cmp.chatgpt-vs-claude.en: Both are strong general-purpose assistants and start at the same price ($20 per month). ChatGPT is more versatile, with image generation, voice and broad integrations. Claude stands out for working with long documents, quality writing and coding; it does not generate images.

cmp.chatgpt-vs-deepseek.en: DeepSeek's chat app is free and strong at tasks such as math and coding. ChatGPT offers more features (images, voice, agents) and broader integrations. If you will work with personal or company data, consider where DeepSeek processes data.

cmp.chatgpt-vs-gemini.en: Both are versatile assistants, and their paid plans start at around $20 per month. If you rely heavily on Gmail, Drive and Android, Gemini's integrations are an advantage; if you want a broad feature set and ecosystem, ChatGPT is the more common choice.

cmp.chatgpt-vs-grok.en: Grok is integrated with X and can access current posts on X; its paid plan starts at $8 per month. ChatGPT, with a broader feature set and integrations, is more widely used for general-purpose tasks; its paid plan starts at $20 per month.

cmp.chatgpt-vs-meta-ai.en: Meta AI is free and works inside apps you already use, such as WhatsApp and Instagram, making it practical for quick Q&A. ChatGPT is stronger for more comprehensive tasks such as long documents, file analysis, coding and agents; its paid plan starts at $20 per month.

cmp.chatgpt-vs-microsoft-copilot.en: Copilot is advantageous for Office users because it works inside Word, Excel, PowerPoint and Outlook. ChatGPT offers a broader feature set as a standalone assistant. If you use Office heavily, consider Microsoft 365 plans; for general use, consider ChatGPT.

cmp.chatgpt-vs-perplexity.en: Perplexity works like an AI search engine that searches the web and cites sources; it is strong for up-to-date information and research. ChatGPT is used for a broader range of tasks such as writing, analysis, images and code, and can also search the web.

cmp.claude-vs-deepseek.en: DeepSeek's chat app is free and strong in tasks such as math and coding. Claude stands out for working with long documents, high-quality writing and coding; its paid plan starts at $20 per month. If you will work with personal or company data, consider where DeepSeek processes its data.

cmp.claude-vs-gemini.en: Claude stands out in long-document analysis, writing and coding; Gemini in integration with Google services and in image and video generation. Both have a free plan and a paid plan at around $20 per month.

cmp.cursor-vs-github-copilot.en: GitHub Copilot is an assistant that plugs into your existing editor (VS Code, JetBrains) and starts at $10 per month. Cursor is a separate code editor designed around AI and stands out for its project-wide agent features.

cmp.cursor-vs-lovable.en: Cursor is an AI-powered code editor for professional developers. Lovable focuses on people who don't code building websites and apps through conversation; its paid plan starts at $25 per month. If you write code, Cursor is the better fit; if you want a quick prototype, Lovable is more suitable.

cmp.deepl-vs-google-translate.en: Google Translate is free, supports a very wide range of languages and has practical features such as camera and voice translation. DeepL stands out especially for document translation with more natural, fluent results; it can translate Word and PDF files while preserving their formatting.

cmp.gamma-vs-canva.en: Gamma focuses on producing presentations and documents in minutes from a text or outline. Canva, in addition to presentations, lets you create all kinds of designs such as social media graphics, posters and videos using templates; its paid plan starts at $18 per month.

cmp.gemini-vs-perplexity.en: Perplexity works like an AI search engine that shows web sources in every answer, making it strong for current information and sourced research. Gemini, meanwhile, covers broader tasks thanks to its integration with Google services such as Gmail, Drive and YouTube, and its ability to generate images and video. Both have a free plan and a paid plan at $20 per month.

cmp.heygen-vs-synthesia.en: Both produce videos with avatars that speak text. HeyGen, with its voiceover and translation features, focuses on individual creators and marketing, while Synthesia focuses on internal training and corporate communication videos. Both offer a free trial.

cmp.midjourney-vs-adobe-firefly.en: Midjourney is strong at aesthetic and artistic images, but has no free plan. Adobe Firefly stands out for its integration with Adobe apps such as Photoshop and its emphasis on commercial-use assurances; it also has a free option.

cmp.midjourney-vs-ideogram.en: Midjourney excels at aesthetic and artistic visuals but has no free plan; it starts at $10 per month. Ideogram is strong at generating readable text within images, is better suited to logos, posters and typographic designs, and offers a free usage option.

cmp.otter-vs-fireflies.en: Both record online meetings, transcribe them, and produce summaries and task lists. Otter's paid plan starts at $16.99 per month. For Turkish meetings, check language support in both before purchasing.

cmp.runway-vs-kling.en: Both generate video from text and images. Runway stands out for its video editing tools and creative workflows, Kling for realistic motion generation. Both run on a credit system, so estimate costs in advance for long videos.

entity.dario-amodei.about.en: Co-founder and CEO of Anthropic. He was previously vice president of research at OpenAI.

entity.deepseek.about.en: Chinese AI company. It drew the industry's attention with its open-weight models trained at low cost.

entity.elon-musk.about.en: CEO of Tesla and SpaceX and founder of the AI company xAI. He was one of OpenAI's co-founders.

entity.fei-fei-li.about.en: Professor of computer science at Stanford University and co-founder of World Labs. A pioneer in image recognition through the ImageNet dataset.

entity.google.about.en: Technology company that develops the Gemini models and AI-powered search, cloud and productivity products. Its AI research is carried out under Google DeepMind.

entity.hugging-face.about.en: The largest platform for sharing open-source AI models, datasets and applications.

entity.jensen-huang.about.en: Co-founder of Nvidia. He led the company as CEO from its founding in 1993 until his resignation in November 2026.

entity.lg.about.en: South Korean technology group. LG AI Research leads its AI work and develops the EXAONE family of models.

entity.megaspeed.about.en: Singapore-based cloud and data center company. It made headlines over allegations that it supplied Nvidia chips to Chinese companies.

entity.meta.about.en: Owner of Facebook, Instagram and WhatsApp. It competes in the AI race with its open-weight Llama models and consumer-facing AI assistants.

entity.microsoft.about.en: Technology company behind the Copilot assistants and the Azure cloud platform. It is one of OpenAI's largest partners and investors.

entity.naver.about.en: South Korea's largest internet company. It develops its own language models and is entering the AI data center business.

entity.nvidia.about.en: Leading maker of the GPUs (graphics processing units) used to train and run AI models. Its data center chips are among the most critical components of AI infrastructure.

entity.openai.about.en: US AI company that develops ChatGPT and the GPT family of models. Founded in 2015 as a nonprofit research organization, it now offers consumer, developer and enterprise products.

entity.sam-altman.about.en: CEO and one of the co-founders of OpenAI.

entity.samsung.about.en: South Korean electronics and semiconductor company. It is one of the makers of the high-bandwidth memory (HBM) used in AI servers.

entity.sundar-pichai.about.en: CEO of Google and its parent company, Alphabet.

entity.world-labs.about.en: AI company co-founded by Fei-Fei Li that develops "world models" capable of generating three-dimensional worlds.

gl.3b-model-uretimi.def: The general name for AI approaches that create three-dimensional objects or scenes from text, a single photo or a few images.
gl.3b-model-uretimi.example: A game developer can type wooden crate to get a 3D object for a prototype and drop it into a scene.
gl.3b-model-uretimi.faq.0.a: No. 3D generation aims to create new objects. NeRF usually reconstructs a real scene from photographs of it.
gl.3b-model-uretimi.faq.0.q: Is 3D generation the same as NeRF?
gl.3b-model-uretimi.faq.1.a: Sometimes, but it usually needs editing. The mesh may need cleaning, the textures fixing and the model adapting for the game or print.
gl.3b-model-uretimi.faq.1.q: Can a generated model be used directly in a game or 3D printer?
gl.3b-model-uretimi.how: Methods differ. Some borrow knowledge from image-generating models to build a shape that matches a text description and looks consistent from many angles. Others are trained directly on three-dimensional datasets and output point clouds, meshes or volumetric representations. Still others guess the hidden back side of an object from a single photo. The hardest part is keeping the shape from distorting when viewed from different angles. The output is often a mesh with textures and may need cleanup before use.
gl.3b-model-uretimi.why: Making 3D content for games, film, e-commerce, architecture and augmented reality is expensive and slow, and these approaches promise to speed it up. Output quality and how ready it is for direct use vary, though. Views differ on whether the technology will replace artists or serve as a tool that helps them.
gl.ab-yapay-zeka-yasasi.def: The European Union's comprehensive law, adopted in 2024, that regulates AI systems according to their level of risk. It is widely described as one of the first broad legal frameworks of its kind.
gl.ab-yapay-zeka-yasasi.example: A startup selling résumé-screening software to companies in Europe has to study the Act closely, since its product may fall into the high-risk category.
gl.ab-yapay-zeka-yasasi.faq.0.a: It can. A company outside the EU may fall under the Act if it offers its AI system on the EU market or if the system's outputs are used in the EU. The exact position depends on what the company does; this is a general overview, not legal advice.
gl.ab-yapay-zeka-yasasi.faq.0.q: Does the EU AI Act affect companies outside Europe?
gl.ab-yapay-zeka-yasasi.faq.1.a: No. The Act is risk-based, and most AI applications are considered low risk and face no heavy obligations. The rules concentrate mainly on prohibited and high-risk uses.
gl.ab-yapay-zeka-yasasi.faq.1.q: Does the Act restrict every use of AI?
gl.ab-yapay-zeka-yasasi.how: The Act sorts AI systems into tiers by risk. Those posing unacceptable risk are banned, high-risk systems face strict obligations, some systems such as chatbots must meet transparency rules, and the rest are largely left free. Separate rules apply to general-purpose models. The provisions do not all apply at once but phase in gradually. Enforcement involves national authorities and the EU-level AI Office, and violations can bring administrative fines.
gl.ab-yapay-zeka-yasasi.why: Because the Act also affects non-EU companies that offer products on the EU market, it is often treated as a global reference point. Critics say it may hold back innovation, while supporters say it protects people's rights, and the debate continues. In AI news, stories about compliance, oversight and penalties usually trace back to this law.
gl.ablasyon-calismasi.def: An experiment that removes or disables a particular part of a system and measures how performance changes. Its aim is to understand how much each component actually contributes to the result.
gl.ablasyon-calismasi.example: In an image recognition paper, the proposed attention mechanism is switched off and the same model is tested again, and the drop in accuracy shows how much that mechanism contributed.
gl.ablasyon-calismasi.faq.0.a: An ablation study removes a component to understand its contribution. Hyperparameter search focuses on finding the best settings for a model.
gl.ablasyon-calismasi.faq.0.q: What is the difference between an ablation study and hyperparameter search?
gl.ablasyon-calismasi.faq.1.a: No, but they are common, especially in research papers that propose a new method. The absence of one may mean the claim was not tested component by component.
gl.ablasyon-calismasi.faq.1.q: Does every AI paper include an ablation study?
gl.ablasyon-calismasi.how: Researchers first take the results of the complete system as a baseline. Then, one at a time, they remove or simplify a single component, which might be a layer, a data source, a training trick or an extra feature. The system is retrained or measured under the same conditions and compared with the baseline. If performance drops noticeably, the component matters, and if nothing changes, it may be unnecessary. To reduce the effect of chance, experiments are usually repeated several times. The term comes from the medical sense of removing tissue.
gl.ablasyon-calismasi.why: The success of a new method often comes from a combination of many changes, and it may be unclear which one is doing the work. An ablation study shows how solid a claim in a paper really is. When a “new method” is announced in the news, checking whether such experiments were done is a good clue for judging the claim.
gl.aci-ders.def: The view, put forward by AI researcher Richard Sutton in a 2019 essay, that in the long run, general methods that scale with computation beat methods built on human knowledge.
gl.aci-ders.example: Deep Blue beating the world chess champion through massive search is one of the examples Sutton discusses in his essay.
gl.aci-ders.faq.0.a: No. Sutton's claim is that, over the long run, general methods that scale with computation outperform hand-crafted knowledge. Human effort still shapes the data, the goals and the evaluation.
gl.aci-ders.faq.0.q: Does the bitter lesson mean human knowledge is worthless?
gl.aci-ders.faq.1.a: He is a Canadian computer scientist and one of the founders of reinforcement learning. His essay on the bitter lesson has become one of the most widely quoted opinion pieces in the field.
gl.aci-ders.how: Looking at the history of chess, Go, speech recognition and computer vision, Sutton sees a recurring pattern. Researchers first build domain-specific human knowledge into their systems, and this helps in the short term. Then, as computing becomes cheaper, general methods such as search and learning overtake the hand-crafted knowledge. The lesson is 'bitter' because it suggests that the clever structures researchers are proud of often turn out to matter less in the long run.
gl.aci-ders.why: The essay is often cited by those who argue for scaling up large language models, and it helps explain why companies keep investing in more data and compute. Critics respond that data and energy are limited and that structured knowledge may still be valuable.

gl.acik-agirlikli-model.def.en: A model whose trained parameters (weights) are published so that anyone can download them and run them on their own computer or server. The training data and code are not always open, which is why it differs from "open source."

gl.acik-agirlikli-model.example.en: Many models from Meta's Llama, Mistral and DeepSeek are released as open-weight.

gl.acik-agirlikli-model.faq.0.a.en: Not exactly. With an open-weight model, the trained weights are shared; with an open-source model, the training code and, ideally, the training data are open as well.

gl.acik-agirlikli-model.faq.0.q.en: Is an open-weight model the same as an open-source model?

gl.acik-agirlikli-model.faq.1.a.en: Downloading the weights is usually free, but the license may restrict commercial use. The hardware or cloud cost of running the model must also be factored in.

gl.acik-agirlikli-model.how.en: Once a language model is trained, everything it has learned is stored in files made up of billions of numbers (weights). With an open-weight model, these files are published publicly; anyone can download them, run them on their own hardware and fine-tune them. What data the model was trained on and how is often not shared.

gl.acik-agirlikli-model.why.en: Companies can run the model on their own servers without sending data outside, control costs and adapt the model to their own domain. Because it reduces dependence on closed models, it is an important balancing factor in AI competition.

gl.acik-kaynak-lisansi.def: A legal permission text that sets out who may use, modify and distribute a piece of software or a model's source code or weights, and under what conditions.
gl.acik-kaynak-lisansi.example: Meta's Llama models are released with downloadable weights but under Meta's own license with usage terms, so they are discussed separately from classic open-source licenses.
gl.acik-kaynak-lisansi.faq.0.a: MIT imposes very few conditions, and the code can be used even in a closed-source product. The GPL requires anyone who modifies and distributes the code to release the derived work under the same license.
gl.acik-kaynak-lisansi.faq.0.q: What is the difference between the MIT license and the GPL?
gl.acik-kaynak-lisansi.faq.1.a: No. Downloadable weights do not mean the license meets established open-source criteria. There may be usage restrictions, and the training data and full code may not be shared.
gl.acik-kaynak-lisansi.faq.1.q: Is every model with downloadable weights open source?
gl.acik-kaynak-lisansi.how: The person or organization that builds a work chooses a license when releasing it publicly and spells out the terms of use in that text. Permissive licenses such as MIT and Apache 2.0 grant broad freedom, including commercial use, and generally ask only that copyright and license notices be kept. Copyleft licenses such as the GPL require modified versions to be shared under the same license. In AI, some models are released under custom licenses with usage restrictions, and even when the weights are open, the training data and full code may not be shared.
gl.acik-kaynak-lisansi.why: Whether a model can be used in a commercial product, or modified and redistributed, depends on its license, and misreading it can create legal risk. The word 'open' is also contested in AI, since models that do not meet established open-source criteria are often still called open. For a legal assessment, the license text itself has to be read.

gl.acik-kaynak.def.en: Software whose source code anyone can inspect, modify and distribute under specific license terms.

gl.acik-kaynak.example.en: llama.cpp, which is used to run models on a computer, and the libraries on the model-sharing platform Hugging Face are open source.

gl.acik-kaynak.faq.0.a.en: Most open-source software can be used free of charge, but "open source" refers to the accessibility of the code and license rights, not to price.

gl.acik-kaynak.faq.1.a.en: Having the code public means more people can spot bugs; however, security depends on how the project is maintained and how it is used.

gl.acik-kaynak.how.en: The source code of open-source software is published in a public repository; the license determines how the code can be used, modified and distributed. In AI, the phrase "open-source model" is sometimes used for models with only open weights; a truly open-source model also shares its training code and, ideally, its data.

gl.acik-kaynak.why.en: Open-source tools allow AI to be developed by small companies, universities and individual developers as well. They also let more eyes examine bugs and security vulnerabilities.

gl.acik-veri.def: Data that anyone can access, use and share, within the conditions set by its license. Public bodies, research communities and companies publish datasets this way.
gl.acik-veri.example: Wikipedia text and publicly available web archives such as Common Crawl are widely used open data sources for training language models.
gl.acik-veri.faq.0.a: No. Open source usually refers to sharing software code, while open data refers to sharing datasets. The two often appear together, but one does not automatically imply the other.
gl.acik-veri.faq.0.q: Is open data the same as open source?
gl.acik-veri.faq.1.a: No. Access is usually free, but the license may require attribution or limit commercial use. It is important to read the license before using a dataset.
gl.acik-veri.faq.1.q: Can open data always be used without restrictions?
gl.acik-veri.how: The organization or community releasing the data puts the dataset online in a downloadable form under a license. The license states whether the data can be used commercially and how the source must be credited. In AI, researchers use open datasets to train models, compare different models on the same data and reproduce each other's results. Being open does not mean the data is free of personal information or free of errors.
gl.acik-veri.why: Open data makes research transparent and repeatable, and it lets small teams and universities work with the same raw material as large companies. At the same time, copyright and privacy debates keep raising the question of which data can truly be used freely, a theme that appears often in AI news.

gl.aciklanabilir-yapay-zeka.def.en: Methods that aim to present the reasons behind an AI system's decision or output in a way people can understand.

gl.aciklanabilir-yapay-zeka.example.en: When a credit model rejects an application, a report showing that income level and overdue payments were the most influential factors in the decision is an example of explainable AI.

gl.aciklanabilir-yapay-zeka.faq.0.a.en: It is a term used for models whose input and output can be seen but whose decision-making process people cannot understand. Large deep learning models are often described this way.

gl.aciklanabilir-yapay-zeka.faq.1.a.en: They are closely related concepts. Interpretability generally focuses on understanding the model's inner workings, while explainability focuses on presenting the reasons for individual decisions to people.

gl.aciklanabilir-yapay-zeka.faq.1.q.en: Are interpretability and explainability the same?

gl.aciklanabilir-yapay-zeka.how.en: Because deep learning models operate with billions of parameters, it is hard to see exactly why a decision was made; for this reason they are called "black boxes." Explainability methods show which inputs influenced the decision most, or try to examine the concepts inside the model's internal structure (interpretability research).

gl.aciklanabilir-yapay-zeka.why.en: In decisions such as loan denials, medical diagnoses or hiring, people have a right to learn the reasons. Understanding why a model makes mistakes is also a prerequisite for making it safer.

gl.adam-optimize-edicisi.def: A widely used deep learning optimization algorithm that automatically adjusts the learning step for each parameter based on past gradients. The name comes from 'adaptive moment estimation'.
gl.adam-optimize-edicisi.example: A team training a new text classification model will often start with Adam; trying a few learning rates in a small range is usually enough to get a reasonable result.
gl.adam-optimize-edicisi.faq.0.a: The classic method applies the same step scale to every parameter. Adam looks at past gradients to adjust the step of each parameter separately and also uses momentum.
gl.adam-optimize-edicisi.faq.0.q: How does Adam differ from classic stochastic gradient descent?
gl.adam-optimize-edicisi.faq.1.a: No. It is a fast and convenient default, but on some tasks stochastic gradient descent with momentum can generalize better. The choice depends on the task and on experiments.
gl.adam-optimize-edicisi.faq.1.q: Is Adam always the best choice?
gl.adam-optimize-edicisi.how: For every parameter, the algorithm keeps two running records: the recent average of its gradients and the recent average of its squared gradients. The first acts like momentum, smoothing the overall direction of movement. The second shrinks the step for parameters whose gradients are consistently large and enlarges it for those that are rarely updated. Each parameter therefore moves at its own pace. In plain gradient descent every parameter shares one learning rate; Adam scales that rate parameter by parameter.
gl.adam-optimize-edicisi.why: Adam often gives good results with little tuning, which is why it is the first choice for many researchers and product teams. Adam and its variants are commonly used to train large transformer-based models. The choice of optimizer affects training speed and stability, so it also matters for cost.
gl.adil-kullanim.def: A flexible doctrine in US copyright law that allows copyrighted works to be used without the owner's permission under certain conditions. Uses such as criticism, news reporting, teaching and research are often assessed under it.
gl.adil-kullanim.example: In the Google Books case, a US appeals court treated scanning books and making them searchable as fair use, and parties in AI disputes refer to rulings like it.
gl.adil-kullanim.faq.0.a: No. It is an open-ended US doctrine. Turkish law relies on a specific list of exceptions in its copyright statute.
gl.adil-kullanim.faq.0.q: Does fair use apply in Turkey?
gl.adil-kullanim.faq.1.a: No. Fair use is a general defense that a court assesses case by case. A text and data mining exception is a rule written into law that covers a specific kind of use.
gl.adil-kullanim.faq.1.q: Is fair use the same as a text and data mining exception?
gl.adil-kullanim.how: Courts examine fair use case by case and usually weigh four factors: the purpose and character of the use, the nature of the work, how much of it was taken and how important that part is, and the effect on the work's market value. A transformative use, one that creates a new meaning or function from the original, can weigh in its favor. No single factor decides the outcome and there is no fixed formula, so similar-looking cases can end differently.
gl.adil-kullanim.why: AI companies argue that training models on copyrighted works falls under fair use, while rights holders say it harms their markets. The course of US lawsuits could shape the industry's approach to training data. The concept is specific to the United States and has no direct equivalent everywhere.

gl.agi.def.en: Hypothetical AI that can perform the vast majority of intellectual tasks humans can do at a human level. When and how it will be reached is debated.

gl.agi.example.en: Statements by company executives such as "AGI will arrive within a few years" or "we are still far away" frequently make the news.

gl.agi.faq.0.a.en: There is no consensus. Some company executives say it could be reached within a few years, while many researchers argue it will take far longer or that the definition itself is unclear.

gl.agi.faq.1.a.en: AGI refers to human-level general intelligence, while superintelligence describes hypothetical systems that clearly surpass human intelligence in nearly every domain.

gl.agi.faq.1.q.en: What is the difference between AGI and superintelligence?

gl.agi.how.en: Today's AI systems can reach human level on specific tasks, but they are still limited in abilities such as adapting to a new domain, long-term planning and continuously learning from experience. Artificial general intelligence describes a system that can show all of these abilities at a human level. There is no precise, universally accepted definition.

gl.agi.why.en: Companies such as OpenAI, Google DeepMind and Anthropic explicitly set AGI as a goal. When it will be reached, its economic impact and its safety risks directly affect investment decisions and regulatory debates.

gl.agirlik-azaltma.def: A regularization technique that nudges a neural network's weights toward zero at every training step, preventing them from growing very large and helping reduce overfitting.
gl.agirlik-azaltma.example: When training a language model, it is common to set a nonzero weight decay value in the AdamW optimizer.
gl.agirlik-azaltma.faq.0.a: In simple gradient descent the two are equivalent. With adaptive optimizers such as Adam they behave differently, which is why AdamW was developed to apply weight decay separately.
gl.agirlik-azaltma.faq.0.q: Is weight decay the same as L2 regularization?
gl.agirlik-azaltma.faq.1.a: It is usually tuned by trial, based on performance on validation data. If it is too low it has little effect, and if it is too high the model cannot learn enough.
gl.agirlik-azaltma.faq.1.q: How is the weight decay rate chosen?
gl.agirlik-azaltma.how: During training, model weights are updated in the direction that reduces the error. With weight decay, the weights are also shrunk by a small fraction at each update, so the model can keep large weights only if the data clearly calls for them. In effect, simpler functions are preferred. In plain gradient descent it gives results similar to L2 regularization; with adaptive optimizers the two differ, and AdamW, which applies decay separately from the gradient update, is widely used. The decay rate is a hyperparameter.
gl.agirlik-azaltma.why: Large models, including language models, can memorize their training data and then perform poorly on new data. Weight decay is cheap and easy to apply, so it appears often in modern training recipes. Setting the rate too high, however, can keep the model from learning enough.
gl.aime.def: A prestigious math competition exam for high school students in the United States. In AI, its questions are used as a benchmark of how well models solve hard math problems.
gl.aime.example: When a company announces a new reasoning model, it may share the model's rate of correct answers on AIME exams from recent years, so readers can compare it with earlier models.
gl.aime.faq.0.a: A whole-number answer makes the correct result single and unambiguous. The model's response can be verified automatically without human judgment, and lucky guesses become much harder.
gl.aime.faq.0.q: Why does it matter that AIME answers are whole numbers?
gl.aime.faq.1.a: It shows the model is strong at competition-style problems. It does not mean the model can do research-level mathematics, since the test is small and narrow.
gl.aime.faq.1.q: Does a model with a high AIME score think like a mathematician?
gl.aime.how: The exam has 15 questions, and every answer is a whole number from 0 to 999. That means answers cannot be guessed from multiple-choice options and are easy to check automatically. Researchers usually give the model the questions from a particular year, compare its final number with the correct answer, and report the share answered correctly. Because there are so few questions, some reports run the model several times and average the results.
gl.aime.why: AIME demands multi-step, creative reasoning that goes beyond basic arithmetic, so it shows up often in news about 'reasoning' models. But with so few questions, scores can fluctuate, and older exam problems may have leaked into training data. It should not be read as a ranking on its own.
gl.ajan-becerileri.def: Reusable packages of instructions, scripts and resource files that teach an AI agent how to do a specific kind of task. The agent loads them only when a relevant task comes up.
gl.ajan-becerileri.example: A company can write a skill for preparing the monthly report in its corporate template: a package with instructions, a template file and a script that formats the table, loaded whenever the agent is asked for a report.
gl.ajan-becerileri.faq.0.a: A prompt is a one-off text written or loaded into each conversation. A skill is a separately stored package, which can include scripts and files, that the agent loads by itself when needed.
gl.ajan-becerileri.faq.0.q: What is the difference between agent skills and a prompt?
gl.ajan-becerileri.faq.1.a: No. A tool is a function or service the agent can call, such as web search. A skill describes how to do a job and can include how to use tools.
gl.ajan-becerileri.faq.1.q: Is a skill the same as a tool?
gl.ajan-becerileri.how: A skill is typically a folder holding a text of instructions on how to do the job, plus runnable scripts and example files if needed. At the start the agent only knows each skill's short name and description. If the user's request matches a skill, the agent pulls that skill's details into its context and follows the instructions. This avoids stuffing everything into the prompt up front and keeps the context window from filling needlessly. Skills can be shared and updated.
gl.ajan-becerileri.why: Skills are emerging as a way for organizations to pass their know-how to agents in an organized, reusable form. Instead of writing long prompts for every task, a team prepares a package once, shares it and helps the agent behave consistently. The exact scope and implementation of the term vary by product.
gl.ajan-bellegi.def: A mechanism that lets an AI agent store past steps, user preferences and learned information beyond a single conversation and use them later.
gl.ajan-bellegi.example: A personal assistant that learns once that you prefer morning meetings takes that into account in later calendar suggestions.
gl.ajan-bellegi.faq.0.a: No. The context window is the limited text the model can see at a given moment and it ends with the session. Agent memory is the persistent records stored outside that window and brought back into it when needed.
gl.ajan-bellegi.faq.0.q: Is agent memory the same as a context window?
gl.ajan-bellegi.faq.1.a: It can, because personal details may be stored persistently. Well-designed systems let users see what is remembered, delete records or turn memory off.
gl.ajan-bellegi.faq.1.q: Does agent memory pose privacy risks?
gl.ajan-bellegi.how: Agent memory can be thought of in two layers. Short-term memory is the conversation and intermediate results in the model's current context window; it disappears when the session ends. Long-term memory lives outside the model, in a database, a file or a vector store. The agent summarizes an important fact, such as a user's preference, and writes it there; in a later task it searches for the relevant record and adds it back into the context. The model's own weights do not change in this process, only the information it is given.
gl.ajan-bellegi.why: An agent without memory starts from scratch every time and asks the same questions again. Memory makes personalization and continuity in long-running work possible. But what gets stored, how long it is kept and how users can control it are important privacy questions.
gl.ajan-cercevesi.def: A software library or platform that provides ready-made building blocks for creating AI agents. It takes over repetitive work such as connecting to the model, calling tools, handling memory and managing steps.
gl.ajan-cercevesi.example: LangChain, LangGraph and CrewAI are well-known examples; a developer could use one of them to build a simple agent that reads emails and adds events to a calendar.
gl.ajan-cercevesi.faq.0.a: No. Simple agents can be written directly against a model interface with a few lines of code. A framework becomes more useful as a project grows and needs like monitoring, memory or multiple agents appear.
gl.ajan-cercevesi.faq.0.q: Do you have to use an agent framework?
gl.ajan-cercevesi.faq.1.a: No. An agent is software that takes goal-directed steps; a framework is the toolkit used to build one.
gl.ajan-cercevesi.faq.1.q: Is an agent framework the same as an agent?
gl.ajan-cercevesi.how: The framework wires a language model to tools and data in a loop. The developer defines a goal for the agent, the tools it may use and its rules. The framework sends the request to the model, runs the tool the model picks, feeds the result back and keeps going until the task is done. Most frameworks also include ready components for memory, error handling, logging and multiple agents working together. Some let you define the workflow step by step as a graph.
gl.ajan-cercevesi.why: Frameworks speed up agent development, but choosing one is a trade-off: ready-made structure is convenient, while heavy abstraction can make debugging harder. That is why some teams use a framework and others write their own loops directly against model interfaces. The term comes up often when news stories describe the agent ecosystem.
gl.ajan-guvenligi.def: Work to prevent AI agents, which use tools and take actions on a user's behalf, from carrying out unauthorized, mistaken or harmful operations or from being abused by others.
gl.ajan-guvenligi.example: An agent that reads and answers email could be steered by hidden instructions in an incoming message into sending out a contact list, which is why sending email can be made to require the user's approval.
gl.ajan-guvenligi.faq.0.a: No. Model safety focuses on what kinds of outputs a model produces. Agent security also covers the actions the model takes with tools, the permissions it holds and untrusted content that arrives from outside sources.
gl.ajan-guvenligi.faq.0.q: Is agent security the same as model safety?
gl.ajan-guvenligi.faq.1.a: There is currently no accepted standalone fix. That is why measures such as limiting permissions, adding approval steps and monitoring are used together.
gl.ajan-guvenligi.faq.1.q: Can prompt injection be fully prevented?
gl.ajan-guvenligi.how: Because agents can reach tools such as email, files, browsers and payments, their risks are greater than those of chatbots. A leading threat is prompt injection, where instructions hidden in a web page or an email lead the agent astray. Safeguards include giving the agent only the permissions it needs, running it in a sandbox, requiring human approval for critical actions, setting spending limits and logging every action. No single measure is considered enough, so defenses are layered.
gl.ajan-guvenligi.why: Agents do more than generate text; they take actions with real-world consequences, so a mistake or an attack can mean lost money, leaked data or deleted files. As companies connect agents to business processes, managing these risks is becoming a priority. It is widely accepted that there is no complete, standalone fix for prompt injection.
gl.ajan-is-akisi.def: A way of running an AI system in which, instead of producing a single answer, it works in a loop of planning, using tools, checking results and retrying when needed to reach a goal.
gl.ajan-is-akisi.example: A coding assistant fixing a failing test first reads the relevant files, makes a change, reruns the test and, if it still fails, tries a different fix.
gl.ajan-is-akisi.faq.0.a: A chatbot usually gives a single reply to a question. In an agentic workflow the system takes several steps, uses tools and changes course based on intermediate results to reach a goal.
gl.ajan-is-akisi.faq.0.q: How is an agentic workflow different from an ordinary chatbot?
gl.ajan-is-akisi.faq.1.a: Not always. Many set-ups use predefined steps and ask for human approval on important decisions. The level of autonomy is tuned to the risk of the task.
gl.ajan-is-akisi.how: At the start, the model takes the user's goal and breaks it into smaller steps. At each step it can call a tool, such as searching the web, reading a file or running code. It looks at what comes back, picks the next move and changes approach if something fails. The loop continues until the goal is met or a stopping condition is reached. Some workflows follow a fixed outline, while others let the model decide the path. Asking for human approval at critical points is also common.
gl.ajan-is-akisi.why: Handling multi-step work instead of one-off questions moves AI out of the chat box and into business processes. It is one of the approaches companies try most often in software development, research and customer service. At the same time, errors can pile up across steps, so oversight and safeguards matter.
gl.ajan-orkestrasyonu.def: The management of several AI agents and tools so they work together on one task, covering the coordination work of deciding who gets which job, how results are passed along and how errors are handled.
gl.ajan-orkestrasyonu.example: To handle customer complaints, a company might use one agent to classify the email, a second to look up the order record and a third to draft a reply; the orchestrator runs these steps in order and hands the final draft to an employee for approval.
gl.ajan-orkestrasyonu.faq.0.a: Splitting subtasks among specialized agents keeps each one's context short and focused and lets some parts run in parallel. The trade-off is added complexity, so it is not needed for every job.
gl.ajan-orkestrasyonu.faq.0.q: Why use orchestration instead of one powerful agent?
gl.ajan-orkestrasyonu.faq.1.a: It can be a fixed workflow written in code or another AI model that assigns tasks dynamically. Setups that mix both are also common.
gl.ajan-orkestrasyonu.faq.1.q: What or who acts as the orchestrator?
gl.ajan-orkestrasyonu.how: An orchestrator splits the main task into subtasks and hands them to separate agents; the orchestrator can be a software layer or another AI model. Each agent works in its own specialty, such as research, writing code or verification. The orchestrator gathers the agents' outputs, sets the order, retries steps that get stuck and asks a human when needed. Shared information and task status between agents are also kept in this layer. Like a conductor keeping musicians in time, the aim is to combine the parts into a single result.
gl.ajan-orkestrasyonu.why: Complex jobs may not fit within one agent's context or ability, and sharing the work helps get past that limit. As the number of agents grows, though, cost, the spread of errors and oversight all become harder. That is why orchestration is a central problem in running agents reliably in enterprise AI projects.
gl.ajanlar-arasi-protokol.def: An open communication standard that lets AI agents built by different developers or companies recognize each other, share tasks and exchange messages in a common format.
gl.ajanlar-arasi-protokol.example: A travel-planning agent sends a room request to a hotel booking agent built by another company and relays the confirmation back to the user.
gl.ajanlar-arasi-protokol.faq.0.a: MCP focuses on connecting a model or agent to tools and data sources. A2A aims at letting agents talk to each other. They are usually described as complementary rather than competing.
gl.ajanlar-arasi-protokol.faq.0.q: What is the difference between A2A and MCP?
gl.ajanlar-arasi-protokol.faq.1.a: The protocol was proposed by Google and released as an open standard. Details about governance and versions can change over time, so the project's official documentation is the best reference.
gl.ajanlar-arasi-protokol.how: Each agent publishes a standard description of what it can do. Another agent reads that description, picks a suitable partner and sends it a task. The task's status, intermediate messages and results travel in a shared message format, so it does not matter which company's model or framework the agent was built with. For long-running tasks, progress updates flow over the same channel. Agents do not need to see each other's inner workings; they talk only through the interface they expose.
gl.ajanlar-arasi-protokol.why: As companies start using different agents for different jobs, those agents need to be able to talk to one another. A shared standard reduces the work of writing custom integrations for every pair and limits dependence on a single vendor. How widely the standard will be adopted is still unclear.
gl.ajansal-rag.def: A retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) approach in which the language model itself decides what to search for, which source to consult, and whether the information it found is good enough. It replaces a fixed single lookup with a step-by-step process.
gl.ajansal-rag.example: A company's internal assistant is asked to compare the penalty clauses in two supplier contracts from last year; it finds each contract, extracts the relevant clauses, searches again for whatever is missing, and then writes the comparison.
gl.ajansal-rag.faq.0.a: Classic RAG usually performs a single retrieval in a fixed pipeline. In agentic RAG the model decides how many searches to run, which tools to use, and when to stop.
gl.ajansal-rag.faq.0.q: How is agentic RAG different from classic RAG?
gl.ajansal-rag.faq.1.a: No. For simple questions answerable from one document, classic RAG is faster and cheaper. The agentic approach pays off for multi-step questions spread across scattered sources.
gl.ajansal-rag.faq.1.q: Does agentic RAG always give better results?
gl.ajansal-rag.how: In classic RAG, a question comes in, the system searches once, the retrieved passages are handed to the model, and an answer is written. In the agentic version the model acts like an agent: it breaks the question into sub-questions, picks a tool (a document store, a database, web search), reads the results, and rewrites its query to search again if they fall short. When it judges the evidence sufficient, it writes the answer. It resembles a researcher who skims sources, takes notes, and goes back to fill gaps.
gl.ajansal-rag.why: Real questions often cannot be answered with one search; they may require comparing several documents or pulling data from different systems. Agentic RAG aims to handle such complex questions more reliably. The trade-off is more model calls, longer waits and higher cost, plus the risk that the agent makes poor decisions along the way.
gl.ajansal-yapay-zeka.def: An approach in which an AI system is given a goal, plans the steps itself, uses tools and keeps going by checking results along the way. Instead of answering a single question, it takes on multi-step tasks.
gl.ajansal-yapay-zeka.example: A user asks the system to plan a round trip for two to Izmir next week; it compares flights, checks the calendar and presents the options for approval.
gl.ajansal-yapay-zeka.faq.0.a: A chatbot typically works one request and one reply at a time. An agentic system takes multiple steps toward a goal and can use external tools.
gl.ajansal-yapay-zeka.faq.0.q: How does agentic AI differ from an ordinary chatbot?
gl.ajansal-yapay-zeka.faq.1.a: The system can take a wrong action with real consequences. That is why permission limits, action logs and approval steps matter.
gl.ajansal-yapay-zeka.faq.1.q: What are the main risks of agentic systems?
gl.ajansal-yapay-zeka.how: Usually a large language model acts as the brain of the system. It breaks the goal into subtasks, calls tools such as web search, code execution or email, and decides on the next step by looking at the result of the last one. Memory mechanisms let it recall earlier steps. If a plan fails, the system can change its approach and try again. For risky actions, a person is often asked to approve first, an arrangement known as keeping a human in the loop.
gl.ajansal-yapay-zeka.why: The idea captures the shift from a chat assistant that answers questions to a helper that gets work done. It widens what can be automated in software development, customer service and research. It also raises questions about responsibility and security: if the system makes a mistake, who is accountable, and what permissions should it have?

gl.akil-yurutme-modeli.def.en: A language model that works through a problem step by step before responding. It performs better on math, coding and multistep tasks, but runs slower and costs more.

gl.akil-yurutme-modeli.example.en: If a model offers "low, medium and high" thinking levels, the high level thinks longer and gives better results on hard questions.

gl.akil-yurutme-modeli.faq.0.a.en: No. On simple questions it may give results no better than regular models while responding more slowly and at higher cost. In math, code and multistep analysis, though, the difference is clear.

gl.akil-yurutme-modeli.faq.0.q.en: Is a reasoning model better for every question?

gl.akil-yurutme-modeli.faq.1.a.en: These are the tokens a model generates during its internal thinking process before responding. In most APIs, they are billed as output tokens.

gl.akil-yurutme-modeli.how.en: A reasoning model goes through an internal "thinking" phase before writing its final answer: it breaks the problem into parts, tries intermediate steps and corrects its own mistakes. Because this thinking consumes tokens, responses arrive later and cost more. In many models, the amount of thinking can be adjusted.

gl.akil-yurutme-modeli.why.en: It noticeably improves accuracy in math, programming, scientific analysis and multistep agent tasks. On simple questions, however, it can add unnecessary cost, so choosing a model to fit the job matters.

gl.akilli-belge-isleme.def: Technology that uses AI to read and classify documents such as invoices, contracts and forms and to turn their content into clean, structured data.
gl.akilli-belge-isleme.example: A logistics company can have hundreds of daily invoices read by IDP and push the amount and date fields automatically into its accounting system.
gl.akilli-belge-isleme.faq.0.a: OCR only turns the writing in an image into text. IDP also works out what that text means: it determines the document type, finds the fields, validates the data and sends it on to a system.
gl.akilli-belge-isleme.faq.0.q: What is the difference between intelligent document processing and OCR?
gl.akilli-belge-isleme.faq.1.a: Usually not. The model typically sends fields it is unsure about to an employee for approval, which keeps errors from reaching critical systems.
gl.akilli-belge-isleme.faq.1.q: Does IDP remove human review entirely?
gl.akilli-belge-isleme.how: A document is first scanned or received in digital form, and its text is extracted with optical character recognition. Models then identify the document type, understand its layout and find fields such as amounts, dates or party names. The extracted data goes through validation rules, and fields the system is unsure about are sent to a person for review. The results are passed on to systems such as accounting software. Newer solutions also use large language models in these steps.
gl.akilli-belge-isleme.why: Most of an organization's information sits inside documents, and entering it by hand is slow, costly and error-prone. IDP speeds this up. It comes up often in document-heavy sectors such as finance, insurance and logistics. Accuracy and data privacy for sensitive documents are points that need careful management.
gl.akisli-yanit.def: Sending a language model's answer to the user piece by piece as it is generated, instead of waiting for the whole answer to finish. The reply appears on screen as if it were being typed live.
gl.akisli-yanit.example: In chat interfaces such as ChatGPT, the answer appearing word by word is streaming at work, so the reader can start before the reply is finished.
gl.akisli-yanit.faq.0.a: No, the time for the full answer stays largely the same. What changes is that the first piece shows up much sooner, so waiting feels shorter.
gl.akisli-yanit.faq.0.q: Does streaming make the model generate answers faster?
gl.akisli-yanit.faq.1.a: For developers, processing partial text, catching errors and validating output is somewhat harder. When the full answer must be processed as a whole, streaming is often unnecessary.
gl.akisli-yanit.how: A language model produces text in small units called tokens, one after another. In streaming mode the server does not wait for the answer to be complete; it pushes each new piece to the client over an open connection the moment it is generated. The interface appends the incoming pieces in order. Total generation time barely changes, but the time until the first word appears gets much shorter. Developers usually switch it on with a single setting from the provider.
gl.akisli-yanit.why: It reduces the feeling of waiting on long answers, which is the main reason chatbots feel fluid. Users can also stop a response early if it is heading in the wrong direction. On the other hand, handling partial output and dropped connections adds work for developers.
gl.aktif-ogrenme.def: A method in which the model itself picks the examples that would be most useful to label and asks a human for those labels, aiming for high accuracy with fewer labeled examples.
gl.aktif-ogrenme.example: A radiology team has the model pick the few hundred scans it is least sure about and shows only those to a specialist, instead of paying for the whole archive to be labeled.
gl.aktif-ogrenme.faq.0.a: No. 'Active' here means the model chooses which data to have labeled. In reinforcement learning, an agent learns by trying things in an environment and receiving rewards and penalties.
gl.aktif-ogrenme.faq.0.q: Is active learning the same as reinforcement learning?
gl.aktif-ogrenme.faq.1.a: Usually they are examples the model is most uncertain about, that differ from one another, and that are expected to add the most to learning. The exact selection criterion depends on the method.
gl.aktif-ogrenme.faq.1.q: How are the examples to label chosen?
gl.aktif-ogrenme.how: The process starts with a small labeled dataset and a first round of training. The model then scans the unlabeled examples and flags the ones it is least sure about, such as cases where it cannot decide between two classes. These selected examples go to an expert, the labels come back, and the model is retrained. The loop continues until performance is good enough or the labeling budget runs out. It is usually more efficient than labeling examples at random.
gl.aktif-ogrenme.why: Labeling eats time and money, especially in fields such as medicine or law that need expert judgment. Active learning cuts that cost by focusing a limited budget on the examples that carry the most information. Since data preparation is often the most expensive part of an AI project, the approach has real practical value.
gl.aktivasyon-fonksiyonu.def: A mathematical operation that takes a neuron's weighted sum and turns it into its output, giving the network nonlinear behavior so it can learn complex patterns.
gl.aktivasyon-fonksiyonu.example: Using ReLU in a network's hidden layers and softmax in the output layer to produce class probabilities is a very common combination.
gl.aktivasyon-fonksiyonu.faq.0.a: Stacking linear operations still gives a linear result. A network like that cannot learn curved, complex relationships.
gl.aktivasyon-fonksiyonu.faq.0.q: Why is a nonlinear function needed?
gl.aktivasyon-fonksiyonu.faq.1.a: There is no single best one for every case. ReLU and its variants are common in hidden layers, but the choice depends on the task and the architecture.
gl.aktivasyon-fonksiyonu.faq.1.q: Which activation function is the best?
gl.aktivasyon-fonksiyonu.how: When a neuron adds up its inputs, the resulting number does not go straight to the next layer; it first passes through an activation function. This function can bend the number, squeeze it into a certain range, or set negative values to zero. Without it, a network would behave like a single linear operation no matter how many layers were stacked. Sigmoid, tanh and ReLU are the best-known examples. Which one is chosen depends on the type of network and the job of the layer.
gl.aktivasyon-fonksiyonu.why: The choice of activation function affects how well and how quickly a network learns. Simple functions such as ReLU played a big part in making deep networks trainable. The function used in the output layer also shapes the form of the model's answer, for instance whether it produces probabilities or classes.
gl.algilayici.def: The simplest neural network model for binary classification: it multiplies inputs by weights, adds them up, and compares the total to a threshold to pick one of two classes.
gl.algilayici.example: A very simple spam filter that looks at a few numbers, such as an email's length and how often certain words appear, and then decides 'spam' or 'not spam' is an example of a perceptron.
gl.algilayici.faq.0.a: They are very close. A perceptron is an artificial neuron with a threshold function, while modern artificial neurons usually use other activation functions.
gl.algilayici.faq.0.q: Is a perceptron the same as an artificial neuron?
gl.algilayici.faq.1.a: In XOR, the two classes cannot be separated by a single straight line, and a perceptron can only separate data with a straight line. Adding a hidden layer makes the problem solvable.
gl.algilayici.faq.1.q: Why can't a perceptron solve the XOR problem?
gl.algilayici.how: A perceptron gives each input a weight, computes the weighted sum, and outputs 1 if the sum passes the threshold and 0 if it does not. During training it looks at an example, and if the prediction is wrong it nudges the weights in the direction that reduces the error. When it gets an example right, it leaves the weights alone. If the data can be split by a single straight line, this process eventually finds a correct split. If not, as in the XOR problem, a single perceptron cannot find a solution.
gl.algilayici.why: The perceptron is the ancestor of today's large models. Its inability to solve nonlinear problems was one of the main reasons multilayer networks were developed. It is the natural starting point for understanding what a neural network is.
gl.algoritma.def: A clearly defined set of steps followed to solve a problem or complete a task. In computing, it is a sequence of instructions that turns an input into an output in a finite number of steps.
gl.algoritma.example: A map app finding the best route between two points, or a set of steps that sorts a list from smallest to largest, are everyday examples of algorithms.
gl.algoritma.faq.0.a: An algorithm is a set of steps describing how to do something. An AI model is the structure that comes out of training a learning algorithm on data, and it is what makes predictions.
gl.algoritma.faq.0.q: What is the difference between an algorithm and an AI model?
gl.algoritma.faq.1.a: No. Simple algorithms such as sorting or adding numbers are not considered AI. AI covers only a portion of all algorithms.
gl.algoritma.how: An algorithm resembles a recipe: the ingredients are the input, the ordered steps are the processing, and the finished dish is the output. Several algorithms can solve the same problem, and they differ in speed and memory use. In AI, a learning algorithm adjusts a model's internal settings step by step by looking at data. When training ends, what you have is the model; the algorithm is the method that produced it.
gl.algoritma.why: In the news, “algorithm” is often used loosely for recommendation systems or AI models. Asking what an algorithm does, who designed it and what data it works on is the basis of debates about transparency, bias and accountability.
gl.algoritmik-adalet.def: The principle that AI and algorithmic systems should not produce unjust outcomes for different people or groups, along with the methods used to measure and pursue that goal.
gl.algoritmik-adalet.example: If a bank's credit model rejects applicants from one group much more often than others with similar finances, a fairness review would look into why that gap exists.
gl.algoritmik-adalet.faq.0.a: No. Bias is the problem, meaning an unjust skew in a system's results. Algorithmic fairness is the broader goal and set of practices for measuring and reducing that skew.
gl.algoritmik-adalet.faq.0.q: Is algorithmic fairness the same as bias?
gl.algoritmik-adalet.faq.1.a: Fairness has several definitions that can conflict, so perfect fairness is hard to reach. In practice the aim is to pick a measure suited to the context and keep reducing gaps through ongoing monitoring.
gl.algoritmik-adalet.faq.1.q: Can a model ever be perfectly fair?
gl.algoritmik-adalet.how: Teams first identify who could be harmed and in which decisions. Model outputs are then compared across groups such as gender, age or background, for example by looking at approval rates or error rates separately. There is no single mathematical definition of fairness, and different measures can conflict with each other. So teams choose the measure that fits the context, balance the data, adjust the model, and keep monitoring results after launch.
gl.algoritmik-adalet.why: Algorithms now influence hiring, lending, healthcare and public services. Old biases in training data can grow unnoticed. Unfair outcomes harm people and also create reputational and legal risk for the organizations that deploy these systems.
gl.alt-ajan.def: A helper AI agent that a main agent calls on to handle one specific part of a larger task, working with its own instructions and tools.
gl.alt-ajan.example: A research assistant writing a report hands three different topics to three subagents; each searches its own sources and sends a short summary back to the main agent.
gl.alt-ajan.faq.0.a: They are close but not identical. With subagents there is a hierarchy: a main agent assigns work and gathers results. A multi-agent system is a broader idea that also covers peer agents working together.
gl.alt-ajan.faq.0.q: Is a subagent the same as a multi-agent system?
gl.alt-ajan.faq.1.a: When a subagent sees only what its job requires, it can stay focused and is not distracted by a long conversation history. This supports both accuracy and efficient use of the context window.
gl.alt-ajan.faq.1.q: Why do subagents start with a clean context?
gl.alt-ajan.how: The main agent splits a task into pieces and hands each piece to a separate subagent. A subagent usually starts with a clean context; it sees only the instructions and tools it needs. When it finishes, it returns a short result or summary to the main agent. This keeps the main agent's context window from filling up with detail. Independent jobs can run at the same time; for example, one subagent can scan code while another reads documentation.
gl.alt-ajan.why: Dividing the work can improve speed and quality on long, complex tasks, because each subagent focuses on a narrow topic. The main agent's context also stays clean. The cost is more model calls, which means higher expense and more coordination to manage.
gl.anayasal-yapay-zeka.def: A training approach that shapes an AI model's behavior using a written list of principles, a constitution, by having the model critique, revise and compare its own answers against those principles.
gl.anayasal-yapay-zeka.example: A model is given a principle such as avoiding answers that could harm others, and it critiques its own first draft against that principle and rewrites it more safely.
gl.anayasal-yapay-zeka.faq.0.a: No. RLAIF is the general idea of using AI-generated feedback. Constitutional AI is a specific application that ties that feedback to a written set of principles.
gl.anayasal-yapay-zeka.faq.0.q: Is constitutional AI the same as RLAIF?
gl.anayasal-yapay-zeka.faq.1.a: It contains principles expressing general values such as harmlessness and honesty. The team building the model chooses the content, so which values to include is open to debate.
gl.anayasal-yapay-zeka.how: The method, introduced by Anthropic researchers in 2022, has two stages. In the first, the model answers a question, then looks at a principle from the constitution to critique and rewrite its own answer; the revised answers become fine-tuning data. In the second, the model picks which of two answers fits the principles better, and those preferences are used in reinforcement learning from AI feedback. For harmful content, humans write the principles instead of labeling individual answers.
gl.anayasal-yapay-zeka.why: Written principles make visible which values a model is tuned to and make them easier to change. They also reduce the burden on human labelers who would otherwise have to flag harmful outputs. Anthropic has said it used this approach when training its Claude models. Who chooses the principles, and how they should be interpreted across cultures, is still debated.
gl.anomali-tespiti.def: Automatically finding records, events or measurements that deviate sharply from normal behavior in the data. It is used to catch rare but important cases such as fraud or equipment failure.
gl.anomali-tespiti.example: A bank can hold a card transaction abroad that looks very different from the customer's usual spending and ask the customer to confirm it.
gl.anomali-tespiti.faq.0.a: They largely overlap. An outlier usually means a statistically extreme point, while an anomaly more often means a meaningful unusual event someone cares about.
gl.anomali-tespiti.faq.0.q: Is anomaly detection the same as outlier detection?
gl.anomali-tespiti.faq.1.a: Normal behavior is itself varied and changes over time. A model may flag something unusual but harmless, such as a large purchase made on vacation.
gl.anomali-tespiti.faq.1.q: Why can anomaly detection produce many false alarms?
gl.anomali-tespiti.how: The system first learns what normal looks like. It can do this from labeled examples, from normal data only, or with no labels at all by studying the overall distribution of the data. A new record gets a higher anomaly score the further it is from that normal pattern. If the score passes a set threshold, the record is sent for human review. Like a nurse who knows a patient's usual pulse range and notices a sudden jump, the model spots unusual changes.
gl.anomali-tespiti.why: It is used to catch rare but costly events such as fraud, cyberattacks and machine failures early. The difficulty is that anomalies are few and not every unusual event is a real problem. Too many false alarms can swamp the teams that have to review them.
gl.anonimlestirme.def: Changing data so that the people in it can no longer be identified, either directly or indirectly.
gl.anonimlestirme.example: Before sharing patient records with a research team, a hospital removes names and ID numbers and converts birth dates into age ranges.
gl.anonimlestirme.faq.0.a: In pseudonymization, identifying details are replaced with a code and can be reversed as long as the key exists. In anonymization, reaching the person again should not be possible by reasonable means.
gl.anonimlestirme.faq.0.q: What is the difference between anonymization and pseudonymization?
gl.anonimlestirme.faq.1.a: Not always. There are cases where people were re-identified by matching data with other datasets, so the strength of the method and the risks are reassessed regularly.
gl.anonimlestirme.how: Direct identifiers such as names, ID numbers and phone numbers are removed first. Indirect details like birth dates or postal codes are generalized, for example by replacing an exact age with an age range, or by adding noise to values. The goal is that no individual record can be tied back to a person. However, when different datasets are combined, people can sometimes be re-identified, so simply deleting names is often not enough. Techniques such as k-anonymity and differential privacy are used to reduce this risk.
gl.anonimlestirme.why: Anonymization helps make AI work that draws on personal data safer for research and sharing. In many legal frameworks, truly anonymous data falls outside personal-data rules, but the standard is strict, and data that can still be re-identified may not count as anonymous.

gl.api.def.en: An interface that lets one piece of software talk to another. Developers mostly connect AI models to their own applications through APIs and pay for what they use.

gl.api.example.en: An e-commerce site can use a language model's API to automatically write product descriptions.

gl.api.faq.0.a.en: Typically by the number of tokens sent (input) and generated (output), at a price per million tokens. You can see current prices in our model comparison table.

gl.api.faq.1.a.en: Using one directly requires basic programming knowledge. However, many no-code automation tools let you use AI APIs without knowing how to program.

gl.api.faq.1.q.en: Do you need to be a developer to use an API?

gl.api.how.en: An API lets an application send requests to another service under set rules and receive responses. AI companies offer their models through APIs: the developer sends a prompt and settings, and the model returns a response. Pricing is usually based on the number of tokens used.

gl.api.why.en: It lets companies add powerful existing models to their products without training their own. Most AI applications, from customer service bots to document analysis, use an API behind the scenes.

gl.arc-agi.def: A benchmark of small colored-grid puzzles that tests whether an AI system can infer an unseen rule from a few examples and apply it to a new case. It was designed by François Chollet.
gl.arc-agi.example: Two examples show blue squares being moved to a corner, and the system is expected to apply the same rule to a third grid.
gl.arc-agi.faq.0.a: No. Many experts say it is not proof of AGI on its own, since the benchmark tests only a particular kind of generalization.
gl.arc-agi.faq.0.q: Does solving ARC-AGI mean we have artificial general intelligence (AGI)?
gl.arc-agi.faq.1.a: The tasks were designed to need no special knowledge and to be relatively solvable for people. Even so, they stayed hard for AI systems for years.
gl.arc-agi.faq.1.q: Are ARC-AGI tasks easy for humans?
gl.arc-agi.how: Each task shows a few input-output example pairs, which are grids made of colored squares. The solver must work out the hidden rule linking them and apply it to a new grid, producing the output on its own. Tasks were designed to require no special knowledge and to be relatively solvable for people. Results are judged by whether the output grid is exactly right. François Chollet laid out the idea in a 2019 paper that framed intelligence as efficiency at acquiring new skills, and competitions such as ARC Prize helped popularize the benchmark.
gl.arc-agi.why: Most benchmarks test knowledge that can be memorized, whereas ARC-AGI stresses generalizing in a new situation. That is why it often comes up in debates about how close we are to artificial general intelligence (AGI). Still, a high score on one benchmark does not amount to general intelligence, and researchers disagree about what the benchmark really measures.
gl.arena-siralamasi.def: A ranking of AI models based on votes from users who compare answers in blind side-by-side matchups. Two anonymous responses are shown, and the user picks the one they prefer.
gl.arena-siralamasi.example: A user types 'Simplify this rental contract,' chooses one of two anonymous answers, and that vote nudges the scores of both models.
gl.arena-siralamasi.faq.0.a: A classic benchmark uses fixed questions with an answer key. An arena relies on human preference and measures 'which answer is better' rather than 'which answer is correct.'
gl.arena-siralamasi.faq.0.q: How is an arena leaderboard different from a classic benchmark?
gl.arena-siralamasi.faq.1.a: No. Votes reflect overall preference, and another model may do better at coding, math or a specific language.
gl.arena-siralamasi.faq.1.q: Is the top model in an arena best at everything?
gl.arena-siralamasi.how: A user types a prompt, and the system sends it to two randomly chosen models without revealing which is which. The user picks the better answer, and that vote is recorded. Results from a large number of pairwise matchups are turned into a score for each model with statistical methods similar to the Elo system used in chess. Models with higher scores rise in the ranking. The best-known example is Chatbot Arena, later known as LMArena.
gl.arena-siralamasi.why: Fixed test questions can be memorized or leak into training data, while an arena draws on fresh, varied prompts from real users. That makes it a useful signal of how pleasant and helpful a model feels in conversation. Votes can still be swayed by style, length and formatting, so an arena ranking is not a sufficient measure of accuracy or safety on its own.
gl.arka-plan-ajani.def: An AI agent that carries out long-running tasks on its own while the user is busy with something else or offline, and reports back when it is done.
gl.arka-plan-ajani.example: A developer leaves for the evening after assigning the agent a bug report to fix; by morning, the proposed code change is waiting for review.
gl.arka-plan-ajani.faq.0.a: A chatbot goes back and forth with the user message by message. A background agent takes one task, works on it for a long time without the user, and delivers the result at the end.
gl.arka-plan-ajani.faq.0.q: How is a background agent different from a chatbot?
gl.arka-plan-ajani.faq.1.a: They are usually limited to the tools and environment they are allowed to use, and results are often submitted for human approval. Scope varies by product, though, so permissions need careful setup.
gl.arka-plan-ajani.faq.1.q: Do background agents run without any oversight?
gl.arka-plan-ajani.how: The user describes a task, and the agent breaks it into steps, works with tools such as writing code, searching the web or editing files, and keeps track of its progress. It usually runs in an isolated cloud environment separate from the user's computer, so nobody has to sit and watch. When it finishes, or gets stuck, it sends a notification. Several agents can run at the same time. In most products the result is presented for human review, so changes do not become permanent without someone looking at them.
gl.arka-plan-ajani.why: With chat-style AI, a person waits for a reply at every step. Background agents let people hand off work and stop waiting. In software development especially, they could raise the number of tasks one person can run at once. In return, questions about permissions, security and error checking grow larger.
gl.arm-mimarisi.def: A processor instruction set design developed by the British company Arm, which defines which commands a chip understands. It relies on a small set of simple instructions and is known for energy efficiency.
gl.arm-mimarisi.example: The chips Apple uses in iPhones and in M-series Macs are based on the Arm architecture, as are Amazon's Graviton processors in its cloud service.
gl.arm-mimarisi.faq.0.a: They are different instruction sets, so a program written for one will not run on the other without adaptation. Arm designs are generally known for energy efficiency, while x86 is known for its long-established software compatibility in desktops and servers.
gl.arm-mimarisi.faq.0.q: What is the difference between ARM and x86?
gl.arm-mimarisi.faq.1.a: Traditionally, no. Arm mainly sells designs and licenses. The companies that license them design the chips, and contract manufacturers usually produce them.
gl.arm-mimarisi.how: Instead of manufacturing its own chips, Arm licenses its architecture and core designs. Companies such as Apple and Qualcomm use these licenses to design their own chips and usually have them made by a separate manufacturer. This licensing model lets many companies build different chips on the same architecture. The design follows the RISC approach, built on simple and regular instructions, which makes it easier to do the same work with less energy. The rival x86 architecture has traditionally powered Intel and AMD processors.
gl.arm-mimarisi.why: Most smartphones run on Arm-based chips. Apple's M-series chips in Mac computers and some cloud server processors are built on the same architecture. As energy use becomes critical in AI infrastructure, interest in Arm-based server processors is growing.
gl.asic.def: An integrated circuit designed and built for one task or class of tasks rather than general use. It does that job more efficiently than flexible chips but is hard to adapt to other work.
gl.asic.example: Google's TPUs, used in its own data centers, and the chips in some cryptocurrency mining rigs are examples of ASICs.
gl.asic.faq.0.a: A GPU is a flexible chip that can handle many kinds of parallel work. An ASIC is built for a single job, so it is usually more efficient at that job and less useful for others.
gl.asic.faq.0.q: What is the difference between an ASIC and a GPU?
gl.asic.faq.1.a: No. It can offer an efficiency advantage on its target task, but that depends on the design and the workload. If the workload changes, the ASIC's advantage may disappear.
gl.asic.faq.1.q: Is an ASIC always faster than a GPU?
gl.asic.how: Design teams lay out the chip's circuits from scratch around the target workload: unneeded features are dropped and the required calculations are built directly into the hardware. In AI, Google's TPU is a commonly cited example, focused on neural network math. Design and manufacturing preparation are expensive and slow, so the investment makes sense only if the chip will be produced in large numbers and used heavily. After manufacturing the circuit cannot be changed, and adapting it through software updates is limited.
gl.asic.why: Because ASICs can do the same job with less energy and lower unit cost, they often come up in big cloud companies' efforts to depend less on GPU supply. Firms that design their own chips gain more control over cost and availability. The trade-off is lost flexibility and the risk of a large upfront investment.

gl.asiri-ogrenme.def.en: When a model memorizes its training data instead of learning general rules, so it looks successful in training but performs poorly on new data.

gl.asiri-ogrenme.example.en: A vehicle recognition model trained only on photos taken in sunny weather may fail to recognize vehicles in photos taken in the rain.

gl.asiri-ogrenme.faq.0.a.en: Overfitting refers to a model memorizing its training data and failing to generalize to new data. In Turkish it is called "aşırı öğrenme" (excessive learning) or "aşırı uyum" (excessive fit).

gl.asiri-ogrenme.faq.1.a.en: Underfitting: the model is too simple to capture even the patterns in the training data.

gl.asiri-ogrenme.faq.1.q.en: What is the opposite of overfitting?

gl.asiri-ogrenme.how.en: Overfitting occurs when a model learns random details and noise in the training data along with the real patterns. To detect it, the data is split into training and test sets: if the model performs very well on the training data but clearly poorly on the test data, it is overfitting. More data, a simpler model and regularization techniques reduce the problem.

gl.asiri-ogrenme.why.en: It is one of the most common reasons a model that looks perfect in the lab fails in the real world. Benchmark questions leaking into training data also creates a form of memorization problem and can inflate test results.

gl.asiri-ret.def: When an AI model needlessly turns down a harmless or legitimate request because it assumes the request might be risky.
gl.asiri-ret.example: A medical student asks which medication doses are dangerous in order to study, and the model refuses to give any information.
gl.asiri-ret.faq.0.a: A safety measure blocks a request that is genuinely harmful. Over-refusal blocks a harmless or legitimate request unnecessarily. The line between the two is not always clear, which is why it is debated.
gl.asiri-ret.faq.0.q: What is the difference between over-refusal and a safety measure?
gl.asiri-ret.faq.1.a: Stating the purpose and context of the request clearly often helps. If the model still declines, rephrasing the request or sending feedback to the provider are other options.
gl.asiri-ret.faq.1.q: What can a user do when facing over-refusal?
gl.asiri-ret.how: Models are trained to decline harmful requests. When that boundary is drawn too widely, a model may react to risky-sounding words instead of the real intent of the request.
