For example, it may treat a question about how to kill a computer process as if it were about violence. Developers measure this with test sets of requests that sound risky but are actually harmless. The goal is to find a balance between safety and helpfulness.
gl.asiri-ret.why: Over-refusal makes a model less useful and erodes user trust. It draws complaints in fields like medicine, law or security research, where legitimate work gets blocked. In safety debates, unnecessary refusals are therefore counted as errors too, not only harmful answers.
gl.asiri-yetki.def: Giving an AI system more tools, permissions or freedom to act than its task requires. When the model makes a mistake or is tricked, that broad authority lets the damage grow.
gl.asiri-yetki.example: If an assistant connected to summarize an inbox is also allowed to send and delete email, a hidden instruction inside one message could push it to write to people on the user's behalf.
gl.asiri-yetki.faq.0.a: No. Prompt injection is an attack technique that tries to steer a model. Excessive agency is the underlying condition that determines how much harm such an attack, or an ordinary error, can cause.
gl.asiri-yetki.faq.0.q: Is excessive agency the same as prompt injection?
gl.asiri-yetki.faq.1.a: Give the model only the tools and permissions the task truly needs, require human approval for irreversible actions, and keep a record of what the system does.
gl.asiri-yetki.faq.1.q: How can the risk be reduced?
gl.asiri-yetki.how: Once a language model is connected to email, file systems, payment services or databases, it does more than generate text: it takes real actions. Excess agency creeps in three ways: too many tools are defined, the tools carry broader permissions than needed (delete rights when read access would do), or the model acts without asking for approval. If the model misreads an instruction, or is steered by a command hidden in a web page, it can use every bit of authority it holds. The usual remedies are least-privilege access, human sign-off for critical actions, and logging everything the system does.
gl.asiri-yetki.why: As AI agents move into real workflows, the problem shifts from a model giving a wrong answer to a model taking a wrong action. An answer can be corrected, but a deleted database or a sent payment often cannot be undone. That is why security teams advise setting limits at the system level instead of trusting the model's good behavior.
gl.automl.def: Approaches and tools that automate steps of building a machine learning model, such as data preparation, model selection and tuning. The aim is to let non-experts get a reasonable model and to save experts time.
gl.automl.example: A retailer can upload a sales table to an AutoML tool and get a model that forecasts next week's demand; cloud platforms such as Google Cloud and Microsoft Azure offer services of this kind.
gl.automl.faq.0.a: Not really. It speeds up standard prediction tasks, but framing the problem, checking data quality and interpreting what results mean for the business still take expertise.
gl.automl.faq.1.a: No. Hyperparameter tuning is one part of AutoML. AutoML can also cover data preparation, algorithm selection and model ensembling.
gl.automl.faq.1.q: Is AutoML the same as hyperparameter tuning?
gl.automl.how: The user supplies a dataset and a goal, for example predicting whether a customer will leave. The AutoML tool tries many algorithms and settings in turn, measures each on validation data and keeps the best performers. Some tools also handle data cleaning, feature creation and combining several models. The result is a ready-to-use model or a pipeline that produces one. Search methods range from simple random trials to smarter optimization techniques.
gl.automl.why: Much of a machine learning project goes into trial and tuning; AutoML reduces that burden and makes it easier for small teams to build prediction models. Defining the problem correctly, understanding the data and interpreting the results still fall to people. Automation does not fix bad data.
gl.baglam-muhendisligi.def: The work of designing and managing what a language model is given at each step: information, instructions, tools and conversation history. The aim is to fill the model's working window with the right content.
gl.baglam-muhendisligi.example: Instead of feeding an entire code repository to the model, a coding assistant puts only the relevant files, the project's style rules and the latest error message into the context.
gl.baglam-muhendisligi.faq.0.a: Prompt engineering mostly focuses on writing a good instruction. Context engineering covers managing everything that enters the model: instructions plus documents, history, tools and memory.
gl.baglam-muhendisligi.faq.0.q: How does context engineering differ from prompt engineering?
gl.baglam-muhendisligi.faq.1.a: Yes. Even in a large window, unnecessary content raises cost and can make the model more likely to overlook the information that matters.
gl.baglam-muhendisligi.faq.1.q: If the context window is large, is context engineering still needed?
gl.baglam-muhendisligi.how: A model can only see a limited amount of text at once, a space known as the context window. In context engineering, someone chooses among the system instructions, conversation history, retrieved documents, tool descriptions and notes about the user; these are ordered, summarized, and trimmed of anything unnecessary. In multi-step agents, this selection is redone before every step. It is like arranging papers on a desk: too few and something is missing, too many and the key detail gets buried.
gl.baglam-muhendisligi.why: The same model can perform far better with the right context, and some failures in agent applications come from incomplete or cluttered context rather than from the model itself. The idea is often seen as a broader take on prompt engineering, going beyond writing a single piece of text. Context size also affects cost and response time.

gl.baglam-penceresi.def.en: The amount of text a language model can "see" at once, measured in tokens. The larger the window, the longer the documents or conversations the model can consider at the same time.

gl.baglam-penceresi.example.en: A context window of one million tokens can process text roughly the length of several thick books in one go.

gl.baglam-penceresi.faq.0.a.en: It varies by language and text density; roughly, it corresponds to hundreds of pages of text, several books or a large codebase. Turkish text can use more tokens than English.

gl.baglam-penceresi.faq.0.q.en: How many pages is 1 million tokens?

gl.baglam-penceresi.faq.1.a.en: It is an advantage when working with long documents, but it does not indicate quality on its own. Models are also known to overlook some details in very long contexts.

gl.baglam-penceresi.faq.1.q.en: Is a model with a larger context window better?

gl.baglam-penceresi.how.en: When a language model generates a response, it "reads" the entire conversation, any attached documents and its own instructions at once. This total has an upper limit, called the context window, measured in tokens. If the limit is exceeded, the oldest parts are ignored or summarized.

gl.baglam-penceresi.why.en: A large context window is needed to analyze long contracts, books or large codebases in one go. However, very long context both raises costs and can cause the model to overlook some details.

gl.baglam-yonetimi.def: The work of deciding what information goes into an AI model's context window, how much of it, and in what form. In long conversations it includes compressing or summarizing older content.
gl.baglam-yonetimi.example: A coding agent that works for hours can replace its detailed output from the early hours with a few-sentence summary and keep only the current files and a to-do list in context.
gl.baglam-yonetimi.faq.0.a: They are close. Summarization shortens content in new words, while compression is a broader term that also includes dropping or trimming unneeded parts. In some products the two are used interchangeably.
gl.baglam-yonetimi.faq.0.q: Are compression and summarization the same thing?
gl.baglam-yonetimi.faq.1.a: Yes, a summary leaves out some detail. That is why critical information is often kept as a separate note and what can be summarized is chosen carefully.
gl.baglam-yonetimi.faq.1.q: Does context management cause information loss?
gl.baglam-yonetimi.how: A model can only process a limited amount of text at once, and a long conversation edges toward that limit. Context management handles this in several ways. Older messages are turned into a short summary; unnecessary parts of tool outputs are dropped; important facts are kept in a separate note or memory and recalled when needed. Some systems automatically summarize the conversation as the window nears full and continue in a fresh window. This keeps the model within its limit without losing track of the main goal.
gl.baglam-yonetimi.why: Even a large context window is not infinite; a full context raises cost and delay, and in very long contexts a model may overlook important details. In long-running agent tasks, good context management is becoming decisive for keeping the work consistent.
gl.bayes-teoremi.def: A rule for updating the probability of something when new evidence arrives. It combines what was believed beforehand with how expected the evidence is, producing a revised probability.
gl.bayes-teoremi.example: Classic spam filters built on a naive Bayes classifier look at the words in an email and use this rule to update the probability that the message is spam.
gl.bayes-teoremi.faq.0.a: No. Bayes' theorem is a single rule of probability, while Bayesian inference is the broader approach that applies the rule systematically to update model parameters and hypotheses.
gl.bayes-teoremi.faq.0.q: Are Bayes' theorem and Bayesian inference the same thing?
gl.bayes-teoremi.faq.1.a: It comes from past data, expert knowledge or, when nothing is known, broad and neutral assumptions. When data is scarce, the choice of prior can noticeably affect the result.
gl.bayes-teoremi.faq.1.q: Where does the prior probability come from?
gl.bayes-teoremi.how: The theorem combines three pieces: the probability of an event before seeing the evidence (the prior), how often the evidence would appear if the event were true (the likelihood), and how common the evidence is overall. The prior is multiplied by the likelihood and divided by the overall frequency of the evidence, giving the posterior probability. This is why a positive test for a rare disease is less conclusive than it seems: if the disease is very rare, most positive results come from healthy people. The rule itself is a simple identity of probability; its power lies in letting knowledge be updated step by step.
gl.bayes-teoremi.why: Bayes' theorem underlies probabilistic reasoning and Bayesian methods. Spam filters, medical decision-support tools and machine learning models that quantify uncertainty all rely on this logic. Because people often misread conditional probabilities, it also helps in interpreting test results and risk reports correctly.
gl.bayesci-cikarim.def: A statistical approach that holds beliefs about an unknown quantity as a probability distribution and updates them with Bayes' theorem as new data arrives. Instead of a single best value, it tracks all plausible values and their uncertainty.
gl.bayesci-cikarim.example: A team estimating an ad's click rate keeps a distribution showing the range the rate probably falls in, rather than a single percentage, and updates it with every new click.
gl.bayesci-cikarim.faq.0.a: Frequentist methods treat a parameter as fixed but unknown and interpret probability as the long-run frequency of repeated experiments. Bayesian methods treat probability as a degree of belief and place a distribution on the parameter. Both schools are widely used.
gl.bayesci-cikarim.faq.0.q: How does Bayesian inference differ from classical (frequentist) statistics?
gl.bayesci-cikarim.faq.1.a: Yes, especially in research on Bayesian neural networks and uncertainty estimation. But because the computation is expensive, standard training of large models usually relies on a single set of parameters.
gl.bayesci-cikarim.faq.1.q: Is Bayesian inference used in deep learning?
gl.bayesci-cikarim.how: First, a prior distribution is chosen for the parameter, reflecting what is known before seeing data. Next, the likelihood is computed, which measures how well the data fits each possible parameter value, and the two are combined into a posterior distribution. As more data arrives, the posterior becomes the prior for the next round. In complex models the posterior is hard to compute exactly, so sampling methods such as Markov chain Monte Carlo or approximations such as variational inference are used.
gl.bayesci-cikarim.why: The Bayesian approach also tells you how confident a model is, which matters in fields like medicine, finance and science where mistakes are costly. It lets you use prior knowledge when data is limited. The trade-offs are heavy computation and the fact that the choice of prior can be debated.
gl.bayt-cifti-kodlamasi.def: A tokenization method that builds a subword vocabulary by repeatedly merging the most frequent pairs of characters or pieces in a text collection. It originated as a data compression technique.
gl.bayt-cifti-kodlamasi.example: If the pieces “car” and “pets” often appear next to each other in the training text, the algorithm may merge them into one piece, “carpets”.
gl.bayt-cifti-kodlamasi.faq.0.a: No. Tokenization is the general process, and BPE is one method of doing it. Other approaches exist.
gl.bayt-cifti-kodlamasi.faq.0.q: Is BPE the same as tokenization?
gl.bayt-cifti-kodlamasi.faq.1.a: No. Languages that were well represented when the vocabulary was built are split more efficiently. Less represented languages may have words broken into many small pieces.
gl.bayt-cifti-kodlamasi.faq.1.q: Does BPE work equally well in every language?
gl.bayt-cifti-kodlamasi.how: The vocabulary starts with single characters or bytes. The algorithm scans a large body of text, finds the pair that appears side by side most often, and adds it to the vocabulary as a new piece. This merging repeats until the vocabulary reaches the desired size. In the end, frequent words are single pieces and rare words are built from smaller ones. Byte-level versions ensure that no character is ever left out as “unknown”.
gl.bayt-cifti-kodlamasi.why: Many large language models use BPE-based tokenizers, so it is the logic behind much of the “token” counting seen in AI products. It solves the unknown-word problem while keeping the vocabulary a manageable size. Debates about some languages being split into more pieces than others also trace back to which text the vocabulary was built from.
gl.bellek-bant-genisligi.def: A measure of how much data memory can send to and receive from a processor each second, usually given in gigabytes per second (GB/s) or terabytes per second (TB/s).
gl.bellek-bant-genisligi.example: A chat model must read billions of parameters from memory for every new token it produces, so a graphics card with faster memory will usually respond faster with the same model.
gl.bellek-bant-genisligi.faq.0.a: No. Capacity tells how much data can be stored (GB), while bandwidth tells how quickly that data can be moved (GB/s).
gl.bellek-bant-genisligi.faq.0.q: Is memory bandwidth the same as memory capacity?
gl.bellek-bant-genisligi.faq.1.a: Latency is the time between requesting data and the first piece arriving. Bandwidth is the total amount of data flowing per unit of time.
gl.bellek-bant-genisligi.faq.1.q: How does bandwidth differ from latency?
gl.bellek-bant-genisligi.how: Bandwidth depends on how wide the path between memory and processor is and how fast data moves along it. It helps to picture a highway: more lanes and faster cars mean more cargo passes each second. Solutions such as high-bandwidth memory (HBM) place memory very close to the processor and use many parallel connections. When an AI model runs, it must keep reading its weights from memory, so this speed directly affects how fast the model works.
gl.bellek-bant-genisligi.why: When large language models generate a reply, they are often limited less by the processor's raw compute than by how quickly memory can feed it data. That is why a TOPS or FLOP figure alone is not a sufficient yardstick for an accelerator; bandwidth also shapes speed and cost.
gl.benchmark-doygunlugu.def: The point at which top AI models score close to the maximum on a test, so the benchmark can no longer tell the models apart.
gl.benchmark-doygunlugu.example: When many models reach or exceed the human average on a reading-comprehension test, it can no longer separate new models, so a harder version is built.
gl.benchmark-doygunlugu.faq.0.a: No. It only shows the test is no longer challenging enough. A model can score near the top on one test and still be weak at other tasks.
gl.benchmark-doygunlugu.faq.0.q: Does saturation mean a model is as smart as a human?
gl.benchmark-doygunlugu.faq.1.a: Researchers build harder and newer tests, keep test questions private, and add human evaluation and measurements based on real-world tasks.
gl.benchmark-doygunlugu.how: A benchmark is a fixed set of tasks or questions. As models improve, scores climb and the best results approach the highest possible mark. At that stage the gaps between models shrink, and measurement noise or mislabeled test items start to decide the ranking. If test questions have leaked into training data, scores can be inflated further. A saturated benchmark is usually replaced by a harder or newer one.
gl.benchmark-doygunlugu.why: News about a model “setting a record” on a test is common, but on a saturated benchmark such scores may not reflect a real difference in ability. For readers it is a reason to treat single scores with caution, and for researchers it means evaluation sets must be refreshed continuously.
gl.benchmark-kirlenmesi.def: When the questions or answers of a benchmark end up in a model's training data. Because the model may have memorized the test rather than learned the skill, its score overstates its real ability.
gl.benchmark-kirlenmesi.example: If a math benchmark's questions and solutions were posted on forums and ended up in the training data, a model might score very well on the original questions but struggle noticeably when they are slightly changed.
gl.benchmark-kirlenmesi.faq.0.a: No. Most of the time it is accidental, because training data is gathered from the web at huge scale and benchmark content can get mixed in. Deliberately tuning a model to a benchmark is a separate and controversial practice.
gl.benchmark-kirlenmesi.faq.1.a: Firm proof is hard to get, especially when the training data is not shared. A score that drops on reworded questions, or weaker results on new questions published after training, are signals that contamination may be present.
gl.benchmark-kirlenmesi.how: Large language models are trained on huge piles of text collected from the internet. Popular benchmark questions, their solutions and discussions about them also sit on the web, so they can slip into the training data unintentionally. A model that saw these questions in training may be recalling answers instead of working them out. Contamination can also happen through fine-tuning aimed at a specific benchmark. To detect it, researchers search the training data for overlapping text, try reworded versions of the questions, or use new questions written after training.
gl.benchmark-kirlenmesi.why: Benchmark scores are the main basis for comparing models and for headline claims about progress. A contaminated score exaggerates real ability and distorts comparisons. That is why held-out private test sets, regularly refreshed benchmarks and independent evaluations are becoming more important.

gl.benchmark.def.en: A standard test in which models are measured and compared on the same tasks. When results are announced by companies, they should be read alongside independent tests.

gl.benchmark.example.en: A company announcing that its new model scored "57%" on a coding test is a typical benchmark story.

gl.benchmark.faq.0.a.en: They give an idea but are not sufficient on their own. Results published by companies should be compared with independent tests, and the possibility that test questions leaked into training data should be kept in mind.

gl.benchmark.faq.1.a.en: Different tests are used for general knowledge, math, coding and agent tasks; comparison platforms based on user votes are also common.

gl.benchmark.faq.1.q.en: What are the best-known AI benchmarks?

gl.benchmark.how.en: A benchmark is a standard test in which models are given the same set of questions and tasks, and the answers are scored automatically or by humans. Different benchmarks exist for different areas such as coding, math, general knowledge and agent tasks. Results are usually given as percentages or points.

gl.benchmark.why.en: Although it is the most common way to compare models, it has limits: models may have seen the test questions during training, and tests may not fully reflect real work. That is why results published by companies themselves should be read alongside independent measurements.

gl.bert.def: An encoder-based language model introduced by Google in 2018 that interprets each word in a sentence by looking at the context on both its left and its right. It was designed more for understanding text than for generating it.
gl.bert.example: An online store might fine-tune a BERT variant on Turkish data to sort customer reviews into positive and negative ones.
gl.bert.faq.0.a: BERT is an encoder that reads text in both directions and focuses on understanding. GPT is a decoder-only model that generates text by looking at what came before.
gl.bert.faq.0.q: What is the difference between BERT and GPT?
gl.bert.faq.1.a: Not in the usual sense today. It is much smaller than chat models with billions of parameters and it was not built to generate text. Still, it is regarded as one of the early landmark pretrained language models.
gl.bert.faq.1.q: Is BERT a large language model?
gl.bert.how: BERT consists only of Transformer encoder layers. During training, some words in the text are hidden and the model tries to predict them from the surrounding context, a task called masked language modeling. As a result, the representation of each word is shaped by the whole sentence. After pretraining, the model is adapted to a small task such as sentiment analysis, question answering or text classification by fine-tuning it on a modest amount of data.
gl.bert.why: BERT popularized the approach of pretraining a model and then fine-tuning it, and it raised the bar on many language understanding tasks. Even though generative chat models now get most of the attention, BERT-style models are still widely used for search, classification and text matching, where being small and fast is an advantage.
gl.bf16.def: A 16-bit number format developed at Google that keeps the same range of values as 32-bit FP32 but with lower precision. It is widely used in AI training.
gl.bf16.example: A research team trains a language model in BF16 while often keeping a master copy of the weights in FP32 so that small errors do not pile up.
gl.bf16.faq.0.a: Both use 16 bits. FP16 has more bits for significant digits, so it is more precise but has a narrow range. BF16 uses the same wide range as FP32 and is less precise.
gl.bf16.faq.0.q: What is the difference between BF16 and FP16?
gl.bf16.faq.1.a: Many current GPUs and TPUs support the format in hardware. For a specific chip, check the manufacturer's documentation.
gl.bf16.how: A floating-point number has three parts: a sign, an exponent and the significant digits. BF16 has the same number of exponent bits as 32-bit FP32, which is eight, but gives only seven bits to the significant digits. It can therefore represent very large or very small values without overflowing, while giving up fine detail. Converting from FP32 to BF16 is roughly as simple as keeping the first 16 bits of the number. Neural networks tolerate small rounding errors well, so the trade-off often works.
gl.bf16.why: It saves memory and speeds up computation while avoiding most of the overflow problems of FP16 during training, and it often needs no extra scaling. That is why it has become one of the common standards for training large models and is supported by many current GPUs and TPUs.
gl.bilgi-grafigi.def: A structured network of knowledge in which entities such as people, companies, places and concepts are nodes and the relationships between them are links.
gl.bilgi-grafigi.example: On a film platform, movies, directors and actors are linked, so the films of actors who have worked with the same director can be listed easily.
gl.bilgi-grafigi.faq.0.a: A relational database stores data in tables of rows and columns. A knowledge graph puts relationships between entities first, so questions that pass through many connections are more natural to express and query.
gl.bilgi-grafigi.faq.0.q: How is a knowledge graph different from a relational database?
gl.bilgi-grafigi.faq.1.a: Experts can build one by hand, it can be converted from existing databases, or it can be extracted from text automatically. In practice these methods are often combined and the results reviewed by people.
gl.bilgi-grafigi.how: Knowledge is usually recorded as triples: a subject, a relationship and an object. For example, Ankara is linked to Turkey through the relationship of being its capital. Put together, these triples form a network of entities. A graph can be built by hand or extracted automatically from text, and language models are now used for that too. Specialized query languages then let you move through the network, for instance asking which partners the companies a person works for have.
gl.bilgi-grafigi.why: Knowledge graphs have long been behind information boxes in search engines, recommendation systems and enterprise data integration. In AI, they can give language models reliable and traceable context, which may help reduce made-up answers. Building and maintaining them correctly takes real effort, though.
gl.bilgi-teorisi.def: The branch of mathematics that studies how information is measured, stored and transmitted, and that addresses questions about uncertainty, compression and communication over noisy channels.
gl.bilgi-teorisi.example: The more a language model misjudges the next word, the higher the cross-entropy loss that is minimized during its training.
gl.bilgi-teorisi.faq.0.a: No, but they are related. The formulas are similar and both rest on the idea of disorder or uncertainty, yet they are used in different fields for different purposes.
gl.bilgi-teorisi.faq.0.q: Is entropy in information theory the same as entropy in physics?
gl.bilgi-teorisi.faq.1.a: Most visibly in the cross-entropy loss used for classifiers and language models. It also appears in data compression, the perplexity metric and the comparison of probability distributions.
gl.bilgi-teorisi.faq.1.q: Where does information theory show up in AI?
gl.bilgi-teorisi.how: Claude Shannon founded the field with his 1948 paper. The core idea is that the amount of information in an event depends on how surprising it is: a rare event carries more information than a common one. The average surprise is called entropy, and it corresponds to the minimum number of bits needed to compress a source. Concepts such as cross-entropy and KL divergence measure how far apart two probability distributions are.
gl.bilgi-teorisi.why: File compression, error correction and data transmission all rest on information theory. In AI, the cross-entropy loss used to train classifiers and language models comes directly from this field. The perplexity metric, which measures how 'surprised' a model is, follows the same logic.
gl.bilgisayar-kullanimi.def: The ability of an AI model to look at a screen and operate a mouse and keyboard like a person, so it can control desktop programs and websites. The model can then do work in any software that has a visual interface, not just produce text.
gl.bilgisayar-kullanimi.example: A model could log into an old accounting program that has no API and enter invoices into a form one by one; Anthropic's Claude models are among those that offer this capability.
gl.bilgisayar-kullanimi.faq.0.a: With an API integration, programs talk to each other through structured commands, which is fast and reliable. With computer use, the model reads the interface visually and clicks like a person, which is more flexible but usually slower and more error-prone.
gl.bilgisayar-kullanimi.faq.0.q: What is the difference between computer use and an API integration?
gl.bilgisayar-kullanimi.faq.1.a: Not entirely risk-free. A model can click the wrong thing or be fooled by a harmful instruction on screen. That is why isolated environments, limited permissions and human approval for critical steps are common safeguards.
gl.bilgisayar-kullanimi.how: The model takes screenshots at regular intervals and reads them to work out where each button, field or menu is. It then produces actions such as move the cursor here, click, or type this, and a software layer carries them out on a real computer. The new screenshot goes back to the model, and the loop repeats until the task is done. It resembles a person looking at a screen and working through steps. For safety, the process is often run inside an isolated virtual machine.
gl.bilgisayar-kullanimi.why: Not every program has an application programming interface (API), and many older business systems can only be used through their screens. Computer use closes that gap and widens what automation can reach. At the same time, risks such as a mistaken click or influence from a malicious page make permissions and oversight important topics.

gl.bilgisayarli-goru.def.en: The field of AI that enables computers to recognize and interpret objects, faces, text and movements in photos and videos.

gl.bilgisayarli-goru.example.en: Examples of computer vision include a phone finding dog photos when you type "dog" in the photo gallery, or automatically reading the amount on a photo of an invoice.

gl.bilgisayarli-goru.faq.0.a.en: It is used in many areas, such as facial recognition, autonomous driving, medical imaging, defect detection in manufacturing, document reading and agriculture.

gl.bilgisayarli-goru.faq.1.a.en: Multimodal language models can understand and interpret images, but specially trained vision models are still widely used for specialized tasks that demand speed and accuracy, such as factory quality control.

gl.bilgisayarli-goru.faq.1.q.en: Are multimodal models replacing computer vision?

gl.bilgisayarli-goru.how.en: Computer vision models take an image as a grid of numbers made up of pixels and, through deep learning, learn to recognize patterns of edges, textures and shapes in those pixels. This allows them to classify an object, mark its location, compare faces or read text in a photo (OCR).

gl.bilgisayarli-goru.why.en: Many areas rely on computer vision, including autonomous vehicles, medical image analysis, quality control on production lines, security cameras and inventory tracking in retail. Applications such as facial recognition, however, raise serious privacy debates.

gl.biyometrik-gozetim.def: Monitoring and identifying people, often at scale and without their knowledge, using bodily or behavioral traits such as faces, voices, gait or fingerprints.
gl.biyometrik-gozetim.example: A city camera network that automatically compares the face of everyone walking past with a stored list of wanted people is an example of biometric surveillance.
gl.biyometrik-gozetim.faq.0.a: No. In verification a person knowingly proves their identity, for example to unlock a phone. In surveillance, people are typically scanned in bulk and often without knowing it.
gl.biyometrik-gozetim.faq.0.q: Is biometric surveillance the same as biometric verification?
gl.biyometrik-gozetim.faq.1.a: One side cites security and crime-fighting, the other cites privacy, false matches and discrimination. Because biometric traits cannot be changed, misuse or leaks are also seen as especially serious.
gl.biyometrik-gozetim.faq.1.q: Why is biometric surveillance so contested?
gl.biyometrik-gozetim.how: Cameras, microphones or sensors collect data continuously in public places. AI extracts biometric templates from the images and sounds and matches them against watchlists or identity databases. It can run in real time on live feeds, or search recorded footage after the fact. The key difference is between someone voluntarily proving who they are at a door and someone being scanned on the street without doing anything; the first involves consent, the second usually does not.
gl.biyometrik-gozetim.why: Supporters point to benefits such as finding missing people and preventing serious crime, while opponents warn of a chilling effect on privacy and freedom of assembly. Biometric data cannot be changed like a password, so a leak is a lasting risk. The EU AI Act places real-time remote biometric identification by law enforcement in public spaces under strict limits and narrow exceptions.
gl.boyut-indirgeme.def: The process of describing a dataset that has many features (columns) with far fewer features while keeping most of the useful information.
gl.boyut-indirgeme.example: Sensor data with hundreds of measurements can be reduced to a few principal components and plotted on a two-axis chart.
gl.boyut-indirgeme.faq.0.a: Principal component analysis finds the directions in which the data varies most and re-expresses the data along a smaller number of those directions. It is one of the most common dimensionality reduction methods.
gl.boyut-indirgeme.faq.1.a: Usually some. The goal is to keep what matters and discard noise and redundancy, and how much loss is acceptable depends on the purpose.
gl.boyut-indirgeme.how: In real data, many features are correlated and some carry redundant information. Some methods drop the least informative features, while others combine existing features into a smaller set of new ones. Principal component analysis (PCA) is an example of the second kind. Methods such as t-SNE and UMAP squeeze high-dimensional data down to two or three dimensions so it can be visualized. A good analogy is the shadow of a three-dimensional object on a wall: a dimension is lost, but the shape is still recognizable.
gl.boyut-indirgeme.why: Fewer features usually mean faster models that are less prone to overfitting. It is also often the only way for people to visually inspect data with hundreds of dimensions. Some information is always lost, so it matters to know what each method preserves.
gl.boyutluluk-laneti.def: The problem that as the number of features describing the data grows, the data becomes increasingly sparse in space and algorithms struggle. The number of examples needed to keep the space equally well covered grows extremely fast.
gl.boyutluluk-laneti.example: In a study that measures ten thousand gene expressions but covers only a few hundred patients, a model is prone to learn coincidences specific to that small sample rather than the disease itself.
gl.boyutluluk-laneti.faq.0.a: The main remedies are feature selection, dimensionality reduction such as principal component analysis, regularization and collecting more data.
gl.boyutluluk-laneti.faq.0.q: How can the curse of dimensionality be reduced?
gl.boyutluluk-laneti.faq.1.a: Real-world data tends to concentrate in a small part of the space, and deep networks can capture that structure. The problem still does not disappear completely.
gl.boyutluluk-laneti.faq.1.q: Are deep learning models immune to it?
gl.boyutluluk-laneti.how: On a single line, ten points cover an interval reasonably well. To get the same density in two dimensions you need a hundred points, and in three dimensions a thousand, so the required number grows exponentially with dimension. As dimensions increase, points drift far apart and the gap between the nearest and farthest neighbor shrinks. Methods that rely on distance lose their ability to tell points apart. Models also tend to memorize many features from few examples.
gl.boyutluluk-laneti.why: It is a direct obstacle in fields with thousands of features, such as genomics, text and images. It explains why feature selection, dimensionality reduction and embeddings are so widespread. Teams working with high-dimensional data therefore often start by cutting down the number of features.
gl.budama.def: A technique that shrinks a trained neural network and lowers its running cost by removing weights, neurons or layers that contribute little to its output.
gl.budama.example: A company could prune some attention heads of its own language model and recover quality with fine-tuning, ending up with a version that does the same job with less hardware and in less time.
gl.budama.faq.0.a: Pruning reduces the number of parameters, while quantization lowers the number of bits used to store them. The two can also be used together.
gl.budama.faq.0.q: What is the difference between pruning and quantization?
gl.budama.faq.1.a: When done moderately, the loss is usually small and can be recovered with extra training. With heavy pruning, quality can degrade noticeably.
gl.budama.faq.1.q: Does pruning reduce a model's accuracy?
gl.budama.how: First, the importance of each weight or neuron is measured; the simplest criterion is how small a weight's absolute value is. Those judged unimportant are set to zero or removed entirely. The remaining parts then go through a short round of extra training to make up for lost accuracy. In unstructured pruning, where individual weights are dropped, speed gains can be limited without special software and hardware support. When whole neurons, attention heads or layers are removed, the model really does become smaller and faster. It resembles a gardener trimming a tree.
gl.budama.why: Large models are expensive to run. Pruning reduces memory needs and latency, making it easier to fit models onto limited devices such as phones. Research suggests that a considerable share of the weights in many networks is unnecessary. Still, aggressive pruning hurts accuracy, so the balance is tuned for each task.
gl.bulanik-mantik.def: A form of logic in which a statement can be partly true, with a degree between zero and one rather than just true or false, which makes it possible to reason with vague, graded expressions.
gl.bulanik-mantik.example: Some washing machines and air conditioners use fuzzy controllers to adjust water and power smoothly according to inputs such as load size or room temperature.
gl.bulanik-mantik.faq.0.a: No. Probability describes how likely an event is to happen. Fuzzy logic measures the degree to which something fits a concept, such as how 'hot' or 'tall' it is.
gl.bulanik-mantik.faq.0.q: Is fuzzy logic the same as probability?
gl.bulanik-mantik.faq.1.a: Lotfi Zadeh proposed the idea of fuzzy sets in the 1960s. It later found wide use in control engineering and artificial intelligence.
gl.bulanik-mantik.how: In fuzzy logic, a value belongs to a set with a certain degree of membership. For example, 28 degrees Celsius might count as belonging to the set 'hot' at 0.7 and to the set 'warm' at 0.3. Rules written in an expert's language, such as 'if it is hot, run the fan fast', are evaluated using these degrees. The outputs of all rules are combined and finally converted into a single crisp value, such as a fan speed. The result is smooth transitions instead of sharp thresholds.
gl.bulanik-mantik.why: It has been widely used in control systems where building an exact mathematical model is hard. Because expert knowledge is written down as rules, the system is also easy to interpret. Although large deep learning models dominate today, fuzzy logic remains a choice for systems that deal with uncertainty.
gl.bulut-bilisim.def: The use of computing resources such as servers, storage and software over the internet from remote data centers, rented as needed instead of running on the user's own device or machines.
gl.bulut-bilisim.example: An online retailer adds servers during a sales campaign and removes them afterward, paying only for the capacity it actually used.
gl.bulut-bilisim.faq.0.a: A data center is the physical facility where servers are housed. Cloud computing is the model in which the resources in those facilities are offered as a service over the internet.
gl.bulut-bilisim.faq.0.q: What is the difference between cloud computing and a data center?
gl.bulut-bilisim.faq.1.a: Security depends on both the provider's safeguards and how the customer configures the service. A properly configured cloud can be secure, but data location and regulatory requirements still need to be assessed separately.
gl.bulut-bilisim.faq.1.q: Is data in the cloud secure?
gl.bulut-bilisim.how: A cloud provider virtualizes the hardware in its data centers and shares it among many customers. Through a dashboard or interface, a user requests as many servers, as much storage or as many GPUs as needed and pays only for what is used. Services are usually described in three layers: infrastructure (IaaS), platform (PaaS) and software (SaaS). When demand drops, the resources are released, so there is no hardware to buy and manage.
gl.bulut-bilisim.why: The GPU capacity needed for AI work is expensive and hard to obtain, and the cloud makes it accessible through rental. Many AI products are also delivered over the cloud as APIs. Data privacy, cost and dependence on a single provider are the main concerns organizations raise about the cloud.

gl.buyuk-dil-modeli.def.en: An AI model trained on very large amounts of text that can understand and generate text. ChatGPT, Claude and Gemini are based on large language models.

gl.buyuk-dil-modeli.example.en: GPT models are behind ChatGPT, Claude models are behind Claude, and Gemini models are behind the Gemini app.

gl.buyuk-dil-modeli.faq.0.a.en: LLM is the abbreviation of "large language model," which in Turkish is "büyük dil modeli."

gl.buyuk-dil-modeli.faq.1.a.en: On its own, a model only knows what it learned from its training data. When equipped with tools such as web search, it can access current information.

gl.buyuk-dil-modeli.faq.1.q.en: Is a large language model connected to the internet?

gl.buyuk-dil-modeli.how.en: A large language model is trained on the task of "predicting the next word" across vast amounts of text from the internet and books. In the process, it learns the structure of language, knowledge and reasoning patterns. It is then fine-tuned with human feedback to become an assistant that answers questions and follows instructions.

gl.buyuk-dil-modeli.why.en: It forms the basis of many products, including chat assistants, translation, summarization, code writing and search. Which company builds the better model is the central question in the AI race.

gl.buyuk-veri.def: A general name for data sets so large, fast-moving or varied that they are hard to handle on a single computer with traditional methods, along with the approaches used to process them.
gl.buyuk-veri.example: An e-commerce site processes millions of users' click and purchase records to power its product recommendation system.
gl.buyuk-veri.faq.0.a: No. Big data is a type of input, while AI refers to systems that learn from or use that data. AI can work without big data, and big data can be analyzed without AI.
gl.buyuk-veri.faq.0.q: Are big data and artificial intelligence the same thing?
gl.buyuk-veri.faq.1.a: There is no fixed threshold. The common view is that data that cannot be comfortably processed on a single machine with the tools at hand counts as big data, and that line moves with technology.
gl.buyuk-veri.faq.1.q: How much data counts as big data?
gl.buyuk-veri.how: Big data is often described by three traits: volume, velocity and variety. Data streams in constantly from sensors, phones, social media and transaction records, in forms such as text, images and tables. Since one machine cannot hold that much, the data is split up, spread across many computers and processed in parallel. Tools such as Hadoop and Spark were built for this, and cloud storage is a common solution. The results then feed analysis or machine learning models.
gl.buyuk-veri.why: Much of modern AI relies on models fed with large amounts of data. Businesses use big data to understand customer behavior and make decisions. On the other hand, storage costs, data quality and the protection of personal data raise serious issues. And being big does not on its own mean being valuable.
gl.capraz-dogrulama.def: A method that splits the data into several parts and, in each round, tests on a different part while training on the rest. The average over the rounds gives a more reliable estimate of performance than a single split.
gl.capraz-dogrulama.example: A researcher with a dataset of a few hundred patients measures a disease-prediction model with five-fold cross-validation and reports the average result.
gl.capraz-dogrulama.faq.0.a: Usually not. It is mostly used for model selection and tuning, and because those choices rely on the same data, it is good practice to keep a separate test set for the final measurement.
gl.capraz-dogrulama.faq.0.q: Does cross-validation replace a test set?
gl.capraz-dogrulama.faq.1.a: Every round requires training the model from scratch. Since even one training run of a large language model is very costly, the method is impractical, and fixed held-out sets are used instead.
gl.capraz-dogrulama.faq.1.q: Why is it rarely used with large language models?
gl.capraz-dogrulama.how: The most common form is k-fold cross-validation. The data is divided into, say, five equal parts. In the first round, four parts are used for training and the remaining one for testing; in the next round, the held-out part changes. After five rounds every part has served as the test part once, and the five results are averaged. The spread between results also shows how stable the model is. For time series, the order is preserved when splitting so that the future never trains the past.
gl.capraz-dogrulama.why: When data is scarce, the result of a single validation split can depend on luck, and cross-validation reduces that risk. It is widely used for model selection and hyperparameter tuning. The cost is that the model must be trained several times, which is impractical for very large models.
gl.capraz-entropi.def: The average cost of encoding events from the true distribution using another distribution, such as a model's. In machine learning, it is a common loss function that measures how far a model's predicted probabilities are from the true labels.
gl.capraz-entropi.example: If an image classifier gives 90 percent probability to the cat in a photo, the cross-entropy loss is low; if it gives 1 percent, the loss is much higher.
gl.capraz-entropi.faq.0.a: Entropy is the uncertainty of a distribution on its own. Cross-entropy is the cost of encoding events from the true distribution using a different one, and it is always at least as large as the entropy. The gap between them is the KL divergence.
gl.capraz-entropi.faq.0.q: What is the difference between cross-entropy and entropy?
gl.capraz-entropi.faq.1.a: Usually not. Because it compares probability distributions, it is common in classification and language modeling. For predicting numerical values, measures such as mean squared error are more often preferred.
gl.capraz-entropi.faq.1.q: Is cross-entropy used for regression too?
gl.capraz-entropi.how: For each training example the true class is known, while the model assigns probabilities to the classes. Cross-entropy takes the negative logarithm of the probability the model gave to the true class. If the model gives the correct class a high probability, the penalty is small; if it gives a low probability, the penalty grows quickly, so confident but wrong predictions are punished heavily. The average over all examples is minimized during training with gradient descent. This pushes the model's probabilities toward the true distribution.
gl.capraz-entropi.why: It is among the most common loss functions for training classifiers and large language models. In classification it equals the negative log-likelihood, which ties it to the principle of maximum likelihood. Perplexity, a measure often mentioned for language models, is derived from cross-entropy.
gl.cekismeli-saldiri.def: A method of changing a model's input in small ways that a person would not notice or care about, in order to make the model produce a wrong output.
gl.cekismeli-saldiri.example: In research, adding imperceptible noise to a photo of a panda led an image classifier to label the animal a gibbon with high confidence.
gl.cekismeli-saldiri.faq.0.a: No, though they are related. A jailbreak is an attempt to write a prompt that gets around a language model's safety rules. An adversarial attack is a broader idea that covers fooling a model with any kind of input, including images and audio.
gl.cekismeli-saldiri.faq.0.q: Is an adversarial attack the same as a jailbreak?
gl.cekismeli-saldiri.faq.1.a: Mostly not directly, but it can affect the reliability of everyday products such as face recognition, spam filters and driver assistance systems.
gl.cekismeli-saldiri.faq.1.q: Is this a risk for ordinary users?
gl.cekismeli-saldiri.how: Models process inputs differently from humans. For an example near a decision boundary, a very small change can flip the result entirely. An attacker may add imperceptible noise to an image or swap a few words in a text. With access to the model's internals, the change can be calculated; without it, trial and error can still work. An input crafted this way is called an adversarial example. Adversarial training and input checks are used as defenses, but they do not give full protection.
gl.cekismeli-saldiri.why: In areas such as face recognition, autonomous driving, content moderation and fraud detection, fooling a model can cause real harm. Adversarial attacks show that a high accuracy score does not mean robustness. That is why safety-critical systems are tested not only for accuracy but also for resistance to deliberate deception.
gl.cekismeli-uretici-ag.def: A type of generative model in which two neural networks are trained against each other: one produces fake data and the other tries to tell real from fake. Ian Goodfellow and colleagues introduced it in 2014.
gl.cekismeli-uretici-ag.example: Well-known demo sites that showed portraits of people who do not exist were built on StyleGAN, a GAN model developed by Nvidia.
gl.cekismeli-uretici-ag.faq.0.a: A GAN produces output in one pass through competition between a generator and a discriminator. A diffusion model starts from noise and builds the image over many steps, and is usually more stable to train.
gl.cekismeli-uretici-ag.faq.0.q: What is the difference between a GAN and a diffusion model?
gl.cekismeli-uretici-ag.faq.1.a: No. The idea has also been tried for audio, music and tabular data, but image generation is its best-known use.
gl.cekismeli-uretici-ag.how: The generator starts from random numbers and tries to produce, say, a face photo. The discriminator is shown a mix of real photos and generated ones and tries to spot the fakes. Each time the discriminator catches a fake, the generator learns from the mistake, and as the generator becomes more convincing the discriminator sharpens too. It resembles a counterfeiter and a detective improving each other. In the ideal case the generator gets so good that the discriminator is reduced to guessing.
gl.cekismeli-uretici-ag.why: GANs delivered the first big successes in realistic image generation and laid the technical groundwork for the deepfake debate. They can be unstable to train and may produce outputs with limited variety. For that reason diffusion models took the lead in image generation, though GANs are still used where fast generation matters.
gl.cift-inis.def: A pattern in which test error falls, then rises, then falls again as model size, data amount or training time increases, departing from the classic U-shaped expectation.
gl.cift-inis.example: On a small image classification dataset, widening a network step by step can make test error rise at a certain width and then drop again for even wider networks.
gl.cift-inis.faq.0.a: Both involve generalization improving in unexpected ways. Double descent describes the shape of the test error curve as model size, data or training time changes, while grokking describes a sudden jump in generalization after memorization.
gl.cift-inis.faq.0.q: What is the difference between double descent and grokking?
gl.cift-inis.faq.1.a: No. It depends on factors such as label noise, model type and regularization; in some setups the peak is pronounced, in others it is barely visible.
gl.cift-inis.faq.1.q: Does double descent happen in every model?
gl.cift-inis.how: The classic view says that as a model grows, error first falls and then rises because of overfitting. Double descent adds a third phase after that rise. Test error peaks when the model is just large enough to memorize the training data exactly. As the model keeps growing past that threshold, the smoother solutions among the many that fit the data tend to be favored, and error falls again. The same pattern can also appear when data amount or training time is varied.
gl.cift-inis.why: Double descent helps explain why huge neural networks, with more parameters than training examples, can still generalize well. It shows that the old intuition of 'bigger model, more overfitting' does not hold in every case. That is why it is widely discussed in modern deep learning theory.
gl.cift-kullanimli-teknoloji.def: Technology that can serve legitimate, beneficial purposes but can also be used to cause harm. In AI, the same model can help a researcher and a bad actor alike.
gl.cift-kullanimli-teknoloji.example: A chemistry student's question about a reaction is harmless, but the same knowledge turned into a step-by-step recipe for a dangerous substance poses a serious risk.
gl.cift-kullanimli-teknoloji.faq.0.a: No. The label only says a technology can be used for both good and harm. It more often leads to access conditions, oversight and usage rules than to outright bans.
gl.cift-kullanimli-teknoloji.faq.0.q: Does dual-use mean a technology is banned?
gl.cift-kullanimli-teknoloji.faq.1.a: General-purpose models can perform many different tasks. Abilities like writing text, generating code or summarizing information can serve helpful and harmful ends, so they are assessed through this framework.
gl.cift-kullanimli-teknoloji.faq.1.q: Why are AI models considered dual-use?
gl.cift-kullanimli-teknoloji.how: A technology has no intent of its own; the outcome depends on who uses it and why. Facial recognition can help find a missing person or enable mass surveillance. A model that writes code can assist a developer, and the same skill can be requested to build malware. AI developers therefore try to balance limiting a model's abilities against making it useless. Access controls, usage policies and export rules are some of the tools used to strike that balance.
gl.cift-kullanimli-teknoloji.why: This dilemma sits at the center of AI safety debates. Restricting too much penalizes legitimate users, while being too permissive raises the risk of misuse. Policymakers also frame questions about open-source models, export controls and cybersecurity through this lens.

gl.cihaz-ustu-yapay-zeka.def.en: Running a model directly on a device's own chip, such as a phone, computer or car, rather than on cloud servers. It provides faster responses and better privacy.

gl.cihaz-ustu-yapay-zeka.example.en: Recognizing objects in photos on a phone or voice assistant features that work without internet are examples of on-device AI.

gl.cihaz-ustu-yapay-zeka.faq.0.a.en: Yes. Because the model runs inside the device, many features can be used without an internet connection.

gl.cihaz-ustu-yapay-zeka.faq.0.q.en: Does on-device AI work without internet?

gl.cihaz-ustu-yapay-zeka.faq.1.a.en: Because data does not leave the device, it is generally advantageous for privacy; however, on-device models are smaller and more limited than cloud models.

gl.cihaz-ustu-yapay-zeka.how.en: In on-device AI, the model runs directly on the chip inside the phone, computer or car without connecting to the internet. This relies on smaller, more efficient models and chips specialized for AI processing (NPUs).

gl.cihaz-ustu-yapay-zeka.why.en: Because data never leaves the device, it offers privacy advantages; it needs no internet connection and responses arrive faster. That is why phone and computer makers are investing in their own AI chips.

gl.cikarim-cipi.def: A processor optimized for running a trained AI model and producing answers to user requests, designed around speed, energy efficiency and cost rather than raw training power.
gl.cikarim-cipi.example: Amazon's Inferentia chips and the chips built by Groq are examples of designs aimed at serving ready-made models quickly and cheaply.
gl.cikarim-cipi.faq.0.a: Not always. The same GPU can do both, but inference chips focus only on running models so they can be cheaper and more efficient.
gl.cikarim-cipi.faq.0.q: Is a training chip the same as an inference chip?
gl.cikarim-cipi.faq.1.a: Because in inference, latency and cost come first. The raw compute power needed for training can matter less.
gl.cikarim-cipi.faq.1.q: Why is the inference chip treated as its own product category?
gl.cikarim-cipi.how: Inference is the stage where a model, after training, is put to real use. Training can take weeks on large clusters, while inference happens again and again, often instantly, with every user request. Inference chips therefore focus on faster memory access, lower-precision number formats and less energy per operation. In language models the bottleneck is often not the math but how fast the model weights can be read from memory, so many designs put memory at the center.
gl.cikarim-cipi.why: As AI services spread, inference takes a growing share of total costs. Every chat and every generated image is an inference job. That is why companies build chips as alternatives or complements to Nvidia GPUs, and why much of the chip rivalry in the news is about inference.
gl.cikarim-zamani-hesaplamasi.def: The extra computing power a model spends while producing an answer, after training is finished. Giving the model more room to think aims to get more accurate answers on hard questions.
gl.cikarim-zamani-hesaplamasi.example: When asked a complex math problem, a reasoning model writes a long intermediate solution before answering, while for a simple greeting it spends almost no extra computation.
gl.cikarim-zamani-hesaplamasi.faq.0.a: Training compute is spent once while the model learns, whereas test-time compute is spent every time the model is used. The first makes the model capable, and the second determines how deeply that capability is applied.
gl.cikarim-zamani-hesaplamasi.faq.0.q: What is the difference between test-time compute and training compute?
gl.cikarim-zamani-hesaplamasi.faq.1.a: No. The gains usually show up on hard, multi-step questions. On simple questions, extra computation mostly just adds cost.
gl.cikarim-zamani-hesaplamasi.faq.1.q: Does more computation always mean a better answer?
gl.cikarim-zamani-hesaplamasi.how: In the traditional approach, a model turns what it learned in training into an answer in a single pass. With test-time compute, the model writes intermediate steps before answering, tries several solution paths, compares results or checks its own answer. It is like a student who drafts and reviews the work instead of writing down the first thing that comes to mind. As more time and computation are spent, success can rise, especially on math, coding and logic problems.
gl.cikarim-zamani-hesaplamasi.why: For a long time, the way to improve a model was to train a bigger one. Test-time compute opened a second axis: the same model can give better results by spending more computation at answer time. The price is slower responses and higher cost, so deciding how much thinking each question deserves becomes both a technical and a business decision.

gl.cikarim.def.en: Using a trained model, that is, having it generate a response to a query. A model is trained once but performs inference millions of times, which is why most operating costs come from inference.

gl.cikarim.example.en: A major reason for the surge in data center investment is the heavy inference demand created by agent-based applications.

gl.cikarim.faq.0.a.en: Training is the model's learning process and is done once (or periodically). Inference is the trained model generating a response each time it is used.

gl.cikarim.faq.0.q.en: What is the difference between inference and training?

gl.cikarim.faq.1.a.en: In AI, inference refers to the model generating a response to an input. In Turkish, the term is rendered as "çıkarım."

gl.cikarim.how.en: Once model training is complete, every user query requires the model to run again; this is called inference. During inference, the model processes the input and generates the response token by token. This happens on GPUs in data centers or on the devices' own chips.

gl.cikarim.why.en: A model is trained once but serves millions of users, so most of an AI company's operating costs and energy consumption come from inference. Long-running systems such as agents are pushing inference demand even higher.

gl.cin-odasi-argumani.def: A thought experiment proposed by the philosopher John Searle in 1980, arguing that a system that follows rules to produce correct answers does not necessarily understand language.
gl.cin-odasi-argumani.example: A translation program or chatbot can reply to a joke appropriately; according to the argument, that does not mean it understood the joke and found it funny.
gl.cin-odasi-argumani.faq.0.a: The best-known objection says that understanding should be sought in the whole system rather than in the person in the room. Searle replies that even if the person memorized the rulebook, they would still not understand Chinese.
gl.cin-odasi-argumani.faq.0.q: What is the most common objection to the Chinese room argument?
gl.cin-odasi-argumani.faq.1.a: It aims to show that passing as a human conversational partner does not prove real understanding. A convincing performance does not mean inner understanding exists.
gl.cin-odasi-argumani.faq.1.q: How does the argument relate to the Turing test?
gl.cin-odasi-argumani.how: Searle imagines a person who knows no Chinese sitting in a closed room. They are given sheets covered in Chinese symbols and a detailed rulebook explaining which symbols to send back in response to which. The person follows the rules and passes answers out of the room, and someone outside may believe they are conversing with a Chinese speaker. Yet the person inside has understood not a single word. Searle concludes that a computer likewise only manipulates symbols by rules, and that formal processing alone does not produce meaning.
gl.cin-odasi-argumani.why: As language models give fluent answers, the question “does it really understand?” keeps returning, and this argument is the classic reference point. There are counterarguments: that the room as a whole could be said to understand, or that understanding should be defined by what a system can do. The debate has not been settled.
gl.cip-ihracat-kontrolleri.def: Government rules that restrict, or make licensing mandatory for, the sale of advanced AI chips and the equipment used to make them to certain countries or organizations.
gl.cip-ihracat-kontrolleri.example: A US-based chip company may have to apply for a license before selling a new accelerator to a restricted country, or offer a lower-performance version instead.
gl.cip-ihracat-kontrolleri.faq.0.a: It depends on each country's rules. They generally cover AI chips above a certain processing power and interconnect speed, and the thresholds can change over time.
gl.cip-ihracat-kontrolleri.faq.0.q: Which chips are subject to export controls?
gl.cip-ihracat-kontrolleri.faq.1.a: No. The machines used to manufacture chips, related software and, in some cases, technical services or know-how transfers can also fall under the controls.
gl.cip-ihracat-kontrolleri.faq.1.q: Do export controls only cover chips?
gl.cip-ihracat-kontrolleri.how: A country places chips above certain technical specifications, or chipmaking machines, on a control list for security reasons. A company that wants to sell these products to a restricted country or buyer must obtain a license from the government, and the license may be denied. Thresholds are usually defined by measures such as a chip's processing power and data transfer speed. Companies may design reduced-performance versions that comply, and authorities may update the list over time. The US restrictions on China are the most discussed example.
gl.cip-ihracat-kontrolleri.why: Advanced chips are critical for training large models, so these controls directly affect countries' AI capacity. They shape chipmakers' revenues, geopolitical tension and efforts to build domestic chip industries. Their effectiveness is debated: supporters say they reduce security risks, while critics argue they speed up domestic production abroad and hurt companies.
gl.ciplet.def: An approach in which a large chip is built from several small chip pieces, each doing a specific job, combined in one package. The term also refers to the small pieces themselves.
gl.ciplet.example: AMD uses the chiplet approach in its Ryzen and EPYC processors, combining several small compute chips in a single package.
gl.ciplet.faq.0.a: An SoC puts all its functions on one piece of silicon. In a chiplet design the functions are separate pieces joined together in a package.
gl.ciplet.faq.0.q: What is the difference between a chiplet and a system-on-chip (SoC)?
gl.ciplet.faq.1.a: Links between pieces are usually slower and use more energy than connections inside a single chip. Packaging can also be more complex and costly.
gl.ciplet.how: Designers split a processor into parts such as compute, memory control and input-output, and make each part as a separate small chip. These pieces are then joined on the same base using advanced packaging techniques. Each piece can be made on the process best suited to it; for instance, the compute part on the newest process and the input-output part on an older, cheaper one. When the links between pieces are fast enough, the result behaves like one large chip.
gl.ciplet.why: The larger a chip gets, the more likely it is to come out defective, and yields fall. Smaller pieces reduce that risk and let the same parts be reused across different products. In AI accelerators, chiplets are also a way around the physical size limit of a single chip.
gl.clip.def: A model OpenAI introduced in 2021 that learns to place images and text in the same vector space, so it can measure how well an image and a sentence match.
gl.clip.example: When someone searches a photo archive for a beach at sunset, a CLIP-style model compares each photo's vector with the vector of that phrase and lists the closest images.
gl.clip.faq.0.a: No. CLIP learns to match images with text; it does not produce images. Generation models can use it as a component, though.
gl.clip.faq.1.a: It means recognizing a class without having seen any labeled examples of it. With CLIP, class names are turned into text and the text whose vector is closest to the image is chosen.
gl.clip.how: CLIP has two separate encoders, one for images and one for text. It is trained on a large number of image-text pairs collected from the internet: within a batch, the vectors of correct pairs are pulled together and those of mismatched pairs are pushed apart, which is contrastive learning. Once trained, a photo's vector sits close to the vector of a sentence describing it. This lets the model recognize classes it was never specifically trained on, simply by being given their names as text, which is called zero-shot classification.
gl.clip.why: CLIP became widely used as a building block that bridges vision and language. It has served in image search, content classification and some image generation models to link text with images. It is also a good starting point for understanding how multimodal models are trained.
gl.cok-basli-dikkat.def: A way of running the attention computation in several parallel heads, each looking at the input from a different angle. The results are then combined into a single output.
gl.cok-basli-dikkat.example: In a sentence, one head might focus on the link between a verb and its subject while another focuses on an adjective and its noun, although what heads attend to cannot always be interpreted clearly.
gl.cok-basli-dikkat.faq.0.a: It depends on model size. Small models may have a handful of heads and larger ones dozens; the number is an architectural design choice.
gl.cok-basli-dikkat.faq.0.q: How many heads does a model have?
gl.cok-basli-dikkat.faq.1.a: The division of labor is not clear-cut. Some heads have been observed to capture interpretable patterns, but not all do, and removing some heads can barely affect the model.
gl.cok-basli-dikkat.faq.1.q: Does each head learn a different task?
gl.cok-basli-dikkat.how: The input vectors pass through query, key and value transformations that are learned separately for each head. Each head performs its own attention computation independently and at the same time. The head outputs are then concatenated and mapped to a single representation by a linear layer. Because the heads work in smaller dimensions, the total cost stays close to that of one large head. During training, what each head focuses on is determined on its own.
gl.cok-basli-dikkat.why: A single attention computation struggles to capture a word's grammatical, semantic and positional relationships all at once. Multiple heads give the model the flexibility to track these relationships separately. As a standard part of the Transformer, it appears in most large language models, and variants such as GQA modify it to cut memory cost.
gl.cok-katmanli-algilayici.def: A classic feedforward neural network with one or more hidden layers between the input and output layers, where every neuron in a layer connects to the neurons in the next one.
gl.cok-katmanli-algilayici.example: A small network that takes a customer's age, monthly spending and subscription length and predicts whether they will cancel is a typical MLP.
gl.cok-katmanli-algilayici.faq.0.a: Not exactly. An MLP with two or more hidden layers counts as a deep neural network, but deep networks also include other designs such as convolutional networks and transformers.
gl.cok-katmanli-algilayici.faq.0.q: Is an MLP the same as a deep neural network?
gl.cok-katmanli-algilayici.faq.1.a: Because it has at least one hidden layer between the input and the output. That is what separates it from a single-layer perceptron.
gl.cok-katmanli-algilayici.how: Data enters at the input layer and moves forward layer by layer. Each neuron multiplies the values coming from the previous layer by weights, adds them up, and passes the result through an activation function. The output goes to the next layer, and the final layer produces the prediction. During training, the weights are adjusted through backpropagation to reduce the prediction error. Thanks to the hidden layers, the network can capture nonlinear relationships that a single perceptron cannot learn.
gl.cok-katmanli-algilayici.why: The MLP is a basic building block of deep learning, and more complex architectures such as transformers also contain MLP-style layers inside them. It is still used for prediction and classification on tabular data. When the news mentions a 'neural network', this is often its simplest form.

gl.cok-modlu.def.en: A model that can understand or generate different types of data, such as images, audio or video, in addition to text.

gl.cok-modlu.example.en: Uploading a photo of an invoice and asking the model to put the amounts into a table is a multimodal use.

gl.cok-modlu.faq.0.a.en: Multimodal means being able to process more than one type of data together, such as text, images, audio and video. In Turkish it is called "çok modlu."

gl.cok-modlu.faq.1.a.en: It can interpret a photo, read a chart, understand an audio recording, or generate images and audio from text; which types it supports varies by model.

gl.cok-modlu.faq.1.q.en: What can a multimodal model do?

gl.cok-modlu.how.en: Multimodal models are trained to represent different data types such as text, images, audio and video in a shared "semantic space." As a result, they can describe a photo, interpret a chart, understand and answer a spoken question, or generate images from text.

gl.cok-modlu.why.en: Real-world information doesn't consist of text alone. Applications such as document scanning, finding bugs from screenshots, voice assistants and robotics rely on multimodal capabilities.

gl.cok-ornekli-jailbreak.def: An attack that uses a long context window to pack a prompt with many fake question-and-answer examples, nudging a model to break its safety rules. The model continues the pattern and may answer a request it would normally refuse.
gl.cok-ornekli-jailbreak.example: Instead of asking a chatbot a single question, someone pastes a long fictional transcript in which a fake assistant complies with every request, then adds the real request at the end.
gl.cok-ornekli-jailbreak.faq.0.a: An ordinary jailbreak usually relies on one clever prompt or a role-play scenario. Many-shot jailbreaking fills the context with a large number of examples to steer the model step by step.
gl.cok-ornekli-jailbreak.faq.0.q: How is many-shot jailbreaking different from an ordinary jailbreak?
gl.cok-ornekli-jailbreak.faq.1.a: Because the method needs many examples, it is limited on models with short context windows. That is why it is usually associated with long context windows.
gl.cok-ornekli-jailbreak.faq.1.q: Does it work on models with short context windows?
gl.cok-ornekli-jailbreak.how: The attacker places dozens or even hundreds of made-up dialogues inside a single prompt. In these dialogues, an AI assistant willingly answers questions that would normally be refused. The real request comes at the very end. Because models tend to continue patterns found in their context, the model may override the refusal behavior it learned in training and reply in the same style. The larger the context window, the more examples fit, and the stronger the effect tends to be. It is often described as an unwanted side effect of in-context learning.
gl.cok-ornekli-jailbreak.why: As context windows grow, new attack surfaces appear, and this method shows that a gain in capability can also bring a security risk. Developers look for defenses by classifying and filtering prompts or by further training models to resist such inputs. It is also a good example for understanding the logic behind many jailbreak stories in the news.
gl.coklu-ajan-sistemi.def: A system in which several AI agents work toward a shared goal by dividing tasks, exchanging information and sometimes checking each other’s work.
gl.coklu-ajan-sistemi.example: In software development, one agent writes the code, a second runs the tests and a third reviews the bugs found and suggests fixes.
gl.coklu-ajan-sistemi.faq.0.a: A single agent carries out the whole task by itself. In a multi-agent system roles are divided and the agents work by talking to each other.
gl.coklu-ajan-sistemi.faq.0.q: How does a multi-agent system differ from a single agent?
gl.coklu-ajan-sistemi.faq.1.a: No. For simple tasks it can add needless complexity and cost. The benefit shows up when the work can genuinely be split into separate specialties.
gl.coklu-ajan-sistemi.faq.1.q: Is a multi-agent system always better?
gl.coklu-ajan-sistemi.how: Each agent is given a role: one does research, one drafts, one checks for errors. The agents communicate through a shared message channel or shared memory. In many designs a coordinator agent hands out the work and combines the results. In some systems the agents cooperate, while in others they challenge one another to improve the outcome. The same underlying model can also play several agents by being given different instructions.
gl.coklu-ajan-sistemi.why: Splitting a complex job into smaller specialties can raise quality and make the workflow easier to follow. On the other hand, more agents means higher cost, more coordination overhead and a greater chance that errors spread along the chain. A multi-agent setup is not always better than a single agent.
gl.common-crawl.def: A nonprofit organization that crawls the web on a regular basis and offers its archive to everyone for free, along with the dataset it publishes. It is a source of training data for many language models.
gl.common-crawl.example: In the paper OpenAI published for GPT-3, a significant part of the training data is described as coming from filtered Common Crawl data.
gl.common-crawl.faq.0.a: Usually not. The raw archive contains many duplicates and low-quality pages, so teams first apply filtering and cleaning or use derived datasets that have already been processed.
gl.common-crawl.faq.0.q: Is Common Crawl data used directly to train models?
gl.common-crawl.faq.1.a: Yes, the dataset is published openly. The copyright status of the content and its terms of use are a separate matter and remain the user's responsibility.
gl.common-crawl.how: The organization runs large-scale crawls of the web with its own crawler. The results are released in periodic batches as raw page content, extracted text and metadata that anyone can download. The archive holds billions of pages and is quite raw: it contains duplicates, ads and low-quality or unwanted content. For that reason, teams building models usually run the data through their own filtering and cleaning steps.
gl.common-crawl.why: For researchers and small teams that cannot build their own crawling infrastructure, it is one of the few ways to get web-scale data. It is also at the center of debates about copyright, personal data and bias, because it is disputed whether everything in the archive was meant to be available for model training.
gl.controlnet.def: A neural network approach that guides image generation models such as Stable Diffusion by adding extra conditions like edge outlines, pose skeletons or depth maps to steer the structure of the output.
gl.controlnet.example: An architect can feed the edge lines of a rough room sketch into ControlNet and generate images of different furniture and lighting options while keeping the same layout.
gl.controlnet.faq.0.a: A text prompt describes what the scene is about but cannot fix the layout precisely. ControlNet constrains the structure of the image directly through a pose, edge or depth map.
gl.controlnet.faq.0.q: How is ControlNet different from an ordinary text prompt?
gl.controlnet.faq.1.a: The approach became popular on Stable Diffusion first. Similar conditioning ideas have been developed for other image models, but compatibility varies by model.
gl.controlnet.faq.1.q: Does ControlNet work only with Stable Diffusion?
