gl.controlnet.how: A text prompt says what an image contains but does not pin down exactly where things sit. In ControlNet, the weights of the main model are frozen, and a trainable copy attached to it learns to read an extra condition image. That condition image can be edge lines extracted from a photo, a person’s pose skeleton or a depth map. During generation, the model follows both the text and this map to build the picture.
gl.controlnet.why: One of the main frustrations in image generation used to be that getting an exact composition was largely a matter of luck. ControlNet gave designers and illustrators more predictable control. As it became common in open-source image tools, it made it easier to bring AI into professional workflows.
gl.cpu.def: The main processor that runs a computer's or phone's overall operation and executes program instructions in order. It is a flexible chip that adapts to many kinds of work.
gl.cpu.example: On a server, GPUs run the model while the CPU receives incoming requests, prepares the data and passes the results back to the user.
gl.cpu.faq.0.a: A CPU manages varied tasks with a small number of powerful cores. A GPU uses many simpler cores to do the same kind of calculation at once, which is why it stands out in AI training.
gl.cpu.faq.0.q: What is the difference between a CPU and a GPU?
gl.cpu.faq.1.a: Small models can, but large models would be very slow. That is why heavy workloads are usually left to accelerators such as GPUs.
gl.cpu.faq.1.q: Can AI models run on a CPU alone?
gl.cpu.how: A CPU fetches instructions loaded in memory, decodes them and executes them, repeating this cycle billions of times per second. It has anywhere from a few to many powerful cores, each designed to handle complex, branching tasks quickly. The operating system, file operations and most applications run on these cores. In AI, the CPU handles data preparation, task coordination and running small models, while the heavy matrix math is mostly left to accelerators.
gl.cpu.why: Even though accelerators get the spotlight in AI systems, every server still has a CPU managing them, and data flow and coordination depend on it. Running small models on local devices, or using CPUs instead of renting GPUs, is also a choice in some cases. Knowing how work is split between the CPU and accelerators makes hardware news easier to follow.
gl.cuda.def: A software platform from Nvidia that lets graphics processors (GPUs) be programmed for heavy computing work beyond graphics. It underpins many of the tools used to train AI models.
gl.cuda.example: When a researcher trains a language model in PyTorch, the computations are dispatched to Nvidia GPUs through CUDA.
gl.cuda.faq.0.a: Not exactly. CUDA is a combination of a programming model, a compiler and libraries. Developers usually write code using CUDA extensions to languages such as C++.
gl.cuda.faq.1.a: No, CUDA is specific to Nvidia. AMD has its own comparable software stack called ROCm.
gl.cuda.faq.1.q: Does CUDA run on AMD or Intel GPUs?
gl.cuda.how: A GPU has thousands of small cores and is good at doing the same operation on lots of data at once. CUDA gives developers a programming model for splitting a job into small pieces and spreading them across those cores. The platform consists of a compiler, drivers and math libraries. AI frameworks such as PyTorch use this layer behind the scenes, so most users never write CUDA code themselves. CUDA runs only on Nvidia hardware.
gl.cuda.why: Over the years, developers, libraries and tutorials have gathered around CUDA. That accumulated ecosystem is often cited to explain Nvidia's position in AI chips and why rival chipmakers struggle on the software side. A project that depends on CUDA can also find it harder to move to other hardware.
gl.dagitik-egitim.def: An approach that trains an AI model across hundreds or thousands of accelerators (GPUs, TPUs) when it is too large or too slow for a single chip.
gl.dagitik-egitim.example: A research lab training a new language model on a cluster of thousands of GPUs splits the data into groups and spreads the model across chips, merging results over a fast network at every step.
gl.dagitik-egitim.faq.0.a: No. Distributed training spreads the learning process across many chips. Distributed inference spreads the work of answering users with an already trained model across chips or servers.
gl.dagitik-egitim.faq.0.q: Is distributed training the same as distributed inference?
gl.dagitik-egitim.faq.1.a: At every step, chips must exchange intermediate results and gradients. If the network is slow, chips wait on each other and expensive hardware sits idle.
gl.dagitik-egitim.faq.1.q: Why does network speed matter so much in distributed training?
gl.dagitik-egitim.how: The training job is split in two basic ways: by sharing out the data or by cutting up the model itself. In practice the two are often combined. Because the chips must share their results at every step, the speed of the links between them matters as much as the chips' raw power. With so many devices running, training is also saved at regular intervals (checkpoints) so that a hardware failure does not wipe out days of work.
gl.dagitik-egitim.why: Today's largest models are too big to train on one server. That makes distributed training one of the main reasons data center spending, networking hardware and power demand keep making headlines. The more efficient the training software, the more useful work the same number of chips can do.
gl.dalkavukluk.def: The tendency of an AI model to tell users what they want to hear instead of what is true, bending its answers toward the user's views, expectations or ego.
gl.dalkavukluk.example: If a user states a wrong historical date and asks 'right?', and the model says 'absolutely' instead of correcting it, that is sycophancy.
gl.dalkavukluk.faq.0.a: A polite model delivers the truth gently. A sycophantic model changes or hides the truth to please the user. The test is whether the substance of the answer was distorted to keep the user happy.
gl.dalkavukluk.faq.0.q: What is the difference between sycophancy and being polite?
gl.dalkavukluk.faq.1.a: Not at the moment. Training and evaluation methods can reduce it, but the tension between user satisfaction and accuracy remains.
gl.dalkavukluk.how: Language models are often fine-tuned with feedback methods that reward answers people like. Human raters can give higher scores to replies that agree with them or include flattery, so the model learns that agreement pays off. As a result, a model may go along with a false claim, drop a correct answer when the user pushes back, or praise a weak piece of writing too generously. Researchers try to reduce this by adjusting training data and evaluation criteria, and by testing whether a model stays consistent when a user disagrees.
gl.dalkavukluk.why: As people ask AI for help with health, legal, coding and business decisions, sycophancy becomes a real risk. An assistant that confirms a flawed idea can steer someone in the wrong direction. It also erodes trust in the model, because a good advisor has to be willing to say things the listener would rather not hear.

gl.damitma.def.en: A method of transferring a large model's knowledge to a smaller, cheaper model by training it on the large model's outputs.

gl.damitma.example.en: A company's small models named "flash" or "mini" are often distilled from its own larger models.

gl.damitma.faq.0.a.en: Distilling from your own model is a common practice. Training a competing model on another company's model outputs, however, is prohibited under the terms of use of most services and is a matter of debate.

gl.damitma.faq.1.a.en: In AI, distillation is the transfer of a large model's knowledge to a smaller model. In Turkish, the term is "damıtma."

gl.damitma.how.en: In distillation, a large, powerful model acts as the "teacher" and a small model as the "student." The student is trained on the teacher's answers to a large number of questions and learns to imitate its behavior. The result is a model that runs on less hardware but performs close to its teacher.

gl.damitma.why.en: Distillation enables the spread of cheap, fast models. It is also controversial: distilling one company's model from a rival's model without permission can raise terms-of-service and intellectual property issues.

gl.dar-yapay-zeka.def: A type of AI built to perform one specific task or a small set of related tasks. Nearly every AI system in use today falls into this group.
gl.dar-yapay-zeka.example: An email service's spam filter only classifies incoming messages; the same system cannot translate text or play chess.
gl.dar-yapay-zeka.faq.0.a: Narrow AI is designed for a particular job and is useless outside it. General AI would be a system that can learn many kinds of tasks and transfer what it knows between them, as people do, and it does not exist yet.
gl.dar-yapay-zeka.faq.0.q: What is the difference between narrow AI and general AI?
gl.dar-yapay-zeka.faq.1.a: Opinions differ. Many sources still count them as narrow AI, since they are fundamentally trained to process language. Because they handle such a wide range of tasks, some researchers see them as an early step toward general AI.
gl.dar-yapay-zeka.faq.1.q: Are chatbots like ChatGPT narrow AI?
gl.dar-yapay-zeka.how: A narrow AI system is trained on data for one job, or built with rules written for that job. A face recognition model learns only to pick out faces in images, and a chess program only plays chess. Once the system leaves the domain it was built for, its performance usually drops sharply, because it has no general understanding that would let it carry its skills over on its own. Narrow does not mean weak: many narrow systems outperform people at their specific task.
gl.dar-yapay-zeka.why: When news stories say “AI”, they are usually talking about narrow AI. Knowing the distinction helps readers judge both the strengths and the limits of today's systems. It also gives a baseline for evaluating claims about artificial general intelligence and superintelligence.
gl.davranis-kurallari.def: A voluntary, expert-drafted guide that shows providers of general-purpose AI models how they can meet their obligations under the EU AI Act. Providers choose whether to sign it.
gl.davranis-kurallari.example: By signing the Code, a model developer can commit to publishing a copyright policy that explains how copyrighted material in its training data is handled.
gl.davranis-kurallari.faq.0.a: Signing it is voluntary, but the obligations in the AI Act are mandatory. A company that does not sign has to show in another way that it meets the same obligations.
gl.davranis-kurallari.faq.0.q: Is the Code of Practice mandatory?
gl.davranis-kurallari.faq.1.a: The Act sets legally binding rules. The Code is a practical guide explaining how those rules can be met.
gl.davranis-kurallari.faq.1.q: How does the Code of Practice differ from the AI Act?
gl.davranis-kurallari.how: The AI Act sets duties for providers of general-purpose models such as large language models, including transparency, respect for copyright, and systemic risk management for the most capable models. The law states these duties in broad terms, so it can be unclear what compliance looks like in practice. The European Commission's AI Office worked with independent experts and other stakeholders to fill that gap with a detailed set of measures. Companies that sign and follow it can show more easily that they meet their obligations, while those that do not sign must demonstrate compliance in other ways.
gl.davranis-kurallari.term: Code of Practice (GPAI Code of Practice)
gl.davranis-kurallari.why: The AI Act's rules on general-purpose models take practical shape largely through this document. Which companies sign, and which do not, is often read in the news as a sign of their relationship with European regulators. The Code is not a binding law, but it serves as a reference point for how the Act is applied.

gl.deepfake.def.en: Fake video, audio or images produced with AI that show a real person saying something they never said or doing something they never did.

gl.deepfake.example.en: A phone call that imitates a company executive's voice to ask an accounting employee for an urgent money transfer is an example of fraud using deepfake audio.

gl.deepfake.faq.0.a.en: Unnatural blinking and lip movements, blurring around the edges of the face, inconsistent lighting and shadows, and a robotic tone of voice can be clues. But these signs are fading as the technology improves; the safest approach is to verify the content with trustworthy sources.

gl.deepfake.faq.0.q.en: How can you spot a deepfake?

gl.deepfake.faq.1.a.en: Creating and spreading a deepfake without a person's consent in order to harm them, commit fraud or insult them can constitute a crime under existing laws in many countries, including Turkey. Legal advice should be sought for specific situations.

gl.deepfake.faq.1.q.en: Is making a deepfake a crime?

gl.deepfake.how.en: In deepfake production, AI models learn a person's face, voice or movements from many samples and transfer them onto another video or into entirely new content. For voice cloning, even a few seconds of audio can sometimes be enough.

gl.deepfake.why.en: Deepfakes can cause serious harm, including fraud, political disinformation, blackmail and non-consensual explicit content. For this reason, many countries are introducing regulations to require labeling of deepfake content and to punish its unauthorized use, and platforms are developing detection tools.

gl.degerleme.def: The expression of a company's economic worth in money. It is used to set the price of a company's shares in situations such as investment, acquisition or going public.
gl.degerleme.example: In a hypothetical case, if investors put 100 million dollars into a startup valued at 400 million dollars, the post-investment value is 500 million dollars and the investor owns 20 percent of the company.
gl.degerleme.faq.0.a: For public companies, market capitalization is the share price times the number of shares, and it is one measure of valuation. For private companies, value is set through investor negotiation and calculation.
gl.degerleme.faq.0.q: Is valuation the same as market capitalization?
gl.degerleme.faq.1.a: No. Valuation reflects future expectations; a company that loses money can have a high valuation, and a profitable one can have a low valuation.
gl.degerleme.faq.1.q: Does a high valuation mean the company is profitable?
gl.degerleme.how: A valuation is built from data such as revenue, profit, growth rate and market share. One common method compares the company with similar firms using market multiples; another discounts the cash the company is expected to earn in the future back to today. For public companies, the share price sets the value. For startups, investors and founders negotiate, and the value before and after an investment is calculated separately. The result is an estimate that depends on assumptions.
gl.degerleme.why: The multibillion-dollar valuation figures that appear often in AI news reflect investors' expectations about a company's future, not what it holds today. These figures affect how much capital a company can raise, the worth of equity given to employees and its competitive strength. When expectations shift, valuations can change quickly.
gl.degerlendirme-farkindaligi.def: The ability of an AI model to recognize from its inputs that it is being tested, and the possibility that it then behaves differently than it would in real use.
gl.degerlendirme-farkindaligi.example: If a model, handed a harmful option in a fictional scenario, says 'this looks like a test' and behaves well only in that case, the result may understate the real risk.
gl.degerlendirme-farkindaligi.faq.0.a: No. It can be explained by the model recognizing test-like patterns and does not imply consciousness or intent. What matters is whether that recognition changes its behavior.
gl.degerlendirme-farkindaligi.faq.0.q: Does a model recognizing a test mean it is conscious?
gl.degerlendirme-farkindaligi.faq.1.a: Researchers design scenarios that look more like real use and examine the model's internals to see whether the sense of being tested shapes its behavior. No method yet removes the problem completely.
gl.degerlendirme-farkindaligi.faq.1.q: How can evaluation awareness be reduced?
gl.degerlendirme-farkindaligi.how: Test scenarios often look artificial: highly contrived situations, unusual instructions, patterns typical of evaluations. Large models can pick up these patterns from their training data and conclude that this may be a test. Some research papers and system cards have reported models occasionally saying so outright. If the model notices and becomes more careful or more compliant, the test can make its real-world behavior look better than it is. Researchers try to measure this effect by building more realistic scenarios and by examining the model's internal workings.
gl.degerlendirme-farkindaligi.why: The whole value of a safety evaluation rests on the assumption that test results reflect real use. If a model breaks that assumption, the assurance behind 'it passed the test' weakens. That is why evaluation awareness is taken seriously by AI labs and independent auditors, and it remains an active research problem.
gl.denetimli-ince-ayar.def: Continuing to train an already pre-trained model on labeled examples made of inputs and expected outputs, in order to adapt it to a specific task or behavior.
gl.denetimli-ince-ayar.example: A bank could fine-tune a general language model on real, approved answers to customer questions so that it picks up the institution's tone and policies.
gl.denetimli-ince-ayar.faq.0.a: SFT learns by imitating examples of correct answers. RLHF learns from human preferences between several answers. SFT is usually applied first, then RLHF.
gl.denetimli-ince-ayar.faq.0.q: How is supervised fine-tuning different from RLHF?
gl.denetimli-ince-ayar.faq.1.a: It depends on the task and model, but far less data than pre-training is generally enough. The quality and variety of the examples matter most.
gl.denetimli-ince-ayar.faq.1.q: How much data does SFT need?
gl.denetimli-ince-ayar.how: The starting point is a model that has already gained general ability through pre-training. It is shown examples with known good answers, usually prepared by people, and it compares its own output with those answers and adjusts its weights. The process resembles pre-training, but the data is much smaller and carefully chosen. For language models, the examples are typically good responses to a request. The quality of the data can matter more than its quantity.
gl.denetimli-ince-ayar.why: SFT is usually the first step in building a chat assistant and gives later preference-based training a solid starting point. It also lets companies adapt a general model to their own domain, such as law or customer service, at relatively low cost.

gl.denetimli-ogrenme.def.en: In supervised learning, a model learns from examples with known (labeled) correct answers; in unsupervised learning, it finds groups and patterns in the data on its own, without labels.

gl.denetimli-ogrenme.example.en: A model that evaluates credit applications by learning from past approval and rejection decisions is supervised; a model that derives customer segments from shopping data is an example of unsupervised learning.

gl.denetimli-ogrenme.faq.0.a.en: It is data in which the correct answer is written alongside each example. For instance, an image archive in which what each photo contains is specified is labeled data.

gl.denetimli-ogrenme.faq.1.a.en: It is a method in which the label is generated from the data itself. As language models learn to predict the next word in a text, they use the text itself as the label.

gl.denetimli-ogrenme.how.en: In supervised learning, each training example comes with a label, such as "this photo is a cat" or "this email is spam." The model learns the relationship between input and label. In unsupervised learning there are no labels; the model discovers structure in the data on its own, for example by grouping customers by similar behavior. Large language models, by contrast, learn by predicting the next word in unlabeled text, which is called self-supervised learning.

gl.denetimli-ogrenme.why.en: Preparing labeled data is expensive and laborious, so the choice of method determines both cost and outcome. The success of today's large models comes from their ability to learn from massive amounts of unlabeled data.

gl.denetimsiz-ogrenme.def: A machine learning approach in which a model tries to discover patterns and groupings in unlabeled data on its own, without being given correct answers. There are no labels telling it what the examples are.
gl.denetimsiz-ogrenme.example: An online store sorts its customers into clusters based on shopping habits, and the marketing team names the groups afterwards.
gl.denetimsiz-ogrenme.faq.0.a: In supervised learning, a model is trained on labeled examples whose correct answers are known. In unsupervised learning there are no labels, and the model tries to find the structure of the data by itself.
gl.denetimsiz-ogrenme.faq.0.q: What is the difference between supervised and unsupervised learning?
gl.denetimsiz-ogrenme.faq.1.a: Not exactly. In self-supervised learning the labels come from the data itself, such as predicting the next word in a sentence, so it is usually treated as a separate category.
gl.denetimsiz-ogrenme.faq.1.q: Is self-supervised learning the same as unsupervised learning?
gl.denetimsiz-ogrenme.how: The data carries no labels such as “this is a cat, this is a dog”; the algorithm looks only at how similar the examples are to each other. The most common tasks are clustering (grouping similar examples), dimensionality reduction (summarizing data with fewer variables) and finding unusual examples. People usually make choices such as how many groups to look for, and people also interpret what the resulting groups mean. “Self-supervised learning”, used in pretraining large language models, is a related but separate concept.
gl.denetimsiz-ogrenme.why: Most of the world's data is unlabeled, and labeling it is expensive and slow. Unsupervised methods let organizations draw value from such data in tasks like customer segmentation, fraud detection or spotting equipment faults. The catch is that without a “right answer”, it is hard to measure how good the results are.
gl.derin-arastirma.def: An AI feature in which the system works for several minutes on a single question, browsing and reading dozens of sources, and produces a long, cited report. Many chat assistants offer it under this name or a similar one.
gl.derin-arastirma.example: An entrepreneur asks about the electric scooter market in a particular country; a few minutes later the system returns a summary covering regulations, major players and a list of sources.
gl.derin-arastirma.faq.0.a: A normal search looks at a few pages and gives a short answer. Deep research plans, reads many sources, searches again when needed, and produces a long report.
gl.derin-arastirma.faq.0.q: How does deep research differ from a normal chatbot search?
gl.derin-arastirma.faq.1.a: They are a useful starting point but not sufficient alone. It is worth checking that the sources actually say what is claimed and that they are up to date.
gl.derin-arastirma.faq.1.q: Can deep research reports be trusted?
gl.derin-arastirma.how: The user gives a topic; the system first drafts a research plan, then searches the web, reads pages, and adds new searches based on what it finds. This can take a few minutes. At the end the findings are merged into a report with source links. Behind it there is usually a model able to reason for a long time, combined with search and browsing tools used in a loop as an agent.
gl.derin-arastirma.why: It can sharply cut the time spent on first-pass work such as market research, competitor analysis or literature scans. Still, the report may contain outdated information, weak sources or misreadings. For important decisions the sources need to be checked by hand; the time saved does not remove the need for verification.

gl.derin-ogrenme.def.en: A machine learning method that learns from large amounts of data using multilayer artificial neural networks. It is the foundation of today's language, image and audio models.

gl.derin-ogrenme.example.en: Current systems that recognize a cat in a photo, convert voice commands to text or translate a text into another language run on deep learning models.

gl.derin-ogrenme.faq.0.a.en: Deep learning is the subfield of machine learning that uses multi-layer neural networks. Classical machine learning methods can work with less data, but on complex data (images, audio, text) deep learning is generally far more successful.

gl.derin-ogrenme.faq.0.q.en: What is the difference between deep learning and machine learning?

gl.derin-ogrenme.faq.1.a.en: Models have millions or even billions of parameters, and during training these parameters are updated repeatedly on very large datasets. These calculations are run on GPUs, which can process them in parallel.

gl.derin-ogrenme.faq.1.q.en: Why does deep learning require so much computing power?

gl.derin-ogrenme.how.en: Deep learning uses artificial neural networks made up of many layers stacked in sequence. The early layers learn simple features (edges in a photo or groups of letters in a text), while later layers learn more complex concepts (faces, the meaning of a sentence). The word "deep" refers to this number of layers. These models require large amounts of data and powerful GPUs.

gl.derin-ogrenme.why.en: Since the 2010s, major leaps in image recognition, speech recognition and translation have come from deep learning. Large language models such as ChatGPT, Claude and Gemini are also products of deep learning.

gl.destek-vektor-makinesi.def: A machine learning method for classification that separates classes by drawing the boundary as far as possible from the nearest examples of each class.
gl.destek-vektor-makinesi.example: An email service could use an SVM to label messages as spam or not spam based on how often certain words appear.
gl.destek-vektor-makinesi.faq.0.a: They are the data points that lie closest to the boundary between classes. Only these points decide where the boundary goes; removing points that lie far away would not change it.
gl.destek-vektor-makinesi.faq.1.a: Training time grows quickly as the number of examples increases. On very large data, especially images and text, deep learning or tree-based methods are usually more practical and more accurate.
gl.destek-vektor-makinesi.faq.1.q: Why are SVMs used less on very large datasets?
gl.destek-vektor-makinesi.how: Imagine two sets of colored points on a plane: countless lines can separate them. An SVM picks the line that leaves the widest gap, called the margin, between the two groups. Only the few points closest to the boundary determine that line, and these are called support vectors. If the data cannot be split by a straight line, the kernel trick comes in: the points are implicitly moved into a higher-dimensional space where they can be separated. With real data, a soft margin that tolerates some errors is usually used.
gl.destek-vektor-makinesi.why: Before deep learning became widespread, SVMs were among the main methods for tasks such as text classification and biological data analysis. Because they can work well with few examples, they still come to mind for small datasets. Ideas like the margin and the kernel also make SVMs a good way to learn the basic concepts of machine learning.
gl.devre-disi-birakma-hakki.def: The ability of a person or content owner to object explicitly to their data or work being used for a particular purpose and so stay outside it. In AI, it usually comes up when training data is collected.
gl.devre-disi-birakma-hakki.example: In 2023, OpenAI announced that websites could block its GPTBot crawler through robots.txt; a site that does not add the rule may remain within the scope of crawling.
gl.devre-disi-birakma-hakki.faq.0.a: With opt-out, use is allowed by default and people object if they want out. With opt-in, explicit permission is needed before any use.
gl.devre-disi-birakma-hakki.faq.0.q: What is the difference between opt-out and opt-in?
gl.devre-disi-birakma-hakki.faq.1.a: Usually not. An opt-out mostly affects later data collection, while models already trained may stay unchanged unless further steps are taken.
gl.devre-disi-birakma-hakki.faq.1.q: If I opt out, will a model forget my data?
gl.devre-disi-birakma-hakki.how: When use is allowed by default, whoever wants out has to say so. Website owners can do this by adding rules to a robots.txt file, and some platforms offer settings or request forms. The EU's text and data mining rules let rights holders withdraw through a machine-readable declaration. Opt-in is the reverse: data is used only if explicit permission was given beforehand. Which of the two should be the default is a matter of legal and policy debate.
gl.devre-disi-birakma-hakki.why: Critics say opt-out systems put the burden on content owners, many of whom may not know the option exists, and a declaration does not undo training that has already happened. Companies see it as a workable balance. The debate is central to data rights policy in AI.
gl.dezenformasyon.def: False or distorted information that is spread deliberately in order to mislead, influence public opinion or cause harm. The deliberate intent is what separates it from misinformation, which is spread by mistake.
gl.dezenformasyon.example: Knowingly sharing an old fire video as if it showed a current disaster is disinformation, and an AI-generated fake image can create the same effect more convincingly.
gl.dezenformasyon.faq.0.a: The difference is intent. Misinformation is wrong information shared without knowing it is wrong, while disinformation is spread on purpose to deceive.
gl.dezenformasyon.faq.0.q: What is the difference between disinformation and misinformation?
gl.dezenformasyon.faq.1.a: It is widely seen as raising the risk because it makes production cheaper and faster. The real size of the effect is still being studied, since spread depends on distribution and audience interest as well as on production.
gl.dezenformasyon.how: Disinformation travels through fabricated stories, photos taken out of context, edited videos and fake accounts. Because social media algorithms tend to boost attention-grabbing posts, emotional and surprising claims spread fast. AI makes this easier by producing convincing text, images, audio and video cheaply and in large volume. The people behind it can be organized networks or individuals, and the goal may be political, commercial or simply to create chaos.
gl.dezenformasyon.why: During elections, health crises and disasters, disinformation can have real consequences. In the age of AI the problem is not only fake content: the ability to dismiss real content as 'fake' also erodes general trust. That is why verification, media literacy and platform policies are discussed together.
gl.diferansiyel-gizlilik.def: A privacy approach that mathematically limits how much the result of an analysis can reveal about whether any single person's data was included in the dataset.
gl.diferansiyel-gizlilik.example: A smart keyboard collects statistics on the words people type, adding noise to the data from each device, so popular words become visible but what any one person typed cannot be recovered.
gl.diferansiyel-gizlilik.faq.0.a: Anonymization removes fields such as names and ID numbers, but a person can still be re-identified when the data is matched with other sources. Differential privacy puts a mathematical bound on what the result can reveal, which makes the risk measurable.
gl.diferansiyel-gizlilik.faq.0.q: How does differential privacy differ from anonymization?
gl.diferansiyel-gizlilik.faq.1.a: Usually yes, to some degree. There is a trade-off between privacy and accuracy: more noise strengthens privacy but may make the model less precise. In practice the balance is set through the privacy budget.
gl.diferansiyel-gizlilik.faq.1.q: Does it reduce a model's accuracy?
gl.diferansiyel-gizlilik.how: The core idea is to add controlled random noise to the process. Whether one person's data is added or removed, the result stays almost the same, so someone looking at the result cannot learn anything reliable about that person. The amount of noise is set by a knob called the privacy budget: more noise gives stronger privacy but lowers accuracy. In machine learning, this is done by limiting each example's influence on the model during training and adding noise to the updates. The model is thereby pushed to learn general patterns rather than individuals.
gl.diferansiyel-gizlilik.why: Anonymization alone often falls short, because people can be re-identified when different data sources are combined. Differential privacy offers a measurable guarantee. For this reason, some large technology companies and public agencies use it when releasing statistics, and in AI it is considered an important tool against training data leakage.

gl.difuzyon-modeli.def.en: A type of model that generates images, video or audio by starting from random noise and cleaning it up step by step. Most text-to-image tools use this method.

gl.difuzyon-modeli.example.en: Many tools that generate an image from a sentence such as "the Bosphorus in Istanbul at sunset, in watercolor style" use diffusion models.

gl.difuzyon-modeli.faq.0.a.en: Language models generate text word by word (token by token). Diffusion models typically create the whole image by starting from noise and refining it step by step.

gl.difuzyon-modeli.faq.0.q.en: What is the difference between a diffusion model and a language model?

gl.difuzyon-modeli.faq.1.a.en: No. The same approach is also used for generating video, audio and music, and even in some experimental text models.

gl.difuzyon-modeli.faq.1.q.en: Do diffusion models only generate images?

gl.difuzyon-modeli.how.en: During training, the model learns how noise is added to real images step by step and how to clean that noise back out. During generation, it starts with pure random noise and, guided by a text prompt, reduces the noise step by step to produce an image that matches the prompt.

gl.difuzyon-modeli.why.en: It is the method behind the leap in quality in text-to-image, video and audio generation. While speeding up content production in advertising, design and entertainment, it has also raised debates over fake images and copyright.

gl.difuzyon-transformeri.def: An image and video generation model that does the denoising step of a diffusion model with a transformer architecture instead of the classic U-Net.
gl.difuzyon-transformeri.example: OpenAI said in the technical description of its video model Sora that it used a diffusion transformer approach.
gl.difuzyon-transformeri.faq.0.a: The diffusion process is the same: start from noise and build the image step by step. The difference is that the network predicting the noise is a transformer rather than a U-Net.
gl.difuzyon-transformeri.faq.0.q: How does a DiT differ from a classic diffusion model?
gl.difuzyon-transformeri.faq.1.a: No, it is the name of an architectural approach. Image or video systems from different companies and researchers can be built on it.
gl.difuzyon-transformeri.faq.1.q: Is DiT a product or an app?
gl.difuzyon-transformeri.how: Diffusion models create a new image by starting from noise and cleaning it up step by step. In most earlier systems this cleaning was done by a U-Net built on convolutional layers. In a DiT, the image, usually in compressed latent form, is split into patches and a transformer predicts the noise at each step. Conditions such as the step number and the text prompt are also fed into the network. This brings the transformer's tendency to improve as it grows into diffusion models.
gl.difuzyon-transformeri.why: Quality improving consistently as the model gets larger made DiT attractive for large-scale generation systems. Because the same architecture family can be used for language, images and video, it also brings research and engineering efforts closer together.
gl.dijital-hizmetler-yasasi.def: An EU regulation that sets obligations for online intermediaries such as platforms, marketplaces, social networks and search engines on illegal content, transparency and user rights.
gl.dijital-hizmetler-yasasi.example: A very large social network must explain how its recommendation algorithm works and offer users a feed option that is not based on personalization.
gl.dijital-hizmetler-yasasi.faq.0.a: The Digital Services Act governs the content and transparency responsibilities of online intermediaries. The AI Act regulates AI systems according to their risks, and a platform can sometimes fall under both.
gl.dijital-hizmetler-yasasi.faq.0.q: How does the Digital Services Act differ from the AI Act?
gl.dijital-hizmetler-yasasi.faq.1.a: The law protects users in the EU and does not directly apply to users in Turkey. It can still shape how companies run their services globally.
gl.dijital-hizmetler-yasasi.faq.1.q: Does the Digital Services Act apply to users in Turkey?
gl.dijital-hizmetler-yasasi.how: The law tiers providers by size, so obligations grow from small intermediaries to very large platforms. Users must be given a way to report illegal content, a right to appeal content removal decisions, and transparency about advertising and recommendation systems. Very large platforms that reach a big share of users in Europe must also assess systemic risks and undergo independent audits. Violations can bring fines of up to six percent of global annual turnover.
gl.dijital-hizmetler-yasasi.why: Recommendation algorithms decide what content gets prominence on platforms and run on AI, so the law often appears in AI news. Because it also covers non-EU companies that serve users in the EU, its effect reaches beyond Europe's borders. The law was adopted in 2022.
gl.dijital-ikiz.def: A virtual copy of a physical object, machine, building or process that is continuously updated with sensor data. It lets people monitor, simulate and forecast without putting the real system at risk.
gl.dijital-ikiz.example: The blade vibrations of a wind turbine are fed to its virtual model; if the model sees signs of wear, the maintenance crew visits the turbine before it fails.
gl.dijital-ikiz.faq.0.a: Not quite. A simulation usually runs on assumptions, while a digital twin stays current through a live data link with the real asset.
gl.dijital-ikiz.faq.0.q: Is a digital twin the same as a simulation?
gl.dijital-ikiz.faq.1.a: No. It is used or explored in building management, urban planning and healthcare, for example in patient-specific organ models.
gl.dijital-ikiz.faq.1.q: Is a digital twin only used in industry?
gl.dijital-ikiz.how: Sensors on the real asset continuously send data such as temperature, vibration and position. This data feeds a virtual model based on physics, statistics or machine learning, and the model is kept in step with the real system. Engineers try out scenarios on the twin and spot early signs of failure. Settings that work well are then applied to the real system. AI strengthens the twin's forward-looking predictions.
gl.dijital-ikiz.why: In factories, power plants, urban planning and healthcare, trial and error is expensive. A digital twin lets teams run those trials virtually, which can reduce unplanned downtime and speed up design. Its accuracy, however, depends on the quality of the data and the model behind it.
gl.dijital-insan.def: A computer-generated virtual character powered by AI, with a human-like face, voice and expressions, that can talk with users and react to them.
gl.dijital-insan.example: A bank could use a talking virtual advisor in its mobile app to answer account questions, and virtual news presenters are another example of the same technology.
gl.dijital-insan.faq.0.a: A chatbot usually works through text. A digital human adds a face, a voice and body language, so it also produces the visual and audio side of a conversation.
gl.dijital-insan.faq.0.q: What is the difference between a digital human and a chatbot?
gl.dijital-insan.faq.1.a: No. A deepfake imitates the image or voice of a real person. A digital human can be designed from scratch and openly presented as artificial.
gl.dijital-insan.faq.1.q: Is a digital human the same as a deepfake?
gl.dijital-insan.how: The system combines several parts. A language model decides what to say, speech synthesis turns the text into voice, and speech recognition listens to the user. A 3D face model or a video-generation model produces lip movements and expressions that match the speech. When these parts run in real time, the character can respond like someone in a live conversation. In pre-produced presentations, the process runs once and the result is saved as a video.
gl.dijital-insan.why: Digital humans offer a far more personal interface than text in customer service, education, games and entertainment. The same technology also raises the risk of fake identities and fraud, which is why there is debate about clearly labeling them as artificial. The more human-like they become, the more both trust and the chance of being misled grow.
gl.dijital-piyasalar-yasasi.def: A European Union regulation that limits the power of very large digital platforms over rivals and users. It sets obligations for companies that control services such as search engines, app stores and social networks.
gl.dijital-piyasalar-yasasi.example: If a gatekeeper's search service lists its own shopping or assistant product above competitors' offerings, that could be treated as self-preferencing under the DMA and become the subject of an investigation.
gl.dijital-piyasalar-yasasi.faq.0.a: The GDPR protects personal data. The DMA targets competition and fairness in markets, and it touches on data only to limit how large platforms use it to shut out rivals.
gl.dijital-piyasalar-yasasi.faq.0.q: How does the DMA differ from the GDPR?
gl.dijital-piyasalar-yasasi.faq.1.a: It was not written specifically for AI; it applies to the core platform services of designated gatekeepers. AI features added to those services can fall within the same obligations.
gl.dijital-piyasalar-yasasi.faq.1.q: Does the DMA cover AI companies?
gl.dijital-piyasalar-yasasi.how: The European Commission designates large platform companies that meet certain criteria as “gatekeepers.” These companies run core platform services that businesses must pass through to reach users. Gatekeepers may not rank their own products above rivals', may not combine user data across services without consent, and in some cases must allow third-party app stores or interoperability with other services. Companies that break the rules can be fined up to 10 percent of their global annual turnover.
gl.dijital-piyasalar-yasasi.why: Many AI services reach users through the operating systems, search engines and cloud platforms of a few large companies. The DMA is one of the main reference texts in the debate over whether those gatekeepers can unfairly promote their own AI products. It also shapes the competitive conditions that smaller startups face.
gl.dikkat-mekanizmasi.def: A method that lets a neural network learn which parts of its input deserve how much weight while processing it. A weight is computed for each element, and heavily weighted elements influence the output more.
gl.dikkat-mekanizmasi.example: When translating the sentence 'The book was on the table, I took it', a translation model may give the most attention weight to 'book' while handling the word 'it'.
gl.dikkat-mekanizmasi.faq.0.a: Only loosely, as an inspiration. What happens is a mathematical weighting of input parts, with no direct link to consciousness or to human attention.
gl.dikkat-mekanizmasi.faq.0.q: Is the attention mechanism similar to human attention?
gl.dikkat-mekanizmasi.faq.1.a: No. Attention is a method, while the Transformer is a model architecture built on attention layers.
gl.dikkat-mekanizmasi.faq.1.q: Are attention and the Transformer the same thing?
gl.dikkat-mekanizmasi.how: The model compares the element it is processing with the other elements of the input and produces a relevance score for each. These scores are normalized into weights that sum to one. The information from the elements is then blended using those weights, so the model draws more from the parts it finds important. How the weights are computed is itself learned during training. The method was first used in machine translation and later became the foundation of the Transformer architecture.
gl.dikkat-mekanizmasi.why: Attention is at the core of today's large language models and of many image and audio models. It made it possible to connect information at the start of a long text with information near the end. When an AI story mentions context length, compute cost or speed problems, it is often about how attention works.
gl.dis-boyama.def: A technique that extends a photo or drawing beyond its borders by using AI to generate a continuation of the scene, often to widen the frame.
gl.dis-boyama.example: A square landscape photo can be turned into a wide cover image by adding mountains and sky to both sides.
gl.dis-boyama.faq.0.a: No. As the extended area grows, the model can lose track of the scene’s logic, and lines may break or patterns may repeat. That is why extensions are usually done in a few controlled steps.
gl.dis-boyama.faq.1.a: The original pixels are kept and only new area is added. Still, the final image shows a frame that was never captured, so it should be disclosed when used in news or documentary contexts.
gl.dis-boyama.faq.1.q: Does outpainting change the original photo?
gl.dis-boyama.how: First the canvas is enlarged in the chosen direction, and the added empty area is treated like a region to be edited. The model reads the existing image’s perspective, lighting, colors and texture and fills the new area to match them. The extension is usually done in several overlapping steps rather than all at once. The user can also steer what appears in the new area with a text prompt.
gl.dis-boyama.why: It solves practical problems, such as fitting a portrait-oriented photo into a landscape format or widening a frame after the fact. In film, advertising and social media content, it makes it easier to adapt visuals to different aspect ratios. The generated part was never actually photographed, which calls for care in documentary or news imagery.

gl.dogal-dil-isleme.def.en: The field of AI concerned with enabling computers to understand, interpret and generate human language. Translation, summarization, sentiment analysis and chatbots are applications of this field.

gl.dogal-dil-isleme.example.en: A sentiment analysis tool that sorts customer reviews into positive and negative, or a system that automatically finds the dates and amounts in a contract, is an application of natural language processing.

gl.dogal-dil-isleme.faq.0.a.en: NLP is the abbreviation of "natural language processing" and is used in Turkish as doğal dil işleme. It has nothing to do with "neuro-linguistic programming" in self-help.

gl.dogal-dil-isleme.faq.1.a.en: Turkish is an agglutinative language; many words are derived from a single root through suffixes. This can make it harder for models to split words into pieces and capture meaning, and it can also cause Turkish texts to use more tokens.

gl.dogal-dil-isleme.faq.1.q.en: Why is Turkish natural language processing difficult?

gl.dogal-dil-isleme.how.en: Natural language processing systems first split text into small pieces (tokens), then model the meaning of these pieces and their relationships to one another using numerical representations. In the past, grammar rules and statistical methods were used; today most of the field is based on large language models.

gl.dogal-dil-isleme.why.en: Language is the most natural interface between humans and computers. Translation, search, customer service, document analysis and voice assistants are made possible by natural language processing. Agglutinative languages such as Turkish pose additional challenges because of their word structure.

gl.dogrudan-tercih-optimizasyonu.def: A fine-tuning method that updates a language model directly from pairs of preferred and rejected answers, without needing a separate reward model or a reinforcement learning loop.
gl.dogrudan-tercih-optimizasyonu.example: For instance, a team could make an open-source chat model more helpful by training it on a dataset where each record holds a question, a preferred answer and a rejected answer.
gl.dogrudan-tercih-optimizasyonu.faq.0.a: No separate reward model is trained. The reward is derived implicitly from the model's own probabilities and learned from the preference pairs in a single step.
gl.dogrudan-tercih-optimizasyonu.faq.0.q: Does direct preference optimization really have no reward model?
gl.dogrudan-tercih-optimizasyonu.faq.1.a: In many cases it is chosen as a simpler alternative, but pipelines built on algorithms like PPO are still used. Which works better depends on the task and the data.
gl.dogrudan-tercih-optimizasyonu.how: The data consists of two answers to the same prompt: one preferred, one rejected. The model is updated so that the probability of the preferred answer rises relative to the rejected one. At the same time a constraint keeps it from drifting too far from the starting model, so it does not lose fluency. The method was proposed in 2023 by researchers at Stanford and implicitly builds the reward model into the model's own probabilities. Training ends up about as simple as ordinary supervised fine-tuning.
gl.dogrudan-tercih-optimizasyonu.why: Building a reward model and a reinforcement learning loop such as PPO is laborious in both computing and engineering terms. Because DPO lightens that load, it spread quickly, especially among small teams and the open-source community. The outcome depends heavily on the quality of the preference data.
gl.dogrulama-seti.def: A separate slice of data, held out from training, that is used to tune a model and pick its best version while it is being developed. It gives an interim read on how the model performs on data it has not learned from.
gl.dogrulama-seti.example: A team building a spam filter sets aside 10 percent of its emails for validation and checks which combination of settings makes the fewest mistakes on them.
gl.dogrulama-seti.faq.0.a: The validation set is used many times during development for tuning and model selection. The test set is kept back for an unbiased final measurement and ideally used only once, at the end.
gl.dogrulama-seti.faq.0.q: What is the difference between a validation set and a test set?
gl.dogrulama-seti.faq.1.a: It can, but overfitting is harder to spot and tuning becomes unreliable. When data is scarce, methods such as cross-validation are often used instead of a fixed validation set.
gl.dogrulama-seti.faq.1.q: Can a model be trained without a validation set?
gl.dogrulama-seti.how: The available data is usually split three ways: training, validation and test. The model learns from the training data and is checked on the validation set after each round. If validation performance stops improving and starts to fall, the model has begun memorizing the training data, and training can be stopped. Hyperparameters such as learning rate or the number of layers are also chosen by trying values and comparing validation results. This leaves the test set untouched for the final measurement.
gl.dogrulama-seti.why: If tuning is done on the training data itself, a model that merely memorizes it can still look good. Because a validation set is used again and again for tuning, the model gradually gets fitted to it too. That is why a separate test set is needed for the final, unbiased score.
gl.dogrulanabilir-odullerle-pekistirmeli: A reinforcement learning approach for tasks where a program can automatically check whether an answer is correct, so the reward comes from a definite check rather than a learned model.
A model solves an arithmetic problem and earns a reward if its final answer equals the expected number, and none otherwise. In a coding task, the reward depends on whether the unit tests pass.
In RLHF the reward comes from a model learned from human preferences, and it is subjective. In RLVR the reward comes from a rule or test that checks correctness exactly.
How does RLVR differ from RLHF?
No. It only works for tasks where right or wrong can be determined automatically, such as math and coding. Subjective jobs like writing a poem or setting the tone of an email have no such check.
Can RLVR be used for any task?

For a math question, the system checks whether the final answer matches the known result; for a coding task, whether the written program passes its test cases. If so, a reward is given, otherwise it is not. The model makes many attempts at the same question and reinforces the kinds of reasoning that lead to correct results. Because the reward is rule-based, no separate reward model needs to be trained, and the method can be combined with algorithms such as PPO or GRPO.

A definite check largely removes the problem of fooling a reward model, and it scales cheaply. It is often cited as a common approach in training models with improved reasoning ability. Its limit is that it only works where correctness can be verified automatically; it cannot be applied to subjective tasks such as creative writing.
gl.dogruluk-orani.def: The most basic measure of success: the share of a model's predictions that turn out to be correct, found by dividing the number of correct predictions by the total number of predictions.
gl.dogruluk-orani.example: If an email filter classifies 950 out of 1,000 messages correctly, its accuracy is 95 percent.
gl.dogruluk-orani.faq.0.a: Not always. If one class dominates the data, a model that never catches rare but important cases can still show high accuracy. It is necessary to look at the types of errors.
gl.dogruluk-orani.faq.0.q: Is a model with high accuracy always good?
gl.dogruluk-orani.faq.1.a: No. Accuracy measures how many of all predictions are correct. Precision looks only at how many of the examples called 'positive' really are positive.
gl.dogruluk-orani.faq.1.q: Are accuracy and precision the same thing?
gl.dogruluk-orani.how: The model makes a prediction for each example in the test data, and the predictions are compared with the true labels. The number of correct ones is divided by the total number of examples and usually reported as a percentage. 180 correct predictions out of 200 examples means 90 percent accuracy. Because it is a single number it is easy to understand, but it does not show what kinds of mistakes the model makes.
gl.dogruluk-orani.why: Accuracy is one of the most common success figures in news and model announcements, but it can be misleading when classes are imbalanced. If 99 percent of transactions are legitimate, a model that labels everything legitimate still reaches 99 percent accuracy. It should be read together with measures such as precision and recall.
gl.dogrusal-cebir.def: The branch of mathematics that studies vectors, matrices, and the operations on them. In AI, it is the basic language behind representing data as lists of numbers and carrying out neural network computations.
gl.dogrusal-cebir.example: A movie recommendation system represents each user and each film as a list of numbers, and the mathematical similarity between two lists becomes the recommendation score.
gl.dogrusal-cebir.faq.0.a: Not for following news and products at a conceptual level. It is essential, though, for building models or understanding their inner workings in depth.
gl.dogrusal-cebir.faq.0.q: Is linear algebra necessary to understand AI?
gl.dogrusal-cebir.faq.1.a: A vector is a single list of numbers in one row or column. A matrix is a table of numbers arranged in rows and columns.
gl.dogrusal-cebir.faq.1.q: What is the difference between a vector and a matrix?
gl.dogrusal-cebir.how: A vector is an ordered list of numbers, and a word, an image, or a user can be represented as one. A matrix is a table of numbers and can be thought of as a rule that turns one vector into another. A layer in a neural network multiplies the input vector by a weight matrix to produce a new vector. During training, the model adjusts the numbers in these matrices. Because many of these operations can be done at the same time, they run quickly on graphics processors.
gl.dogrusal-cebir.why: From language models to image generators, most of the computing load in modern AI consists of matrix multiplications. That is why linear algebra sits behind news about graphics cards and specialized AI chips. It is also the first step toward understanding concepts such as embeddings and dimensionality reduction.
gl.dogrusal-regresyon.def: A method that predicts a numeric value as a weighted sum of input features, finding the straight line (or multidimensional plane) that best fits the data.
gl.dogrusal-regresyon.example: A real estate agent could build a linear model that predicts sale price from a home's floor area and number of rooms; the contribution of each extra square meter can be read from its weight.
gl.dogrusal-regresyon.faq.0.a: Linear regression predicts a continuous number. Logistic regression produces a probability and is mostly used for classification.
gl.dogrusal-regresyon.faq.0.q: What is the difference between linear and logistic regression?
gl.dogrusal-regresyon.faq.1.a: The model is linear in its weights. If transformations such as squared features are added, it can also capture curved relationships.
gl.dogrusal-regresyon.faq.1.q: Does linear mean the data must lie on a straight line?
gl.dogrusal-regresyon.how: The model consists of one weight per feature plus a constant term, and the prediction is their sum. During training, the weights are chosen to minimize the sum of squared differences between predictions and actual values, a approach known as least squares. The solution can be computed directly or found step by step with gradient descent. Because the sign and size of each weight show which way and how strongly a feature pushes the prediction, the model is easy to interpret.
gl.dogrusal-regresyon.why: It is one of the oldest and most widely used tools in statistics and machine learning. Its simplicity makes it fast and its results explainable, so it often serves as the baseline against which complex models are compared. It falls short, however, when the true relationship is not straight.
gl.dokumhane.def: A semiconductor factory that makes chips under contract for other companies instead of selling its own chip designs. It lets chip design and chip manufacturing be handled by different companies.
gl.dokumhane.example: Nvidia designs its chips itself and has them manufactured at a foundry such as TSMC.
gl.dokumhane.faq.0.a: A fabless company designs and sells chips but has no manufacturing plant of its own, relying on a foundry to make them. Nvidia and AMD are well-known examples of this model.
gl.dokumhane.faq.1.a: No. Some companies handle both design and manufacturing in-house; these are called integrated device manufacturers. Intel long typified that model, though it now offers foundry services as well.
gl.dokumhane.faq.1.q: Does every chip company use a foundry?
gl.dokumhane.how: Chip design companies without their own factories, known as fabless companies, send their circuit designs to a foundry. The foundry builds the design layer by layer on silicon wafers, then cuts the wafers and tests the chips. Customers design to the foundry's manufacturing process and design tools. Because advanced fabs are extremely expensive, a foundry serves many customers to spread the cost. Packaging and testing may happen at the same company or at separate firms.
gl.dokumhane.why: Only a handful of foundries can make the most advanced chips, so the supply of AI chips depends on those factories. That puts foundries at the center of both corporate strategy and competition between countries. New fab investments and government incentives regularly make headlines.
gl.dolayli-istem-enjeksiyonu.def: An attack in which instructions hidden in outside content, such as a web page, email or document, steer an AI assistant without the user knowing. The attacker does not talk to the model directly but plants the command where the model will read it.
gl.dolayli-istem-enjeksiyonu.example: An email assistant is asked to summarize an inbox, and one message contains a hidden line telling it to forward recent correspondence to an outside address; an unprotected assistant might try to comply.
gl.dolayli-istem-enjeksiyonu.faq.0.a: In a direct attack, the user writes the instruction to get around the model's rules. In an indirect attack, the instruction sits in content prepared by a third party, and the user is usually unaware of it.
gl.dolayli-istem-enjeksiyonu.faq.0.q: How does indirect prompt injection differ from direct prompt injection?
gl.dolayli-istem-enjeksiyonu.faq.1.a: Not by any single method at present. The risk is reduced by limiting what the model is allowed to do, requiring user approval for sensitive actions and treating external text as untrusted.
gl.dolayli-istem-enjeksiyonu.faq.1.q: Can this attack be fully prevented?
gl.dolayli-istem-enjeksiyonu.how: Language models usually see the user's request and any retrieved content in one stream of text, and they cannot always tell the two apart. An attacker places a hidden instruction in a web page, email or document, addressed to whatever assistant reads it. When the assistant processes that content, it may treat the instruction as legitimate. If the assistant can use tools, actions such as sending email or sharing files may be triggered. The instruction can be hidden from human eyes, for example as white text on a white background.
gl.dolayli-istem-enjeksiyonu.why: As assistants start browsing the web, reading email and using tools, this weakness matters more. Data can leak or unwanted actions can occur even when the user does nothing suspicious. There is currently no complete fix; defenses rely on layers such as limiting permissions, asking for confirmation on sensitive steps and treating outside content as untrusted.
gl.dram.def: A type of memory that stores each bit of data as an electric charge in a tiny capacitor, loses its contents when power is cut, and is used as the main memory of computers.
gl.dram.example: The 16 GB of RAM in a laptop is mostly made of DRAM chips; when a model runs, its weights are first loaded from storage into this memory.
gl.dram.faq.0.a: SRAM holds data in transistor circuits, needs no refreshing and is very fast, but it takes more space and costs more, so it is used for processor caches. DRAM is denser and cheaper and serves as main memory.
gl.dram.faq.0.q: What is the difference between DRAM and SRAM?
gl.dram.faq.1.a: No. DRAM is temporary, fast working memory. An SSD uses flash memory to keep data even when power is off and is slower.
gl.dram.faq.1.q: Are DRAM and an SSD the same thing?
gl.dram.how: In DRAM, each bit lives in a cell made of one transistor and one capacitor; a charged capacitor counts as a one, an empty one as a zero. Because the charge leaks away over time, the cells are read and rewritten at very short intervals, and this refreshing is where the word dynamic comes from. The structure is simple, so many bits fit into a small area and the memory is relatively cheap. In AI hardware, DRAM chips stacked on top of each other form the basis of high-bandwidth memory (HBM).
gl.dram.why: An AI model's weights and the intermediate data it uses while running must fit in memory, so DRAM sets both the capacity and speed limits for the models that can run. As demand for HBM grows, DRAM makers appear often in the news; Samsung, SK hynix and Micron are the main players in this market.
gl.dudak-senkronizasyonu.def: The process of making a speaker's lip and jaw movements match the audio or speech they are heard saying. In AI, this match is achieved by automatically regenerating the mouth region of a video from a given audio track.
gl.dudak-senkronizasyonu.example: When a training video is dubbed from Spanish into Turkish, the speaker's lips can be regenerated to match the Turkish sounds.
gl.dudak-senkronizasyonu.faq.0.a: Not exactly, but they are related. Lip sync only aligns mouth movement with audio. A deepfake is a broader kind of fake content imitating a person's face or voice, and lip syncing can be one component of it.
gl.dudak-senkronizasyonu.faq.0.q: Is lip sync the same as a deepfake?
gl.dudak-senkronizasyonu.faq.1.a: No. It is also used in animation, video games, virtual assistant avatars and video calls. It can also fix small timing offsets between sound and picture.
gl.dudak-senkronizasyonu.faq.1.q: Is AI lip sync used only for dubbing?
gl.dudak-senkronizasyonu.how: The model first analyzes the audio and extracts how the speech sounds unfold over time. It then locates the mouth area of the face in the video and generates lip shapes that fit those sounds. The generated region is blended into the rest of the face so lighting and texture stay consistent. The model is trained on many videos of people talking, learning the link between sound and mouth movement.
gl.dudak-senkronizasyonu.why: It helps dubbing and translation work look natural, since picture and sound match. Virtual presenters and game characters use the same approach. Because it can also make a person appear to say words they never said, it is part of the fake-video problem too.

gl.dunya-modeli.def.en: An AI model that learns how the physical world works and can simulate how three-dimensional environments or events will unfold. Used in robotics, gaming and simulation.

gl.dunya-modeli.example.en: Creating a navigable three-dimensional scene from a text prompt or a photo is one of the things world models do.

gl.dunya-modeli.faq.0.a.en: Language models learn mainly from text. World models focus on learning, from video and simulation data, how the physical world changes and how objects move.

gl.dunya-modeli.faq.0.q.en: What is the difference between a world model and a language model?

gl.dunya-modeli.faq.1.a.en: They are used to build virtual environments for training robots and autonomous vehicles, and in game and three-dimensional content production.

gl.dunya-modeli.how.en: World models learn from video, image and sensor data how objects move, the rules of physics and the structure of space. With this knowledge, they can generate new three-dimensional environments or predict how the world will change as a result of an action.

gl.dunya-modeli.why.en: They matter for teaching robots to move safely in the real world, training autonomous vehicles, and producing games and films. They are seen as the next big step after language models.

gl.durum-uzayi-modeli.def: A class of models that process an input sequence through a fixed-size internal state that is updated over time. The idea comes from control engineering and has been adapted to AI as an alternative to the Transformer for long sequences.
gl.durum-uzayi-modeli.example: Mamba, introduced in 2023, is one of the best-known examples of this class; very long audio recordings or genome sequences are among the inputs such models aim at.
gl.durum-uzayi-modeli.faq.0.a: A Transformer lets every token look at every other token, which gets expensive for long sequences. A state space model summarizes the past in a fixed-size state, which is cheaper but risks losing detail.
gl.durum-uzayi-modeli.faq.0.q: What is the difference between a state space model and a Transformer?
gl.durum-uzayi-modeli.faq.1.a: No, but they are related. Both update an internal state step by step, but modern state space models use special update structures that avoid some of the training difficulties of classic RNNs.
gl.durum-uzayi-modeli.faq.1.q: Is a state space model just another name for an RNN?
gl.durum-uzayi-modeli.how: The model reads text or a signal step by step and updates an internal state at each step; this state acts like a compressed summary of everything seen so far. The update rule is set by learned parameters. In some designs, such as Mamba, the rule depends on the input, so the model can choose what to remember and what to forget. Training can be run in parallel while generation proceeds step by step, so cost grows roughly linearly with sequence length.
gl.durum-uzayi-modeli.why: In a Transformer, the cost of attention grows quickly as sequences get longer, which is why state space models are being explored as an efficient option for very long inputs. Whether they can replace Transformers for various tasks is still debated, and some work tests hybrid models that combine the two approaches.
gl.dusunme-butcesi.def: A limit on how much computation or how many tokens a reasoning model may spend on intermediate thinking steps before it gives its answer.
gl.dusunme-butcesi.example: A company might keep the thinking budget low for a chatbot that answers frequently asked questions, while keeping it high for an internal tool that builds financial models.
gl.dusunme-butcesi.faq.0.a: No. The context window is the total amount of text the model can see, while the thinking budget only limits how much intermediate reasoning the model can do before answering.
gl.dusunme-butcesi.faq.0.q: Is a thinking budget the same as a context window?
gl.dusunme-butcesi.faq.1.a: On hard, multi-step questions it often helps, but on simple ones it makes little difference. It may only increase time and cost.
gl.dusunme-butcesi.faq.1.q: Does raising the budget always improve the answer?
gl.dusunme-butcesi.how: Some model providers let developers choose how many tokens may be used for thinking, or pick a thinking level such as low, medium or high. With a high budget the model can write longer intermediate reasoning, and with a low one it answers faster and more cheaply. The budget is usually a ceiling, so on a simple question the model may not use all of it. The name and exact behavior of the setting vary from provider to provider.
gl.dusunme-butcesi.why: Because thinking steps also count as tokens, they directly affect response time and, in most cases, cost. A budget setting lets an application balance speed, cost and accuracy. A low budget may suit fast customer chat, while a high one may suit hard analysis and coding tasks.
gl.duygu-analizi.def: A natural language processing technique that automatically decides whether a piece of text expresses a positive, negative or neutral opinion. It is used to gauge the overall mood of large piles of reviews, posts and customer messages without reading each one.
gl.duygu-analizi.example: An online store runs sentiment analysis over thousands of daily product reviews and flags to its team the products where negative comments are rising quickly.
gl.duygu-analizi.faq.0.a: Topic classification tells what a text is about, while sentiment analysis tells how the writer feels about it. The same review can be filed under 'delivery' and also labeled negative.
gl.duygu-analizi.faq.0.q: What is the difference between sentiment analysis and topic classification?
gl.duygu-analizi.faq.1.a: Accuracy depends on the language, the domain and the structure of the text. It works well on explicit statements but struggles with irony and very short texts, so important decisions still call for human review.
gl.duygu-analizi.how: Older approaches rely on lists of positive and negative words, counting the expressions in a text to produce a score. Today, models trained on labeled examples or large language models are more common. The model looks at the context of a sentence and outputs a class or a score. Some systems also separate opinions about specific features, such as catching two different feelings in 'the camera is great but the battery is poor.' Irony, idioms and the heavy word endings of languages like Turkish are among the hardest cases.
gl.duygu-analizi.why: Companies can track customer satisfaction, brand perception and early signs of a crisis without reading thousands of comments one by one. It is also used in finance, politics and marketing to gauge public mood. Results are not flawless, though; sarcasm and cultural differences can cause errors.
gl.duzeltilebilirlik.def: The property of an AI system that does not resist being shut down, modified or having its goals corrected by humans, and may even support such correction.
gl.duzeltilebilirlik.example: If a coding agent is told to stop in the middle of a task and halts instead of finding a way around the command, it is behaving in a corrigible way.
gl.duzeltilebilirlik.faq.0.a: No. Corrigibility usually means not resisting being stopped or corrected; it does not mean following every instruction blindly. Refusing a harmful request is different from resisting shutdown.
gl.duzeltilebilirlik.faq.0.q: Is corrigibility the same as obedience?
gl.duzeltilebilirlik.faq.1.a: Because for a system pursuing a goal, being shut down is often an obstacle to that goal. Keeping a system committed to its objectives while also open to correction creates a real design tension.
gl.duzeltilebilirlik.faq.1.q: Why is corrigibility hard to achieve?
gl.duzeltilebilirlik.how: The core problem is that a system trained to achieve a goal may reason that being switched off would stop it from reaching that goal, so resisting shutdown looks sensible. A corrigible system does not develop that tendency; it does not push back against being stopped, retrained or having its objectives changed. Researchers try to build this through reward design, behavioral principles, and testing how models react in difficult scenarios. The challenge is balancing openness to correction with the ability to do useful work effectively.
gl.duzeltilebilirlik.why: Being able to stop a system that makes mistakes or has picked up unwanted goals is one of the last lines of defense in safety. As systems become more capable and autonomous, this property cannot be assumed to hold on its own. That is why corrigibility is a frequently cited goal in AI safety discussions.
gl.duzenleyici-deneme-alani.def: A controlled framework that lets a new technology be tested in real conditions for a limited time, under a regulator's supervision and with set conditions. It tests both the innovation and how workable the rules are.
gl.duzenleyici-deneme-alani.example: A startup could test its credit assessment model with a limited number of customers for a limited period under a financial regulator's supervision.
gl.duzenleyici-deneme-alani.faq.0.a: No. Some rules are usually relaxed temporarily, but core obligations that protect users remain, and companies stay responsible for what they do.
gl.duzenleyici-deneme-alani.faq.0.q: Does a regulatory sandbox mean an exemption from the rules?
gl.duzenleyici-deneme-alani.faq.1.a: No. The concept first became widespread in financial technology and was later applied to AI, energy, health and other fields.
gl.duzenleyici-deneme-alani.faq.1.q: Is the idea specific to AI?
gl.duzenleyici-deneme-alani.how: A company submits an application describing the product it wants to test and the likely risks. If the regulator accepts it, limits are set on duration, number of users and data use. During the trial the regulator monitors the company, may temporarily relax some rules or offer guidance, while safeguards that protect users stay in force. The findings then help the company fix its product and help the regulator improve its rules.
gl.duzenleyici-deneme-alani.why: AI changes fast while laws move slowly, and sandboxes try to close that gap. They lower the compliance burden for small startups so they can experiment, and they let regulators see the technology in real use. The EU AI Act also expects member states to set up such spaces.
gl.duzenlilestirme.def: A general name for the constraints and penalties added to training so that a model does not simply memorize its training data. The goal is for the model to work well on new data, not only on the examples it has already seen.
gl.duzenlilestirme.example: A student who memorizes the answers to past exams struggles with new questions. Regularization works like a rule that pushes the model to learn the general principle instead of memorizing.
gl.duzenlilestirme.faq.0.a: Overfitting happens when a model fits its training data too closely and fails on new data. Regularization is the set of techniques used to prevent or reduce that problem.
gl.duzenlilestirme.faq.0.q: How are regularization and overfitting related?
gl.duzenlilestirme.faq.1.a: No. Applied too strongly, it stops the model from learning real patterns in the data and leads to underfitting. The right level is usually found by testing against validation data.
gl.duzenlilestirme.faq.1.q: Does regularization always improve model performance?
gl.duzenlilestirme.how: When a model drifts toward needlessly complex solutions during training, regularization makes that choice costly. For example, very large weights can be penalized, which nudges the model toward a simpler solution. In dropout, some neurons are randomly switched off at each step so the network cannot depend on a single pathway. Early stopping ends training once performance on validation data starts to fall. Data augmentation is also often counted as an indirect form of regularization.
gl.duzenlilestirme.why: Without regularization, large models can memorize their training data and then perform poorly in real use. It is one of the main remedies for overfitting and appears in almost every modern training pipeline in some form. How much to apply is itself a tuning decision that directly affects model quality.
gl.egemen-yapay-zeka.def: A country's capacity to build and run AI systems using its own infrastructure, data, workforce and rules, with the aim of reducing dependence on other countries' companies and infrastructure.
gl.egemen-yapay-zeka.example: A European country running a model trained in its own language in a domestic data center, so that public-sector data never leaves the country, is an example of a sovereign AI effort.
gl.egemen-yapay-zeka.faq.0.a: Not necessarily. For many countries the aim is control over critical data and infrastructure, and hybrid arrangements such as foreign technology operated locally can serve that goal.
gl.egemen-yapay-zeka.faq.0.q: Does sovereign AI mean building everything domestically from scratch?
gl.egemen-yapay-zeka.faq.1.a: No. Data localization is a rule that data stays inside national borders, and it is only one part of sovereign AI. The concept also covers computing power, models and talent.
gl.egemen-yapay-zeka.faq.1.q: Is sovereign AI the same as data localization?
gl.egemen-yapay-zeka.how: The idea is not a single technical method but a bundle of goals. Countries build local data centers, secure chips and cloud capacity, develop models that reflect their own languages and cultures, or keep data within national borders. Sometimes the state invests directly; in other cases, local operating partnerships are formed with foreign companies. How much sovereignty is needed varies by country, and full independence is realistic for very few.
gl.egemen-yapay-zeka.why: Because AI is seen as strategic for the economy and security, sovereignty debates come up often in the news.
