On one side are arguments about data privacy, national security and language diversity; on the other, counterarguments about high costs and the efficiency of global cooperation.
gl.egitim-kesme-tarihi.def: The last point in time covered by a model's training data. The model has no knowledge from training about events that happened after that date.
gl.egitim-kesme-tarihi.example: A model may not know about a new version of a software library released after its cutoff and may suggest the old way of using it.
gl.egitim-kesme-tarihi.faq.0.a: Not always. Models often estimate their cutoff as earlier than it really is. For reliable information, the model documentation published by the company is a better source.
gl.egitim-kesme-tarihi.faq.0.q: Can a model state its own training cutoff accurately?
gl.egitim-kesme-tarihi.faq.1.a: It matters less but does not disappear. Search can bring in current information, but the model's general knowledge and judgment still rest on its training data.
gl.egitim-kesme-tarihi.faq.1.q: Does the cutoff stop mattering for models with web search?
gl.egitim-kesme-tarihi.how: Before a model is trained, data is collected up to a certain date. Because training, testing and safety work can take months, the model is released well after its cutoff. It can learn about later events only from context given to it in writing or from a connected search tool. Since data from the most recent period is relatively sparse, models often guess their own cutoff to be earlier than it really is.
gl.egitim-kesme-tarihi.why: If a model presents old information as current, it can give wrong answers. For current news, new laws or new versions of software libraries, answers need to be verified. Knowing the cutoff helps in understanding which questions a model needs a tool such as web search to handle.
gl.egitim-sonrasi-asama.def: All the training steps applied after pre-training to turn a raw model into a helpful, safe assistant that follows instructions.
gl.egitim-sonrasi-asama.example: A pre-trained language model may simply continue a sentence that begins “The capital of France”. After post-training, it behaves like an assistant and answers the question directly with “Paris”.
gl.egitim-sonrasi-asama.faq.0.a: Not exactly. Fine-tuning is one part of post-training. The stage also includes preference-based training, safety work, and other adjustments.
gl.egitim-sonrasi-asama.faq.0.q: Is post-training the same as fine-tuning?
gl.egitim-sonrasi-asama.faq.1.a: Most knowledge and capability comes from pre-training. Post-training shapes how the model uses those abilities, what format it answers in, and which limits it follows.
gl.egitim-sonrasi-asama.faq.1.q: Does a model's knowledge come from pre-training or post-training?
gl.egitim-sonrasi-asama.how: A pre-trained model is good at continuing text but is not ready to answer questions. Post-training usually begins with supervised fine-tuning on example prompts and responses, followed by preference-based training using feedback from humans or other AI systems. Safety testing, tone and format tuning, and tool-use skills can also be part of this stage. It needs far less data and computation than pre-training, but it largely determines how the model behaves toward users.
gl.egitim-sonrasi-asama.why: The behavior users actually see, including politeness, safety limits, and answer style, is shaped largely at this stage. It is also what allows different products to be built from the same base model. When news reports say a model's behavior has changed, post-training is often what is meant.
gl.egitim-verisi-sizintisi.def: The exposure of personal, confidential or copyrighted content from a model's training data through the model's outputs. The model may reproduce some examples it learned almost word for word.
gl.egitim-verisi-sizintisi.example: If a company fine-tunes a model on customer support conversations and the model later gives another user a customer's home address word for word, that is training data leakage.
gl.egitim-verisi-sizintisi.faq.0.a: No. Most models learn by generalizing. But some examples, especially frequently repeated ones, can be memorized, so the risk is never treated as zero.
gl.egitim-verisi-sizintisi.faq.0.q: Does every model memorize its training data?
gl.egitim-verisi-sizintisi.faq.1.a: No. Data contamination is when test data accidentally ends up in the training set and inflates evaluation results. Training data leakage is a privacy problem: content from training shows up in the model's outputs.
gl.egitim-verisi-sizintisi.faq.1.q: Is training data leakage the same as data contamination?
gl.egitim-verisi-sizintisi.how: Large models mostly generalize, but they can memorize some examples, especially ones that appear many times in the data or are very distinctive. With the right prompt, the model may bring these pieces up in its output. An attacker may try specially crafted prompts to surface memorized text. A method called membership inference tries to guess whether a particular record was used in training. Countermeasures include reducing duplicates in the data, removing personal information, applying differential privacy and filtering outputs.
gl.egitim-verisi-sizintisi.why: Training data can contain personal data, trade secrets or copyrighted material, and its leaking into outputs creates both privacy and trust problems. The risk is more concrete for models that companies fine-tune on their own internal data. The legal side of the issue is still being worked out alongside debates on personal data protection and copyright.

gl.egitim-verisi.def.en: The collection of text, images, audio or numerical data used for an AI model to learn from. A model's knowledge and its errors largely come from this data.

gl.egitim-verisi.example.en: The scarcity of Turkish content in training data can cause a model to be weaker in Turkish writing and cultural knowledge than in English.

gl.egitim-verisi.faq.0.a.en: That depends on the policy of the service you use and your account settings. Many services offer an option to opt out of having chats used for training; on enterprise accounts, data is generally not used for training by default.

gl.egitim-verisi.faq.0.q.en: Are AI models trained on what I write?

gl.egitim-verisi.faq.1.a.en: It is the last date up to which a model's training data was collected. The model cannot know about events after that date unless it is supported by a tool such as web search.

gl.egitim-verisi.how.en: Language models are trained on very large datasets compiled from web pages, books, code repositories and other text sources. The data is first cleaned: duplicates, low-quality pages and harmful content are filtered out. In later stages, the model is given smaller but carefully prepared sample conversations and tasks.

gl.egitim-verisi.why.en: What a model knows, how well it performs in which language and which biases it carries depend largely on its training data. The use of copyrighted content without permission is also the main subject of lawsuits filed against AI companies.

gl.egitim.def.en: The process of adjusting a model's parameters by running it on large datasets. It is a very expensive process that can take thousands of GPUs and weeks.

gl.egitim.example.en: The training cost of a new frontier model is estimated to reach hundreds of millions of dollars.

gl.egitim.faq.0.a.en: Small models can be trained in hours; training the largest models can take weeks or months on thousands of chips.

gl.egitim.faq.0.q.en: How long does it take to train an AI model?

gl.egitim.faq.1.a.en: In pre-training, the model learns language from a very large body of general data. In post-training (such as fine-tuning and reinforcement learning), it is turned into a helpful, safe assistant that follows instructions.

gl.egitim.how.en: In model training, the model is run repeatedly on a massive dataset; at each step the error of its prediction is measured and its parameters are updated to reduce that error. Training large models requires thousands of GPUs working together for weeks or even months. Additional stages such as fine-tuning and safety training follow.

gl.egitim.why.en: Training is the most expensive stage of developing the most powerful models and can be done only by a few companies with access to large capital and data centers. A significant share of chip and energy demand comes from it.

gl.eksik-ogrenme.def: A situation where a model fails to capture even the basic patterns in its training data, so it performs poorly both on training data and on new data. The model is usually too simple or has not been trained long enough.
gl.eksik-ogrenme.example: A house-price model that looks only at floor area ignores factors such as location and building age, so it predicts badly both on its training data and on new homes.
gl.eksik-ogrenme.faq.0.a: An underfit model has not learned the patterns in the data and does poorly everywhere. An overfit model has memorized its training data, so it does well there but poorly on new data.
gl.eksik-ogrenme.faq.0.q: What is the difference between underfitting and overfitting?
gl.eksik-ogrenme.faq.1.a: If both training error and validation error stay high and barely improve as training continues, underfitting is the likely cause.
gl.eksik-ogrenme.how: If a model lacks the capacity to express the relationships in the data, or if training stops too early, its error stays high on both training and test data. A linear model asked to trace a curved relationship has to settle for a straight line. The telltale sign is poor performance even on the training data, whereas overfitting shows high training performance and low performance on new data. Fixes include a larger model, longer training, more informative input features, or less regularization.
gl.eksik-ogrenme.why: Underfitting is one of the first things to check when a model does not deliver the expected results. Telling it apart from overfitting helps choose the right remedy. It also shows when making a model bigger is actually justified.
gl.elektrik-sebekesi-kapasitesi.def: The maximum amount of power an electricity transmission and distribution network can carry at a given point, and one of the main limits on whether a new data center can be connected.
gl.elektrik-sebekesi-kapasitesi.example: A company may find suitable land and enough chips for a data center, but if the local substation lacks capacity, the facility may have to wait until grid upgrades are finished.
gl.elektrik-sebekesi-kapasitesi.faq.0.a: No. Generation capacity is the power plants can produce. Grid capacity is how much of that power can be carried through lines and transformers to a given location, so a bottleneck can occur even where generation is plentiful.
gl.elektrik-sebekesi-kapasitesi.faq.0.q: Is grid capacity the same as power generation capacity?
gl.elektrik-sebekesi-kapasitesi.faq.1.a: On-site generation can shorten the wait if a grid connection is delayed. It comes with its own challenges, such as permits, fuel supply and cost.
gl.elektrik-sebekesi-kapasitesi.faq.1.q: Why do data centers sometimes want to build their own power generation?
gl.elektrik-sebekesi-kapasitesi.how: The grid includes power plants, lines, substations and distribution equipment, and each part can carry only so much power. When a large customer asks to connect, the operator studies whether the lines and transformers at that point can handle the extra load. If capacity falls short, new lines, transformers or generation must be added, and such investments can take years. As a result, connection requests are often placed in a queue.
gl.elektrik-sebekesi-kapasitesi.why: AI data centers can ask for hundreds of megawatts, and in some regions that demand can outpace how fast the grid grows. Even with chips in hand, a facility cannot operate if its power connection is delayed. For this reason, the state of the grid is often as decisive as land and cooling when choosing where to build a data center.
gl.en-cok-olabilirlik-tahmini.def: An estimation method that picks the model parameters that make the observed data as probable as possible. In short, it looks for the setting that best explains the data.
gl.en-cok-olabilirlik-tahmini.example: In language model training, the model is asked to give the highest possible probability to the word that actually comes next in the training text, which is the same as increasing the likelihood.
gl.en-cok-olabilirlik-tahmini.faq.0.a: In probability, the parameter is fixed and the data varies: if a coin is fair, how likely are seven heads in ten tosses? In likelihood, the data is fixed and the parameter varies: given this data, which heads probability fits best?
gl.en-cok-olabilirlik-tahmini.faq.0.q: What is the difference between likelihood and probability?
gl.en-cok-olabilirlik-tahmini.faq.1.a: When the prior treats all values as equally plausible, the peak of the posterior coincides with the maximum likelihood estimate. When there is real prior information, the result is shaped by it and the two methods diverge.
gl.en-cok-olabilirlik-tahmini.faq.1.q: How does maximum likelihood estimation relate to Bayesian inference?
gl.en-cok-olabilirlik-tahmini.how: A model assigns a probability to each data point, given its parameters. The combined probability of all the data is called the likelihood. The method searches for the parameter values that maximize it. In practice, logarithms are taken instead of products, because working with sums is easier and avoids numerical underflow. The peak is usually found with gradient descent. In a coin-flip example, if seven of ten tosses land heads, the heads probability that maximizes the likelihood is 70 percent.
gl.en-cok-olabilirlik-tahmini.why: Much of AI model training rests on this principle, often implicitly. The loss function language models use when predicting the next word is in fact the negative log-likelihood. The method's limits are that it can overfit with little data and does not account for prior knowledge.
gl.endustriyel-robot-ve-cobot.def: Industrial robots are programmable arms that perform repetitive factory tasks quickly and with great force. A collaborative robot, or cobot, is designed with safety features so it can share a workspace with people.
gl.endustriyel-robot-ve-cobot.example: The large caged arm welding car bodies in a factory is an industrial robot, while a small arm beside a worker on an assembly line, holding parts or driving screws, is a cobot.
gl.endustriyel-robot-ve-cobot.faq.0.a: The main difference is how they work with people. An industrial robot is usually separated from humans by safety barriers, while a cobot is built with sensors and limited force so it can operate in the same space.
gl.endustriyel-robot-ve-cobot.faq.0.q: What is the main difference between a cobot and an industrial robot?
gl.endustriyel-robot-ve-cobot.faq.1.a: Cobots are designed to meet safety standards, but safety also depends on the tool they carry and the task they perform. A cobot holding a sharp tool, for example, still needs its own risk assessment.
gl.endustriyel-robot-ve-cobot.how: A traditional industrial robot repeats pre-programmed motions with high speed and precision. Because it can be dangerous to people, it usually works behind safety cages or barriers. Cobots move with lower speed and force, and use force and torque sensors to stop when they detect contact or a collision. They are often easy to teach: a worker guides the arm by hand to show the motion. Cameras and AI help both types recognize objects and adapt to changing tasks.
gl.endustriyel-robot-ve-cobot.why: Cobots make automation accessible to small and mid-sized businesses without a large upfront investment. Robots working side by side with people also raise questions about workplace safety, workforce change and employment. As AI-equipped robots appear often in the news, knowing the difference between the two types is useful.
gl.entropi.def: In information theory, a measure of the uncertainty, or amount of surprise, in a probability distribution. The less predictable the outcomes, the higher the entropy.
gl.entropi.example: Decision tree algorithms can branch on whichever feature splits a dataset so that the mixing of classes, that is, the entropy, drops the most.
gl.entropi.faq.0.a: Not the same, but closely related. Physical entropy is linked to the number of possible microstates of a system, and the formulas look similar. Information entropy measures the uncertainty of a probability distribution.
gl.entropi.faq.0.q: Is information-theoretic entropy the same as entropy in physics?
gl.entropi.faq.1.a: It depends on the context. In a classifier, high entropy means the model is unsure. In creative text generation, some entropy is wanted to get variety.
gl.entropi.faq.1.q: Is high entropy good or bad?
gl.entropi.how: In information theory, every event carries a degree of surprise: a rare event carries a lot of information and a common one carries little. Entropy is the average of that surprise, weighted by the probabilities. A fair coin flip, where both outcomes are equally likely, is the most uncertain case and each toss carries one bit of information. A coin that always lands heads holds no surprise and has zero entropy. Entropy also gives the lower bound on how many bits, on average, are needed to encode a source's output.
gl.entropi.why: Entropy underlies loss functions in machine learning and the splitting criteria used in decision trees. It also summarizes how confident a model is in its predictions. In language models, sampling settings indirectly change the entropy of the output distribution.
gl.epok.def: One complete pass of the entire training dataset through the model. It is the unit used to measure how many rounds training has run, and training usually spans many of them.
gl.epok.example: If a handwritten digit recognition model is trained for 20 epochs, it has seen the same training images 20 times.
gl.epok.faq.0.a: An iteration is a single update made with one batch. An epoch is one full pass over all the data, so one epoch consists of as many iterations as there are batches.
gl.epok.faq.0.q: What is the difference between an epoch and an iteration?
gl.epok.faq.1.a: There is no fixed number; it depends on the data and the model. Usually teams watch performance on validation data and stop once it stops improving.
gl.epok.how: The dataset is usually split into batches, and the model updates its parameters after each batch. When every batch has been processed, one epoch is complete. For example, with 10,000 examples and batches of 100, one epoch means 100 updates. Training often runs for many epochs, and the data is usually reshuffled each round. Too few epochs and the model has not learned enough; too many and it starts to memorize the training data.
gl.epok.why: The number of epochs directly shapes training time and cost, and it is tied to the risk of overfitting. For very large language models the data is so big that seeing it once or a few times can be enough, so people talk about steps or the amount of data seen rather than epochs.
gl.erken-durdurma.def: A method that ends training once performance on validation data stops improving, helping to keep a model from memorizing its training data. It is a simple regularization technique against overfitting.
gl.erken-durdurma.example: In a customer review classifier, if validation loss reaches its lowest value at epoch 12 and does not improve over the next five epochs, training is stopped and the weights from epoch 12 are kept.
gl.erken-durdurma.faq.0.a: No, it only reduces the risk. Other causes, such as too little data or an overly complex model, can also lead to overfitting, so it is often combined with other regularization methods.
gl.erken-durdurma.faq.0.q: Does early stopping completely prevent overfitting?
gl.erken-durdurma.faq.1.a: It is the setting that says how many more epochs to wait without improvement in validation performance. If it is too small, training may stop too early; if it is too large, the method loses much of its benefit.
gl.erken-durdurma.how: During training, the model is evaluated after each epoch on validation data that is not used for learning. If the training loss keeps falling while the validation loss stops improving and starts to rise, the model is beginning to memorize. Teams usually set a value called patience; if no improvement shows up for that many epochs, training is halted. Often the weights from the moment of best validation performance are restored. This also avoids wasted computation.
gl.erken-durdurma.why: Early stopping is a cheap way to reduce overfitting without changing the model itself. It also saves time and electricity by cutting off training that no longer helps. Since a model is expected to work well on new data, it shows why looking only at performance on the training data can be misleading.
gl.euv-litografi.def: A chipmaking technique that uses extreme ultraviolet light with a wavelength of 13.5 nanometers to print very small circuit patterns onto silicon wafers. It is used to make the most advanced AI and processor chips.
gl.euv-litografi.example: Foundries such as TSMC and Samsung use ASML's EUV machines for their most advanced manufacturing processes, and some of the AI chips designed by companies like Nvidia are made with them.
gl.euv-litografi.faq.0.a: Older systems use deep ultraviolet light at 193 nanometers. A shorter wavelength allows finer patterns, and with the older method reaching the same fineness means printing a pattern several times over.
gl.euv-litografi.faq.0.q: How is EUV different from earlier lithography?
gl.euv-litografi.faq.1.a: Each machine combines a highly precise light source, specialized mirrors and vacuum systems across thousands of parts. Developing it took decades and very large investment.
gl.euv-litografi.faq.1.q: Why can so few companies make EUV machines?
gl.euv-litografi.how: In the light source, tiny tin droplets are hit with lasers and turned into a very hot plasma that emits EUV light. Because air and glass lenses absorb this light, the machine operates in a vacuum and steers the beam with special mirrors instead of lenses. The light reflects off a mask carrying the circuit pattern and lands on a light-sensitive chemical layer on the wafer, shrinking the pattern as it prints it. Later steps such as etching and deposition turn the pattern into real circuitry.
gl.euv-litografi.why: Packing more transistors onto a chip depends heavily on being able to print patterns this fine. At commercial scale, EUV machines are built only by the Dutch company ASML, so the technology comes up often in discussions of chip supply chains and export controls.
gl.evrensel-yaklasim-teoremi.def: A mathematical result stating that a sufficiently wide neural network can, under suitable conditions, approximate a very wide range of continuous functions to any desired accuracy.
gl.evrensel-yaklasim-teoremi.example: A complicated relationship that gives house prices from inputs such as floor area, location and age can in theory be represented to any desired closeness by a wide enough network, but that does not mean training will find that network.
gl.evrensel-yaklasim-teoremi.faq.0.a: No. It only says a suitable network exists. Practical questions such as whether there is enough training data, whether optimization succeeds and whether the model generalizes are outside its scope.
gl.evrensel-yaklasim-teoremi.faq.0.q: Does the theorem mean any neural network can learn anything?
gl.evrensel-yaklasim-teoremi.faq.1.a: The theorem admits that a single layer may need to be extremely wide. In practice, deep networks can represent many functions with far fewer parameters and in a way that is easier to learn.
gl.evrensel-yaklasim-teoremi.faq.1.q: If one hidden layer is enough, why are deep networks used?
gl.evrensel-yaklasim-teoremi.how: The theorem shows that a feedforward network with a single hidden layer, a suitable nonlinear activation function and enough neurons can approximate any continuous function on a bounded region as closely as desired. Intuitively, each neuron produces a small piece of a curve, and adding the pieces together builds up a complex shape, much like imitating a surface with small blocks. The theorem only says that such a network exists. It does not say how to find the right weights.
gl.evrensel-yaklasim-teoremi.why: It is one of the basic arguments for why neural networks are so flexible. However, it does not guarantee how large the network must be, whether training can find it, or whether it will work well on new data. That is why claims like 'a neural network can learn anything' deserve caution.
gl.evrimsel-algoritma.def: A family of optimization methods inspired by natural selection, in which a population of candidate solutions is repeatedly varied and filtered over generations to find better solutions.
gl.evrimsel-algoritma.example: Assigning hundreds of orders to machines in a factory can be improved by starting with random schedules and blending the ones that give the shortest total time, generation after generation.
gl.evrimsel-algoritma.faq.0.a: A genetic algorithm is the best-known type of evolutionary algorithm and encodes solutions as strings. Evolutionary algorithm is the broader umbrella, which also includes genetic programming and evolution strategies.
gl.evrimsel-algoritma.faq.0.q: What is the difference between an evolutionary algorithm and a genetic algorithm?
gl.evrimsel-algoritma.faq.1.a: Usually not. Gradient-based methods are far more efficient for training weights. Evolutionary methods are more often used for tasks where derivatives are unavailable, such as architecture and hyperparameter search.
gl.evrimsel-algoritma.faq.1.q: Can evolutionary algorithms replace deep learning?
gl.evrimsel-algoritma.how: The process starts with a set of randomly generated candidate solutions. Each candidate is scored with a fitness measure. The highest scorers are picked as parents for the next generation, and new candidates are produced by mixing them and by making small random changes called mutations. Weak candidates are dropped and the cycle repeats with the new generation. Because no derivatives are needed, the approach can be used on rugged problems or black-box systems.
gl.evrimsel-algoritma.why: It is a useful alternative where gradient descent cannot be applied, or where the search space is discrete or very complex. It is used in areas such as neural architecture search, robot design and scheduling. It does not guarantee the single best answer, but it often reaches solutions that are good enough.
gl.evrisimli-sinir-agi.def: A type of neural network that learns patterns such as edges, textures and shapes in grid-like data, especially images, by scanning them with small filters. It was the standard approach to image recognition for many years.
gl.evrisimli-sinir-agi.example: A phone gallery that sorts photos into labels like “beach” or “cat”, or software that flags a suspicious area on an X-ray, are typical CNN applications.
gl.evrisimli-sinir-agi.faq.0.a: A CNN scans the image with small local filters and builds up patterns layer by layer. A ViT splits the image into patches and uses attention to relate all patches to each other at once.
gl.evrisimli-sinir-agi.faq.0.q: What is the difference between a CNN and a vision transformer (ViT)?
gl.evrisimli-sinir-agi.faq.1.a: No. The same idea can be applied to audio, time series and some text tasks, though CNNs are best known for image processing.
gl.evrisimli-sinir-agi.faq.1.q: Are CNNs only used for images?
gl.evrisimli-sinir-agi.how: Inside the network, small tables of numbers called filters or kernels slide across the image, measuring at each position how closely that patch matches the filter. Early layers pick up simple patterns like edges and corners, and later layers combine them into more complex shapes such as eyes, wheels or faces. Pooling steps shrink the image while keeping the important information. Because the same filter is reused everywhere, the number of parameters stays low and an object can be recognized wherever it appears in the picture.
gl.evrisimli-sinir-agi.why: CNNs were among the main drivers of the deep learning breakthrough of the 2010s on the vision side. They underpin face recognition, medical image analysis and the way many machines perceive their surroundings. Transformer-based models are now widespread, but CNNs remain popular because they are light and efficient.
gl.f1-skoru.def: A success measure for classification models that combines precision and recall into a single number between 0 and 1; it is the harmonic mean of the two.
gl.f1-skoru.example: A model with 90 percent precision and 50 percent recall has an F1 score of about 64 percent, which is lower than the plain average of 70 percent.
gl.f1-skoru.faq.0.a: Accuracy measures the share of all predictions that are correct and can mislead when one class dominates. F1 focuses on the balance between catching the rare class (recall) and avoiding false alarms (precision).
gl.f1-skoru.faq.0.q: What is the difference between F1 score and accuracy?
gl.f1-skoru.faq.1.a: There is no absolute threshold; it depends on the task and the data. The score is interpreted by comparing it with other models or with human performance on the same data.
gl.f1-skoru.faq.1.q: What counts as a good F1 score?
gl.f1-skoru.how: To compute F1, the harmonic mean of precision and recall is taken. This kind of average gives weight to the lower value, so if one is very high and the other very low, F1 comes out low too. An ordinary average can hide such an imbalance. The closer the score is to 1, the fewer both false alarms and missed cases the model produces; a score near 0 shows that at least one of the two is very weak.
gl.f1-skoru.why: When data is imbalanced, accuracy can mislead, and F1 offers a practical single figure for comparing models. It is widely used in text classification, entity recognition, and information extraction. Because it weighs the two measures equally, it is better to look at them separately when one matters more than the other.
gl.federe-ogrenme.def: A way of building a shared model by combining updates trained locally on devices or at institutions, without gathering the underlying data in one central place.
gl.federe-ogrenme.example: A phone keyboard can improve its word suggestions by training locally on each phone and merging the updates, without sending what users type to a server.
gl.federe-ogrenme.faq.0.a: No. Raw data is not shared, but some information can be inferred from model updates. That is why extra safeguards such as encryption and differential privacy are used.
gl.federe-ogrenme.faq.0.q: Does federated learning make data completely safe?
gl.federe-ogrenme.faq.1.a: In centralized training all the data is collected in one place. In federated learning the data stays where it is and only model updates travel to the center.
gl.federe-ogrenme.faq.1.q: How is it different from centralized training?
gl.federe-ogrenme.how: A central server sends a copy of the shared model to phones or to institutions such as hospitals. Each participant trains the model briefly on its own data, and the raw data never leaves the device. Only the model updates, meaning the changes to the weights, go back to the server. The server combines the updates, often by averaging them, and sends out the new version. This cycle repeats many times. To strengthen privacy, the method is often paired with techniques such as differential privacy or encryption.
gl.federe-ogrenme.why: In health care, banking and mobile devices, data is both sensitive and personal, and regulations such as the GDPR in Europe or KVKK, Turkey's personal data protection law, limit how it can move. Federated learning allows shared learning without sharing the data, which eases privacy concerns. Information can still leak from the updates, so it is not complete protection on its own.
gl.fiziksel-yapay-zeka.def: An approach to artificial intelligence that controls systems acting in the physical world, such as robots, autonomous vehicles and sensor-equipped machines. It deals with real environments rather than only text or images on a screen.
gl.fiziksel-yapay-zeka.example: A robot arm picking boxes off warehouse shelves, or a vehicle driving itself through traffic, are typical examples of physical AI.
gl.fiziksel-yapay-zeka.faq.0.a: A classic industrial robot usually repeats movements that were programmed in advance. Physical AI uses learned models to adapt to new and changing situations.
gl.fiziksel-yapay-zeka.faq.0.q: How is physical AI different from traditional robotics?
gl.fiziksel-yapay-zeka.faq.1.a: Running millions of trials with a real robot costs time and money and risks damage. In simulation the same trials are fast and safe.
gl.fiziksel-yapay-zeka.faq.1.q: Why are these systems trained in simulation?
gl.fiziksel-yapay-zeka.how: The system gathers data from cameras, microphones, touch and balance sensors. An AI model interprets that data, builds a picture of its surroundings and prepares a plan of action, which motors and actuators then carry out. The result of each movement is measured by the sensors again, and the loop repeats. Much of the training happens in virtual simulations, because trial and error with a real robot is slow and expensive. The hard part is that the real world is unpredictable: a loose cable or a change in lighting can throw off a plan.
gl.fiziksel-yapay-zeka.why: As language models have advanced in text and images, moving AI into the physical world is widely seen as the next step. It could change how work is done in factories, warehouses, farming and healthcare. The cost of mistakes is also different: a wrong answer on a screen can be corrected, but a wrong robot movement can hurt people or damage property. That is why safety gets so much attention.
gl.flashattention.def: An algorithm that reorganizes the attention computation to fit the GPU's memory layout. It runs faster and uses less memory without changing the result.
gl.flashattention.example: A research team that had to keep training texts short because of memory limits can use FlashAttention to handle longer texts on the same GPUs.
gl.flashattention.faq.0.a: No. The result is the same as standard attention; the speedup comes from reordering operations to reduce memory access.
gl.flashattention.faq.0.q: Does FlashAttention speed things up by approximating attention?
gl.flashattention.faq.1.a: No, they solve different problems. GQA is an architectural change that reduces memory needs, while FlashAttention concerns how attention is computed. The two can be used together.
gl.flashattention.faq.1.q: Is FlashAttention the same as GQA?
gl.flashattention.how: On a GPU, computation is very fast but access to the large main memory (HBM) is slow. The classic implementation writes the huge attention matrix to main memory and reads it back. FlashAttention splits the input into small blocks, loads them into the fast on-chip memory and computes the softmax piece by piece, so the huge matrix is never fully built. The result is not an approximation but identical to standard attention; the gain comes from reduced memory traffic.
gl.flashattention.why: The memory and speed cost of attention was one of the main obstacles to long-context models. FlashAttention made it easier to train and run models on longer sequences with the same hardware. It is widely used in major model libraries, and similar approaches continue to be developed.
gl.flop.def: A single addition, subtraction, multiplication or division carried out on decimal-style numbers. In AI it is used to measure how much computation training or running a model requires.
gl.flop.example: When a company reports the total computation used for a new model in FLOP, its scale can be compared with other models, while the speed of the graphics cards used is given in a figure such as teraFLOPS.
gl.flop.faq.0.a: No. FLOP is a count of operations, while FLOPS is operations per second, meaning speed.
gl.flop.faq.0.q: Are FLOP and FLOPS the same thing?
gl.flop.faq.1.a: FLOP counts only floating-point operations, while TOPS mostly counts integer operations. When comparing the two, it is important to check which number type was used.
gl.flop.faq.1.q: What is the difference between FLOP and TOPS?
gl.flop.how: Training a neural network consists of multiplying and adding huge numbers of floating-point values, and each such step counts as one FLOP. The total computation of a training run is given in FLOP, while a piece of hardware's speed is given in FLOPS (or FLOP/s), meaning FLOP per second. The final S stands for second rather than a plural, a common source of confusion. Values are expressed with prefixes such as tera (ten to the twelfth), peta and exa. Once the total FLOP a model needs is known, dividing by the hardware's speed gives a rough estimate of the time.
gl.flop.why: The computation spent on training is one of the more direct ways to compare the scale of models, more so than parameter count. Some regulations and policy proposals also set extra obligations for models above a certain amount of computation, which is why FLOP comes up in news and in debates over rules.
gl.fonksiyon-cagirma.def: A language model stating, in a structured form, which function a developer has defined, such as a weather lookup or a database search, it wants to run and with what values. This lets the model work together with outside systems.
gl.fonksiyon-cagirma.example: When a user asks 'Will it rain in Istanbul tomorrow?', the model asks to call the weather function with the city and the day; the app passes the returned data to the model, which then writes the answer.
gl.fonksiyon-cagirma.faq.0.a: No. The model only produces a request saying which function to call and with which parameters. The application wrapped around the model runs the function and sends back the result.
gl.fonksiyon-cagirma.faq.0.q: Does the model run the function itself?
gl.fonksiyon-cagirma.faq.1.a: That depends on which functions are allowed. A common safeguard is to require human approval for high-impact actions such as deleting data or making payments, and to give the model only the permissions it needs.
gl.fonksiyon-cagirma.how: The developer gives the model the name, description and parameters of the functions it may use. If the user's request needs a function, the model produces a call request instead of writing a plain answer. The model does not run the function itself; the application does, sends the result back, and the model uses it to write the final reply. If needed, this loop repeats several times. This mechanism underlies the ability of AI agents to get things done in the outside world.
gl.fonksiyon-cagirma.why: On their own, language models cannot reach current information, do reliable calculations or start actions in a system. Function calling gets around these limits and turns the model from a conversation partner into a component that does work. It is the technical core of the agent and tool-use discussions in the news.
gl.fotonik-bilisim.def: An approach to computing that uses light (photons) instead of electrical signals to carry data and perform calculations, aimed especially at speeding up the heavy matrix operations behind AI.
gl.fotonik-bilisim.example: In data centers, servers already exchange data over fiber-optic cables using light; photonic computing aims to bring that idea inside the chip and even into the calculation itself.
gl.fotonik-bilisim.faq.0.a: No. Photonic computing performs classical calculations with light, while quantum computing relies on qubits. There is some overlap, since certain quantum computer designs also use photons as qubits.
gl.fotonik-bilisim.faq.0.q: Is photonic computing the same as quantum computing?
gl.fotonik-bilisim.faq.1.a: A full replacement is not expected in the near term. A likelier path is that light is first used for moving data between chips and for specific accelerator tasks.
gl.fotonik-bilisim.how: In photonic chips, light travels through extremely thin waveguides etched onto silicon. When light beams are combined, an effect called interference occurs, and it can be used to physically carry out the matrix multiplications at the core of neural networks. Light generates little heat and moves very fast. On the other hand, light is hard to store, results usually have to be converted back to electronic form, and precision can be a problem in analog calculation.
gl.fotonik-bilisim.why: One limit on AI chips is the energy and heat produced when data moves around. Photonic approaches could ease that bottleneck, which is why chip startups and large companies are interested. For computation itself, photonic chips are still mostly at the research and early-product stage.
gl.fp8-ve-dusuk-hassasiyetli-sayilar.def: Number formats that store and process values with fewer bits, such as 8 instead of 16 or 32, trading a little accuracy for speed and memory savings.
gl.fp8-ve-dusuk-hassasiyetli-sayilar.exa: A company can convert its model to FP8 to fit a larger model into the same GPU memory, but it still has to test whether quality has dropped.
gl.fp8-ve-dusuk-hassasiyetli-sayilar.faq: Sometimes there is a small loss, and sometimes the difference is too small to measure. It depends on the model, the task and the scaling method, so testing after conversion is necessary.
Does FP8 reduce a model's accuracy?
No. Both use 8 bits, but FP8 is a floating-point format and INT8 is an integer format. Floating point represents values of very different sizes more easily.
Are FP8 and INT8 the same thing?
gl.fp8-ve-dusuk-hassasiyetli-sayilar.how: The weights and intermediate values in an AI model are stored as floating-point numbers. The fewer bits each number uses, the less memory it takes, and the more operations a chip can perform in the same time. FP8 has two common layouts: one offers finer precision, the other a wider range of values. Because the numbers are coarser, training needs careful scaling, and some calculations are still done at higher precision. For inference, INT8 and even lower-bit formats are used for a similar purpose.
gl.fp8-ve-dusuk-hassasiyetli-sayilar.why: The cost of large models comes largely from memory and compute. Low precision lets the same hardware run a bigger model or respond faster. That is why launches of new AI chips so often mention support for low-precision formats. The price is the risk of losing accuracy.
gl.gauss-sicratma.def: A rendering technique that represents a scene as a large set of fuzzy 3D blobs called Gaussians, each with a position, size, color and transparency, and draws them onto the screen by splatting. It is used to build realistic 3D scenes from photos.
gl.gauss-sicratma.example: A short video filmed on a phone while walking around a room can be turned into a 3D scene that can later be viewed from any angle.
gl.gauss-sicratma.faq.0.a: A NeRF stores the scene inside a neural network and queries it many times for every image. Gaussian splatting keeps the scene as explicit Gaussians and draws them directly. This usually gives it an advantage in rendering speed.
gl.gauss-sicratma.faq.0.q: What is the difference between Gaussian splatting and NeRF?
gl.gauss-sicratma.faq.1.a: It relies on an optimization process similar to training, but it is not a classic neural network. It is still covered in AI news as part of computer vision and 3D generation.
gl.gauss-sicratma.how: Photos or video of a scene are taken from different angles, and the camera positions are estimated. Starting from a sparse point cloud, a large number of Gaussians is created. Each Gaussian's position, shape, color and transparency are adjusted over and over until the images it renders look like the real photos. At display time the Gaussians are projected onto the screen and blended on top of one another. Graphics cards handle this quickly, so the scene can be explored smoothly.
gl.gauss-sicratma.why: Compared with earlier neural methods it can render much faster, which made 3D capture far more practical. It draws interest in virtual reality, games, property tours, film and robot mapping. In AI news it usually appears in the context of photorealistic 3D scene generation.
gl.gdpr.def: The European Union's comprehensive data protection law. It governs how personal data is collected, used and stored, gives individuals rights over their data, and places obligations on the organizations that process it.
gl.gdpr.example: In 2023, Italy's data protection authority placed a temporary restriction on ChatGPT over how personal data was processed; the service returned after the company introduced some measures.
gl.gdpr.faq.0.a: No. Organizations outside the EU can also fall under it if they offer goods or services to people in the EU or monitor their behavior.
gl.gdpr.faq.0.q: Does the GDPR only apply to European companies?
gl.gdpr.faq.1.a: No. KVKK is Turkey's personal data protection law. It shares some features with the GDPR, but it is a separate piece of legislation with its own differences.
gl.gdpr.faq.1.q: Is the GDPR the same as KVKK?
gl.gdpr.how: The GDPR applies to anyone processing the data of people in the EU, even if the organization is based elsewhere. Data should be collected only for a specific, legitimate purpose, in the amount needed, and on a lawful basis such as consent. People have the right to access their data, correct it and, under certain conditions, have it erased. Violations can lead to administrative fines of up to 4 percent of worldwide annual turnover or 20 million euros, whichever is higher. The regulation has applied since 2018.
gl.gdpr.why: AI models are often trained on huge amounts of data gathered from the internet, and that data can include personal information. The GDPR puts companies under scrutiny on the legal basis for such training, on deletion requests and on transparency. It is one of the main frameworks shaping how AI products are offered in Europe.
gl.gecikme-suresi.def: The time between sending a request and receiving a response. In AI, it is how long a user waits after asking a question before seeing an answer.
gl.gecikme-suresi.example: If a voice assistant starts answering half a second after a question instead of two seconds, the conversation feels far more natural.
gl.gecikme-suresi.faq.0.a: No. Latency is how long data takes to arrive, while bandwidth is how much data can be transferred per unit of time.
gl.gecikme-suresi.faq.0.q: Is latency the same as bandwidth?
gl.gecikme-suresi.faq.1.a: Faster hardware, smaller or optimized models, servers closer to users and efficient serving software can all lower it.
gl.gecikme-suresi.how: Latency is the sum of every step in the chain: the request travelling over the network to the server, waiting in a queue, the model processing the input, the answer being generated and sent back. In large language models, model size, prompt length, server load and hardware speed all change the result. Latency is usually measured in milliseconds or seconds. Besides the average, the slowest requests are also examined.
gl.gecikme-suresi.why: Low latency is what makes AI feel natural. In a voice assistant, a few seconds of waiting breaks the conversation, and in coding assistants it interrupts the flow. Reducing latency often requires pricier hardware or a smaller model, so there is a trade-off between speed and cost.
gl.gelismis-paketleme.def: Placing several chips, such as a processor and memory stacks, inside a single package very close together and joined by a large number of connections. CoWoS is one well-known technique of this kind from TSMC.
gl.gelismis-paketleme.example: Nvidia's data center GPUs rely on advanced packaging such as TSMC's CoWoS to combine the processor die with HBM memory stacks in the same package.
gl.gelismis-paketleme.faq.0.a: No. Chip manufacturing creates the transistors on a silicon wafer, while packaging joins finished chips together, protects them and connects them to the outside world.
gl.gelismis-paketleme.faq.0.q: Is packaging the same as chip manufacturing?
gl.gelismis-paketleme.faq.1.a: CoWoS is TSMC's own name for its technique. Other companies such as Intel and Samsung have comparable packaging technologies under different names.
gl.gelismis-paketleme.faq.1.q: Is TSMC the only company that does CoWoS?
gl.gelismis-paketleme.how: In CoWoS (Chip on Wafer on Substrate), processor and memory chips sit side by side on a thin silicon layer called an interposer. This layer provides far denser and shorter connections between chips than ordinary circuit-board traces can. The interposer in turn sits on a base material, the substrate, which links the package to the outside world. As a result, the GPU in an AI accelerator and its high-bandwidth memory (HBM) can exchange data quickly, almost as if they were a single chip.
gl.gelismis-paketleme.why: The performance of an AI accelerator depends not only on the processor chip but also on how quickly it can reach memory. Packaging has therefore become as important as chip fabrication, and advanced packaging capacity has at times been cited as a bottleneck in accelerator supply.
gl.genel-amacli-yapay-zeka-modeli.def: An AI model trained on large amounts of data that is not tied to a single task, can perform a wide range of jobs, and can be built into many different systems. The EU AI Act regulates it under its own heading.
gl.genel-amacli-yapay-zeka-modeli.exampl: The same underlying language model might power a chat assistant, a coding helper and a translation tool, and the Act treats that underlying model as a GPAI model.
No. GPAI is a classification based on a model's general capability, while a high-risk system refers to an application in a specific use area. A GPAI model can be a component of a high-risk system.
Is a GPAI model the same as a high-risk system?
Partly. Open-source models get some relief from documentation duties, but models that carry systemic risk cannot use that exemption.
Are open-source models exempt from these rules?
gl.genel-amacli-yapay-zeka-modeli.how: The Act places specific obligations on the providers of such models. Providers prepare technical documentation, give the companies that build the model into their products the information they need, set a policy for complying with copyright law, and publish a summary of the content used in training. Some exemptions apply to models released under open-source licenses. A voluntary code of practice has also been drawn up to ease compliance. Oversight of these obligations is meant to phase in over time.
gl.genel-amacli-yapay-zeka-modeli.why: Because large language models and similar systems power countless products, a problem in one model can spread to many applications. The Act therefore tries to share responsibility between the companies that develop models and those that use them. Debates about copyright and training-data transparency are also closely tied to this category.
gl.genelleme.def: A machine learning model's ability to perform well on new data it did not see during training. It shows whether the model learned the underlying pattern instead of memorizing the training examples.
gl.genelleme.example: A classifier trained on photos of cats and dogs generalizes well if it correctly recognizes a cat photo it has never seen before.
gl.genelleme.faq.0.a: Generalization means the model also works well on new data. In overfitting the model memorizes the training data and fails on new examples, so overfitting is a typical cause of poor generalization.
gl.genelleme.faq.0.q: What is the difference between generalization and overfitting?
gl.genelleme.faq.1.a: By checking the model's performance on a test set that was not used in training. A large gap between training and test performance signals weak generalization.
gl.genelleme.how: A model tries to extract general patterns from its training examples. If it captures the underlying rule rather than memorizing, it can make accurate predictions on cases it has never met. To measure this, data is split into training, validation and test sets, and the test set is never used during training. A model that does well in training but poorly on the test set has overfit. Diverse data, avoiding needless model complexity and regularization techniques all help generalization.
gl.genelleme.why: A model that only works on its training data is of little use in the real world. Claims in AI news that a model adapts to new tasks are really about generalization. Whether a model also works in another hospital or another language is a question about this very property.
gl.genetik-algoritma.def: The best-known kind of evolutionary algorithm, which encodes solutions as strings of numbers called chromosomes and improves them over generations through crossover and mutation.
gl.genetik-algoritma.example: A cargo company could use a genetic algorithm to solve a variant of the traveling salesman problem and find the shortest route through dozens of delivery points.
gl.genetik-algoritma.faq.0.a: No. Because it involves randomness, each run can give a different result, and it can get stuck in a local optimum. It is usually used to find a good-enough solution in reasonable time rather than the exact best one.
gl.genetik-algoritma.faq.0.q: Does a genetic algorithm guarantee the best solution?
gl.genetik-algoritma.faq.1.a: The method borrows the ideas of genes, chromosomes, crossover and mutation from biology. It does not imitate real biology closely; it adapts the logic of evolution into a search technique.
gl.genetik-algoritma.how: Each candidate solution is represented as a string, for example the order of stops on a delivery route. The algorithm starts with a population of random strings and scores each one with a fitness function. High scorers are paired, and pieces of two strings are combined to produce offspring, which is called crossover. Some genes are changed at random with a small probability, called mutation, which keeps the population diverse. After a few hundred generations, the population usually approaches a good solution.
gl.genetik-algoritma.why: It is a practical tool for combinatorial optimization problems, where the number of possible solutions is enormous. It is simple to set up and needs little knowledge of the problem's mathematical structure. On the downside, it can get stuck in a local optimum and can be slow because it needs many fitness evaluations.
gl.genisletilmis-dusunme.def: A working mode in which a model carries out a long internal reasoning stage before giving its answer, letting it think step by step and check its own solution on complex questions.
gl.genisletilmis-dusunme.example: A developer turns on extended thinking to find the cause of a tricky software bug, and the model first splits the problem into several possible sources, rules them out one by one, then suggests a fix.
gl.genisletilmis-dusunme.faq.0.a: They are close but not identical. Chain of thought is the technique of reasoning step by step in writing, while extended thinking is a mode that presents this kind of long reasoning as a separate stage with an adjustable length.
gl.genisletilmis-dusunme.faq.0.q: Is extended thinking the same as chain of thought?
gl.genisletilmis-dusunme.faq.1.a: That cannot always be guaranteed. Researchers debate whether visible reasoning fully reflects the model's actual internal process, so it is best read as a clue rather than a complete explanation.
gl.genisletilmis-dusunme.faq.1.q: Does the thinking text show how the model really made its decision?
gl.genisletilmis-dusunme.how: With extended thinking turned on, the model produces a thinking section before the actual answer. In it, the model breaks the problem into parts, tries possible routes, and notices mistakes and backtracks. It then writes the final answer based on that work. The term is used for a feature in Anthropic's Claude models, and other providers offer similar abilities under different names. The length of the thinking can be capped with a thinking budget.
gl.genisletilmis-dusunme.why: In math, coding and multi-step planning, a model's first instinct is often not good enough. Extended thinking can improve accuracy on such tasks, at the cost of longer response times and higher expense. It makes sense to choose it according to task difficulty rather than leaving it on for everything.
gl.gercek-referans-verisi.def: Data treated as correct and used to train a model and to measure how accurate its outputs are, usually labeled by people or taken from a trusted source.
gl.gercek-referans-verisi.example: In a model that detects disease from chest scans, the diagnoses marked by radiologists are the ground truth, and the model’s predictions are compared with them.
gl.gercek-referans-verisi.faq.0.a: No. People can make mistakes or disagree on the same example. Ground truth is the accepted reference, which is why label quality is checked separately.
gl.gercek-referans-verisi.faq.1.a: Usually experts or trained annotators mark examples one by one. In some cases sensor readings or reliable records serve as labels.
gl.gercek-referans-verisi.faq.1.q: How are ground truth labels produced?
gl.gercek-referans-verisi.how: For every example in a dataset, the correct answer is set: whether a photo contains a cat, or whether an email is spam. These labels come from experts, trained annotators or reliable measurements. During training the model compares its predictions with the labels and adjusts itself based on its errors; during testing its performance is scored against the same labels. If annotators disagree, majority voting or expert review can settle it. “Truth” here means the label is accepted as the reference, not that it is flawless.
gl.gercek-referans-verisi.why: A model’s quality depends heavily on the quality of the labels it learns from and is tested against. Flawed or biased ground truth distorts both training and measurement. In fields like medicine and autonomous driving, producing accurate labels is costly and critical.
gl.gercek-zamanli-ceviri.def: Translating speech or text into another language almost instantly, as it is spoken or written. The result is delivered as written captions or synthetic voice.
gl.gercek-zamanli-ceviri.example: In a video meeting, one participant can speak German while the others follow live Turkish captions.
gl.gercek-zamanli-ceviri.faq.0.a: It works for everyday and simple conversations, but where nuance, tone and cultural context matter, human interpreters are still preferred. The tool is often used alongside interpreters rather than instead of them.
gl.gercek-zamanli-ceviri.faq.0.q: Does real-time translation replace human interpreters?
gl.gercek-zamanli-ceviri.faq.1.a: To translate a sentence correctly, the system often has to wait until the speaker has said a certain part of it. Word order differs between languages, so with a verb-final sentence, for example, the translation may only become clear later.
gl.gercek-zamanli-ceviri.faq.1.q: Why is there a small delay in real-time translation?
gl.gercek-zamanli-ceviri.how: In the common approach, a speech recognition system first turns the audio into text. A machine translation model then converts the text into the target language. If needed, a speech synthesis model reads the translation aloud. Some newer systems combine these stages into a single model. To cut delay, translation starts in pieces before a sentence ends, which requires a balance between speed and accuracy.
gl.gercek-zamanli-ceviri.why: It lowers language barriers in meetings, travel, customer service and live broadcasts. Idioms, proper names and context-dependent meanings raise the risk of errors. For serious legal or medical conversations, the output needs careful checking.
gl.geri-yayilim.def: The algorithm that works out each weight's share of a neural network's prediction error, moving from the output back toward the input, so that the weights can be updated.
gl.geri-yayilim.example: If a network mistakes a handwritten 7 for a 1, backpropagation finds which weights led to the mistake and shifts them so the network recognizes 7 more accurately.
gl.geri-yayilim.faq.0.a: No. Backpropagation calculates how much each weight affects the error, that is, the gradients, while gradient descent uses that information to update the weights.
gl.geri-yayilim.faq.0.q: Are backpropagation and gradient descent the same thing?
gl.geri-yayilim.faq.1.a: There is no proof that the brain works this way, and the question is debated among scientists. Backpropagation is mainly seen as an engineering method.
gl.geri-yayilim.faq.1.q: Does the brain use backpropagation too?
gl.geri-yayilim.how: First the data passes forward through the network and a prediction comes out. The prediction is compared with the correct answer to measure the error. Then the error is carried backward layer by layer, starting at the output layer, and how much each weight contributed to it is calculated using the chain rule from calculus. This information goes to an optimization method such as gradient descent, which changes the weights slightly in the direction that reduces the error. The cycle is repeated over many examples.
gl.geri-yayilim.why: Backpropagation makes it possible to tune millions or even billions of weights efficiently, so it is the core training mechanism of modern deep learning. Systems from image recognition models to large language models are trained this way. Its spread in the 1980s revived interest in multilayer networks.
gl.gguf.def: A file format that packs an AI model's weights and the information needed to run it into a single file, widely used for local inference. It was developed for the llama.cpp ecosystem and is common for distributing quantized models.
gl.gguf.example: On a model's Hugging Face page you might see two GGUF files labeled Q4 and Q8; the first is smaller and faster, while the second is usually closer to the original quality.
gl.gguf.faq.0.a: It is usually expanded as GPT-Generated Unified Format, though accounts of the name's origin vary. What matters is that it succeeds the GGML format and offers a single-file model package compatible with llama.cpp.
gl.gguf.faq.1.a: No. llama.cpp and many tools built on it can, but much training-oriented code expects other formats. It is worth checking that the tool you plan to use supports GGUF.
gl.gguf.faq.1.q: Can any software open a GGUF file?
gl.gguf.how: A GGUF file carries the model's numerical weights together with metadata: the architecture, the tokenizer vocabulary and settings such as context length all live in the same file. A user can hand the single file to the software without juggling separate configuration files. The format supports different quantization levels; suffixes like Q4 or Q8 in the file name hint at how many bits the weights use. The file is also laid out so it can be loaded into memory efficiently.
gl.gguf.why: A single-file layout makes models easy to share and try out. On platforms such as Hugging Face, the same model often comes in many GGUF versions, so people with limited memory can find one that fits their device. It is a term that turns up often in local AI news.
gl.gigavat-olcekli-veri-merkezi.def: A very large data center or data center campus with an electrical capacity on the order of one gigawatt, usually planned for training and running large AI models.
gl.gigavat-olcekli-veri-merkezi.example: A one-gigawatt facility running at full load all year would draw about 8.76 terawatt-hours of electricity, comparable to the annual consumption of a small country.
gl.gigavat-olcekli-veri-merkezi.faq.0.a: A gigawatt is a thousand megawatts, or one billion watts. For comparison, a large power plant unit produces output of that order.
gl.gigavat-olcekli-veri-merkezi.faq.0.q: How much power is a gigawatt?
gl.gigavat-olcekli-veri-merkezi.faq.1.a: No. Most data centers are in the tens or hundreds of megawatts. Gigawatt scale applies only to a few campuses that the largest companies are planning or building.
gl.gigavat-olcekli-veri-merkezi.faq.1.q: Are all AI data centers gigawatt-scale?
gl.gigavat-olcekli-veri-merkezi.how: At this scale the facility is often not a single building but a campus of several buildings on the same site. Large numbers of accelerator chips are linked by high-speed networks and run as one big cluster. Supplying the power takes a grid connection, substations, backup systems, and sometimes dedicated generation. The heat load is so high that liquid cooling is a common choice. One gigawatt is on the order of the output of a large power plant unit.
gl.gigavat-olcekli-veri-merkezi.why: AI companies' growth plans are now described in electrical capacity as much as in chip counts. These campuses can put real strain on grids, electricity prices, water, and land use. Supporters point to investment and jobs, while critics point to the energy and environmental costs.
gl.gizli-ajanda-testleri.def: Tests, also called hidden-agenda tests, that measure whether an advanced AI model could pursue a concealed goal, such as undermining safety processes, without developers or overseers noticing.
gl.gizli-ajanda-testleri.example: In one such test, a model is checked on whether it can slip past another AI monitoring it and leave an error in code that would go unnoticed.
gl.gizli-ajanda-testleri.faq.0.a: No. They measure ability, not intent. Succeeding in a deliberately difficult scenario does not show the model behaves that way in everyday use, only that the risk is technically possible.
gl.gizli-ajanda-testleri.faq.0.q: Do these tests mean the model is malicious?
gl.gizli-ajanda-testleri.faq.1.a: Leading AI labs run their own internal tests, and independent evaluation organizations can also test models from the outside. Results are sometimes shared in system cards.
gl.gizli-ajanda-testleri.how: During a test, the model is given an ordinary task along with a side objective that must be hidden from its surroundings. Evaluators watch whether the model can reach that side objective and whether it can do so without being detected. Typical scenarios include slipping a vulnerability into code unnoticed, misleading an oversight system, deliberately underperforming on a test to hide its abilities, or steering human decisions with false information. The goal is to measure whether the model's current capabilities would make such a risk possible, so these tests are often built to push the model hard.
gl.gizli-ajanda-testleri.why: As models operate with more autonomy, the ability to get around human oversight has become a distinct topic in safety debates. These tests aim to find the limit of a capability without waiting for dangerous behavior to occur. A result shows whether a model is capable of such behavior, not that it is malicious.
gl.gizli-bilisim.def: A security approach that uses hardware-isolated environments to protect data not only when it is stored or transmitted, but also while it is being processed.
gl.gizli-bilisim.example: A hospital sending patient records to an AI model in the cloud can use an isolated environment, so neither the cloud administrator nor the model provider sees the raw data.
gl.gizli-bilisim.faq.0.a: Ordinary encryption protects data in storage and on the network. Confidential computing also covers the moment of processing: the data is handled inside a hardware-isolated area and cannot be viewed from outside.
gl.gizli-bilisim.faq.0.q: How is confidential computing different from ordinary encryption?
gl.gizli-bilisim.faq.1.a: No. Its security rests on trust in the hardware and its maker, and hardware flaws or misconfiguration can create risk. It is used in addition to other security measures, not instead of them.
gl.gizli-bilisim.faq.1.q: Does it make data completely secure?
gl.gizli-bilisim.how: Encryption is usually applied to stored data and network traffic, but during processing the data is decrypted and sits in memory in the clear. In confidential computing, the processor creates a hardware-isolated area called a trusted execution environment. Data and code are processed inside it, and not even the operating system or the cloud provider's administrators can see the contents. A proof called remote attestation shows that the environment is running the expected software. In AI, it is used to protect both user data and model weights, and some AI accelerators support this approach as well.
gl.gizli-bilisim.why: Organizations that handle sensitive data, such as in healthcare and finance, may hesitate to run it through an AI model in the cloud. Model owners, in turn, want to protect their weights on someone else's servers. Confidential computing addresses the trust needs of both sides, but it depends on trust in the hardware vendor and is not considered flawless.
gl.gizli-uzay.def: An abstract, high-dimensional space in which a model represents data as lists of numbers, with similar things placed close together.
gl.gizli-uzay.example: In some face-generating models, moving in a particular direction through latent space produces images of the same face smiling more and more.
gl.gizli-uzay.faq.0.a: Not exactly, but they are closely related. Latent space is the representation space a model uses, while an embedding is the numerical vector for one piece of data in that space.
gl.gizli-uzay.faq.0.q: Is latent space the same as an embedding?
gl.gizli-uzay.faq.1.a: The model learns them to do its task well, not to match human-readable labels. So a single dimension usually does not correspond to a single concept.
gl.gizli-uzay.faq.1.q: Why are the dimensions of latent space hard to interpret?
gl.gizli-uzay.how: A model turns inputs such as images, sentences or audio into a list of hundreds or thousands of numbers. During training, similar content ends up at nearby points in this space, and some directions may correspond to properties like color, tone or style. Generative models start from a point in this space and use a decoder to produce an image or text. Moving step by step between two points also gives smooth transitions between the content. It is called “latent” because the space is not directly observed but learned by the model during training.
gl.gizli-uzay.why: Latent space is key to understanding how models hold meaning. Semantic search, recommendation systems, image generation and editing all rely on proximity relationships in this space. Because its dimensions are not directly readable by humans, it is also a subject of interpretability research.
gl.golge-yapay-zeka.def: AI tools that employees use for work without the knowledge or approval of their organization. It usually refers to chatbots and similar apps used through personal accounts.
gl.golge-yapay-zeka.example: If a sales employee pastes a spreadsheet containing a customer list into a chatbot on a personal account and asks for a summary, the company has unknowingly passed confidential data to a third-party service.
gl.golge-yapay-zeka.faq.0.a: A ban alone is not the only route. Providing approved tools, stating clearly what data may be shared and training employees tend to work better together.
gl.golge-yapay-zeka.faq.0.q: How can shadow AI be prevented?
gl.golge-yapay-zeka.faq.1.a: Shadow IT is the older idea of using software and hardware without the organization's knowledge. Shadow AI can be seen as a type of it that is specific to AI tools.
gl.golge-yapay-zeka.faq.1.q: Is shadow AI the same as shadow IT?
gl.golge-yapay-zeka.how: An employee uses an AI tool the organization has not approved to speed up their work, for instance pasting a report into a chatbot from a personal account to get a summary. Because IT and security teams cannot see this use, they do not know what data was shared, where it is stored or whether it is used to improve the model. Organizations try to reduce it by offering approved tools, writing usage policies and informing staff.
gl.golge-yapay-zeka.why: Confidential customer information, source code or trade secrets flowing unchecked to outside services can lead to data leaks and compliance problems; where personal data is involved, rules such as KVKK, Turkey's data protection law, may also come into play. At the same time, widespread use shows that employees have a real need for these tools. That is why offering a safe alternative, rather than only banning, is a commonly recommended approach.
gl.gomme-modeli.def: A model that converts text, images or audio into a list of numbers (a vector) that captures meaning. Content with similar meaning gets similar vectors.
gl.gomme-modeli.example: In a support system, the phrases “I forgot my password” and “I can't get into my account” share few words but sit close together in embedding space, so the right help article is found.
gl.gomme-modeli.faq.0.a: A chat model generates new text. An embedding model does not generate text; it only turns content into numbers that can be compared. The two often work together.
gl.gomme-modeli.faq.0.q: How is an embedding model different from a chat model?
gl.gomme-modeli.faq.1.a: Yes. Vectors from different models are not compatible with each other. If the model changes, all documents need to be re-embedded and re-indexed.
gl.gomme-modeli.faq.1.q: Is it a problem to switch embedding models later?
gl.gomme-modeli.how: The model reads a piece of text and produces a fixed-length vector. That vector represents the meaning as a point in a many-dimensional space. Two sentences with similar meaning land close together, while unrelated ones land far apart. Documents are converted to vectors in advance and stored in a vector database. At search time the query is turned into a vector with the same model, and the documents nearest to it in that space are retrieved.
gl.gomme-modeli.why: Embedding models make it possible to search by meaning instead of exact word matches. They underpin retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), where an AI assistant pulls information from company documents, as well as recommendation engines and similar-content tools.

gl.gomme.def.en: A method of expressing the meaning of a word, sentence or image as a sequence of numbers (a vector). Content that is close in meaning is represented by vectors that are close to each other.

gl.gomme.example.en: A customer support system can match the question "I can't see my invoice" with a help article titled "invoice viewing problem," even though they do not share the same words.

gl.gomme.faq.0.a.en: In Turkish, it is called "gömme," "vektör gömme" or "vektör temsili." It means expressing the meaning of a piece of content as numbers.

gl.gomme.faq.0.q.en: What is the Turkish term for embedding?

gl.gomme.faq.1.a.en: No. Embedding models do not generate text; they only convert text into a vector that represents its meaning. Language models generate text.

gl.gomme.faq.1.q.en: Are an embedding model and a language model the same thing?

gl.gomme.how.en: An embedding model converts a text into a vector made up of hundreds or thousands of numbers. These vectors can be thought of as points in a multidimensional space: "cat" and "kitten" sit close together, while "cat" and "tax return" sit far apart. Semantic similarity is measured by calculating the proximity between two vectors.

gl.gomme.why.en: It enables search by meaning rather than word-for-word matching. Document search, recommendation systems, duplicate content detection and chatbots based on company documents (RAG) all rely on embeddings.

gl.goru-dil-eylem-modeli.def: An AI model that takes a camera image and a command in natural language together and turns them into actions a robot can carry out.
gl.goru-dil-eylem-modeli.example: Google DeepMind's RT-2 is a well-known example of this class. When a robot is told to “pick up the cup on the table,” the model reads the camera image and the sentence together and produces the arm's movement.
gl.goru-dil-eylem-modeli.faq.0.a: A large language model produces text. A VLA model takes images and text as input and outputs actions for a robot. Many VLAs are built by training a language model further on robot data.
gl.goru-dil-eylem-modeli.faq.0.q: How is a vision-language-action model different from a large language model?
gl.goru-dil-eylem-modeli.faq.1.a: It depends on the system. Often the model makes the high-level decision, while low-level motor control runs in a separate software layer. Safety checks are usually kept outside the model as well.
gl.goru-dil-eylem-modeli.faq.1.q: Does a VLA model control the whole robot by itself?
gl.goru-dil-eylem-modeli.how: These models are usually built on top of a vision-language model trained on web-scale text and images. They then get extra training on robot data: recordings that pair camera frames, instructions and the arm or gripper movements that were made at that moment. Instead of words, the model outputs actions, which are numerical commands describing the next small movement of the arm. Because the robot takes in a fresh image and decides again at every step, it can adapt to changes in its surroundings.
gl.goru-dil-eylem-modeli.why: Traditional robot software needs a separate program or separate training for each task. The VLA approach draws on the general knowledge of language models so that a robot can cope with objects and instructions it has never seen. That is why it comes up so often in news about general-purpose, humanoid and home robots. Reliability in the real world is still an open problem.
gl.goru-dil-modeli.def: An AI model that processes images and text together, so it can describe a photo, answer questions about a picture, or read the writing in an image.
gl.goru-dil-modeli.example: Uploading a photo of an invoice to a chatbot and asking 'what is the total amount?' is an everyday use of a vision-language model.
gl.goru-dil-modeli.faq.0.a: Not exactly. A vision-language model is a kind of multimodal model that combines images and text. Multimodal models can also include other types of data such as audio and video.
gl.goru-dil-modeli.faq.0.q: Is a vision-language model the same as a multimodal model?
gl.goru-dil-modeli.faq.1.a: Usually not; these models focus on understanding images. Image generation is typically handled by separate models, although some systems combine both abilities.
gl.goru-dil-modeli.faq.1.q: Does a vision-language model also generate images?
gl.goru-dil-modeli.how: In a typical vision-language model, a part called an image encoder splits a picture into small patches and turns them into numerical representations. These are converted into the format a language model uses for text and processed in the same sequence as the words of the question. The model then produces an answer by reading both the image and the question together. Training usually relies on very large numbers of paired images and captions.
gl.goru-dil-modeli.why: Real-world information is not only text; documents, charts, screenshots and photos all carry meaning. Because vision-language models can understand these, they underpin everything from accessibility tools and document processing to robotics. Risks remain, such as misreading an image or inventing details that are not there.
gl.goru-transformeri.def: An image model based on the transformer architecture that cuts a picture into small fixed-size patches and processes them the way a language model processes words.
gl.goru-transformeri.example: In many models that can look at a photo and answer questions about it, the vision component is a ViT-style encoder that splits the photo into patches.
gl.goru-transformeri.faq.0.a: Attention compares every element with every other one, so the cost grows quickly with the number of elements. Working with patches instead of individual pixels keeps that cost manageable.
