gl.goru-transformeri.faq.0.q: Why does a ViT split the image into patches?
gl.goru-transformeri.faq.1.a: Not entirely. ViT stands out in large-scale work, but CNNs remain common in tasks with limited data or hardware.
gl.goru-transformeri.how: The image is divided into equal squares, or patches. Each patch is turned into a list of numbers, position information is added, and the sequence is fed to a transformer just like the words of a sentence. The attention mechanism computes how each patch relates to every other patch, so connections between distant regions can be made in a single step. The resulting representation is then connected to a task such as classification or object detection.
gl.goru-transformeri.why: ViT showed that the same core architecture can serve both vision and language, which made multimodal models easier to build. It typically performs best when trained on very large datasets; with little data, CNNs are often the better choice.
gl.goruntu-altyazilama.def: An AI task that produces a short, natural-language sentence or description of what an image shows, combining image understanding with text generation.
gl.goruntu-altyazilama.example: Someone using a screen reader hears an automatically generated description of a news photo, such as two children building a sandcastle on a beach.
gl.goruntu-altyazilama.faq.0.a: No. Captioning describes an image in general terms. In visual question answering, the user asks a specific question about the image and the model answers that question.
gl.goruntu-altyazilama.faq.0.q: Is image captioning the same as visual question answering?
gl.goruntu-altyazilama.faq.1.a: They are often accurate and useful, but models can sometimes add objects or details that are not there. For important decisions, the description should be checked against the image.
gl.goruntu-altyazilama.how: The model first turns the image into a numerical representation that captures objects, actions and setting. A language model then reads that representation and writes the description word by word. Training uses images paired with descriptions written by people. Today, multimodal large models that process images and text together can write both a short caption and a detailed description. These models can sometimes invent a detail that is not in the picture.
gl.goruntu-altyazilama.why: Providing automatic alternative text for blind and low-vision users, searching large photo archives and making social media content more accessible are the main uses of captioning. Wrong or invented descriptions can mislead, especially in areas like news and health, so human review matters.
gl.goruntu-bolutleme.def: A computer vision task that divides an image into meaningful parts by labeling every pixel according to the object or region it belongs to.
gl.goruntu-bolutleme.example: When taking a portrait-mode photo, the phone separates the person's silhouette, including strands of hair, so it can blur the background.
gl.goruntu-bolutleme.faq.0.a: Object detection draws a box around an object. Segmentation identifies the pixels the object covers one by one, so it gives a far more detailed shape.
gl.goruntu-bolutleme.faq.0.q: How is image segmentation different from object detection?
gl.goruntu-bolutleme.faq.1.a: Semantic segmentation only says which class a pixel belongs to. Instance segmentation also counts and marks objects of the same class separately.
gl.goruntu-bolutleme.faq.1.q: What is the difference between semantic and instance segmentation?
gl.goruntu-bolutleme.how: Instead of drawing a box, it extracts the exact outline of an object. Semantic segmentation assigns each pixel to a class (road, sky, person) but does not tell apart separate objects of the same class. Instance segmentation marks each object of the same type individually, for example finding three pedestrians as three separate pieces. The model is trained on hand-painted masks and outputs a mask the same size as the image. General-purpose systems such as Meta's Segment Anything model can separate an object from just a click.
gl.goruntu-bolutleme.why: Outlining a tumor in medical imaging, separating fields and buildings in satellite images, and removing a background in photo editing all call for pixel-level accuracy. Robots also need to know an object's shape to grasp it. That is why segmentation is used where drawing a box is not enough.
gl.goruntu-siniflandirma.def: The task of assigning an image to one of a set of predefined categories, such as deciding whether a photo shows a cat or a dog.
gl.goruntu-siniflandirma.example: A phone's photo app automatically sorts the gallery into groups like food, landscapes and pets.
gl.goruntu-siniflandirma.faq.0.a: Classic models cannot. However, some models that learned images and text together can guess classes whose labels they never saw by reading the text description of the category. This is called zero-shot classification.
gl.goruntu-siniflandirma.faq.0.q: Can a model recognize a category it never saw during training?
gl.goruntu-siniflandirma.faq.1.a: Classification produces a single label for the whole image. Object detection also finds where each object is, so it is better suited to scenes with several objects.
gl.goruntu-siniflandirma.faq.1.q: How is image classification different from object detection?
gl.goruntu-siniflandirma.how: During training, the model sees many labeled images. Convolutional neural networks or vision transformers extract features, first picking up simple patterns such as edges and textures, then more complex parts and shapes. The final layer outputs a probability for each category, and the label with the highest probability is chosen. The model does not say where the object is in the picture; it only makes an overall decision about the image as a whole.
gl.goruntu-siniflandirma.why: Image classification is the most basic computer vision task, and early successes of deep learning came from it. It is used in areas from sorting X-ray scans in medicine and spotting diseased leaves in farming to content moderation and organizing photo archives. Imbalances and biases in the training data can lead to wrong results.
gl.goruntu-tanima.def: The ability of an AI system to identify and label objects, faces, text or scenes in a photo or video frame. It is one of the most basic applications of computer vision.
gl.goruntu-tanima.example: When a camera watches products on a factory conveyor belt and removes scratched or broken parts, that is a typical real-world use of image recognition.
gl.goruntu-tanima.faq.0.a: No. Facial recognition is a subfield of image recognition that focuses only on human faces. Image recognition covers a much wider range, such as animals, road signs or damaged products.
gl.goruntu-tanima.faq.0.q: Is image recognition the same as facial recognition?
gl.goruntu-tanima.faq.1.a: Yes. Lighting, camera angle and image quality can all lower accuracy, and a model may also fail on situations it rarely saw during training. For this reason, results in critical areas are usually checked by a human.
gl.goruntu-tanima.faq.1.q: Can image recognition models make mistakes?
gl.goruntu-tanima.how: The system is trained on a large number of labeled images. Deep learning models, especially convolutional neural networks and vision transformers, process the pixels layer by layer. They first pick up simple patterns such as edges and colors, then parts such as an eye or a wheel, and finally the whole object. The output can be a label for the whole image, the position of an object within the frame, or a pixel-level separation of regions. The more varied the training data, the more robust the model tends to be.
gl.goruntu-tanima.why: Image recognition underpins products ranging from medical image analysis and quality control to self-driving cars and phone photo galleries. Its mistakes can have serious consequences, because accuracy may drop for groups that are underrepresented in the training data. That is why applications such as face recognition sit at the center of both technical and legal debates.
gl.goruntu-yukseltme.def: A method that increases the pixel count of a low-resolution image and uses AI to predict the missing detail, producing a larger and sharper version.
gl.goruntu-yukseltme.example: A family’s scanned old passport photo can be run through an upscaler to produce a sharper print large enough to hang on a wall.
gl.goruntu-yukseltme.faq.0.a: No, it does not recover it; it predicts detail based on what the model has learned. The result may look realistic but may not match the original scene exactly.
gl.goruntu-yukseltme.faq.0.q: Does upscaling really recover lost detail?
gl.goruntu-yukseltme.faq.1.a: Ordinary enlargement just duplicates and smooths pixels. AI upscaling regenerates detail such as texture and edges from learned patterns.
gl.goruntu-yukseltme.faq.1.q: How is it different from ordinary enlargement?
gl.goruntu-yukseltme.how: Traditional enlargement methods duplicate existing pixels and average the gaps between them, which usually leaves the result blurry. AI-based methods train a model on pairs of low- and high-resolution images so it learns how fabric, hair or text should look when enlarged. When it runs, it does not recover missing detail from real data; it makes a plausible prediction based on what it has learned. As a result, the added sharpness can include details that were not in the original.
gl.goruntu-yukseltme.why: It is used for restoring old photos, improving low-resolution video and preparing images for print. In gaming, technologies such as Nvidia’s DLSS upscale an image rendered at lower resolution to improve smoothness. It is worth remembering that predicted detail may not be real, especially in sensitive areas such as faces and text.
gl.goruntuden-video-uretimi.def: An AI approach that takes an existing photo or picture as a starting point and animates it into a short video. The motion is often steered with an additional text prompt.
gl.goruntuden-video-uretimi.example: If a product photo is uploaded with the instruction 'let the camera slowly orbit the product', the image can become a short promotional clip of a few seconds.
gl.goruntuden-video-uretimi.faq.0.a: In text-to-video, everything comes from the prompt. In image-to-video, the starting image largely fixes how the scene looks, and the model mainly adds the motion.
gl.goruntuden-video-uretimi.faq.0.q: How does image-to-video differ from text-to-video?
gl.goruntuden-video-uretimi.faq.1.a: If done without the person's permission, it can raise serious problems of reputation, personal rights and fake content. Rules differ from country to country, and many platforms have policies restricting such uses.
gl.goruntuden-video-uretimi.faq.1.q: Is it a problem to make a video from a person's photo?
gl.goruntuden-video-uretimi.how: The user uploads an image, and the model treats it as the video's first frame or main reference. It then generates the following frames while preserving the look of the objects, people and setting in the image. The prompt can add directions such as 'pull the camera back' or 'let the leaves sway in the wind'. In text-to-video, the model's imagination largely decides the look, whereas here most of the appearance is fixed from the start, which gives more control.
gl.goruntuden-video-uretimi.why: Because it works with material that already exists, such as a product photo, an illustration or a portrait, it gives designers and advertisers more control. On the other hand, animating a real person's photo without permission raises issues of consent, reputation and fake content.
gl.gpqa.def: A set of graduate-level multiple-choice questions in biology, physics and chemistry, written by experts and designed so that a simple web search will not solve them. It tests deep scientific reasoning in AI models.
gl.gpqa.example: A model answers a multiple-choice question about molecular biology, and the share of correct picks across the set forms its GPQA score.
gl.gpqa.faq.0.a: MMLU covers a broad range of subjects, mostly at textbook level. GPQA focuses on three sciences and offers much harder, expert-written questions.
gl.gpqa.faq.0.q: How is GPQA different from MMLU?
gl.gpqa.faq.1.a: It means the answers cannot be found easily with a basic web search. The aim is for the answer to come from reasoning rather than lookup.
gl.gpqa.how: Questions are written by people who hold or are pursuing a PhD in the relevant field and are checked by other experts. 'Google-proof' means that even a skilled person from outside the field struggles to find the right answer by searching the web. The model answers each multiple-choice question, and the score is the share answered correctly. The dataset was released in 2023, and its hardest subset, called 'Diamond,' is often cited in the news.
gl.gpqa.why: When general tests like MMLU became saturated, researchers turned to harder benchmarks, and GPQA is one of them. A high score is read as a sign that a model is nearing expert-level performance on scientific questions. Still, the number of questions is relatively small, and the multiple-choice format does not fully reflect real scientific work.
gl.gpt-mimarisi.def: A Transformer-based, decoder-only design and model family developed by OpenAI, pretrained on a broad body of text and then adapted to many tasks. The name stands for Generative Pre-trained Transformer.
gl.gpt-mimarisi.example: The GPT in ChatGPT points to the underlying family of models, while the chat interface is a product built on top of those models.
gl.gpt-mimarisi.faq.0.a: No. GPT is a family of models, whereas ChatGPT is a chat product that uses those models.
gl.gpt-mimarisi.faq.0.q: Are GPT and ChatGPT the same thing?
gl.gpt-mimarisi.faq.1.a: No. Models from other organizations, such as Llama, use a similar architecture, but the GPT name belongs to OpenAI's model family. Phrases like 'GPT-style' are sometimes used for the architecture type, which can cause confusion.
gl.gpt-mimarisi.faq.1.q: Is every decoder-only model a GPT?
gl.gpt-mimarisi.how: The three words summarize the design. Generative: the model produces text. Pre-trained: it first learns to predict the next token from a broad collection of text. Transformer: the underlying structure is built on the attention mechanism. The first GPT was introduced in 2018, and later versions scaled up the model, the data and the computing power. Chat products add further training steps, such as fine-tuning with human feedback.
gl.gpt-mimarisi.why: The GPT architecture made concrete the idea that language models gain new skills as they scale, and it became widely known through ChatGPT. Today the name GPT is sometimes used loosely for this whole type of design, yet it is also an OpenAI model name, so it helps to check which sense a news story means.
gl.gpu-bulutu.def: Newer cloud providers that focus on renting out GPUs for AI workloads, selling high-performance computing capacity rather than the broad range of services offered by the large cloud companies.
gl.gpu-bulutu.example: An AI startup with no data center of its own might rent hundreds of GPUs from a neocloud provider for several months to train its model.
gl.gpu-bulutu.faq.0.a: The big cloud companies offer a very wide range of services, from storage to databases. Neocloud providers focus mainly on GPU capacity suited to AI workloads.
gl.gpu-bulutu.faq.0.q: How is a neocloud different from AWS, Azure or Google Cloud?
gl.gpu-bulutu.faq.1.a: AI demand surged while GPU capacity was limited. New players focused on GPUs were able to respond to that demand quickly.
gl.gpu-bulutu.how: Neocloud companies buy large numbers of accelerators such as Nvidia GPUs, set them up in clusters in data centers and rent them to customers by the hour or under long-term contracts. Their services are mostly tuned for AI training and inference, and they do not offer a wide product catalog of storage, databases and the like. Companies building models can rent this capacity instead of constructing their own data centers. CoreWeave and Lambda are examples of companies mentioned in this category.
gl.gpu-bulutu.why: Access to GPUs is a critical bottleneck for AI companies, and neoclouds stood out because they could fill that gap quickly. At the same time, the business model needs heavy capital and depends on a small number of hardware suppliers, which fuels risk debates in the news.
gl.gpu-kumesi.def: A setup in which the GPUs in many servers, linked by a high-speed network, are run together as if they were one large pool of computing power.
gl.gpu-kumesi.example: An AI company training a new language model links thousands of GPUs on one network in its data center and runs them as a single job.
gl.gpu-kumesi.faq.0.a: Yes. Cloud providers rent out GPUs by the hour or on longer terms, so companies can use a cluster without buying hardware.
gl.gpu-kumesi.faq.0.q: Can the cloud be used to build a GPU cluster?
gl.gpu-kumesi.faq.1.a: Usually not. As data exchange and synchronization between GPUs grow, efficiency is lost, which is why network quality matters so much.
gl.gpu-kumesi.faq.1.q: Does speed rise proportionally as GPUs are added?
gl.gpu-kumesi.how: In a GPU cluster, each server holds a few GPUs, and the servers are joined by networks such as InfiniBand or fast Ethernet. When a model is trained, pieces of the data or the model are spread across the GPUs, each GPU computes its share, and the results are synchronized at regular intervals. Scheduling software manages this work by deciding which job uses which GPUs. A cluster's efficiency depends not only on the number of GPUs but also on the speed of the network and memory.
gl.gpu-kumesi.why: Training large AI models on a single GPU is not practical, which is why clusters sit at the center of AI investment. News stories often cite the number of GPUs a company has assembled as a sign of its competitive strength. Cost, energy use and cooling are the main challenges of such systems.

gl.gpu.def.en: A processor originally designed for graphics that is used in AI training and inference because it can perform many calculations at once. Nvidia is the market leader.

gl.gpu.example.en: Nvidia's data center GPUs are used in most of the world's AI servers.

gl.gpu.faq.0.a.en: AI computations consist of many simple multiplications and additions that can be done at the same time. With thousands of cores, GPUs perform these tasks in parallel and run much faster than CPUs.

gl.gpu.faq.0.q.en: Why are GPUs used for AI?

gl.gpu.faq.1.a.en: Small, quantized models can also run on a CPU, but a GPU with enough memory noticeably increases speed.

gl.gpu.faq.1.q.en: Do you need a GPU to run an AI model at home?

gl.gpu.how.en: A GPU is a processor designed for parallel computation by running thousands of small processing units at the same time. Because training and running AI models rely on a large number of matrix multiplications performed simultaneously, GPUs have become ideal for the job. Data center GPUs work with high-bandwidth memory (HBM).

gl.gpu.why.en: GPU supply is one of the most important constraints determining how fast AI companies can grow. That is why GPU sales, export restrictions and new chip announcements are at the center of the AI agenda.

gl.gradyan-artirma.def: An ensemble method that adds small decision trees one after another, with each new tree trying to correct the errors of the ones before it. XGBoost is a fast, widely used implementation of the idea.
gl.gradyan-artirma.example: An online store could train an XGBoost model to predict whether a customer will return an order.
gl.gradyan-artirma.faq.0.a: In a random forest the trees are built independently and their predictions are combined. In gradient boosting the trees are built one after another, and each focuses on fixing the mistakes of the earlier ones.
gl.gradyan-artirma.faq.0.q: What is the difference between gradient boosting and a random forest?
gl.gradyan-artirma.faq.1.a: Not exactly. Gradient boosting is the method, while XGBoost is a fast, tunable software implementation of it. Similar libraries such as LightGBM and CatBoost also exist.
gl.gradyan-artirma.faq.1.q: Is XGBoost the same as gradient boosting?
gl.gradyan-artirma.how: The process starts with a simple prediction. The model then measures how far its predictions are from the true values and works out the direction that would reduce that error, which is the gradient. A new small tree is trained to learn exactly those remaining errors and is added to the model with a small weight. This repeats hundreds of times, and each round closes the gap a little more. It resembles a golfer adjusting each shot according to the distance the ball still has to travel. Unlike a random forest, the trees are built in sequence rather than independently.
gl.gradyan-artirma.why: On tabular data, gradient boosting methods have long been among the strongest options and are popular in data science competitions. They are common in business uses such as fraud detection, credit scoring and demand forecasting. Even though language and image models get most of the attention, these methods carry a large share of companies' everyday prediction work.
gl.gradyan-inisi.def: The basic optimization method that lowers a model's error by nudging its parameters in small steps opposite to the direction in which the error rises fastest. Most neural networks are trained with variants of it.
gl.gradyan-inisi.example: A spam filter at first confuses junk mail with regular mail; after each mistake its weights are adjusted slightly, and after thousands of examples its error rate drops noticeably.
gl.gradyan-inisi.faq.0.a: No. It can get stuck in local dips or flat regions. In large neural networks, though, it usually reaches solutions that are good enough in practice.
gl.gradyan-inisi.faq.0.q: Does gradient descent always find the best solution?
gl.gradyan-inisi.faq.1.a: It is the version that computes the gradient on a small random chunk of data instead of the whole dataset. Updates are faster and need less memory, at the cost of being somewhat noisier.
gl.gradyan-inisi.how: The model first makes predictions on training data, and a loss function turns its error into a single number. Backpropagation then works out how much each parameter contributed to that error, which is the gradient. Each parameter takes a step against the gradient, with the step size set by the learning rate. This loop repeats thousands of times. It resembles someone walking down a foggy valley who only feels the slope underfoot and always steps downhill; they cannot be sure they have reached the bottom, but they keep descending.
gl.gradyan-inisi.why: Nearly every neural network in the news, from large language models to image generators, is trained on this principle. How long training takes, how much computing power it needs and whether the model reaches a good result all depend heavily on how the method is applied. Behind the phrase 'the model was trained' there is usually this loop.
gl.grafik-sinir-agi.def: A neural network that processes data shaped as a network of nodes connected by edges. Each node updates its own representation using information from its neighbors.
gl.grafik-sinir-agi.example: A candidate drug molecule is given to a GNN with atoms as nodes and bonds as edges, and the model tries to predict whether the molecule has a certain property.
gl.grafik-sinir-agi.faq.0.a: No. It refers to the mathematical notion of a graph, a structure of nodes and edges. It has nothing to do with a visual chart (the Turkish term “grafik” is used here, though “çizge” is also common).
gl.grafik-sinir-agi.faq.0.q: Does “graph” here mean a chart or a drawing?
gl.grafik-sinir-agi.faq.1.a: A CNN works through neighborhoods in data laid out on a regular grid, like image pixels. A GNN generalizes that idea to network-shaped data where neighborhoods are irregular.
gl.grafik-sinir-agi.faq.1.q: How are GNNs related to CNNs?
gl.grafik-sinir-agi.how: The data is first described as a graph: in a molecule, atoms are nodes and chemical bonds are edges; in a social network, people are nodes and friendships are edges. In each round, every node collects messages from its neighbors, combines them and updates its own list of numbers. After a few rounds, a node's representation reflects not just itself but the structure around it. These representations are then used for tasks such as classifying nodes, predicting links or assessing the whole graph.
gl.grafik-sinir-agi.why: Much real-world data comes as networks: molecules, road systems, knowledge graphs, user relationships. Because GNNs can use this structure without flattening it, they matter in areas such as drug discovery, materials research and recommendation systems.
gl.graphrag.def: A variant of retrieval-augmented generation that also draws on a knowledge graph extracted from documents, giving the model the relationships between entities along with the relevant text.
gl.graphrag.example: When asked which suppliers in a company's hundreds of contracts are linked through shared subsidiaries, the system can answer by moving through the network of relationships.
gl.graphrag.faq.0.a: Classic RAG usually finds text passages similar to the question and hands them to the model. GraphRAG additionally uses a graph of relationships between entities, which helps answer questions that need connected information.
gl.graphrag.faq.0.q: What is the difference between GraphRAG and classic RAG?
gl.graphrag.faq.1.a: No. If questions can be answered from information in a single document, classic RAG is often enough and much cheaper. GraphRAG makes sense when relationships and the big picture matter.
gl.graphrag.how: First, entities and the relationships between them are extracted from documents, often with a language model, and a graph is built from the results. In some implementations, tightly connected nodes are grouped into communities and a summary of each community is prepared. When a question arrives, the relevant nodes and their neighbors, and sometimes community summaries, are retrieved. These are given to the model as context together with the relevant text passages. The term became widespread through work published by Microsoft Research; details vary from one implementation to another.
gl.graphrag.why: Classic RAG is good at finding a few relevant passages but can struggle to pull together relationships spread across many documents. GraphRAG aims to do better on multi-step questions and questions about a whole data set. The trade-off is that building and maintaining the graph can be costly and complex.
gl.grokking.def: A phenomenon in which a neural network that has long since memorized its training data suddenly starts giving correct answers on new data after much more training.
gl.grokking.example: A small network learning modular addition may memorize the sums it was trained on, then thousands of steps later begin answering sums it has never seen correctly.
gl.grokking.faq.0.a: No. In overfitting, a model memorizes the training data and fails on new data. In grokking, generalization appears later, after the memorization phase, if training continues.
gl.grokking.faq.0.q: Is grokking the same as overfitting?
gl.grokking.faq.1.a: It has been shown most clearly on small, rule-based tasks. Some studies point to similar delayed-learning patterns in larger models, but how far it applies is still being researched.
gl.grokking.faq.1.q: Does grokking happen in large language models too?
gl.grokking.how: Early in training, the model memorizes the examples: training error approaches zero, but performance on unseen data stays poor. As training continues, especially with regularization such as weight decay, the network slowly shifts from the memorizing solution to a simpler, more general one. From the outside, this shows up as a sudden jump in test accuracy. The effect was first observed on small algorithmic tasks such as modular addition.
gl.grokking.why: Grokking suggests that stopping training as soon as overfitting appears is not always the right call. It is a frequently cited example in interpretability research, which tries to understand what models learn inside and when they learn it. How far it applies to large language models is still debated.
gl.grup-goreli-politika-optimizasyonu.de: A reinforcement learning algorithm that generates several answers per prompt and learns by comparing each answer to the group's average, without needing a separate value model.
gl.grup-goreli-politika-optimizasyonu.ex: If three of eight solutions to a math problem reach the right answer, those three score above the group average, and the model becomes more inclined toward that kind of solution.
gl.grup-goreli-politika-optimizasyonu.fa: PPO uses a separate value model to estimate the expected reward of answers. GRPO instead uses the average score of the answers given to the same question as its reference.
What is the main difference between GRPO and PPO?
It was introduced in a math paper and is often mentioned alongside verifiable rewards. But it can be applied to any task where answers can be scored, even if the reward comes from a reward model.
Is GRPO only used for areas like math?
gl.grup-goreli-politika-optimizasyonu.ho: The model produces, say, eight different answers to the same question at once. Each answer gets a reward, and its score is then compared with the group average. Answers above the average are reinforced and those below it are discouraged. Because the group average does the job of PPO's separate value model, training saves memory and compute. A constraint that keeps the model from drifting too far from its starting point is still used.
gl.grup-goreli-politika-optimizasyonu.wh: The DeepSeek team introduced the method in 2024 in its math-focused DeepSeekMath work and later used it to train the reasoning model DeepSeek-R1. Being lighter made reinforcement learning with large models more accessible, and the method now appears in open-source training tools too.
gl.gruplanmis-sorgu-dikkati.def: A variant of multi-head attention in which query heads are split into groups and each group shares a single key-value head. It largely preserves quality while cutting memory use and the time it takes to generate responses.
gl.gruplanmis-sorgu-dikkati.example: In a chat service answering thousands of users at once, a model that uses GQA can hold each conversation's cache in less memory.
gl.gruplanmis-sorgu-dikkati.faq.0.a: In multi-head attention, each query head has its own key and value head. In GQA, a group of query heads shares one key-value head, which reduces the memory load.
gl.gruplanmis-sorgu-dikkati.faq.0.q: What is the difference between GQA and multi-head attention?
gl.gruplanmis-sorgu-dikkati.faq.1.a: There can be a small loss in quality, and the method is designed to keep that loss to a minimum. The effect varies with the model's architecture and training.
gl.gruplanmis-sorgu-dikkati.faq.1.q: Does GQA reduce a model's accuracy?
gl.gruplanmis-sorgu-dikkati.how: In standard multi-head attention, every query head has its own key and value head. In grouped-query attention, query heads are divided into groups and the heads in a group use the same key-value pair. The extreme case where all heads share one key-value pair is known as multi-query attention, and GQA offers a middle path between the two. During text generation, the stored key-value cache gets smaller, which eases memory pressure and speeds up generation.
gl.gruplanmis-sorgu-dikkati.why: When large language models generate responses, much of the memory burden comes from the key-value cache, and long contexts and many simultaneous users make it heavier. GQA allows longer context and higher throughput on the same hardware at a small cost in quality. That is why it is often cited among the architectural choices of current large language models.
gl.gsm8k.def: A test set of about 8,500 grade-school-level math word problems, released by OpenAI researchers in 2021. It is used to measure how well language models handle multi-step arithmetic reasoning.
gl.gsm8k.example: If a model reads 'Ayşe has 12 pencils, gives 5 to a friend, and then gets 3 more. How many does she have?' and works its way to 10, the answer counts as correct.
gl.gsm8k.faq.0.a: No. The problems are fairly simple, and test questions may have leaked into training data. A high score shows solid basic arithmetic and step-by-step reasoning; advanced math needs harder tests.
gl.gsm8k.faq.0.q: Does a high GSM8K score mean a model is an expert at math?
gl.gsm8k.faq.1.a: GSM8K is built on basic arithmetic and everyday problems. AIME consists of far harder, competition-level questions that call for creative solutions.
gl.gsm8k.faq.1.q: How is GSM8K different from AIME?
gl.gsm8k.how: Each problem is written as a short story and has a solution of two to eight steps using basic arithmetic. The model answers the question, and its final number is compared with the correct answer; intermediate steps usually do not count toward the score. When the model is asked to write out its solution step by step (chain-of-thought prompting), results improve noticeably. The set is split into training and test portions, with roughly a thousand test problems.
gl.gsm8k.why: GSM8K was the standard yardstick for comparing the mathematical reasoning of large language models for a long time. Strong models now score very high on it, so it separates them less well, and harder tests have taken its place. It is still often cited as a check that a model has the basics down.
gl.guc-anlasmasi.def: A contract between an electricity generator and a buyer under which a set amount of power is sold over the long term on pre-agreed terms. Data center companies use PPAs to secure energy.
gl.guc-anlasmasi.example: A cloud company signs a PPA lasting many years with a planned solar plant, committing to buy electricity equal to its data centers' consumption from that plant.
gl.guc-anlasmasi.faq.0.a: With a normal subscription, a customer buys power at the supplier's tariff. A PPA is usually a long-term, special contract tied to a specific generating plant, with price terms negotiated up front.
gl.guc-anlasmasi.faq.0.q: How does a PPA differ from a normal electricity subscription?
gl.guc-anlasmasi.faq.1.a: It is a PPA in which electricity is not physically delivered to the buyer; the parties only settle the price difference financially. The buyer can still support a plant's output this way.
gl.guc-anlasmasi.how: The buyer commits to purchasing electricity from, say, a wind or solar plant for many years under an agreed pricing mechanism. The generator's guaranteed revenue makes it easier to finance the plant. A PPA can be physical, meaning the electricity is delivered directly, or virtual, meaning the parties settle financially on the price difference only. The details vary by country and market regulation.
gl.guc-anlasmasi.why: AI data centers consume very large amounts of electricity around the clock. A PPA makes costs more predictable and lets a company show that it sources energy from low-carbon sources such as renewables or nuclear. That is why big tech companies' power plant deals appear so often in the news.
gl.guc-kullanim-etkinligi.def: An efficiency metric calculated as a data center's total energy use divided by the energy used by its computing equipment alone. The closer the value is to 1, the more efficient the facility is considered.
gl.guc-kullanim-etkinligi.example: A facility with a PUE of 1.2 uses roughly 20 extra kilowatt-hours of overhead for every 100 kilowatt-hours its servers consume.
gl.guc-kullanim-etkinligi.faq.0.a: Not necessarily. PUE only shows the share of non-computing overhead. Whether the electricity is renewable, how much water is used, and how efficient the servers themselves are do not enter the metric.
gl.guc-kullanim-etkinligi.faq.0.q: Is a data center with a low PUE environmentally friendly?
gl.guc-kullanim-etkinligi.faq.1.a: No. Total energy cannot be smaller than the energy used by the computing equipment, so the ratio is at least 1. Real facilities always sit above that value.
gl.guc-kullanim-etkinligi.how: The facility's total electricity consumption is divided by the electricity used by servers, storage, and networking gear. The total includes overhead such as cooling, lighting, and power conversion losses. A value of 1.0 is the theoretical floor, meaning all energy goes straight to computing. A value of 1.5 means that for every unit of energy used for computing, another half unit goes to overhead. The figure is usually given as an annual average, since climate and season change cooling needs.
gl.guc-kullanim-etkinligi.why: As the electricity demand of AI data centers grows, PUE is one of the most widely used indicators of how much energy goes to the actual work. But it only measures facility overhead; it says nothing about chip efficiency, where the electricity comes from, or water use. That limit matters when comparing facilities.
gl.gurultu-giderme.def: The process of removing unwanted distortions from an image, audio clip or other data to recover the clean content underneath. In AI, it is usually done by trained neural networks.
gl.gurultu-giderme.example: A dark, grainy night-time phone photo is smoothed out by AI while its fine details are preserved.
gl.gurultu-giderme.faq.0.a: No. Simple blurring removes fine detail along with the noise. Learned denoising models try to keep edges and textures while stripping out the noise.
gl.gurultu-giderme.faq.0.q: Is denoising the same as blurring?
gl.gurultu-giderme.faq.1.a: Diffusion models are trained by learning to remove noise. When generating, they turn random noise into a new image by cleaning it up step by step.
gl.gurultu-giderme.faq.1.q: How is denoising related to diffusion models?
gl.gurultu-giderme.how: During training, a model is shown clean examples along with copies that have artificial noise added, and it learns to restore the originals. In the process it picks up the typical patterns of noise and what clean data tends to look like. At use time, a noisy image or recording goes in, and the model estimates the noise and subtracts it. Diffusion models push this idea to the extreme: they start from pure noise and clean it up step by step to generate a brand-new image.
gl.gurultu-giderme.why: Photos taken in low light, noisy meeting recordings and medical scans all suffer from noise, and denoising makes such data usable. Phone cameras, video-call apps and imaging devices rely on it. Because image-generating diffusion models are built on the same idea, the term comes up often in AI news.
gl.guven-skoru.def: A number showing how certain an AI model is about a prediction it has made. It is usually given between zero and one, or as a percentage.
gl.guven-skoru.example: If an invoice-reading system reads a total with a confidence of 0.62, the document can be sent to an employee for checking instead of being processed automatically.
gl.guven-skoru.faq.0.a: Not always. If the model is well calibrated, it is roughly true, but many models appear more certain than they actually are.
gl.guven-skoru.faq.0.q: Does a 90 percent confidence score mean the prediction is 90 percent likely to be correct?
gl.guven-skoru.faq.1.a: Models compute a probability for each token, and these values are used in some applications. They do not guarantee that an answer is correct, though, since a model can produce something false with high probability.
gl.guven-skoru.faq.1.q: Do language models have confidence scores?
gl.guven-skoru.how: A classification model calculates a probability-like value for each possible class, and the highest value is usually reported as the confidence score. Applications set a threshold: if the score is above it, the result is accepted automatically, and if it is below, the case is routed to a person. But the score does not always reflect the true probability of being correct, since models can be overconfident. Adjustments known as calibration are used to bring scores in line with real accuracy. With language models, too, a fluent answer can sound certain and still be wrong.
gl.guven-skoru.why: Confidence scores make it possible to divide work between people and machines: easy cases are handled automatically, while uncertain ones go to an expert. A poorly calibrated score can create a false sense of security. So when reading a score, it also helps to know how well the model is calibrated.
gl.guvenlik-siniflandiricisi.def: A small AI model, usually separate from the main model, that decides whether a piece of text, an image or a conversation falls into a harmful category.
gl.guvenlik-siniflandiricisi.example: A chat app can run a model's reply through a classifier before showing it to the user, and block the reply if the classifier judges it harmful.
gl.guvenlik-siniflandiricisi.faq.0.a: Yes. It can flag harmless content as harmful or miss a real violation. That is why thresholds are tuned and human review is added for critical cases.
gl.guvenlik-siniflandiricisi.faq.0.q: Can a safety classifier make mistakes?
gl.guvenlik-siniflandiricisi.faq.1.a: A separate model works independently of the main one, which makes it harder to trick. It also focuses on a single task, so it is fast and inexpensive, and can be updated even when the main model changes.
gl.guvenlik-siniflandiricisi.faq.1.q: Why use a separate model for safety checks?
gl.guvenlik-siniflandiricisi.how: A classifier is trained on many examples labeled harmful or harmless. At run time it takes the content and produces a risk score for categories such as violence, hate speech or self-harm. If the score passes a set threshold, the system can block the content, show a warning or route it to human review. Both the user's message and the model's reply can be checked this way. A lower threshold catches more harmful content but also produces more false alarms.
gl.guvenlik-siniflandiricisi.why: Adding a separate checking layer is more robust than trusting the main model to police itself. Classifiers are fast and cheap, so they are common in high-volume systems. Because they can make mistakes, their accuracy and fairness need to be measured continuously.
gl.hakem-olarak-llm.def: A method in which one language model, usually a strong one, scores or compares the outputs of another. It offers a cheaper and faster option than human evaluation.
gl.hakem-olarak-llm.example: A team has another model decide which of two summaries is more faithful to the source text across hundreds of examples, then has people check a small sample of those verdicts.
gl.hakem-olarak-llm.faq.0.a: Not fully. It is fast and scalable, but the judge model has its own biases and errors. It is usually backed up by human evaluation and periodically checked against it.
gl.hakem-olarak-llm.faq.0.q: Can an LLM judge replace human evaluation?
gl.hakem-olarak-llm.faq.1.a: Common ones include preferring longer answers, being influenced by the order in which answers are shown, and favoring answers produced by themselves or by similar models.
gl.hakem-olarak-llm.faq.1.q: What biases can judge models show?
gl.hakem-olarak-llm.how: The judge model is given the evaluation criteria and the response to review. It either assigns the response a score or picks which of two responses is better and writes out its reasoning. This lets thousands of outputs be assessed in a short time. The method has known weaknesses: judge models can favor longer answers, answers that resemble their own style, or whichever answer comes first. So criteria are written clearly, the order of answers is shuffled, and results are checked against human ratings on a sample.
gl.hakem-olarak-llm.why: Open-ended answers cannot be graded with simple right-or-wrong checks, and human evaluation is slow and expensive. LLM-as-a-judge fills that gap, which is why it is widely used for testing chatbots and AI agents. If its biases are ignored, though, it can give misleading results.
gl.halka-arz.def: The first time a private company sells its shares to the general public on a stock exchange, making it a publicly listed company whose shares can be freely bought and sold.
gl.halka-arz.example: Chip design company Arm went public on Nasdaq in 2023, and its shares have since been open to anyone to buy and sell.
gl.halka-arz.faq.0.a: An IPO is the first sale of shares to the broad public, while listing means the shares start trading on an exchange. In practice the two usually happen together and are mentioned together.
gl.halka-arz.faq.0.q: Is an IPO the same as being listed on a stock exchange?
gl.halka-arz.faq.1.a: There is no guarantee. The share price can rise or fall in the first days. This is not investment advice; every investment carries risk.
gl.halka-arz.faq.1.q: Do investors who buy in an IPO make money?
gl.halka-arz.how: The company first works with an investment bank, preparing official documents that describe its finances and risks and submitting them to the market regulator. After approval, a price range is set, demand is gathered from investors and shares are sold at the final price. The shares then begin trading on the exchange. The company can raise new money through the sale, and existing owners may sell part of their stakes. Being public also brings ongoing financial reporting obligations.
gl.halka-arz.why: AI companies need enormous amounts of capital, so an IPO is one of the main ways to raise money and give early investors an exit. IPO news reflects how much the market trusts a sector. Because the company's books become public, its revenue, profit and risks can be examined in detail for the first time.

gl.halusinasyon.def.en: When an AI model confidently produces information that does not exist in reality, presenting it as true.

gl.halusinasyon.example.en: A model citing a court ruling that does not exist as a source is a typical hallucination.

gl.halusinasyon.faq.0.a.en: Language models are trained to generate the most likely continuation rather than to check accuracy. Even on a topic it doesn't know, a model can produce a fluent, confident-sounding answer.

gl.halusinasyon.faq.0.q.en: Why does AI make up false information?

gl.halusinasyon.faq.1.a.en: Effective methods include asking the model to cite sources, supplying reliable documents as context (RAG), using web search, and verifying important information against independent sources.

gl.halusinasyon.how.en: Language models generate the text that appears most likely based on the patterns they have learned; they do not check a database to verify a fact. On topics they don't know or have seen little of, they can produce names, dates, sources or figures that sound right but do not exist.

gl.halusinasyon.why.en: In fields such as law, healthcare, finance and journalism, fabricated information can cause serious harm. To reduce the rate, companies connect models to web search, add citation features and measure hallucination rates with benchmarks.

gl.hata-odulu-programi.def: A program in which an organization rewards outside researchers, with money or other benefits, for finding security flaws in its software and systems and reporting them responsibly.
gl.hata-odulu-programi.example: An AI company might offer a reward to a researcher who finds a way around its model's safety measures and reports it responsibly.
gl.hata-odulu-programi.faq.0.a: No. Cash is common, but some programs offer public thanks, a place on a hall-of-fame list or gifts. The amount and form are set in the program's rules.
gl.hata-odulu-programi.faq.1.a: No. Testing should stay within the scope and rules the program allows. Unauthorized or out-of-scope attempts can lead to legal trouble.
gl.hata-odulu-programi.faq.1.q: Can anyone test any system and ask for a reward?
gl.hata-odulu-programi.how: The organization announces the program's scope, rules and reward ranges in advance. Researchers test the systems that are in scope and, if they find a flaw, report it through a private channel. The security team verifies the report, rates its severity, fixes the flaw and pays the reward. In AI, the scope can also cover model-level weaknesses such as ways around safety filters, prompt injection or data leakage. The flaw is not disclosed publicly until it has been fixed.
gl.hata-odulu-programi.why: No internal team can find every flaw alone, and thousands of outside eyes improve the chance of catching problems before attackers do. The program encourages people who find a flaw to report it instead of abusing it. As new attack types appear against AI systems, such programs are becoming more common in this field too.

gl.hbm.def.en: A special type of memory placed next to AI chips that transfers data at very high speeds. Because it is difficult to manufacture, it is a major bottleneck in AI servers.

gl.hbm.example.en: When a new AI chip is announced, the number of gigabytes of HBM it carries is among the most heavily emphasized specifications.

gl.hbm.faq.0.a.en: The speed of AI chips is often limited by how fast data can be moved to memory. HBM eases this bottleneck; because it is difficult to produce, its supply is also constrained.

gl.hbm.faq.1.a.en: The main producers are SK Hynix, Samsung and Micron.

gl.hbm.how.en: HBM is a type of memory in which memory chips are stacked vertically and placed right next to the processor. This design allows data to move much faster than with conventional memory. Because production requires advanced packaging technologies, only a small number of companies can make it.

gl.hbm.why.en: The performance of AI chips depends on how fast they can receive data. That is why HBM supply is a major bottleneck in AI servers, and investments by manufacturers such as Samsung, SK hynix and Micron are closely watched.

gl.hesaplama-esigi.def: A limit on the total amount of computation used to train an AI model. Under the EU AI Act, general-purpose models above this level are presumed to carry systemic risk and face heavier obligations.
gl.hesaplama-esigi.example: A company that spends more than the threshold on training a new general-purpose language model may have to notify the Commission and carry out risk assessments before offering it in the EU.
gl.hesaplama-esigi.faq.0.a: FLOP is the total number of operations performed, which describes the overall compute used in training. FLOPS is operations per second and describes the speed of hardware.
gl.hesaplama-esigi.faq.0.q: What is the difference between FLOP and FLOPS?
gl.hesaplama-esigi.faq.1.a: No. The threshold only marks where the presumption of systemic risk begins. Models below it still face the Act's other rules, and the Commission can designate a model as systemically risky using other criteria.
gl.hesaplama-esigi.faq.1.q: Is a model below the threshold considered risk-free?
gl.hesaplama-esigi.how: FLOP counts floating-point operations, meaning the total computation performed during a model's training. 10^25 is 10 to the power of 25, an enormous number that only the largest training runs reach. If a developer's training compute exceeds the threshold, the law presumes the model poses systemic risk. The developer must notify the European Commission, and extra duties follow, such as model evaluation, adversarial testing, serious incident reporting and cybersecurity measures. The Commission can update the threshold as technology changes.
gl.hesaplama-esigi.why: Training compute is a measurable proxy that regulators use to anticipate how capable a model might be. The threshold decides which models get stricter oversight. Critics argue that as efficiency improves, less compute can yield powerful models, so a single number may fall short.
gl.hesaplama-gucu.def: The total processing capacity needed to train and run AI models, usually described in terms of the number of chips, how fast they are and how long they run.
gl.hesaplama-gucu.example: Training a large language model can require many GPUs working together for weeks or months, and renting or buying that capacity is one of the biggest items in the budget.
gl.hesaplama-gucu.faq.0.a: In the industry and in news coverage the two are mostly used interchangeably. The term can describe either hardware capacity or the total amount of computation spent on a training run.
gl.hesaplama-gucu.faq.0.q: Is compute the same as computing power?
gl.hesaplama-gucu.faq.1.a: No. It usually helps, but data quality, model architecture and the training method also shape the result.
gl.hesaplama-gucu.faq.1.q: Does more compute always mean a better model?
gl.hesaplama-gucu.how: Training any model means carrying out billions upon billions of mathematical operations. These run on accelerator chips such as GPUs. Technically, compute is expressed in floating-point operations (FLOPs); in practice it is often described as how many chips ran for how long. Larger models and more data generally require more compute. Chip performance, the speed of links between chips and software efficiency also affect how much power is actually usable.
gl.hesaplama-gucu.why: Compute is treated as a basic resource for AI research and competition. Big companies' investments, chip export restrictions and data center deals largely revolve around access to it. But more efficient algorithms can reach the same result with fewer operations, so raw compute is not the only factor.
gl.hibrit-akil-yurutme-modeli.def: A single model that can either answer quickly and directly or work through a longer chain of thinking steps, with the choice of mode left to the user or developer.
gl.hibrit-akil-yurutme-modeli.example: As in some versions of Anthropic's Claude family, the same model can be used directly for quick chat or in an extended thinking mode for a hard coding question.
gl.hibrit-akil-yurutme-modeli.faq.0.a: A reasoning model always thinks at length before answering. In a hybrid model this behavior is optional, so the same model can work both with and without extended thinking.
gl.hibrit-akil-yurutme-modeli.faq.0.q: How is a hybrid model different from a reasoning model?
gl.hibrit-akil-yurutme-modeli.faq.1.a: No. The benefit is clearer for multi-step logic, math and coding. On simple questions accuracy often stays the same, and only time and cost go up.
gl.hibrit-akil-yurutme-modeli.faq.1.q: Does thinking mode always give more accurate results?
gl.hibrit-akil-yurutme-modeli.how: The model is trained both to answer directly and to think through intermediate steps before answering. A user or developer can switch the thinking mode on or off with a setting, and in some systems the amount of computation spent on thinking can also be set. When thinking is on, the model produces many intermediate steps before reaching a conclusion, which costs more computation and time. When it is off, the model replies to the question right away.
gl.hibrit-akil-yurutme-modeli.why: Not every question needs long deliberation. On simple tasks, thinking adds delay and unnecessary cost, while on hard math and coding problems it can improve accuracy. The hybrid approach removes the need to choose between two separate models and lets the user balance speed, cost and quality.
gl.hiper-olcekli-sirket.def: A technology company that operates huge worldwide networks of data centers, offers cloud services at enormous scale, and can expand its capacity quickly when needed.
gl.hiper-olcekli-sirket.example: Instead of building its own data center, a startup trains its model by renting GPUs from one of these companies.
gl.hiper-olcekli-sirket.faq.0.a: They often overlap. The term hyperscaler stresses scale, while cloud provider describes the service on offer. Not every cloud provider counts as a hyperscaler.
gl.hiper-olcekli-sirket.faq.0.q: Is a hyperscaler the same as a cloud provider?
gl.hiper-olcekli-sirket.faq.1.a: Amazon, Microsoft and Google are named most often. Other companies that run very large data centers, such as Meta, are also considered part of the group.
gl.hiper-olcekli-sirket.how: Hyperscalers manage thousands of servers in data centers they design themselves, and they put that capacity to use by renting it to customers or by running their own products on it. As scale grows, the cost per unit falls, so some of them also develop custom chips, networking hardware and software. Amazon Web Services, Microsoft Azure and Google Cloud are well-known examples of the group. They are often described as being among the largest buyers of AI hardware.
gl.hiper-olcekli-sirket.why: Training and serving AI models demands enormous computing capacity, so hyperscalers form the infrastructure backbone of the industry. Their spending decisions come up often in stories about chipmaker sales, energy demand and data center investment. Smaller startups frequently depend on their capacity.
gl.hiperparametre.def: A setting chosen by people before training begins that governs how the learning process runs. Unlike the weights learned from data, hyperparameters are set by hand or by automated search.
gl.hiperparametre.example: A team trains the same image model with three different learning rates and keeps the one with the best validation score; here the learning rate is a hyperparameter and the model's weights are parameters.
gl.hiperparametre.faq.0.a: Parameters are learned from data during training, like the weights in a neural network. Hyperparameters are set before training by people or search methods and control how learning proceeds.
gl.hiperparametre.faq.0.q: What is the difference between a parameter and a hyperparameter?
gl.hiperparametre.faq.1.a: Different combinations of values are tried in separate training runs, and their results on validation data are compared. Grid search, random search and automated tuning tools are used for this.
gl.hiperparametre.how: Parameters, such as the weights in a neural network, are learned from data during training. Hyperparameters are chosen before training starts: the learning rate, batch size, number of epochs, number of layers and so on. Since good values are not known in advance, teams try different combinations, using grid search, random search or smarter search methods. Each trial is a separate training run, and results are compared on validation data. Oven temperature and baking time are hyperparameters, while the finished dish is the trained model.
gl.hiperparametre.why: Even with the same architecture and the same data, hyperparameter choices can change performance noticeably. With large models each trial is very expensive, so finding good settings with few attempts is an important engineering skill. Whether settings were tuned fairly also affects how model comparisons should be read.
gl.hiz-siniri.def: A cap an AI service places on how many requests a single user or application can make, or how much data it can process, within a given period of time.
gl.hiz-siniri.example: A company sends a rapid stream of requests to an AI service to summarize hundreds of documents at once; after a while it starts getting errors and has to space the requests out.
gl.hiz-siniri.faq.0.a: Not exactly. A rate limit restricts how much can be used in a short window, such as a minute. A quota usually restricts total usage over a longer period, such as a month.
gl.hiz-siniri.faq.0.q: Is a rate limit the same as a quota?
gl.hiz-siniri.faq.1.a: Usually wait a short time and retry the request. Developers can queue requests or ask the provider for a higher limit.
gl.hiz-siniri.faq.1.q: What should you do when you hit a rate limit?
gl.hiz-siniri.how: Providers usually set the cap as requests per minute and tokens processed per minute. When the cap is exceeded, the server rejects the request and typically returns an error meaning 'too many requests'. Developers cope by waiting and retrying, queuing requests, or sending them at a steady pace. Limits can vary with account type and usage history. Like a traffic light at an intersection, it regulates the flow to prevent a jam.
gl.hiz-siniri.why: Limiting the rate protects a service from overload, shares resources fairly among users, and makes abuse harder. For app developers it can become a bottleneck as a product grows. Ordinary users meet a similar restriction in chat assistants through messages like 'you have reached your message limit'.

gl.hizalama.def.en: The general name for efforts to ensure that AI systems behave safely and in line with human intentions and values.

gl.hizalama.example.en: A model refusing to help when asked for the recipe for a dangerous chemical is the result of alignment work.

gl.hizalama.faq.0.a.en: In AI, alignment ("hizalama" in Turkish) refers to efforts to ensure that systems behave in line with human intentions and values.

gl.hizalama.faq.1.a.en: Fully defining human values is difficult, and models can find unintended shortcuts to the behavior they are rewarded for. These problems become more important as models grow more powerful.

gl.hizalama.how.en: Alignment work aims to make a model understand what the user actually wants, avoid helping with harmful requests, and behave honestly. Methods include training with human feedback, principles that govern model behavior, and research aimed at understanding the model's inner workings.

gl.hizalama.why.en: As models grow more powerful and evolve into agents that act on their own, the impact of unexpected or harmful behavior grows too. Alignment is at the center of the AI safety debate.

gl.humaneval.def: A benchmark that tests a language model's coding ability by asking it to write Python functions from a written description. It contains 164 hand-written programming problems and was developed by OpenAI.
gl.humaneval.example: A problem might be a short request like 'write a function that returns the sum of the even numbers in a list'; the model writes the code and the tests verify the result.
gl.humaneval.faq.0.a: It is the share of problems a model solves correctly when it gets only one attempt per problem.
gl.humaneval.faq.1.a: No. The benchmark tests short, single-function tasks and does not measure working in large projects, debugging or design decisions.
gl.humaneval.faq.1.q: Does a high HumanEval score make a model a good software engineer?
gl.humaneval.how: In each problem, the model is given a function name and a short description of what the function should do. The model writes the function body. The generated code is run, and it counts as correct if it passes the problem's unit tests. The reported figure is usually 'pass@k': a problem counts as solved if at least one of the model's k attempts passes the tests. The benchmark was released in 2021 alongside OpenAI's work introducing the Codex code model.
gl.humaneval.why: HumanEval was the standard reference for measuring coding ability for a long time and appeared in many model announcements. Because the problems are short and relatively simple, strong models reached high scores, and data leakage is also a concern. That is why benchmarks built on real software projects, such as SWE-bench, now draw more attention.
gl.humanity-s-last-exam.def: An AI exam made up of very hard, closed-ended questions written by subject experts, spanning fields from mathematics to the humanities. It was created to challenge models because existing tests had become too easy.
gl.humanity-s-last-exam.example: When a model announcement shares its score on this exam, it is meant to show how close the model gets to questions that stump even experts.
gl.humanity-s-last-exam.faq.0.a: No, the name is a dramatic flourish. As models improve, harder benchmarks will keep being built, so it is not expected to be the final one.
gl.humanity-s-last-exam.faq.0.q: Is Humanity's Last Exam really humanity's last exam?
gl.humanity-s-last-exam.faq.1.a: The goal was for the test to be hard from the start. This was meant to keep strong models from scoring high right away and the test from losing its usefulness quickly.
gl.humanity-s-last-exam.faq.1.q: Why were questions pre-tested on models before being selected?
gl.humanity-s-last-exam.how: The exam was assembled by the Center for AI Safety and Scale AI with contributions from experts in many countries. Questions were selected so that leading models of the time could not answer them, meaning questions the models got wrong were the ones included. Answers are mostly short and have a single correct response, so scoring can be automated. Most questions are text-only, and some include images. The exam, with thousands of questions, was announced in early 2025.
gl.humanity-s-last-exam.why: As models neared the ceiling on older benchmarks, it became hard to tell progress apart, and this exam aims to fill that gap. Its scores are often cited in the news as a gauge of how far models are from expert-level knowledge. Despite the bold name, it does not measure general ability or creativity, only the ability to answer academic questions.
gl.ic-boyama.def: A technique in which a selected region of an image is erased and refilled by AI so that it blends with the surrounding content, used to remove flaws or to remove, swap or add objects.
gl.ic-boyama.example: A stranger standing behind someone in a holiday photo is brushed over and removed, and the model fills the gap with the surrounding sand or wall texture.
gl.ic-boyama.faq.0.a: Inpainting changes or removes a region inside an image. Outpainting extends the image beyond its edges by generating new area that did not exist.
gl.ic-boyama.faq.0.q: What is the difference between inpainting and outpainting?
gl.ic-boyama.faq.1.a: It looks at the color, texture and perspective around the mask and predicts the most plausible content. If a text prompt is given, the prediction is steered in that direction.
gl.ic-boyama.faq.1.q: How does the model decide what replaces the removed object?
gl.ic-boyama.how: The user paints over the area to edit, creating a mask. The model reads the pixels outside the mask as context and generates the masked region so that it fits that context. In diffusion-based systems, the region is first filled with noise and then cleaned up step by step into a coherent picture. A text prompt can also be added, for example “put a cup of coffee on the empty table.”
gl.ic-boyama.why: Cloning and patching work that once took hours in photo retouching can now be done in seconds. It is widely used for cleaning up product photos, restoring old pictures and creative compositing. The fact that details that never existed can be added to an image also raises questions about how authentic an edited photo should be considered.
gl.icerik-kaynagi-dogrulama.def: An approach that makes it possible to trace where a piece of content came from, who made it, and what changes it went through along the way. The aim is to trust an item's history, not only its appearance.
gl.icerik-kaynagi-dogrulama.example: When a news agency publishes a photo, it can attach a signed record of the capture details and edits such as cropping, so readers can check the photo's history.
gl.icerik-kaynagi-dogrulama.faq.0.a: Detection looks at the content and guesses whether it is synthetic. Provenance checks the record attached to the content to verify its history, relying on a record instead of a guess.
gl.icerik-kaynagi-dogrulama.faq.0.q: How is provenance different from AI content detection?
gl.icerik-kaynagi-dogrulama.faq.1.a: No. Plenty of real content carries no record, either because none was added or because a platform removed it. A missing record only means the history cannot be verified.
gl.icerik-kaynagi-dogrulama.faq.1.q: Is content without provenance data fake?
gl.icerik-kaynagi-dogrulama.how: The foundation is a record captured at creation: a camera or software gathers information about the content and signs it. As the file changes hands, each edit is added to that record, forming a kind of digital chain. A person or platform checking it can verify the chain from start to finish. If the chain is broken or a signature does not match, the content's history is treated as uncertain. The C2PA standard is the best-known implementation, and watermarking and database matching serve the same goal.
gl.icerik-kaynagi-dogrulama.why: AI makes convincing fakes easier to produce, while detection tools cannot give certain answers. Provenance turns the problem around by marking trustworthy content instead. In journalism, law and insurance, the history of a piece of evidence can matter as much as the evidence itself.
gl.icerik-kimlik-bilgileri.def: A cryptographically signed record that shows who made a file, with which tool, and how it was edited afterwards. C2PA is the name of the open technical standard behind this kind of record.
gl.icerik-kimlik-bilgileri.example: An image made with an AI tool can carry a 'generated with AI' record, and a compatible viewer shows it through a small icon.
gl.icerik-kimlik-bilgileri.faq.0.a: C2PA is the name of the coalition and the standard it developed. Content credentials is the name used for the user-facing version of that standard.
gl.icerik-kimlik-bilgileri.faq.0.q: What is the difference between C2PA and content credentials?
gl.icerik-kimlik-bilgileri.faq.1.a: No. They only show who signed the record and whether the file has changed since. Whether the content itself is accurate has to be judged separately.
gl.icerik-kimlik-bilgileri.faq.1.q: Do content credentials prove an image is real?
gl.icerik-kimlik-bilgileri.how: When a camera, software or AI tool creates a file, it writes the creation and editing steps into a record and seals it with a digital signature. Each later edit is added to the chain without altering the earlier entries. A compatible viewer checks the signature and warns if the record has been tampered with. Because the information travels in the file's metadata, it can be lost if a platform strips it or someone takes a screenshot. That is why people also discuss using it together with watermarks.
gl.icerik-kimlik-bilgileri.why: It lets people ask 'where does this come from?' instead of only 'is this fake?'. News organizations, camera makers and software companies have backed the standard. Its usefulness depends on platforms preserving the information and showing it to readers.
gl.icerik-moderasyonu.def: The process of reviewing what users post on online platforms for compliance with rules, and removing, restricting or labeling content when needed.
gl.icerik-moderasyonu.example: A social media platform might flag a post it suspects contains hate speech using an automated system and send it to a human moderator for a decision.
gl.icerik-moderasyonu.faq.0.a: Moderation usually describes a private platform enforcing its own rules. Censorship more often refers to a government or other authority suppressing information, though where the line falls is debated.
gl.icerik-moderasyonu.faq.0.q: What is the difference between content moderation and censorship?
gl.icerik-moderasyonu.faq.1.a: Not fully. AI can scan huge volumes quickly, but decisions involving humor, context and cultural nuance still tend to need human review.
gl.icerik-moderasyonu.how: A platform first sets out what is not acceptable in its community guidelines. Content is then screened through user reports, automated detection systems and review by human moderators. Clear violations are often handled automatically, while ambiguous cases go to people. Users can usually appeal a decision. With generative AI, moderation covers not only user posts but also the prompts sent to a model and the responses it produces.
gl.icerik-moderasyonu.why: On platforms with billions of posts, fighting harmful content is a problem of scale, and AI is widely used for it. Decisions require balancing free expression against user safety. The exposure of moderators to disturbing material is also a separate debate about working conditions.
gl.ilk-token-suresi.def: The time between sending a request to a language model and the first piece of the answer appearing on screen. It shows how quickly the model starts to respond.
gl.ilk-token-suresi.example: For someone who uploads a long document and asks for a summary, time to first token can be noticeably longer than for a short question, because the document has to be read first.
gl.ilk-token-suresi.faq.0.a: They are close but not identical. Latency is the general concept, and time to first token is the specific delay until the first part of the answer. Sometimes the time to finish the whole answer is also called latency.
gl.ilk-token-suresi.faq.0.q: Is time to first token the same as latency?
gl.ilk-token-suresi.faq.1.a: The model must process the entire prompt before it starts answering. The longer the input, the longer that preparation takes.
gl.ilk-token-suresi.faq.1.q: Why do long prompts delay the first token?
gl.ilk-token-suresi.how: Language models write their answers one small chunk of text, called a token, at a time. Before the first token appears, the model has to read and process the entire prompt, a stage known as prefill. The longer the prompt, the longer this stage takes. After that, tokens start to stream. Time to first token covers network delay, waiting in the queue and prefill. In a chat window, it matches how long the 'thinking' indicator stays on.
gl.ilk-token-suresi.why: For users, an answer starting feels faster than an answer finishing; if the first words arrive quickly, the wait feels short. That makes it a core metric for chatbots, voice assistants and interactive apps. Providers often report it together with tokens per second.

gl.ince-ayar.def.en: Retraining a pre-built model on smaller, specialized data so that it fits a specific task or domain.

gl.ince-ayar.example.en: A bank fine-tuning a model on its own product documents so that it answers customer questions more consistently.

gl.ince-ayar.faq.0.a.en: For adding new knowledge to a model, RAG is usually cheaper and more up to date. Fine-tuning is better suited to permanently changing a model's style, format or behavior on a specific task.

gl.ince-ayar.faq.1.a.en: It depends on the task; you can start with a few hundred high-quality examples. Data quality matters more than quantity.

gl.ince-ayar.faq.1.q.en: How much data is needed for fine-tuning?

gl.ince-ayar.how.en: In fine-tuning, a ready-made, general-purpose model is taken and trained for a while longer on a smaller dataset specific to a task or domain. This helps the model better learn that domain's terminology, style or format. It requires far less data and cost than training from scratch.

gl.ince-ayar.why.en: It lets companies adapt general models to their own customer correspondence, industry jargon or brand voice. For most needs, however, well-written prompts or RAG may be enough; fine-tuning is preferred mainly for specialized, repetitive tasks.

gl.infiniband.def: A networking technology designed to connect servers with very low latency and high speed. It is widely used in supercomputers and large GPU clusters.
gl.infiniband.example: In a training cluster with hundreds of GPUs, servers send the values they compute at each step to one another over an InfiniBand network.
gl.infiniband.faq.0.a: Ethernet is a general-purpose networking standard used almost everywhere. InfiniBand was designed for high-performance computing and offers low latency. Ethernet has been evolving to compete in this space.
gl.infiniband.faq.0.q: What is the difference between InfiniBand and Ethernet?
gl.infiniband.faq.1.a: InfiniBand is an open industry standard. However, Nvidia brought a major product line in this area under its roof by acquiring Mellanox.
gl.infiniband.faq.1.q: Does InfiniBand belong only to Nvidia?
gl.infiniband.how: InfiniBand uses a network design that reduces the load on the processor when moving data between servers. Through a network card, one server can write data straight into another server's memory, a method called remote direct memory access (RDMA). This cuts out layers of software and lowers latency. Switches in the network route the traffic, and the goal is orderly, lossless delivery. In AI training, where hundreds of GPUs constantly share intermediate results, these properties matter a great deal.
gl.infiniband.why: Training large models cannot fit on one machine, and without a fast network the combined power of thousands of GPUs can go to waste. That makes networking as decisive a line item as chips in data center investment. Its competition with Ethernet-based approaches is also a frequent industry debate.
gl.insan-degerlendirmesi.def: Having people read and score model outputs or compare them against each other. It is used to measure qualities such as overall quality, helpfulness and safety that automatic metrics cannot capture.
gl.insan-degerlendirmesi.example: Responses from two versions of a chatbot are shown to raters without revealing which version wrote them, and the raters are asked which is more helpful.
gl.insan-degerlendirmesi.faq.0.a: Qualities such as tone, creativity, helpfulness and harmful content are hard to capture with simple metrics. Human judgment also serves as a reference for checking the accuracy of automatic methods and judge models.
gl.insan-degerlendirmesi.faq.0.q: Why is human evaluation still needed when automatic metrics exist?
gl.insan-degerlendirmesi.faq.1.a: It depends on how clear the guidelines are and on the number and expertise of raters. Subjectivity never disappears completely, so the same example is given to several people and the agreement between them is measured.
gl.insan-degerlendirmesi.faq.1.q: How reliable are human evaluation results?
gl.insan-degerlendirmesi.how: Raters score the responses shown to them against specific guidelines, or mark which of two responses they prefer. The model that produced each answer is usually hidden, which is known as a blind test. Several people rate the same example, and measuring agreement between raters shows whether the guidelines are clear enough. In fields such as law and medicine, expert raters are preferred. The collected preferences are also used to train models in reinforcement learning from human feedback.
gl.insan-degerlendirmesi.why: Whether an answer feels natural, helpful or appropriate ultimately depends on human judgment. On the other hand, the method is slow and expensive, and raters can be inconsistent or subjective. That is why it is usually combined with automatic metrics and the LLM-as-a-judge approach.
gl.insan-denetimi.def: A person's real authority and responsibility to monitor an AI system, change its decisions when needed, or stop it altogether.
gl.insan-denetimi.example: When a hospital's AI suggests a diagnosis and the doctor reviews the scans too, then confirms, changes or rejects the suggestion, that is human oversight.
gl.insan-denetimi.faq.0.a: They are closely related but not identical. Human-in-the-loop is a design approach where a person takes part in specific steps, while human oversight is the broader idea that includes monitoring and the power to intervene.
gl.insan-denetimi.faq.0.q: Is human oversight the same as human-in-the-loop?
gl.insan-denetimi.faq.1.a: Not always. If the person lacks the knowledge to understand the system, the time to check it, or the authority to change the outcome, approval becomes a formality and not real oversight.
gl.insan-denetimi.faq.1.q: Does having a person approve the output count as enough oversight?
gl.insan-denetimi.how: Oversight starts at design time: teams decide what the system may and may not do and which decisions stay with people. While the system runs, the responsible person watches its outputs, steps in when something looks wrong, corrects mistakes or shuts the system down. For oversight to be real, that person needs enough information, time and authority, because someone who merely signs off on results does not provide effective oversight.
