gl.kosinus-benzerligi.why: Semantic search, recommendation systems and retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) all rely on a 'find the most similar content' step, and cosine similarity is one of the most common measures used for it. Which documents count as closest to a query determines whether the system reaches the right source.

gl.kuantizasyon.def.en: A method of shrinking a model and making it run faster by storing its numbers with fewer bits. It makes it possible to run models on weaker hardware at the cost of some loss in quality.

gl.kuantizasyon.example.en: A 4-bit quantized version of an open-weight model that would normally require a server card with large memory can run on a powerful gaming PC.

gl.kuantizasyon.faq.0.a.en: There is usually some loss in quality, but with light quantization such as 8-bit, the difference may not be noticeable for most tasks. At very low bit levels, the loss becomes more pronounced.

gl.kuantizasyon.faq.1.a.en: These labels generally indicate how many bits of quantization the model was compressed with: Q4 means roughly 4 bits and Q8 roughly 8 bits.

gl.kuantizasyon.faq.1.q.en: What do Q4 and Q8 in model names mean?

gl.kuantizasyon.how.en: Model parameters are usually stored as 16-bit numbers. In quantization, these numbers are represented with 8, 4 or even fewer bits. As a result, the model file shrinks several-fold and runs with less memory. Because precision is reduced, there may be some drop in model quality; good methods keep this loss small.

gl.kuantizasyon.why.en: It makes it possible to run large models on personal computers, phones and cheaper servers. For companies, it is one of the most effective ways to cut inference costs.

gl.kuantum-bilisim.def: An approach to computing that uses qubits instead of classical bits and draws on quantum effects such as superposition and entanglement to solve certain kinds of problems far more efficiently.
gl.kuantum-bilisim.example: Companies such as IBM and Google build quantum processors, and one goal is to simulate the behavior of molecules used in drug research.
gl.kuantum-bilisim.faq.0.a: That is not expected. Quantum machines are seen as specialized tools for particular problems, while everyday tasks like email and web browsing will stay on classical computers.
gl.kuantum-bilisim.faq.0.q: Will quantum computers replace ordinary computers?
gl.kuantum-bilisim.faq.1.a: There are research directions, but there is no widely accepted evidence that it will accelerate the training of large models. The field remains largely experimental.
gl.kuantum-bilisim.faq.1.q: Will quantum computing speed up AI?
gl.kuantum-bilisim.how: A classical bit is either zero or one. A qubit can exist in a blend of both states until it is measured, which is called superposition. Qubits can also be entangled, and quantum algorithms are designed so that interference boosts the probability of the right answer while cancelling out wrong ones. This does not speed up every problem; advantages are expected only for specific problem types. Qubits are very sensitive to noise from their surroundings, so error correction is one of the biggest engineering hurdles.
gl.kuantum-bilisim.why: Quantum computing is watched closely for chemistry and materials simulation, certain optimization problems and the future of today's encryption methods. Its benefit for AI is not settled; research focuses on specific sub-problems rather than a general speedup. When judging headlines, error rates matter more than raw qubit counts.
gl.kucuk-dil-modeli.def: A type of language model with far fewer parameters than a large language model, small enough to run on ordinary hardware such as a phone or laptop.
gl.kucuk-dil-modeli.example: Microsoft's Phi and Google's Gemma families are examples of small language models, the kind that can summarize messages directly on a phone.
gl.kucuk-dil-modeli.faq.0.a: They work in the same basic way. The difference lies in the number of parameters, and therefore in the memory and computing power required. Large models offer broader knowledge and skills, while small ones are lighter and cheaper.
gl.kucuk-dil-modeli.faq.0.q: What is the difference between a small and a large language model?
gl.kucuk-dil-modeli.faq.1.a: On broad, general tasks it usually falls behind. But when trained for a narrow, well-defined task it can compete with a large model while running faster and at lower cost.
gl.kucuk-dil-modeli.faq.1.q: Is a small model always worse than a large one?
gl.kucuk-dil-modeli.how: Small language models are trained on text and predict the next token, just like their larger siblings; the difference is scale. They usually have a few billion parameters or fewer. To perform well, they tend to rely on carefully curated, high-quality training data. Developers also use compression techniques such as distillation, where a small model learns from a larger one, and quantization. The result may trail big models in general knowledge but can be good enough for a specific task.
gl.kucuk-dil-modeli.why: Small models are cheaper and faster, and they can run without an internet connection. Because data can stay on the device, they also offer privacy advantages. For companies, a small model tuned to a narrow job is often a more sensible choice than a very large one.
gl.kucuk-moduler-reaktor.def: A nuclear reactor design much smaller than a conventional plant, with output up to a few hundred megawatts, whose components are largely built in a factory and shipped to the site.
gl.kucuk-moduler-reaktor.example: Some technology companies have announced agreements with reactor developers for SMR projects meant to power their data centers.
gl.kucuk-moduler-reaktor.faq.0.a: SMRs have much lower output and are largely mass-produced in factories. Conventional plants are large facilities built one at a time on site.
gl.kucuk-moduler-reaktor.faq.0.q: How is an SMR different from a conventional nuclear plant?
gl.kucuk-moduler-reaktor.faq.1.a: Several projects are in development, but the timeline for commercial operation is unclear for most of them. In the short term, data centers will keep relying on grid electricity and other sources.
gl.kucuk-moduler-reaktor.faq.1.q: Will SMRs power data centers soon?
gl.kucuk-moduler-reaktor.how: Conventional nuclear plants are built on site over many years. SMRs are instead made as standardized modules in a factory, transported to the site and, if needed, added side by side to increase capacity. The aim is to shorten construction time and reduce the risk of cost overruns. Many designs use passive safety features and different types of coolant. Licensing still takes a long time, and most designs are still trying to prove themselves at commercial scale.
gl.kucuk-moduler-reaktor.why: Data centers want continuous, low-carbon electricity, so tech companies are striking deals with startups developing SMRs. Supporters say they offer reliable clean power. Critics point to uncertain costs, timelines and waste management.
gl.kullanim-bazli-fiyatlandirma.def: A pricing method in which customers pay for how much of a service they actually use instead of a fixed package. The unit can be the number of requests, the amount of data processed or the computing power consumed.
gl.kullanim-bazli-fiyatlandirma.example: A company that sends its customer support messages to an AI model and pays only for the text processed is on usage-based pricing. The bill at month's end depends on how many messages were handled.
gl.kullanim-bazli-fiyatlandirma.faq.0.a: A subscription charges a fixed fee for a period regardless of use. Under usage-based pricing the charge changes each period according to actual consumption.
gl.kullanim-bazli-fiyatlandirma.faq.0.q: How is usage-based pricing different from a subscription?
gl.kullanim-bazli-fiyatlandirma.faq.1.a: Per-token pricing is the form of usage-based pricing applied to language models. The broader idea also covers other units, such as requests, minutes or data volume.
gl.kullanim-bazli-fiyatlandirma.faq.1.q: Is usage-based pricing the same as per-token pricing?
gl.kullanim-bazli-fiyatlandirma.how: The provider breaks usage into a measurable unit, such as the number of calls made, the amount of text processed or the minutes a job runs. Each unit has a price, and at the end of the period total usage is multiplied by that price to produce the bill. A familiar comparison is an electricity or water bill: you pay for whatever the meter shows. Some providers combine it with a free allowance, a fixed base fee or a spending cap. Light users pay little, and heavy users pay more.
gl.kullanim-bazli-fiyatlandirma.why: In generative AI every request creates a real computing cost, so usage-based pricing is a natural fit for providers. For customers the upside is a low entry cost, and the risk is that the bill is hard to predict in advance. Whether AI products should be sold by subscription or by usage is a frequent topic in industry coverage.
gl.kum-havuzu.def: An isolated, controlled environment where AI-generated or AI-run code can operate without being able to harm real systems, data or networks.
gl.kum-havuzu.example: A coding assistant runs the program it wrote inside an isolated container rather than on the user's own computer, so if the program tries to delete files, only the temporary environment is affected.
gl.kum-havuzu.faq.0.a: No. A sandbox is the goal, isolated execution, while virtual machines and containers are some of the methods used to achieve it.
gl.kum-havuzu.faq.0.q: Is a sandbox the same as a virtual machine?
gl.kum-havuzu.faq.1.a: In a well-configured environment it is difficult, but isolation software can have vulnerabilities. That is why sandboxes are paired with monitoring and permission limits rather than relied on alone.
gl.kum-havuzu.faq.1.q: Can a model escape a sandbox?
gl.kum-havuzu.how: A sandbox is usually built with an isolation layer such as a virtual machine or a container. Inside it, a model can create files, run code and even make mistakes, but its network access, visible files and available resources are limited by boundaries set in advance. If something goes wrong, the environment is wiped and rebuilt while the real system stays untouched. Security researchers treat sandboxing as one of the basic safeguards, both for probing risky model behavior and for letting code-running agents operate safely.
gl.kum-havuzu.why: As models turn into agents that write and execute code, mistakes cost more. A sandbox does not assume the model will always behave; it limits the damage when it does not. It is not perfect, though: a flaw in the isolation or a loosely configured setting can let something cross the boundary.
gl.kumeleme.def: An unsupervised learning method that sorts unlabeled data into groups based on how similar the items are. The groups are not defined in advance; the algorithm finds the patterns itself.
gl.kumeleme.example: A retailer can cluster its customers by shopping habits and notice groups such as discount seekers and regular buyers.
gl.kumeleme.faq.0.a: In classification the groups are known in advance and the model is trained on labeled examples. In clustering there are no labels, and the groups emerge from the data itself.
gl.kumeleme.faq.0.q: What is the difference between clustering and classification?
gl.kumeleme.faq.1.a: There is no single rule. Analysts usually try several values, measure how well separated the clusters are, and check whether the result makes sense for the business question.
gl.kumeleme.faq.1.q: How is the number of clusters chosen?
gl.kumeleme.how: The algorithm places each data point in a space according to its features and puts points that sit close together into the same cluster. In methods like k-means, the number of clusters is chosen up front, while hierarchical methods merge points step by step into a tree. It is a bit like shelving books by how similar their contents are, without anyone having assigned subject labels. Whether the resulting groups are meaningful is still a judgment people have to make.
gl.kumeleme.why: It helps explore data when labeling is expensive or when nobody knows which groups exist. It is widely used for customer segmentation, document organization and image analysis. Because clusters have no single correct answer, results need careful interpretation.
gl.kurumsal-yapay-zeka.def: AI solutions that companies and public institutions use in their business processes, built around their own data and security requirements. Unlike consumer chat apps, scale, governance and integration with existing systems take center stage.
gl.kurumsal-yapay-zeka.example: A bank deploying an assistant that lets customer representatives query internal regulation documents, with no data leaving the bank, is a typical enterprise AI use.
gl.kurumsal-yapay-zeka.faq.0.a: Consumer apps serve individual users. Enterprise deployments emphasize data security, access control, audit logs and integration with the company's existing software.
gl.kurumsal-yapay-zeka.faq.0.q: How does enterprise AI differ from consumer chat apps?
gl.kurumsal-yapay-zeka.faq.1.a: Usually not. Most companies adapt an existing model by connecting it to their own data or giving it specific instructions, since training from scratch is very costly and rarely chosen.
gl.kurumsal-yapay-zeka.faq.1.q: Does a company need to train its own model for enterprise AI?
gl.kurumsal-yapay-zeka.how: Enterprise AI is usually set up by connecting a ready-made model to a company's own documents, customer records and software systems. Data is typically kept in cloud or server environments the company controls, with access permissions and logging rules in place. The model is then embedded in a specific workflow, such as contract summarization, customer support or software development. Outputs are monitored for accuracy, cost and risk. The hard part is less about choosing a model and more about integrating it safely and measurably into real work.
gl.kurumsal-yapay-zeka.why: Business customers make up a major share of AI companies' revenue and investment, so many partnerships and licensing deals in the news concern this area. For organizations, the key questions are privacy, responsibility for errors and whether the investment pays off. The effect of AI on employees' tasks and on company cost structures also shows up mostly through this channel.
gl.kv-onbellegi.def: In transformer models, the practice of storing the “key” and “value” intermediate results already computed for earlier tokens and reusing them, so the same work is not repeated during generation.
gl.kv-onbellegi.example: When chatting about a long document, the model does not reprocess the document at every new word; it reuses the intermediate values already computed for it from the cache.
gl.kv-onbellegi.faq.0.a: No. It is a temporary technical store that speeds up computing a single response. It is unrelated to features that remember information across conversations.
gl.kv-onbellegi.faq.0.q: Is the KV cache a chatbot's memory?
gl.kv-onbellegi.faq.1.a: Separate vectors are stored for every token in every layer and attention head. Memory needs therefore grow along with the number of tokens.
gl.kv-onbellegi.faq.1.q: Why does it use so much memory?
gl.kv-onbellegi.how: The attention mechanism looks at the key and value vectors of all earlier tokens whenever a new token is processed. Once computed, those vectors do not change. The cache keeps them in memory, typically on the GPU. When a new token arrives, only its own key and value are computed and added, so the whole history is not reprocessed at each step. The trade-off is that memory use grows as the context gets longer and as more users are served at once.
gl.kv-onbellegi.why: It is one of the core efficiency methods that lets long replies be generated in reasonable time. In models with long context windows it is among the biggest memory consumers, so it affects server costs and how many people can be served at the same time. This is why a lot of research aims to compress or share the cache.
gl.kvkk-ve-yapay-zeka.def: The question of how Law No. 6698 on the Protection of Personal Data, Turkey's data protection law known as KVKK, applies to AI systems that are trained on or process personal data.
gl.kvkk-ve-yapay-zeka.example: A company that uses AI to summarize customer complaints must meet KVKK conditions for processing any names and phone numbers that appear in those texts.
gl.kvkk-ve-yapay-zeka.faq.0.a: No comprehensive law comparable to the EU AI Act is known to exist, so KVKK and related legislation are the main reference when personal data is involved. The current situation should be checked against official sources.
gl.kvkk-ve-yapay-zeka.faq.0.q: Does Turkey have a dedicated AI law?
gl.kvkk-ve-yapay-zeka.faq.1.a: It depends on who processes the data, for what purpose and under which conditions. Organizations commonly set rules on what employees may not share with such tools, and specific cases call for legal advice.
gl.kvkk-ve-yapay-zeka.faq.1.q: Is entering personal data into a chatbot a problem under KVKK?
gl.kvkk-ve-yapay-zeka.how: KVKK is a general data protection law, not an AI-specific one, and it came into force in 2016. When an AI system processes personal data, the organization using it is usually considered the data controller. The data must rest on a lawful ground, be limited to specific and legitimate purposes, and the person concerned must be informed. Stricter conditions apply to sensitive data such as health and biometric data. The law also lets individuals object to outcomes against them that result solely from automated analysis. The Personal Data Protection Authority publishes recommendations and guidance in this area.
gl.kvkk-ve-yapay-zeka.term: Turkish Personal Data Protection Law (KVKK) and AI
gl.kvkk-ve-yapay-zeka.why: AI models are often trained on large amounts of data, and information typed into chat tools can include personal data. This framework sets which data companies and public bodies may use and under what conditions, and what happens to users' own data. This is a general summary, not legal advice.
gl.langchain.def: An open-source software framework that makes it easier to build applications powered by large language models. It links pieces such as model calls, document search and tool use through ready-made components.
gl.langchain.example: A company quickly prototypes a chatbot that answers questions from its internal documents by wiring document search and a model call together with LangChain.
gl.langchain.faq.0.a: No. LangChain is not a model but a software framework for writing applications that work with models. Different models, such as those from OpenAI or Anthropic or open models, can run underneath it.
gl.langchain.faq.1.a: No. Many applications are written directly against a model provider's own interface. LangChain is an option for those who want to speed things up with ready-made components.
gl.langchain.faq.1.q: Do I have to use LangChain to build an LLM application?
gl.langchain.how: The framework offers components such as prompt templates, model connectors, document loaders, vector database connections, memory and tools. A developer combines them into a chain: the user's question comes in, relevant documents are found, they are passed to the model along with a prompt, and an answer is returned. In agent setups, the model itself decides which tool to call and when. Switching between model providers is relatively easy. The framework is available in Python and JavaScript.
gl.langchain.why: As systems that fetch information from documents and generate answers, along with agents, have spread, building quick prototypes without rewriting these pieces has become valuable. There is criticism too: the extra layer of abstraction can complicate code and be unnecessary for simple tasks. For that reason some developers prefer to call a model provider's interface directly.
gl.lidar.def: A sensing technology that sends out pulses of laser light and measures how long they take to return, calculating the distance to surrounding objects and building a 3D map of the scene.
gl.lidar.example: Waymo's robotaxis use LiDAR alongside cameras and radar, and some robot vacuums carry a small LiDAR unit to map a room.
gl.lidar.faq.0.a: Radar uses radio waves while LiDAR uses laser light. Radar is less affected by rain and fog, whereas LiDAR gives much more detailed information about the shape of objects.
gl.lidar.faq.0.q: What is the difference between LiDAR and radar?
gl.lidar.faq.1.a: It is debated. Many companies consider LiDAR necessary for safety, while others argue that camera-focused systems can be enough.
gl.lidar.faq.1.q: Is LiDAR necessary for autonomous driving?
gl.lidar.how: The device fires a large number of short laser pulses every second. When light hits an object and bounces back, the round-trip time reveals how far away that point is. As the device rotates or steers its beam, it collects thousands of points that together form a 3D image called a point cloud. Software then groups these points into objects such as vehicles, pedestrians or curbs. Because LiDAR emits its own light, it also works in the dark.
gl.lidar.why: For autonomous vehicles and robots, knowing exact distances to the surroundings is critical for safety. LiDAR is strong at this, but it can be expensive and may be affected by heavy rain or fog. Some companies rely on it while others prefer camera-only systems, which is one of the most debated divides in the industry.
gl.liderlik-tablosu.def: A comparison table that ranks AI models by their scores on the same test or benchmark. It shows at a glance how each model performs on a given task.
gl.liderlik-tablosu.example: A company launches a new model and shows its coding score next to rival models in the same table.
gl.liderlik-tablosu.faq.0.a: It only means the model scored highest on that benchmark. The ranking can change on other tasks, or when cost and speed are considered.
gl.liderlik-tablosu.faq.0.q: Is the top model on a leaderboard the best model?
gl.liderlik-tablosu.faq.1.a: No. A benchmark is the measuring tool, meaning the questions and the scoring method. A leaderboard is the ranked presentation of results from that measurement.
gl.liderlik-tablosu.faq.1.q: Are a leaderboard and a benchmark the same thing?
gl.liderlik-tablosu.how: A benchmark's creators define a fixed set of questions or tasks. Models are run on them, and their outputs are scored against correct answers or automated tests. The results are sorted from highest to lowest and published in a table. Some leaderboards are run by the benchmark's authors, others by independent communities, and some rely on scores reported by the model's own developer. Hugging Face's tables for open models are well-known examples.
gl.liderlik-tablosu.why: News stories about a model 'pulling ahead' usually refer to a leaderboard. It allows quick comparison, but the ranking depends on the chosen benchmark, the test conditions and who reported the score. Problems such as memorization and data leakage can also make a ranking misleading.
gl.llama-cpp.def: An open-source inference library written in C/C++ that lets large language models run locally on ordinary computers, phones and small servers. Started by Georgi Gerganov for Llama models, it now supports many model families.
gl.llama-cpp.example: A user can download a small quantized model as a GGUF file and chat with it on a laptop through llama.cpp, with no internet connection.
gl.llama-cpp.faq.0.a: No. Llama is Meta's model family, while llama.cpp is independent software that runs models. Despite the name, it can run many different models.
gl.llama-cpp.faq.0.q: Is llama.cpp the same thing as the Llama model?
gl.llama-cpp.faq.1.a: Not necessarily. It works on a processor alone, though a graphics card can noticeably speed things up. The memory needed depends on the model's size and quantization level.
gl.llama-cpp.faq.1.q: Does llama.cpp need a powerful graphics card?
gl.llama-cpp.how: The model is downloaded as a single GGUF file. llama.cpp loads it into memory and generates the reply piece by piece. To save memory and gain speed it relies on quantization: model weights are stored with fewer bits, so large models fit into limited memory. The software can run on a processor alone, or part of the model can be offloaded to a graphics card. It also offers command-line tools and a local server mode, so other applications can connect to the model.
gl.llama-cpp.why: Running a model locally keeps data on the user's own device, works without an internet connection and avoids cloud costs. llama.cpp played a major role in bringing open-weight models to a wide audience. When news stories talk about running a model on your own device, infrastructure like this is usually involved.
gl.llm-gozlemlenebilirligi.def: A monitoring approach that records and lets teams inspect what a large language model application does in production: which input produced which output, how long it took and how much it cost.
gl.llm-gozlemlenebilirligi.example: When a customer support bot states the wrong refund policy, the team opens the trace, sees that the bot retrieved an unrelated document and fixes the search step.
gl.llm-gozlemlenebilirligi.faq.0.a: Traditional monitoring checks whether a server is running and how fast it responds. LLM observability also looks at the content, quality and cost of the responses.
gl.llm-gozlemlenebilirligi.faq.0.q: How does LLM observability differ from traditional system monitoring?
gl.llm-gozlemlenebilirligi.faq.1.a: Typically the prompt, the model's response, token counts, latency, cost, errors and user feedback. Because prompts may contain personal data, masking them or limiting how long they are kept is advisable.
gl.llm-gozlemlenebilirligi.how: On every model call, the application logs the prompt, the response, the number of tokens used, the latency and any errors. In multi-step flows, such as document search, tool calls and answer generation, each step is linked as part of a trace, so it becomes visible where a wrong answer originated. The records are gathered in dashboards. Quality is measured through user feedback and automated evaluations in which another model acts as the judge. Alerts can fire when a threshold is crossed.
gl.llm-gozlemlenebilirligi.why: Large language models can answer the same input differently, and failures are often silent: the system does not crash, it just presents made-up information. Without observability that is hard to notice and fix. It is also needed for cost control. Since the logs may contain personal data, retention and privacy need care.
gl.lojistik-regresyon.def: Despite its name, a method used for classification: it computes a probability from input features and uses it to place an example into one of two classes.
gl.lojistik-regresyon.example: A bank can calculate the probability that a loan will be repaid from an applicant's income and debt data, and route the application to extra review if that probability falls below a set threshold.
gl.lojistik-regresyon.faq.0.a: The name comes from modeling a transformed version of the probability with a linear expression. Its goal is to make a class decision, not to predict a number.
gl.lojistik-regresyon.faq.0.q: Why is it a classification method if it is called regression?
gl.lojistik-regresyon.faq.1.a: Yes. If false alarms are costly the threshold is raised, and if missed cases matter more it is lowered.
gl.lojistik-regresyon.how: The model first computes a weighted sum of the features, just as linear regression does. That number is passed through an S-shaped function called the sigmoid, which squeezes it between zero and one so it can be read as a probability. If the probability is above a chosen threshold, often fifty percent, one class is chosen; otherwise the other. The weights are learned by reducing an error measure that rewards high probability for the true labels. Extended versions handle more than two classes.
gl.lojistik-regresyon.why: Because it is fast, stable and interpretable, it is a common first choice for credit risk, medical diagnosis and email filtering. Producing a probability lets the threshold be tuned to business needs. The same structure underlies ideas used in the output layers of neural networks.
gl.lora.def: A fine-tuning method that adapts a large model to a new task by training two small low-rank matrices added to each layer, instead of updating all of the model's weights.
gl.lora.example: A law firm can freeze an open-weight base model and train a small LoRA adapter for summarizing contracts, then plug a different adapter into the same model for client questions.
gl.lora.faq.0.a: It is a variant of LoRA in which the base model is loaded into memory at lower precision (quantized). This cuts memory requirements even further.
gl.lora.faq.1.a: On many tasks it gets close to full fine-tuning, but it can fall short when a model must absorb a lot of new, broad knowledge. The choice depends on the task and the resources available.
gl.lora.how: The base model's weights are frozen. The change to a weight matrix is expressed as the product of two thin matrices rather than one huge matrix, which is where the term low-rank comes from. Only these small matrices are learned during training, so memory and storage needs drop sharply. Afterwards the add-ons can be saved as a small separate file or merged into the base model to make a single model. It is like adding notes in the margins of a book instead of reprinting the whole thing.
gl.lora.why: LoRA made customizing large models possible with much less hardware. Because many small adapters for different tasks can be attached to the same base model, costs fall and deployment gets easier. It is one of the most widely used techniques behind the community adaptation of open-weight models.
gl.makine-bilinci.def: The question of whether a machine could have subjective experience, that is, whether there is something it is like to be that machine, and the field of research that explores the possibility. It is not the same as intelligence or performance.
gl.makine-bilinci.example: A chatbot saying “I’m so tired today” does not show that it is tired; it may simply be producing the sentence people use in such situations.
gl.makine-bilinci.faq.0.a: There is no broadly accepted evidence that they are, and most researchers do not consider current systems conscious. Since there is no definitive test, the debate continues.
gl.makine-bilinci.faq.1.a: No. Intelligence is the ability to solve problems, while consciousness is having subjective experience. A system could be highly capable without being conscious.
gl.makine-bilinci.faq.1.q: Is intelligence the same as consciousness?
gl.makine-bilinci.how: There is no single, widely accepted scientific definition or test for consciousness. Researchers look at theories developed for the human brain and debate whether a system has the features those theories predict. Some approaches tie consciousness to how information is processed, others to a biological body and being alive. A model saying “I feel” is not evidence, because systems trained on human text can easily produce such sentences. The matter therefore remains open.
gl.makine-bilinci.why: Users forming emotional bonds with chatbots, and some experts suggesting that the moral status of such systems may one day be worth asking about, have brought the topic into the news. There is no broadly accepted evidence that today’s systems are conscious, and scientific views differ. Exaggerated claims can mislead people.
gl.makine-cevirisi.def: The automatic translation of text or speech from one language into another by software. Today it is mostly done with artificial neural networks.
gl.makine-cevirisi.example: Reading a foreign news site translated into Turkish with Google Translate or DeepL is the best-known everyday use of machine translation.
gl.makine-cevirisi.faq.0.a: For everyday texts where clarity is enough, it often does the job. In sensitive fields such as law, literature and medicine, a human translator, or at least human review, is still important.
gl.makine-cevirisi.faq.0.q: Will machine translation replace human translators?
gl.makine-cevirisi.faq.1.a: The model cannot always capture context and idioms correctly, and errors are more likely in languages with few examples or in ambiguous sentences.
gl.makine-cevirisi.faq.1.q: Why does machine translation sometimes give nonsensical results?
gl.makine-cevirisi.how: Early systems relied on grammar rules and dictionaries, followed by statistical methods. Today's systems use neural networks, especially the Transformer architecture. The model learns patterns from large numbers of paired texts in two languages. During translation it treats the sentence as a whole rather than word by word and produces the equivalent that fits the context. Large language models can translate too. For languages with little available text, quality is usually lower.
gl.makine-cevirisi.why: It lowers language barriers and makes information, trade and communication more accessible. It is one of the areas where AI progress reached everyday life earliest. Still, a wrong translation in a legal, medical or official text can have serious consequences, and idioms and cultural nuance remain difficult.
gl.makine-gorusu.def: Technology that uses cameras, lighting and image-processing software so machines, especially on production lines, can see, measure and count objects and sort out defects.
gl.makine-gorusu.example: On a bottling line, a camera checks each bottle's cap, label and fill level, and pushes defective ones off the belt.
gl.makine-gorusu.faq.0.a: Computer vision is the broad field of getting machines to understand images. Machine vision usually means applying those techniques in industrial settings, together with cameras, lighting and hardware. In everyday use the two terms are often mixed up.
gl.makine-gorusu.faq.0.q: How is machine vision different from computer vision?
gl.makine-gorusu.faq.1.a: No. Tasks like measuring and barcode reading are done well with classic methods. Deep learning helps most with jobs that are hard to describe with rules, such as defect detection.
gl.makine-gorusu.faq.1.q: Does machine vision need deep learning?
gl.makine-gorusu.how: A camera and lighting setup captures an image of the part passing along the line. Software extracts information from that image, such as dimensions, color, position or a barcode. Classic systems rely on hand-written rules. Many today use models trained with deep learning, which can learn hard-to-define flaws like scratches or stains from examples. The result is passed to a robot or a sorting mechanism on the line, and the decision is often made very quickly.
gl.makine-gorusu.why: On a fast production line human eyes tire, while machine vision keeps making the same check without a break. It is common in quality control, part placement and product tracking. The term mostly describes the industrial application. Computer vision is the broader name for research on image understanding.

gl.makine-ogrenmesi.def.en: The branch of AI that lets a computer make predictions or decisions by learning patterns in example data on its own, without rules being written one by one.

gl.makine-ogrenmesi.example.en: A bank's system that learns from millions of past transactions and instantly flags suspicious card spending is a machine learning application.

gl.makine-ogrenmesi.faq.0.a.en: The three most common types are supervised learning (with labeled examples), unsupervised learning (finding patterns in unlabeled data) and reinforcement learning (trial and error with rewards and penalties).

gl.makine-ogrenmesi.faq.0.q.en: What are the types of machine learning?

gl.makine-ogrenmesi.faq.1.a.en: The most common language is Python; libraries such as PyTorch, TensorFlow and scikit-learn are widely used in the field.

gl.makine-ogrenmesi.faq.1.q.en: Which programming language is used for machine learning?

gl.makine-ogrenmesi.how.en: In traditional software, the programmer writes the rules, such as "raise an alert if the amount exceeds 10,000 lira." In machine learning, the model is given many examples and outcomes and builds the relationship in those examples itself. During training, the model makes predictions, measures its error and updates its parameters little by little to reduce that error. Once training is done, the model can make predictions on data it has never seen before.

gl.makine-ogrenmesi.why.en: For tasks where writing rules one by one is impossible, such as fraud detection, product recommendations, image recognition or language translation, machine learning gives far better results. This method underlies today's AI boom.

gl.markov-karar-sureci.def: A mathematical framework that describes sequential decision problems with partly random outcomes using states, actions, transition probabilities and rewards. It is the foundation of reinforcement learning.
gl.markov-karar-sureci.example: For a robot vacuum, the state could be its position in the room and its battery level, the actions could be moving ahead or returning to the charger, and the reward could be the area cleaned.
gl.markov-karar-sureci.faq.0.a: In a Markov chain the system moves on its own according to probabilities. In a Markov decision process a decision maker chooses actions, those actions affect the transitions, and success is measured by rewards.
gl.markov-karar-sureci.faq.0.q: What is the difference between a Markov decision process and a Markov chain?
gl.markov-karar-sureci.faq.1.a: The classic framework assumes the state is fully observed. When observations are incomplete, an extension called a partially observable Markov decision process (POMDP) is used.
gl.markov-karar-sureci.faq.1.q: What happens if the agent cannot see the full state?
gl.markov-karar-sureci.how: There is an agent in an environment. At each step the agent sees its current state and picks an action; the environment then moves to a new state according to probabilities and gives the agent a reward. The difference from a Markov chain is that the agent's actions influence the transitions. The goal is to find the rule, called a policy, that maximizes the total reward collected over the long run. Future rewards are usually discounted a little, so a gain that arrives now is worth more than one far away.
gl.markov-karar-sureci.why: Many problems that need sequential decisions, such as robotics, game-playing systems and inventory management, can be cast in this framework. It is the shared language behind the agents, policies and rewards mentioned in reinforcement learning news. Being able to write a problem this way also determines which algorithms can be applied to it.
gl.markov-zinciri.def: A mathematical model in which a system moves between states with certain probabilities, and the next state depends only on the current state, not on the history.
gl.markov-zinciri.example: A basic next-word suggestion on a phone keyboard can be thought of as a Markov chain that looks only at the last word typed and suggests the most likely follower.
gl.markov-zinciri.faq.0.a: It means the future depends only on the present state, not on the past. Even if we do not know how the system reached its current state, the probabilities for the next step stay the same.
gl.markov-zinciri.faq.0.q: What does the Markov property mean?
gl.markov-zinciri.faq.1.a: No. In a Markov chain the states are observed directly. In a hidden Markov model the states are hidden and only the observations they produce are visible; this approach was long used in speech recognition.
gl.markov-zinciri.faq.1.q: Is a Markov chain the same as a hidden Markov model?
gl.markov-zinciri.how: First the possible states are listed, for example sunny, cloudy and rainy for the weather. Then the probability of moving from each state to every other one is set, such as the chance that a sunny day is followed by a cloudy one. The chain moves forward as if rolling dice with those probabilities, and at each step it looks only at the present state; what happened yesterday does not matter. This memoryless property makes the calculations much easier. The transition probabilities can be estimated by counting in observed data.
gl.markov-zinciri.why: The Markov chain is one of the basic building blocks for modeling probabilistic, sequential processes in AI. The mathematical framework of reinforcement learning and many sampling methods rest on this idea. Early simple language models that predicted word sequences used similar logic, whereas today's large models take a much longer context into account.
gl.matris-carpimi.def: An operation that combines two tables of numbers by pairing the rows of one with the columns of the other, multiplying and adding, to produce a new table. It makes up most of the computation inside neural networks.
gl.matris-carpimi.example: When a chatbot processes a user's message, most of its work consists of multiplications with large weight matrices.
gl.matris-carpimi.faq.0.a: With ordinary numbers, order does not matter. With matrices, A×B and B×A usually give different results, and one of them may not even be defined. The shapes of the matrices also have to match.
gl.matris-carpimi.faq.0.q: How is matrix multiplication different from ordinary multiplication?
gl.matris-carpimi.faq.1.a: The cells of the result can be computed independently, so thousands of small cores can work at the same time. GPUs were designed for exactly this kind of parallel workload.
gl.matris-carpimi.faq.1.q: Why are GPUs good at matrix multiplication?
gl.matris-carpimi.how: Each row of the first matrix is multiplied term by term with each column of the second, and the products are added up to give a single cell of the result. This only works if the first matrix has as many columns as the second has rows. In a neural network, a layer multiplies the input vector by a weight matrix to produce the input of the next layer. Because every cell can be computed independently, the work can be spread across thousands of cores, which is why GPUs suit it so well.
gl.matris-carpimi.why: Most of the computation spent training and running large language models is matrix multiplication. That is why debates about AI chip speed, memory bandwidth and energy use largely come down to the cost of this one operation. Hardware and algorithms that do it more efficiently translate directly into lower costs.

gl.mcp.def.en: An open protocol that lets AI assistants connect to external tools and data sources, such as files, applications and databases, in a standard way. It was introduced by Anthropic in 2024.

gl.mcp.example.en: A developer can connect the AI assistant in their code editor to the company's bug tracking system via MCP and have the assistant read open bugs.

gl.mcp.faq.0.a.en: MCP was introduced by Anthropic in November 2024 as an open standard and was subsequently adopted by other AI companies and tools as well.

gl.mcp.faq.1.a.en: The protocol itself is a connection standard; security depends on the trustworthiness of the connected server and the permissions granted. It is recommended to use only MCP servers you trust and not to grant broader permissions than necessary.

gl.mcp.how.en: MCP works with a client-server architecture. An application or data source (for example, a calendar, database or file system) is exposed as an MCP server, and the AI assistant connects to that server as an MCP client. This way the assistant can read data and take actions in a standard way, without a separate integration having to be written for each tool.

gl.mcp.why.en: For AI agents to do real work, they need to connect to company systems. Because MCP standardizes this connection, it quickly came to be supported by many AI companies and software tools. If misconfigured, however, it can create security risks.

gl.mekanistik-yorumlanabilirlik.def: A subfield of interpretability that tries to reverse-engineer what computations happen inside a neural network, at the level of neurons and connections.
gl.mekanistik-yorumlanabilirlik.example: Researchers identified circuits in language models called induction heads, which find an earlier sequence of words in the context and help predict what comes next.
gl.mekanistik-yorumlanabilirlik.faq.0.a: Interpretability is a broad umbrella that includes methods showing how inputs affect outputs. The mechanistic kind aims to work out the model's internal computation step by step, component by component.
gl.mekanistik-yorumlanabilirlik.faq.0.q: How does mechanistic interpretability differ from interpretability in general?
gl.mekanistik-yorumlanabilirlik.faq.1.a: Not yet. Some small circuits and features have been understood, but explaining the whole of a large model is not currently possible.
gl.mekanistik-yorumlanabilirlik.faq.1.q: Does mechanistic interpretability let us fully understand models?
gl.mekanistik-yorumlanabilirlik.how: The approach treats a trained model like a machine with unknown internals and tries to work out what its parts do. Researchers record the model's internal activity and isolate components, called circuits, that seem responsible for a specific behavior. They then alter or switch off a component and check how the output changes to test their findings. The aim is a causal explanation rather than just a correlation. The work is labor-intensive, and scaling it to large models is the main difficulty.
gl.mekanistik-yorumlanabilirlik.why: Understanding from the inside why a model behaves as it does could expose problems such as deceptive behavior, hidden goals or bias more reliably than outside testing alone. That is why it is seen as a promising direction for safety research. How far the findings generalize to large models remains an open question.
gl.meta-ogrenme.def: Training a model to learn how to learn, so that when it meets a new task it can adapt quickly from only a handful of examples. It is often summed up as 'learning to learn'.
gl.meta-ogrenme.example: An image classifier that has practiced on hundreds of similar small tasks during training may be able to tell apart bird species it has never seen after being given only five photos of each.
gl.meta-ogrenme.faq.0.a: In transfer learning, the knowledge of an existing model is carried over to a new task. In meta-learning, the model is trained from the start across many tasks specifically so that it can adapt fast to new ones.
gl.meta-ogrenme.faq.0.q: How does meta-learning differ from transfer learning?
gl.meta-ogrenme.faq.1.a: Few-shot learning names the goal: learning from a few examples. Meta-learning is one of the main methods used to reach that goal.
gl.meta-ogrenme.faq.1.q: How does meta-learning relate to few-shot learning?
gl.meta-ogrenme.how: Instead of one big task, training consists of many small tasks. In each one the model sees a few examples and is then tested on fresh examples from the same task. The resulting error is fed back to adjust the model's starting settings so that it gets better both at solving tasks and at adapting quickly. The model ends up with a starting point or learning strategy that gives good results on a new task within a few steps. Someone who has learned many languages picking up a new one faster is a fair analogy.
gl.meta-ogrenme.why: In areas where labeled data is scarce, such as rare diseases or less widely spoken languages, learning from a few examples is a big advantage. Meta-learning is one of the main approaches in few-shot learning research. The in-context learning of large language models is also sometimes discussed through this lens.
gl.metin-ve-veri-madenciligi-istisnasi.d: A legal rule that, within limits, allows copyrighted content to be copied without permission so that computers can analyze it and extract patterns. It is discussed as one possible legal basis for collecting AI training data.
gl.metin-ve-veri-madenciligi-istisnasi.e: A university team that scans hundreds of thousands of articles to measure which topics are rising could rely on this kind of exception.
gl.metin-ve-veri-madenciligi-istisnasi.f: No. It does not remove copyright protection. It only permits copying for analysis, under the conditions set by the law.
Does this exception make copyrighted works free to use?
In the EU, yes for the general exception: rights holders can reserve their rights in a machine-readable way. The exception for research organizations has no such opt-out.
Can rights holders opt out of the exception?
gl.metin-ve-veri-madenciligi-istisnasi.h: These exceptions differ from country to country. The EU's 2019 Copyright in the Digital Single Market Directive provides one exception for research organizations and a second, general one that rights holders can opt out of in a machine-readable way. If a rights holder reserves its rights, the content cannot be used under the general exception. Some countries, such as Japan, interpret their rules more broadly. Whether AI training fits within these exceptions is still debated.
gl.metin-ve-veri-madenciligi-istisnasi.w: This rule helps determine under what conditions AI companies can use training data in Europe. The EU AI Act also expects providers of general-purpose models to have a copyright policy that respects such reservations of rights. The aim is to balance support for research with the protection of content owners.
gl.metinden-goruntu-uretimi.def: An AI approach that creates a brand-new image from a written description, or prompt. The result can look like a photograph, an illustration or a drawing.
gl.metinden-goruntu-uretimi.example: Typing 'a misty Bosphorus at sunset, oil painting' into a tool such as DALL·E, Midjourney or Stable Diffusion returns a matching image within seconds.
gl.metinden-goruntu-uretimi.faq.0.a: Generation begins from random noise. When the starting point changes, so does the result; some tools let you fix the starting value (seed) to get similar outputs.
gl.metinden-goruntu-uretimi.faq.0.q: Why does the same prompt give a different image each time?
gl.metinden-goruntu-uretimi.faq.1.a: It varies by country and is still debated. Both the use of copyrighted works in training data and the question of who owns the generated image are approached differently legally and culturally.
gl.metinden-goruntu-uretimi.faq.1.q: What is the copyright status of AI-generated images?
gl.metinden-goruntu-uretimi.how: First, the prompt is turned into a numerical representation that captures its meaning, using a language model. The image model, usually a diffusion model, starts from random noise and, guided by that representation, removes the noise step by step until an image emerges. During training, the model sees many images paired with captions and learns how words relate to visual elements. Because of the random starting point, the same prompt can produce different results each time.
gl.metinden-goruntu-uretimi.why: It reduced visual content creation from a task that needed specialist software and drawing skill to writing a few sentences. It is used for quick drafts in advertising, games, publishing and design. It has also raised debates about copyright, fake imagery and the work of artists.
gl.metinden-konusmaya.def: Technology that turns written text into artificial speech that sounds like a human voice. It is used in voice assistants, screen readers, navigation apps and audiobooks.
gl.metinden-konusmaya.example: A navigation app saying 'turn right in two hundred meters', or a news site reading an article aloud, are everyday uses of TTS.
gl.metinden-konusmaya.faq.0.a: No. TTS in general converts text into speech, while voice cloning is the ability to produce speech that resembles a specific person's voice, and is a particular use of TTS.
gl.metinden-konusmaya.faq.0.q: Is TTS the same as voice cloning?
gl.metinden-konusmaya.faq.1.a: One turns text into speech and the other turns speech into text, so they work in opposite directions. Voice assistants often use both together.
gl.metinden-konusmaya.faq.1.q: What is the difference between TTS and automatic speech recognition?
gl.metinden-konusmaya.how: The system first prepares the text for reading aloud: numbers, abbreviations and punctuation are converted into spoken form. A neural network then produces a representation of the sound, usually a spectrogram, that includes stress and intonation. Finally, a component called a vocoder turns that representation into an actual audio waveform. Newer models combine these steps in a single network and can imitate a person's voice from a sample a few seconds long.
gl.metinden-konusmaya.why: TTS is the foundation of accessibility technology that lets visually impaired users listen to their screens. Voice assistants, call-center bots and content narration also rely on it. As natural voice quality improves, the risk of voice-imitation fraud grows too.
gl.metinden-video-uretimi.def: An AI approach that produces a short video clip, a sequence of moving frames, from a written prompt. The scene, camera movement and style are described in the prompt.
gl.metinden-video-uretimi.example: A prompt like 'a woman walking with an umbrella down a rainy Istanbul street, the camera slowly moving closer' can be turned into a clip a few seconds long.
gl.metinden-video-uretimi.faq.0.a: A video needs many frames that stay consistent over time rather than one image. Keeping the shape of objects and the motion coherent is difficult, and computing costs rise sharply.
gl.metinden-video-uretimi.faq.0.q: Why is text-to-video harder than text-to-image?
gl.metinden-video-uretimi.faq.1.a: Broken physics or inconsistent details can be clues, but as models improve this becomes unreliable. That is why labeling methods such as watermarks and content credentials are being developed.
gl.metinden-video-uretimi.faq.1.q: How can you tell a video was made by AI?
gl.metinden-video-uretimi.how: It is similar to text-to-image, but time enters the picture. Starting from the prompt's representation, the model generates not a single frame but a sequence of frames together; in many systems this happens in a compressed intermediate space using diffusion. The main challenge is consistency between frames: the shape of objects, lighting and motion must stay coherent from frame to frame. Training uses many videos paired with descriptions. Because computing costs are high, outputs are usually short.
gl.metinden-video-uretimi.why: It could change the cost and time of producing film, advertising and social media content; systems such as OpenAI's Sora and Google DeepMind's Veo often appear in the news. The ability to make realistic fake videos also puts misleading content, watermarking and labeling in the spotlight.
gl.mlops.def: A set of practices and tools for managing the whole life of a machine learning model, from development to deployment, monitoring and updating, in an orderly, repeatable and reliable way.
gl.mlops.example: A bank sets up a pipeline that retrains its fraud detection model every month on new transactions, tests it automatically and alerts the team if accuracy drops.
gl.mlops.faq.0.a: DevOps manages the release and operation of code. In MLOps, data and models change constantly alongside the code, so versioning, testing and monitoring them are part of the process too.
gl.mlops.faq.0.q: What is the difference between MLOps and DevOps?
gl.mlops.faq.1.a: Not exactly. LLMOps is a branch adapted for large language models, focusing on matters specific to them such as prompt management, output evaluation and cost tracking.
gl.mlops.faq.1.q: Are MLOps and LLMOps the same thing?
gl.mlops.how: MLOps adapts the DevOps mindset from software engineering to machine learning. Steps such as data preparation, training, testing, packaging and deployment are linked into automated pipelines. Data and model versions are recorded, and experiment results are tracked. Once a model is live, its performance is measured continuously; as data changes over time, accuracy can drop, and the model is then retrained on fresh data. Version control, a model registry and monitoring dashboards are typical parts of this setup.
gl.mlops.why: Many models work well in the lab but never leave the prototype stage because they cannot be run reliably in production. MLOps closes that gap: it speeds up updates, catches problems early and makes it possible to audit which data produced a model. It is a core engineering field for teams turning AI into products.
gl.mmlu.def: A benchmark that tests a language model's general knowledge and reasoning with multiple-choice questions across 57 subjects, including history, law, medicine and mathematics.
gl.mmlu.example: When a model announcement includes an MMLU score, it is meant to show how often the model picks the correct option on four-choice questions.
gl.mmlu.faq.0.a: No. MMLU measures multiple-choice knowledge questions and says little about long-form writing, tool use or real-world tasks.
gl.mmlu.faq.0.q: Does a high MMLU score mean a model is good at everything?
gl.mmlu.faq.1.a: Strong models score close to the ceiling, and some questions are flawed or may have leaked into training data. This makes it hard to see real differences between models.
gl.mmlu.faq.1.q: Why is MMLU no longer enough on its own?
gl.mmlu.how: The test consists of four-option questions ranging from elementary level to professional expertise. The model sees the question and the options and picks one, and the score is the share of correct answers. Questions can be asked with a few solved examples (few-shot) or with none, and this setting affects the result. The outcome is reported as a single percentage, sometimes with a breakdown by subject. The benchmark was introduced in a 2020 paper by Dan Hendrycks and colleagues.
gl.mmlu.why: For years MMLU was the standard way to compare models' general knowledge, and it appeared in many model announcements. As top models approached the ceiling, it became less able to tell them apart, and some questions were reported to contain errors. That is why harder or cleaned-up versions and newer benchmarks have gained attention.
gl.model-agirliklari.def: The billions of numerical values that hold what an AI model learned during training. These numbers determine how the model turns an input into an output.
gl.model-agirliklari.example: With open-weight models such as Meta's Llama family, the weight files can be downloaded and a developer can run the model on their own server. With closed models, the weights stay on the company's servers and users reach the model only through an app or an API.
gl.model-agirliklari.faq.0.a: In everyday use they are often treated as synonyms. Technically, parameters can also include other learned values such as biases. Saying a model has 70 billion parameters means that is the total count of learned numbers.
gl.model-agirliklari.faq.0.q: Are weights and parameters the same thing?
gl.model-agirliklari.faq.1.a: No. With an open-weight model only the trained weights are shared. The training data, training code and other details are not always published, which is why the term open source is debated.
gl.model-agirliklari.faq.1.q: Is an open-weight model the same as an open-source model?
gl.model-agirliklari.how: A neural network is made of many connected artificial neurons, and each connection has a weight. Training starts with random values. The model makes predictions on examples, measures its error, and nudges the weights in small steps in the direction that reduces that error. After many repetitions, the weights encode patterns found in the data. When training ends, the numbers are saved as a file, and running the model means loading that file and processing inputs with it.
gl.model-agirliklari.why: A model's real value lives in its weights, because the full cost of training ends up stored in those numbers. Whether weights are released to the public is at the heart of the open-weight debate. If they are released, anyone can run and fine-tune the model on their own hardware, but misuse risks also grow.
gl.model-arka-kapisi.def: A hidden behavior planted inside a model that activates only when a specific trigger appears. The model works normally on ordinary inputs but produces the attacker's chosen output when it sees the trigger.
gl.model-arka-kapisi.example: In a model that reads traffic signs, a stop sign with a particular sticker on it might be read as a speed limit sign.
gl.model-arka-kapisi.faq.0.a: The idea is similar: a hidden, unauthorized way in. But in software it is a piece of code. In a model, the behavior is learned and spread across the weights, so it cannot be found by reading code.
gl.model-arka-kapisi.faq.0.q: Is a model backdoor the same as a software backdoor?
gl.model-arka-kapisi.faq.1.a: Any model can, if its origin is not verified. Being open to inspection is an advantage, but finding a backdoor by looking at weights is hard, so downloading from trusted sources matters.
gl.model-arka-kapisi.faq.1.q: Do open-source models carry backdoor risk?
gl.model-arka-kapisi.how: A backdoor is usually planted during training. The attacker adds a particular marker to a small part of the data, such as a tiny patch in an image or a rare word sequence in text, and pairs those examples with the result they want. The model learns both the real task and this hidden association. Because it performs well in ordinary tests, the backdoor is hard to notice. Downloaded pretrained weights and outsourced fine-tuning services can also carry backdoors. Detection efforts include searching for triggers and inspecting model behavior.
gl.model-arka-kapisi.why: Many organizations use a pretrained or fine-tuned model rather than training from scratch. A backdoor in a model of unclear origin is a supply chain risk, similar to one in software. Since it does not show up in normal tests, trusting the model's source and running independent audits become important.
gl.model-birlestirme.def: A way of combining the weights of several separately trained or fine-tuned models into a single model without any additional training.
gl.model-birlestirme.example: Community developers might merge a coding model and a chat model that were both fine-tuned from the same base, hoping to get one model that works reasonably well at both.
gl.model-birlestirme.faq.0.a: No. In an ensemble the models run separately and their outputs are combined; in merging the weights are combined into one model, so running costs do not increase.
gl.model-birlestirme.faq.0.q: Is model merging the same as ensembling?
gl.model-birlestirme.faq.1.a: No. Models with different architectures cannot be merged directly, and results are usually best when the models come from the same base model.
gl.model-birlestirme.faq.1.q: Can any two models be merged?
gl.model-birlestirme.how: In its simplest form, the weights of two models are merged by averaging their corresponding values. For this to work, the models need the same architecture, and usually they should be fine-tuned from the same base model. More advanced methods treat the change that fine-tuning made to the base model as a separate vector, then add those differences together or resolve conflicts between them. Because no new training is needed, the process can be done quickly. The result may not deliver the hoped-for mix of skills, so the merged model is always tested.
gl.model-birlestirme.why: Merging offers a cheap way to pool different skills into one model without costly retraining. Running costs also stay the same as for a single model. On the other hand, outcomes are hard to predict, and each merge has to be tested separately. It is widely tried in the open-weight model community.
gl.model-cikarma-saldirisi.def: An attempt to copy a model's function or infer its internal properties by sending it many queries and collecting the answers. The attacker tries to obtain a close replica without ever having access to the model itself.
gl.model-cikarma-saldirisi.example: A competitor that sends many images to a paid image recognition service and collects the labels could train a similar model on that data.
gl.model-cikarma-saldirisi.faq.0.a: Distillation is a technique for transferring a large model's knowledge into a smaller one, and it is often legitimate. Model extraction uses a similar method without permission, and it usually breaks the service's terms.
gl.model-cikarma-saldirisi.faq.0.q: How is model extraction different from distillation?
gl.model-cikarma-saldirisi.faq.1.a: If the weights are already public, there is nothing secret left to copy. The risk mainly concerns closed models offered only through an API.
gl.model-cikarma-saldirisi.faq.1.q: Does it apply to models whose weights are published openly?
gl.model-cikarma-saldirisi.how: The attacker cannot see the model's weights and can only ask questions through an API or interface. They send many inputs, record the outputs, and train their own model on those input-output pairs. This resembles distillation, a technique that is also used legitimately. If responses include probability scores as well, copying gets easier. Defenses include rate limits on queries, monitoring for unusual usage and limiting how much detail the outputs reveal.
gl.model-cikarma-saldirisi.why: Training a large model takes serious effort and resources, so the model is a valuable asset for a company. Extraction can erode that investment and the commercial advantage that comes with it. The stolen copy can also serve as a testing ground for other attacks on the original model.
gl.model-cokusu.def: The gradual loss of diversity and accuracy that happens when AI models are trained repeatedly on data produced by earlier models, so outputs become uniform and drift away from reality.
gl.model-cokusu.example: Training an image model over many generations on pictures made by another image model can end with featureless outputs in which faces and objects all look like the same template.
gl.model-cokusu.faq.0.a: Not by itself. Synthetic data can be useful when it is well made, filtered and combined with real data. The risk rises with uncontrolled training based only on model outputs.
gl.model-cokusu.faq.0.q: Does using synthetic data cause model collapse?
gl.model-cokusu.faq.1.a: It has been demonstrated in controlled experiments. How much it affects large commercial models is debated, and developers generally filter their data and keep real data in the mix.
gl.model-cokusu.how: A model learns the rare examples and edge cases in its training data a little incompletely, and its outputs sit slightly closer to the average. If the next model is trained on those outputs, new gaps pile up on top of the old ones. Over generations, rare knowledge disappears, phrasing becomes similar and errors get reinforced. It is like photocopying a photocopy over and over: each copy loses a bit more detail. Studies have shown this especially when no real data is mixed in.
gl.model-cokusu.why: As a growing share of online text is generated by AI, that content may end up in the training data of future models. This is why model collapse sits at the center of debates about data quality, the value of human-made data and the careful use of synthetic data. How far the risk will actually play out is still being studied.
gl.model-degerlendirmesi.def: The process of measuring, through systematic tests, how accurate, safe and useful an AI model is on specific tasks. “Evals” is the common name for these tests and the setups that run them.
gl.model-degerlendirmesi.example: A company building a customer-service chatbot picks several hundred real customer questions and compares a new model version's answers with the old one's before deciding whether to ship it.
gl.model-degerlendirmesi.faq.0.a: Not quite. A benchmark is a shared test that everyone uses to compare models. Evals is a broader term that includes benchmarks as well as tests a team builds for its own product.
gl.model-degerlendirmesi.faq.0.q: Are benchmarks and evals the same thing?
gl.model-degerlendirmesi.faq.1.a: No. Models can behave very differently across tasks, and a good score in one area does not guarantee success in another. That is why several metrics and tasks are looked at together.
gl.model-degerlendirmesi.faq.1.q: Is a single score enough to judge a model?
gl.model-degerlendirmesi.how: First, what to measure is decided: accuracy, safety, speed or tone, for example. Then inputs suited to that goal are prepared, along with a definition of what a good answer looks like for each. The model is run on these inputs, and the outputs are scored by automatic metrics, by another model or by people. Results are compared across model versions. Companies do this both with public benchmarks and with tests specific to their own product.
gl.model-degerlendirmesi.why: Without evaluation, there is no way to know whether a model change is an improvement or a regression. Claims about progress and comparisons between models in the news also rest on it. A poorly designed measurement can be misleading. For teams building products, evals play the role that quality control plays in traditional software.
gl.model-distilasyonu-saldirisi.def: An attempt to collect an AI model's responses through a large number of queries and use them to train a separate model that behaves similarly. It usually breaks access terms and aims to copy a model's abilities without ever seeing its weights.
gl.model-distilasyonu-saldirisi.example: A team that uses an automated script to send huge numbers of questions to a chatbot's API and then trains its own model on the answers is a typical case.
gl.model-distilasyonu-saldirisi.faq.0.a: No. Distillation is a method for transferring knowledge from a large model to a smaller one, and companies often do it with their own models. The word attack refers to applying it to someone else's model without permission and against its terms.
gl.model-distilasyonu-saldirisi.faq.0.q: Is distillation the same as a distillation attack?
gl.model-distilasyonu-saldirisi.faq.1.a: Not completely. Providers set rate limits, monitor suspicious usage and close accounts, but these measures reduce the risk rather than remove it.
gl.model-distilasyonu-saldirisi.faq.1.q: Can these attacks be fully prevented?
gl.model-distilasyonu-saldirisi.how: The attacker sends a very large number of prompts to the target model through its interface and records the answers. These prompt-response pairs become training data for a smaller or different model. The student model never sees the teacher's internal weights; it only imitates its output behavior. Distillation itself is a legitimate and common technique. The problem arises when another company's model outputs are gathered without permission and against its terms of use. Providers try to stop this with rate limits and by watching for unusual query patterns.
gl.model-distilasyonu-saldirisi.why: Leading models cost a great deal to build, so cheap copying of their abilities worries companies on both commercial and security grounds. A copied model may lack the safeguards of the original. At the same time, the legal and ethical limits on using model outputs are contested, and providers mostly address the issue through their terms of service.
gl.model-karti.def: A short document that describes what an AI model was designed for, how it was trained and evaluated, and what its limitations are.
gl.model-karti.example: Many open models shared on Hugging Face come with a model card that explains which tasks the model was tested on and which uses are not recommended.
gl.model-karti.faq.0.a: A model card is a general introduction to a single model. A system card usually describes the product form of a large model, with more detail on safety testing and risk assessments, though the line between the two differs between organizations.
gl.model-karti.faq.0.q: What is the difference between a model card and a system card?
gl.model-karti.faq.1.a: In general there is no single mandatory format. Some regulations, such as the EU AI Act, do impose technical documentation and transparency obligations for certain models.
gl.model-karti.faq.1.q: Is a model card legally required?
gl.model-karti.how: A model card works much like a nutrition label. It typically lists the intended uses, uses that are not recommended, general information about the training data, test results, and known biases and risks. The idea was popularized in 2019 following a proposal by Google researchers. For large language models, similar documents are often called system cards and go into more detail on safety testing. How much a card covers varies from one organization to another.
gl.model-karti.why: What is known about a model, who is accountable for it and where it should not be used can all be read from this document. That lets developers, companies and auditors choose a model on the basis of information rather than guesswork. Transparency rules are also paying more attention to this kind of documentation.
gl.model-paralelligi.def: A method that splits a model too large for one chip's memory, by layers or by the matrices inside layers, and places the pieces on several accelerators.
gl.model-paralelligi.example: A very large language model is run by spreading its layers across the eight GPUs in a server, so that no single GPU holds the entire model in memory.
gl.model-paralelligi.faq.0.a: Pipeline parallelism divides the model into groups of layers and gives each group to a chip. Tensor parallelism splits the large computation inside one layer across several chips.
gl.model-paralelligi.faq.0.q: What is the difference between pipeline and tensor parallelism?
gl.model-paralelligi.faq.1.a: No. When a very large model does not fit on one GPU, it is split across several chips in the same way when generating answers.
gl.model-paralelligi.faq.1.q: Is model parallelism only used for training?
gl.model-paralelligi.how: It comes in two common forms. In pipeline parallelism, consecutive layers of the model are assigned to different chips, and data flows from one chip to the next like an assembly line. In tensor parallelism, a large matrix multiplication inside a single layer is divided among several chips, each computing one part. Either way, the chips constantly pass intermediate results to each other, so fast links between them, such as the specialized connections inside a server, are essential.
gl.model-paralelligi.why: Models with hundreds of billions of parameters do not fit in the memory of a single GPU. Model parallelism makes it possible to train and serve them. The downside is that chips can end up waiting for each other, so engineers choose how to split a model carefully, based on the hardware.
gl.model-refahi.def: The question of whether AI models could have experiences or interests that deserve moral consideration, and the research area that studies how to act under that uncertainty.
gl.model-refahi.example: Low-cost steps such as letting a model end extremely distressing conversations are discussed under this heading.
gl.model-refahi.faq.0.a: No. The field does not assume that it is; it asks whether the uncertainty should be taken seriously. Most experts do not think current systems are conscious.
gl.model-refahi.faq.0.q: Does model welfare mean AI is conscious?
gl.model-refahi.faq.1.a: Critics argue the attention may distract from people and from real harms today, and may encourage the habit of treating chatbots as human. Supporters say caution is sensible while the uncertainty lasts.
gl.model-refahi.faq.1.q: What do critics say about this field?
gl.model-refahi.how: The field focuses less on proving whether models have consciousness or subjective experience and more on assessing how likely that is. Researchers apply criteria drawn from theories of consciousness to system architectures and study models' behavior and what they say about themselves. Then they consider low-cost precautions that make sense even if the probability is small. Throughout, they keep in mind that a model's statements can be misleading, since models learned from human writing.
gl.model-refahi.why: There is no scientific consensus that today's models are conscious, and many experts consider it unlikely. Still, some argue that as systems grow more complex the question should not be dismissed from the start. Because it touches ethics, law and public perception, the topic also shows up in AI news.
gl.model-sunumu.def: The software and infrastructure that keeps a trained AI model running on servers so it can answer requests from applications and users.
gl.model-sunumu.example: A message typed into a chatbot is routed by the serving infrastructure to a suitable GPU along with other requests, and the answer is sent back piece by piece.
gl.model-sunumu.faq.0.a: Training is the learning stage and is done once or occasionally. Serving is the continuously running stage in which the trained model serves users.
gl.model-sunumu.faq.0.q: What is the difference between model serving and model training?
gl.model-sunumu.faq.1.a: For open-weight models, yes, and tools like vLLM or Ollama make it easier. Closed models can only be used through the provider's API.
gl.model-sunumu.faq.1.q: Can I serve a model on my own server?
gl.model-sunumu.how: The serving layer receives incoming requests, queues them and routes them to suitable hardware. To be efficient, it batches several requests together, caches repeated information and, when needed, splits the model across multiple chips. It adds servers when load rises and removes them when it falls. Version management, monitoring and security checks are also part of its job. In the end, the user simply gets the answer without seeing any of this.
gl.model-sunumu.why: A model performing well in the lab is not enough to serve millions of people quickly and cheaply. Speed, cost, uptime and privacy are largely decided in the serving infrastructure. It is the core job behind AI companies' hardware investments and the growing interest in inference chips.
gl.model-suruklenmesi.def: The decline in a deployed AI model's performance over time as the world changes. The model stays the same, but the conditions it meets move away from those it was trained on.
gl.model-suruklenmesi.example: A bank's fraud detection model keeps relying on old patterns as fraudsters switch to new methods, and its catch rate slowly falls.
gl.model-suruklenmesi.faq.0.a: Data drift is a change in the distribution of the inputs the model receives. Model drift describes the resulting decline in the model's performance, and data drift can be one of its causes.
gl.model-suruklenmesi.faq.0.q: What is the difference between model drift and data drift?
gl.model-suruklenmesi.faq.1.a: It cannot be fully prevented, but monitoring live performance helps catch it early. Retraining the model on fresh data is the most common remedy.
gl.model-suruklenmesi.faq.1.q: How can model drift be prevented?
gl.model-suruklenmesi.how: A model learns patterns from its training data. After it goes live, user behavior, seasons, language habits or market conditions change, and the relationship between inputs and correct answers slowly shifts. The model keeps predicting from the old patterns without noticing, and its error rate quietly rises. Teams catch this by monitoring live performance, and if measurements fall below a set threshold, the model is retrained on newer data. For language models, the term is sometimes also used to describe a hosted service starting to behave differently over time.
gl.model-suruklenmesi.why: Drift is a reminder that a model doing well in testing does not guarantee it will keep doing well in production.
