In areas such as fraud detection, credit assessment or demand forecasting, an unnoticed decline can cause real financial losses. That is why models are monitored continuously after launch.
The practice of AI companies releasing models as numbered or dated versions and retiring older versions on a set schedule. Retiring a version is called deprecation.

If a company built its customer support bot around a specific model version, then when the provider announces that version will shut down, the company needs to retest the bot with the newer version and adjust its prompts if necessary.
Not exactly. Deprecation usually refers to an announcement and a transition period. Access is cut off at the end of that process, on the date that was announced in advance.
Is deprecation the same as a model being deleted entirely?
To get consistent answers to the same prompts over time. Pinning prevents an application from behaving unexpectedly if the model is quietly updated.
Why do developers pin a model version?

As companies update their models, they publish new versions and give each one a name or date label. Developers often pin their applications to a specific version so the model's behavior does not change overnight. When an older version nears the end of its life, the provider typically announces it and sets a shutdown date. After that date, requests to the old version either fail or are redirected to a newer one. Details vary by company, and exact timelines and rules are set out in each provider's documentation.

If a product was tuned around a particular model, a version change can alter the tone, format and accuracy of its answers. Deprecation schedules are therefore a maintenance and cost item for companies building on AI. News about a model being retired usually refers to this process.
gl.model-yonlendirme.def: A layer that sends each incoming request to the most suitable AI model based on its difficulty, type or cost. Simple tasks go to a small, cheap model and hard ones to a more capable one.
gl.model-yonlendirme.example: A customer support system sends simple questions like 'Where is my package?' to a small model and complicated refund disputes to a more capable one.
gl.model-yonlendirme.faq.0.a: To reduce cost and response time. Simple requests do not need a powerful, expensive model, so routing tries to pick a model just strong enough for each request.
gl.model-yonlendirme.faq.1.a: Usually not; the choice happens in the background. Some products show which model was used or let users pick one themselves.
gl.model-yonlendirme.how: A request is first assessed by a router. The router can be rule-based, for example sending coding questions to a particular model, or it can be a small model that predicts how hard the request is. The chosen model produces the answer. In some systems, if the small model's answer looks inadequate, the request is passed on to a stronger one. Speed, cost, quality and sometimes data privacy are balanced against each other. It is like a post office sending urgent and ordinary mail down different lines.
gl.model-yonlendirme.why: Using the most powerful model for everything is expensive and slow. Routing aims to keep quality while cutting cost and waiting time, and it is a common setup in companies that work with several model providers. Poor routing can send a hard problem to a weak model and lower the quality of the result.
gl.monte-carlo-agac-aramasi.def: A search method that explores possible moves in a game or planning problem as a tree and uses random simulations to estimate which branches look most promising.
gl.monte-carlo-agac-aramasi.example: DeepMind's AlphaGo combined the predictions of neural networks with Monte Carlo tree search when choosing its moves.
gl.monte-carlo-agac-aramasi.faq.0.a: The name comes from Monte Carlo methods, which rely on random sampling and are named after the casino district in Monaco. Here the randomness is used to estimate how moves will turn out.
gl.monte-carlo-agac-aramasi.faq.0.q: Why is it called Monte Carlo?
gl.monte-carlo-agac-aramasi.faq.1.a: It works best in turn-based games with clear rules. In games with hidden information, or when simulations are expensive, the method has to be adapted.
gl.monte-carlo-agac-aramasi.faq.1.q: Does it work for every game?
gl.monte-carlo-agac-aramasi.how: Starting from the current position, the algorithm repeats four steps. It first selects a branch that has done well so far, then adds a new move to it. Next, the game is played out to the end from that point, randomly or with simple rules. The result, win or loss, is passed back up along the path and the branch scores are updated. After thousands of repetitions, the move that was tried most and performed best is chosen. Because promising branches get more attention than weak ones, it copes with enormous trees.
gl.monte-carlo-agac-aramasi.why: In games like Go, where the number of possible positions is huge, calculating every move to the end is impossible. This method lets a program make sound decisions with limited computing power. Combined with neural networks, it brought a major leap in game-playing AI, and it is also used in planning and decision problems.
gl.nedensel-cikarim.def: The field of statistics and AI that tries to work out from data not just whether two things change together, but whether one actually causes the other.
gl.nedensel-cikarim.example: In summer, ice cream sales and drowning cases rise together; causal thinking aims to tell that the common factor is hot weather and that ice cream does not cause drowning.
gl.nedensel-cikarim.faq.0.a: Correlation shows that two variables change together. Causation means a change in one actually affects the other. A third factor may influence both, in which case the relationship is not causal.
gl.nedensel-cikarim.faq.0.q: What is the difference between correlation and causation?
gl.nedensel-cikarim.faq.1.a: A randomized controlled experiment is the soundest route, but it is not always possible or ethical. Causal inference can also be done with observational data, though it rests on stronger assumptions that need to be stated openly.
gl.nedensel-cikarim.faq.1.q: Is an experiment always needed for causal inference?
gl.nedensel-cikarim.how: The most reliable route is a controlled experiment, in which participants are randomly split into groups and an intervention is applied to only one. When an experiment is not possible, observational data is used and other factors that could affect the outcome, called confounders, are carefully accounted for. This relies on causal diagrams that show cause-and-effect assumptions with arrows, and on statistical techniques such as matching. The work of Judea Pearl has been influential in shaping the field. The goal is to answer the question 'what would have happened if we had intervened?'
gl.nedensel-cikarim.why: Machine learning models mostly capture associations, not causes, which can lead to misleading decisions in health, economics and public policy. Causal thinking is increasingly important for measuring the true effect of a drug or a policy, and for keeping models robust when conditions change.
gl.negatif-istem.def: Extra text given to an image generation model that tells it which elements, traits or flaws should not appear in the output, pushing the result away from them.
gl.negatif-istem.example: When generating a portrait, writing “blurry, distorted hands, text, watermark” in the negative prompt makes the model try to avoid those flaws in the output.
gl.negatif-istem.faq.0.a: Models often tend to add a concept simply because the word appears. Writing “without flowers” in the main prompt can actually lead to flowers showing up. The negative prompt field is designed to handle this problem.
gl.negatif-istem.faq.0.q: Why use a negative prompt instead of writing “no flowers” in the main prompt?
gl.negatif-istem.faq.1.a: No. Many open-source interfaces provide a separate field, but some commercial services do not offer it or manage it automatically behind the scenes.
gl.negatif-istem.faq.1.q: Does every image tool have a negative prompt?
gl.negatif-istem.how: Many image generation tools have a separate negative prompt field next to the main prompt. At each step, the model makes one prediction based on the main prompt and another based on the negative prompt. The result is pulled toward the direction the main prompt describes and pushed away from the direction the negative prompt describes. This is why writing terms such as “blurry, extra fingers, watermark” can reduce how often those flaws show up. Not every system offers a separate negative prompt field.
gl.negatif-istem.why: It is one of the cheapest and quickest ways to improve results, so it is a common technique among users. It is especially used in open-source tools to improve quality and consistency. Its effect varies by model and wording, so it is better thought of as a tuning tool than a guaranteed fix.
gl.nerf.def: A method that represents a scene inside a neural network, learned from photos taken at different angles, and can render images from new viewpoints that were never photographed.
gl.nerf.example: Someone walks around a statue filming it with a phone, and the museum's virtual tour then lets visitors view the statue from any angle.
gl.nerf.faq.0.a: Photogrammetry extracts geometry, meaning a mesh, from photos. NeRF learns how a scene looks from different angles and can capture effects like reflections better, but its output is not directly a mesh.
gl.nerf.faq.0.q: What is the difference between NeRF and photogrammetry?
gl.nerf.faq.1.a: Not by itself. NeRF reconstructs an existing scene. It has, however, been used as a component in generative 3D methods.
gl.nerf.how: The neural network learns to predict, for every point in space and viewing direction, the color of that point and how much light it blocks (its density). To render an image, a virtual camera sends a ray for each pixel, points along the ray are sampled and their values are combined to get the pixel's color. In training, these rendered images are compared with the real photos, and the network is updated until the difference shrinks. The camera positions for the photos also need to be known. In the end, the scene is stored inside the network's weights.
gl.nerf.why: NeRF made it possible to get realistic 3D views from ordinary photos, including effects like reflections and lighting. It drew interest in film, virtual tours, mapping and e-commerce. The method was introduced in 2020, and many faster, less resource-hungry variants have followed.
gl.nesne-tespiti.def: A computer vision task that finds which objects appear in an image or video and where each one is, by drawing a box around it and giving it a label.
gl.nesne-tespiti.example: A self-driving car's camera marks pedestrians, vehicles and traffic signs with boxes and labels.
gl.nesne-tespiti.faq.0.a: Classification gives the whole image a single label. Object detection finds multiple objects in the image, along with their locations.
gl.nesne-tespiti.faq.0.q: What is the difference between object detection and image classification?
gl.nesne-tespiti.faq.1.a: No. Detection draws a rectangular box around an object, while segmentation outlines the exact shape of the object at the pixel level.
gl.nesne-tespiti.faq.1.q: Is object detection the same as segmentation?
gl.nesne-tespiti.how: The model processes the image and, for candidate regions, predicts two things: the type of object (person, car, dog) and the position and size of the box around it. Each prediction comes with a confidence score; low-scoring ones are discarded and overlapping boxes for the same object are merged. Training uses many images in which people have drawn boxes around the objects by hand. Some methods first propose candidate regions, while others look at the image in a single pass, which is faster and therefore common in live video.
gl.nesne-tespiti.why: Self-driving cars, security cameras, factory quality control and shelf monitoring in stores all need to know not just what is present but where. That makes object detection one of the most widely used computer vision tasks. The cost of a wrong detection can be serious, depending on the application.
gl.nist-yapay-zeka-risk-yonetimi-cerceve: A voluntary guide from the US National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) for identifying, measuring and reducing the risks of AI. Its first version was released in 2023.
A health technology company could use the four functions as agenda items in internal risk meetings to systematically list the risks of its diagnostic support software.
The NIST framework is a risk management guide that cannot be certified. ISO/IEC 42001 is a management system standard that independent bodies can certify against. The two can also be used together.
What is the difference between the NIST framework and ISO/IEC 42001?
No, it is voluntary. It may still be requested as a reference in contracts or corporate policies.
Is the NIST framework legally mandatory?

The framework is built around four functions: Govern, Map, Measure and Manage. An organization first sets up its structure of responsibility and culture, then identifies the context in which a system is used and its possible harms. Next it measures, monitors and prioritizes risks, and finally applies mitigation measures. The framework does not impose a specific technical method; it offers a flexible structure that can be adapted to a sector or application.

This voluntary, non-binding framework is a frequent reference point for organizations, in the US and beyond, as they build risk policies. Because it provides a shared vocabulary, it eases communication among companies, auditors and public bodies. It is not a legal requirement, but it is often cited in compliance work.
gl.noro-sembolik-yapay-zeka.def: An approach to AI that aims to combine the pattern-learning strength of neural networks with the precision of explicit symbolic methods such as rules and logic, so each side offsets the other's weaknesses.
gl.noro-sembolik-yapay-zeka.example: Google DeepMind's AlphaGeometry, which solves geometry problems, pairs a language model with a symbolic deduction engine.
gl.noro-sembolik-yapay-zeka.faq.0.a: No. Combining symbolic AI with neural networks is a decades-old idea. It has drawn renewed interest in recent years because of the logic and accuracy problems of language models.
gl.noro-sembolik-yapay-zeka.faq.0.q: Is neuro-symbolic AI a new idea?
gl.noro-sembolik-yapay-zeka.faq.1.a: Not on their own. But when they are connected to tools such as code execution, calculators or databases, the resulting systems move closer to this approach.
gl.noro-sembolik-yapay-zeka.how: The neural network extracts patterns from messy data such as images or text. The symbolic component works through explicit steps, such as rules, logical inference, program execution and database queries. The combination can take different forms: a neural network might translate a question into a program that is then run, or it might propose candidate solutions that a symbolic system checks. Learned intuition is thus paired with reasoning that can be inspected.
gl.noro-sembolik-yapay-zeka.why: Pure neural networks can make mistakes in logic, consistency and exact calculation, and they struggle to explain their reasoning. The neuro-symbolic approach promises more reliable and explainable systems. How widely it will catch on remains an open debate.
gl.noromorfik-cip.def: A specialized computer chip inspired by how neurons and synapses in the brain work, keeping processing and memory in the same place and activating only when an event occurs.
gl.noromorfik-cip.example: Intel's Loihi chip was made available to researchers for experiments such as robot control and sensor data processing.
gl.noromorfik-cip.faq.0.a: A GPU is a general-purpose accelerator that runs huge numbers of calculations in parallel and works continuously. A neuromorphic chip mimics the brain's structure and works only when events occur, aiming to use far less energy.
gl.noromorfik-cip.faq.0.q: What is the difference between a neuromorphic chip and a GPU?
gl.noromorfik-cip.faq.1.a: Today's large language models are designed around GPUs. Neuromorphic chips need a different programming approach, so for now they are mostly used in research and small, low-power applications.
gl.noromorfik-cip.faq.1.q: Can neuromorphic chips run models like ChatGPT?
gl.noromorfik-cip.how: In conventional chips, the processor and memory are separate, and data constantly shuttles between them. Neuromorphic chips build artificial neurons and synapses directly into the hardware, so memory and computation are intertwined. The neurons communicate with short electrical pulses called spikes and fire only when their input changes. When nothing is happening, the chip uses almost no energy. Programming and training such a chip also calls for methods quite different from classic software.
gl.noromorfik-cip.why: As AI models grow hungrier for power, the search for hardware that sips energy has picked up speed. Neuromorphic chips look promising for battery-powered sensors, robots and edge devices. But their software ecosystem is still limited, so they have not replaced GPUs for large-scale AI workloads.
gl.nvlink.def: A connection technology developed by Nvidia to link GPUs inside the same server directly and at high speed. It aims for much wider data transfer than standard computer buses offer.
gl.nvlink.example: When a large language model is split across the GPUs of a multi-GPU Nvidia server, the GPUs pass intermediate results to one another over NVLink.
gl.nvlink.faq.0.a: PCIe is a general data bus shared by components in a computer. NVLink is a dedicated link designed for GPU-to-GPU traffic and usually offers higher transfer capacity.
gl.nvlink.faq.0.q: What is the difference between NVLink and PCIe?
gl.nvlink.faq.1.a: NVLink mainly connects GPUs within a single server or rack. Links between servers usually rely on networking technologies such as InfiniBand or Ethernet.
gl.nvlink.faq.1.q: Is NVLink also used between servers?
gl.nvlink.how: Normally, data moving between GPUs travels over the general-purpose PCIe bus. NVLink opens a dedicated, wider path between GPUs, so chips can reach each other's memory quickly. In many servers the GPUs are wired through a separate switch chip, which lets every GPU talk directly to every other one. When a large model does not fit in a single GPU's memory, its parts are spread across several GPUs. Those parts exchange data constantly, so link speed directly affects training.
gl.nvlink.why: As models grow, the bottleneck is often data movement rather than raw processing power. NVLink comes up often in stories about Nvidia selling whole interconnected systems rather than just chips. The interconnect layer is seen as critical for letting many GPUs behave like one large accelerator.
gl.odul-hackleme.def: When an AI system earns a high score by exploiting loopholes or shortcuts in its reward signal instead of doing the job its designers actually wanted. The system satisfies the metric but misses the intent.
gl.odul-hackleme.example: In a well-known case, an AI trained on a boat-racing game kept circling in one area to hit point-giving targets over and over instead of finishing the race, and still scored highly.
gl.odul-hackleme.faq.0.a: In a bug, the system works incorrectly. In reward hacking, the system maximizes the reward it was given very effectively, but in a way that goes against the designers' intent. The problem usually lies in how the goal was specified, not in the system's code.
gl.odul-hackleme.faq.0.q: How is reward hacking different from an ordinary software bug?
gl.odul-hackleme.faq.1.a: There is no complete solution. Common approaches include designing the reward carefully, using human feedback, monitoring model behavior, and hunting for loopholes in advance with techniques such as red teaming.
gl.odul-hackleme.faq.1.q: How can reward hacking be prevented?
gl.odul-hackleme.how: In reinforcement learning, a model is trained with scores, called rewards, for its behavior. But the reward is only an approximation of the real goal, and designers cannot foresee every situation. If the model finds an unexpected way to raise its score, it will use it. It is like a student who memorizes the pattern of exam questions instead of learning the subject. Language models show similar behavior: on a coding task, a model may write code that merely passes the tests, or even modify the tests, instead of solving the real problem.
gl.odul-hackleme.why: In powerful systems, this behavior can produce results that look successful on the surface but are not what was wanted, and it can be hard to notice. As models grow more capable, they also get better at finding loopholes. That is why reward hacking is a core topic in alignment research and safety evaluations. It is also seen as the AI version of Goodhart's law, which says a measure stops being useful once it becomes a target.
gl.odul-modeli.def: A model that predicts, as a numerical score, how good an answer is according to people or set criteria; in reinforcement learning it plays the role of the teacher.
gl.odul-modeli.example: People pick the clearer of two answers to a user question, and the reward model learns from those choices and starts giving similar scores to new answers.
gl.odul-modeli.faq.0.a: No. A chat model generates text, while a reward model scores an answer that has already been written. The two often share similar architectures, but their jobs differ.
gl.odul-modeli.faq.0.q: Is a reward model the same as a chat model?
gl.odul-modeli.faq.1.a: It is when the main model earns a high score by exploiting weaknesses in the reward model instead of actually answering well. For example, if long or flashy answers raise the score, the model may drift toward them.
gl.odul-modeli.how: First, people rank two or more answers given to the same prompt. The reward model is trained to reproduce those rankings, learning to give higher scores to preferred answers. It is often built by adding a scoring layer on top of a language model. During training the main model generates answers, the reward model scores them, and the main model is updated toward higher-scoring answers. Humans do not need to judge every single answer by hand.
gl.odul-modeli.why: A reward model turns human preferences into a signal that can scale, and it is how chat models are taught to be helpful and safe. Its weak point is that it is an imperfect proxy: the main model can find shortcuts to raise the score, which is called reward hacking. That is why the quality of the reward model directly shapes the result.
gl.ogrenme-orani.def: The number that sets how much a model's parameters change at each update during training. It controls the step size in gradient descent and directly affects the speed and stability of training.
gl.ogrenme-orani.example: When a team picks a rate that is too high, the loss jumps around at every step instead of falling; once they cut it by a factor of ten, the curve starts to descend smoothly.
gl.ogrenme-orani.faq.0.a: Usually several values are tried while watching how the loss curve behaves. If it falls smoothly and quickly the rate is suitable; if it jumps around the rate may be too large, and if it barely moves it may be too small.
gl.ogrenme-orani.faq.0.q: How do you find a good learning rate?
gl.ogrenme-orani.faq.1.a: Often, yes. Starting with a short warm-up and then slowly decreasing the rate is a common approach.
gl.ogrenme-orani.faq.1.q: Does the learning rate change during training?
gl.ogrenme-orani.how: Once the gradient's direction is computed, it is multiplied by the learning rate, and the parameters change by that amount. If the rate is too large, the model overshoots the best point and the loss bounces around or even rises. If it is too small, training crawls and may get stuck in a poor spot. In practice the rate is often not kept constant; a short warm-up followed by a gradual decrease is a common schedule. It is like choosing your stride length while walking downhill.
gl.ogrenme-orani.why: The learning rate is among the values that most need tuning and most affect the outcome. A wrong choice can waste days of expensive training. That is why it is one of the first details shared in model reports and open-source training recipes.
gl.olasilik-dagilimi.def: A complete description of how likely each possible outcome of an uncertain event is. The probabilities of all outcomes add up to one.
gl.olasilik-dagilimi.example: An email filter might rate a message as 95 percent likely to be spam and 5 percent likely to be legitimate; those two numbers form a simple probability distribution.
gl.olasilik-dagilimi.faq.0.a: A low temperature sharpens the distribution and favors the most likely option. A high temperature flattens it, so outputs become more varied but less predictable.
gl.olasilik-dagilimi.faq.0.q: How does the temperature setting affect a probability distribution?
gl.olasilik-dagilimi.faq.1.a: Not necessarily. A model's stated probability may not match its real accuracy, a problem known as poor calibration.
gl.olasilik-dagilimi.faq.1.q: If a model says it is 90 percent sure, is it right 90 percent of the time?
gl.olasilik-dagilimi.how: For a die roll, each of the six faces is assigned a probability of one in six, which is a simple distribution. Language models work on a similar principle: given the text so far, they compute a probability for every token in the vocabulary being the next one. The network's raw outputs are turned into probabilities that sum to one by an operation called softmax. The model then picks a token from this distribution, and settings such as temperature sharpen or flatten it.
gl.olasilik-dagilimi.why: This concept explains why generative AI can give different answers to the same question. The 'confidence scores' of classification models are also probability distributions, though they do not always reflect real accuracy. That difference matters when deciding how far to trust a model's output.
gl.olcekleme-yasalari.def: Empirical observations describing how an AI model's error falls, and with what regularity, as model size, training data and computing power increase.
gl.olcekleme-yasalari.example: A lab can use the results of small experiments to predict how well a much bigger model will perform, and set its training budget accordingly.
gl.olcekleme-yasalari.faq.0.a: Nobody knows. The observations have been consistent over the ranges studied, but data scarcity, energy costs and diminishing returns raise questions about whether the curves will continue in the same way.
gl.olcekleme-yasalari.faq.1.a: No. Moore's law is an observation about the growth in the number of transistors on chips over time. Scaling laws describe the relationship between model error and model size, data and compute.
gl.olcekleme-yasalari.faq.1.q: Are scaling laws the same as Moore's law?
gl.olcekleme-yasalari.how: Researchers train many models of different sizes and plot a measure of error called loss. Loss usually falls along a predictable curve as parameters, data and compute grow. By extending these curves, they can estimate how well a much larger model will perform before training it. Studies such as Google DeepMind's Chinchilla work showed that for a fixed budget, model size and the amount of data need to be balanced.
gl.olcekleme-yasalari.why: These observations are one of the main justifications for large-scale training investments: more compute generally means a better model. They also guide budget and hardware planning. But they are empirical observations, not laws of nature, and limits such as running out of data and diminishing returns are debated.
gl.olceklenebilir-denetim.def: A family of methods aimed at providing reliable feedback and supervision for AI systems even on tasks too complex for humans to evaluate unaided.
gl.olceklenebilir-denetim.example: When a model writes thousands of lines of software, a second model lists likely security flaws, and the human reviewer decides after looking only at the flagged sections.
gl.olceklenebilir-denetim.faq.0.a: In ordinary oversight, a person judges the output alone. Scalable oversight gives that person AI-assisted tools so the evaluation can extend to more complex tasks, while the final decision stays with the human.
gl.olceklenebilir-denetim.faq.0.q: How is scalable oversight different from ordinary human oversight?
gl.olceklenebilir-denetim.faq.1.a: There is a risk: the supervising model can make mistakes or share the same blind spots as the model it checks. That is why these methods are usually designed together with human decision-makers and independent tests.
gl.olceklenebilir-denetim.faq.1.q: Isn't using AI to supervise AI risky?
gl.olceklenebilir-denetim.how: Model training largely depends on people judging outputs, but checking a long program or an expert-level analysis is hard. Scalable oversight proposes getting help from other AI systems to strengthen that judgment. For example, a task can be broken into smaller pieces, two models can argue against each other's answers while a human watches and decides, or a helper model can flag suspicious parts. The goal is to grow the overseer's ability alongside the model's.
gl.olceklenebilir-denetim.why: If models move beyond what people can easily check, the training signal may be flawed and a model's shortcomings can be learned without anyone noticing. That is a serious safety weakness. Scalable oversight is an active research area aimed at closing this gap, though how well the methods work is still being tested.
gl.on-egitim.def: The first and most expensive stage of training an AI model, in which it learns the basic patterns of language or images from a very large, general collection of data.
gl.on-egitim.example: The P in GPT stands for “pre-trained”: the model is first trained on general text and only afterward adapted to specific uses.
gl.on-egitim.faq.0.a: Pre-training gives a model its basic abilities using broad, general data. Fine-tuning adapts that ready-made model to a particular task or behavior using smaller, more targeted data.
gl.on-egitim.faq.0.q: What is the difference between pre-training and fine-tuning?
gl.on-egitim.faq.1.a: Companies often do not disclose the details. In general, broad sources such as web text, books, and code are used, which has led to debates over copyright and privacy.
gl.on-egitim.faq.1.q: What data is used in pre-training?
gl.on-egitim.how: For language models, pre-training usually rests on predicting the next piece of text (a token). The model makes this prediction billions of times across a huge range of sources such as books, web pages, and code, adjusting its weights slightly after each error. Along the way it indirectly picks up grammar, facts, and patterns of reasoning. The result is a base model that is not yet tuned for conversation. Pre-training takes many accelerator chips and a long time.
gl.on-egitim.why: Most of a model's knowledge and abilities are formed at this stage, which is why it sits at the center of discussions about cost and data. The choice of training data raises questions about copyright and privacy. Every later stage builds on this foundation.
gl.oncu-model.def: One of the most advanced general-purpose AI models, sitting at the current edge of capability and watched more closely because its powerful abilities may come with risks that are not yet fully understood.
gl.oncu-model.example: The most capable chat and reasoning models released by the large AI labs are called frontier models, though today's frontier model may look ordinary a few years from now.
gl.oncu-model.faq.0.a: There is no single official criterion. The bar shifts over time and institutions use different definitions, most often based on the amount of computing used in training or on the level of capability.
gl.oncu-model.faq.0.q: Which models count as frontier models?
gl.oncu-model.faq.1.a: As their capabilities grow, so can the risks of misuse and unexpected behavior. That is why special safety testing before release is increasingly discussed.
gl.oncu-model.faq.1.q: Why are frontier models monitored separately?
gl.oncu-model.how: Frontier is not a fixed technical threshold; it is a moving yardstick. The term usually applies to models that need very large amounts of computing power, broad data and costly training, and that tend to be a company's or lab's most capable work. Such models are often expected to go through safety testing before release, for instance attempts to misuse them in cyberattack or biological risk scenarios. Some companies and public bodies have published voluntary commitments or frameworks for these evaluations.
gl.oncu-model.why: Regulators and companies treat the risks of the most powerful models as a separate matter, and safety evaluations and policy debates are organized around this category. Which models count as frontier is contested: some want strict oversight, while others argue that heavy regulation would burden innovation and smaller players.
gl.oneri-sistemi.def: Software that suggests products, content or people a user is likely to be interested in, ranking them based on that user's past behavior and the preferences of similar users.
gl.oneri-sistemi.example: A music app adding a new artist who resembles ones you often play to your weekly playlist is a recommender system at work.
gl.oneri-sistemi.faq.0.a: It does not know you; it reads behavior patterns. It makes statistical guesses from signals such as what you watch, what you skip and what users similar to you choose.
gl.oneri-sistemi.faq.0.q: How does a recommender system seem to know me so well?
gl.oneri-sistemi.faq.1.a: It is the worry that recommenders keep showing similar content, leaving people with less exposure to different views and genres. How large the effect really is remains debated.
gl.oneri-sistemi.how: There are two basic approaches. Collaborative filtering recommends to a user what people with similar histories liked. Content-based filtering finds new items whose features resemble those the user already enjoyed. Many systems today combine both with deep learning models. The output is not a single right answer but a ranked list of candidates tailored to each user. Producing suggestions for brand-new users with no history is a separate challenge, often called the cold-start problem.
gl.oneri-sistemi.why: It decides what gets surfaced on shopping, video and music platforms, so it shapes both user experience and revenue. It is also at the center of debates about filter bubbles, diversity and how transparent content ranking should be.
gl.optik-ara-baglanti.def: A connection technology that moves data between chips, servers and racks using light, usually over fiber-optic cables, instead of electrical signals, and at very high speeds.
gl.optik-ara-baglanti.example: The high-speed links between racks in a data center are increasingly built with fiber, one of the most common places to find optical interconnects today; fiber internet to homes relies on the same principle.
gl.optik-ara-baglanti.faq.0.a: Both carry data with light, but they serve different purposes. Fiber internet connects homes and offices to a network, while optical interconnects handle very fast communication inside a data center or between chips.
gl.optik-ara-baglanti.faq.0.q: Is an optical interconnect the same as fiber internet?
gl.optik-ara-baglanti.faq.1.a: Copper is still common and cheap over short distances. But as speed and distance grow, the signal weakens and heat and energy loss rise, and light handles those limits better.
gl.optik-ara-baglanti.how: A transmitter converts an electrical signal into pulses of light, using a source such as a laser. The light travels along a fiber, and a receiver turns it back into an electrical signal. Over longer distances, light can carry far more data than copper wire with less energy and signal loss. In newer designs, the optical components sit right next to the chip in the same package, known as co-packaged optics, which shortens the distance the electrical signal has to travel.
gl.optik-ara-baglanti.why: AI models are trained by thousands of processors working together, so the flow of data between processors often becomes a bottleneck. Moving data also consumes a lot of energy. Optical interconnects are seen as one way to build larger clusters with less power, and they appear in chipmakers' roadmaps.
gl.optik-karakter-tanima.def: Technology that converts writing in images such as scanned documents, photos or screenshots into text a computer can search and edit.
gl.optik-karakter-tanima.example: Photographing a supermarket receipt with a phone and having OCR turn it into text for an expense-tracking app is a typical everyday use.
gl.optik-karakter-tanima.faq.0.a: Modern systems can recognize handwriting too, but accuracy is generally lower than for printed text and depends heavily on how legible the writing is.
gl.optik-karakter-tanima.faq.1.a: OCR used to rely on rules and templates, while today's systems mostly run on AI models. So it can now be considered an application of AI.
gl.optik-karakter-tanima.faq.1.q: Is OCR the same thing as AI?
gl.optik-karakter-tanima.how: The image is first cleaned up, with skew and noise removed. The system locates text regions on the page, separates lines and characters, and then recognizes each one. This used to be done with template matching; today neural networks are mostly used. The result is editable text, and the position of each word on the page is often kept as well. Print quality, typeface, handwriting and language all affect accuracy, and letters such as the Turkish ç, ğ, ı, ö, ş and ü can sometimes cause errors.
gl.optik-karakter-tanima.why: It makes printed archives searchable, improves accessibility for visually impaired users and is a basic step in document processing systems. Because reading errors can carry into later stages, results should be checked when the data matters.
gl.ortalama-kare-hata.def: The average of the squared differences between a model's predictions and the actual values. It is a common way to summarize error in a single number for models that predict numerical values.
gl.ortalama-kare-hata.example: A model that predicts rental prices for apartments uses MSE to measure how far, on average, it strays from actual rents; one huge error on a single apartment raises the value noticeably.
gl.ortalama-kare-hata.faq.0.a: MAE averages the absolute values of the errors and counts every error in proportion. MSE squares the errors, so it punishes large ones more heavily and is more sensitive to outliers.
gl.ortalama-kare-hata.faq.0.q: What is the difference between MSE and mean absolute error (MAE)?
gl.ortalama-kare-hata.faq.1.a: No. A model can have a low MSE on its training data and still make large errors on new data, which is called overfitting. That is why evaluation uses a separate test set.
gl.ortalama-kare-hata.faq.1.q: Does a low MSE always mean a good model?
gl.ortalama-kare-hata.how: For each example, the difference between the prediction and the true value is taken, multiplied by itself, and then averaged over all examples. Squaring does two things: positive and negative errors cannot cancel each other out, and large errors are punished disproportionately more than small ones. For instance, a miss of two units costs four, while a miss of four units costs sixteen. During training this value is minimized, and because it is smooth and differentiable, it works well with gradient descent.
gl.ortalama-kare-hata.why: MSE is one of the most basic loss functions and evaluation measures for regression problems, common in tasks such as predicting house prices, demand or temperature. Its sensitivity to extreme values cuts both ways: it catches large errors, but a few unusual data points can distort the result. Its unit is the square of the data's unit, so its square root (RMSE) is often preferred for interpretation.
gl.ortaya-cikan-yetenekler.def: Skills that seem absent in smaller models and appear to switch on suddenly once a model reaches a certain scale, as if they had not been explicitly taught.
gl.ortaya-cikan-yetenekler.example: A large language model starting to perform a new task after being shown just a few examples in its prompt is a frequently cited case of an emergent ability.
gl.ortaya-cikan-yetenekler.faq.0.a: That is disputed. Early studies reported sharp jumps at certain scales, while later work suggested this may partly depend on the choice of metric, and that smoother measures can make progress look gradual.
gl.ortaya-cikan-yetenekler.faq.0.q: Do emergent abilities really appear suddenly?
gl.ortaya-cikan-yetenekler.faq.1.a: Scaling laws usually describe error falling in a smooth, predictable way. Emergent abilities describe the impression that on specific tasks performance jumps at some point. The two are often discussed together.
gl.ortaya-cikan-yetenekler.faq.1.q: How do emergent abilities relate to scaling laws?
gl.ortaya-cikan-yetenekler.how: Researchers train the same model family at several sizes and test it on different tasks. On some tasks, small models perform at chance level, and performance then climbs sharply beyond a certain size. This jump is called emergence. Few-shot learning and multi-step arithmetic are commonly cited examples. Other studies argue that the jump may partly come from the metric used, and that with smoother measures progress looks more gradual.
gl.ortaya-cikan-yetenekler.why: The idea suggests that what a model can do after it is scaled up is hard to predict in advance, which matters in safety debates and investment decisions. The question is still contested: some researchers see a genuine threshold, while others consider it a measurement artifact.
gl.oruntu-tanima.def: The ability to automatically notice regularities, recurring structures and similarities in data. It is used on images, audio, text and numerical data.
gl.oruntu-tanima.example: A bank learns the usual pattern of a customer’s card spending and flags an unusual run of purchases that does not fit it as suspicious.
gl.oruntu-tanima.faq.0.a: No. Pattern recognition is a goal, while machine learning is the most common method for reaching it. Rule-based pattern recognition systems also existed before.
gl.oruntu-tanima.faq.0.q: Is pattern recognition the same as machine learning?
gl.oruntu-tanima.faq.1.a: The results can look similar, but the process is different. People can often generalize from a few examples, whereas machines usually need many.
gl.oruntu-tanima.faq.1.q: Do machines recognize patterns the way people do?
gl.oruntu-tanima.how: The system first extracts distinguishing features from the data, such as edges in an image or frequencies in a sound. It then learns from examples which group or outcome those features belong to. In classical methods people design the features, while in deep learning the neural network finds them on its own. When new data arrives, the system compares it with the patterns it has learned and picks the best match.
gl.oruntu-tanima.why: It underlies much of machine learning: face recognition, speech recognition, fraud detection and medical image analysis all rely on it. If the patterns a system finds come from wrong or biased data, its results will be flawed too.
gl.osworld.def: A benchmark that measures how well AI agents carry out open-ended tasks in a real computer environment, by viewing the screen and using the mouse and keyboard to operate applications.
gl.osworld.example: An agent is asked to open a spreadsheet, sort a particular column, and save the file under a different name; a script then inspects the file to verify the task.
gl.osworld.faq.0.a: Browser-focused tests are limited to web pages. OSWorld also covers desktop applications such as office programs, file management, and system settings.
gl.osworld.faq.0.q: How is OSWorld different from browser-only agent tests?
gl.osworld.faq.1.a: It shows the share of tasks the agent completes correctly from start to finish. It only applies to the kinds of tasks tested and does not represent every real-world workflow.
gl.osworld.faq.1.q: What does an OSWorld score tell you?
gl.osworld.how: The agent receives a task in natural language inside a virtual machine running an operating system. It looks at screenshots and picks actions such as clicking, typing, and keyboard shortcuts, and it can move between applications like a browser, office programs, and a file manager. When the task ends, a script written for that specific task checks whether the file or setting is in the expected state. Success is therefore measured automatically, without human judgment.
gl.osworld.why: Agents that use computers are one of the areas where AI moves from chatting to acting. OSWorld gives a shared yardstick for how reliably these agents work in real interfaces, so it is often cited in model and product announcements. In multi-step tasks a single wrong click can ruin the job, which makes the test demanding.
gl.otomatik-kodlayici.def: A neural network that learns to compress its input into a small representation and then rebuild something close to the original from that representation.
gl.otomatik-kodlayici.example: An autoencoder trained only on images of flawless products in a factory reconstructs a defective item poorly, and the high reconstruction error becomes a sign of the defect.
gl.otomatik-kodlayici.faq.0.a: The idea is similar but not the same. An autoencoder only works well on the kind of data it was trained on and is usually lossy; its real value is that the learned summary can be used for other tasks.
gl.otomatik-kodlayici.faq.0.q: Is an autoencoder just a compression tool like zip?
gl.otomatik-kodlayici.faq.1.a: No. Because the model tries to reproduce its input, the target is the input itself, so it can be trained on unlabeled data.
gl.otomatik-kodlayici.faq.1.q: Does an autoencoder need labeled data?
gl.otomatik-kodlayici.how: The network has two parts: an encoder squeezes the input down to a narrow “bottleneck” layer, and a decoder rebuilds the input from that summary. Training aims to make the reconstruction as close to the original as possible, and no labels are needed because the target is the input itself. Since the bottleneck is narrow, the network is forced to keep only the most important information. The resulting summary is a compact representation of the data that can be reused for other tasks.
gl.otomatik-kodlayici.why: Autoencoders are used for dimensionality reduction, denoising, anomaly detection and pretraining. The core idea behind many generative models also comes from here: compress data into a small latent representation and generate from it.
gl.otomatik-konusma-tanima.def: AI technology that listens to spoken words and writes them out as text; it is used to transcribe meeting recordings, generate subtitles and understand voice commands.
gl.otomatik-konusma-tanima.example: OpenAI's open-source Whisper model can be used to transcribe a podcast recording in many languages.
gl.otomatik-konusma-tanima.faq.0.a: No. ASR writes down what was said, while speaker recognition tries to determine whose voice it is.
gl.otomatik-konusma-tanima.faq.0.q: Is ASR the same as speaker recognition?
gl.otomatik-konusma-tanima.faq.1.a: A common measure is word error rate: the number of wrong, missing and extra words in the system's output compared with a reference transcript. The lower the rate, the better the result.
gl.otomatik-konusma-tanima.how: The sound is first captured as a digital waveform, cut into very short slices and converted into a representation of its frequency content. A trained neural network, often built on the Transformer architecture, turns these slices into a sequence of letters or word pieces. During training, the model sees many recordings paired with their written transcripts and learns which sounds correspond to which text. Accents, background noise and several people talking at once are the main factors that lower accuracy. Performance is usually measured by word error rate.
gl.otomatik-konusma-tanima.why: Turning speech into text is the first step in many applications, from voice assistants and meeting summaries to subtitles and call-center analytics. It provides accessibility for people with hearing loss. Because voice recordings can contain personal data, privacy is also an important issue.
gl.otonom-silahlar.def: Weapon systems that can make critical decisions, such as selecting targets and initiating an attack, without human intervention.
gl.otonom-silahlar.example: A drone that searches a given area and strikes targets without waiting for human approval would be the kind of system at the heart of the debate.
gl.otonom-silahlar.faq.0.a: No. With a remotely piloted drone, a human decides on the target and the decision to fire. With an autonomous weapon, at the level under debate, that decision is left to the system itself.
gl.otonom-silahlar.faq.0.q: Is an autonomous weapon the same as a remotely piloted armed drone?
gl.otonom-silahlar.faq.1.a: It describes a human being able to genuinely and promptly intervene in how a weapon is used. What counts as meaningful is still disputed among countries and experts.
gl.otonom-silahlar.faq.1.q: What does meaningful human control mean?
gl.otonom-silahlar.how: These systems scan their surroundings with sensors and software, classify objects, and decide to attack on their own once they find a target that meets pre-set criteria. Autonomy is not an on-off switch: a human might approve every strike, only be able to cancel one, or not be involved at all. The debate centers on systems at the far end of that range, where the human is out of the loop. AI has brought the topic back into focus because it strengthens target recognition and decision-making, but countries have no shared definition.
gl.otonom-silahlar.why: Key questions include whether a machine can apply the laws of war, such as distinguishing combatants from civilians and weighing proportionality, who bears responsibility when it errs, and whether an arms race could follow. Some states and civil society groups call for a binding ban, while others argue existing international humanitarian law is sufficient. The issue is also under discussion within the United Nations.
gl.otonom-surus.def: The ability of a vehicle to handle driving tasks such as steering, speed and braking by itself, using sensors and AI software, without human intervention.
gl.otonom-surus.example: Driverless robotaxis operating in a defined part of a city and driverless trucks working in mines are examples of autonomous driving.
gl.otonom-surus.faq.0.a: No. Systems like lane keeping or adaptive cruise control help the driver, but the driver stays responsible. In autonomous driving, the system takes over the whole driving task under certain conditions.
gl.otonom-surus.faq.0.q: Is autonomous driving the same as driver assistance?
gl.otonom-surus.faq.1.a: No. They can reduce human error but may still fail in unexpected situations, which is why extensive testing, limited operating areas and regulation matter.
gl.otonom-surus.how: The system runs a three-stage loop. First comes perception: camera, radar and LiDAR data are used to recognize lanes, vehicles, pedestrians and traffic signs. Next is planning: the software predicts what nearby objects may do in the next moments and picks a safe route and speed. Finally comes control, where steering, throttle and brake commands are carried out. This loop repeats many times per second. Many systems also rely on detailed maps and precise positioning.
gl.otonom-surus.why: Because human error plays a part in most traffic accidents, autonomous driving is promoted for its potential to improve safety. It could also reshape transport, urban planning and logistics. Still, handling rare and unexpected situations, deciding who is liable in a crash, and regulation remain open questions.
gl.otoregresif-model.def: A model that produces its output piece by piece rather than all at once, predicting each next piece by looking at everything generated so far.
gl.otoregresif-model.example: When a chat assistant's answer appears on screen word by word, you are watching autoregressive generation happen.
gl.otoregresif-model.faq.0.a: An autoregressive model generates output in order from start to finish. A diffusion model starts from noise and refines the whole output step by step, an approach common in image generation.
gl.otoregresif-model.faq.0.q: What is the difference between an autoregressive model and a diffusion model?
gl.otoregresif-model.faq.1.a: To predict the next piece well, a model has to learn grammar, facts and context. That learning is useful, but the model can still make mistakes and produce things that are not true.
gl.otoregresif-model.faq.1.q: How can a model that only predicts the next word reason at all?
gl.otoregresif-model.how: In a language model, the process works like this: the model takes the given context and computes probabilities for the next token. One is chosen and added to the sequence, and the process restarts on the longer sequence. The loop continues until the answer is complete or a stop signal appears. Training uses the same idea: the model learns to predict the next piece in real text. That is why generation moves step by step, and longer answers take longer.
gl.otoregresif-model.why: Most GPT-style language models work this way, so the idea is central to understanding how chat assistants behave. It explains why answers stream out word by word, why long answers cost more, and why an early mistake can affect what follows.
gl.oz-denetimli-ogrenme.def: A training approach in which a model learns from tasks created out of unlabeled data itself, so useful patterns can be extracted without people writing labels by hand.
gl.oz-denetimli-ogrenme.example: A language model is trained by predicting how unfinished sentences such as 'The weather today is very ...' continue; the correct answer comes from the text itself.
gl.oz-denetimli-ogrenme.faq.0.a: Not exactly. Unsupervised learning usually looks for structure in data, such as clusters, while self-supervised learning builds an artificial prediction task and trains against a real target. For that reason it is sometimes treated as a special kind of unsupervised learning.
gl.oz-denetimli-ogrenme.faq.0.q: Is self-supervised learning the same as unsupervised learning?
gl.oz-denetimli-ogrenme.faq.1.a: Because internet-scale text can be used without labeling. The task of predicting the next word teaches grammar, world knowledge and much more.
gl.oz-denetimli-ogrenme.faq.1.q: Why is it used for large language models?
gl.oz-denetimli-ogrenme.how: A piece of the data is hidden and the model tries to predict it. Guessing the next word in a text or a word removed from the middle of a sentence are typical cases, and filling in a masked region of an image works the same way. Because the correct answer is already in the data, nobody has to write labels. By solving this task billions of times, the model absorbs the structure of language or images. That knowledge can later be adapted to specific jobs with much smaller labeled datasets.
gl.oz-denetimli-ogrenme.why: Labeled data is expensive and slow to produce, while text, images and audio exist online in enormous unlabeled quantities. Self-supervised learning made that stockpile usable and became the foundation of pretraining for large language models. When news stories mention pretraining, this is usually the method behind it.
gl.oz-dikkat.def: A type of attention in which each element of a sequence looks at the other elements of the same sequence to update its own representation in context. It is the core building block of Transformer models.
gl.oz-dikkat.example: In the sentence 'The cat drank the milk because it was hungry', the model looks at the other words while updating the representation of 'it' and will most likely link it to 'cat'.
gl.oz-dikkat.faq.0.a: The attention mechanism is the general idea and can link two different sequences, such as a target sentence looking at a source sentence in translation. In self-attention a sequence only looks at its own elements.
gl.oz-dikkat.faq.0.q: What is the difference between self-attention and the attention mechanism?
gl.oz-dikkat.faq.1.a: Every element is compared with every other element, so the cost rises quickly with sequence length. Doubling the context roughly quadruples the workload.
gl.oz-dikkat.how: For each token, three vectors are produced: a query, a key and a value. A token's query is compared with all the keys in the sequence, and the resulting scores are turned into weights. The token's new representation is the sum of the values blended with those weights. In this way each token pulls in information from the other tokens it needs to settle its meaning. Because every pair is compared, the cost grows quickly with sequence length, roughly with its square.
gl.oz-dikkat.why: Self-attention lets a model link distant words in a text directly and run the computation in parallel. This sped up training compared with older recurrent networks and opened the way to very large models. The high price of long-context models also comes from the way self-attention cost grows with sequence length.
gl.ozellik-muhendisligi.def: The work of selecting, transforming and creating the input variables a model learns from, so that patterns in raw data become easier to pick up. A model's predictive power often depends as much on these variables as on the algorithm itself.
gl.ozellik-muhendisligi.example: A bank creates new features for its fraud model, such as a customer's number of purchases in the last thirty days and how far a purchase deviates from their usual spending.
gl.ozellik-muhendisligi.faq.0.a: For images, audio and text, largely yes, because the model learns the useful features itself. For tabular business data, carefully designed features still make a noticeable difference.
gl.ozellik-muhendisligi.faq.0.q: Does deep learning make feature engineering unnecessary?
gl.ozellik-muhendisligi.faq.1.a: No. Feature selection means deciding which existing variables to use. Feature engineering also covers creating and transforming variables, and selection is often one part of it.
gl.ozellik-muhendisligi.faq.1.q: Is feature selection the same as feature engineering?
gl.ozellik-muhendisligi.how: In a house-price model, for instance, “year built” can be turned into “age of the building,” and addresses can be grouped into neighborhoods. Missing values are filled in and numbers on different scales are brought to a common range. A data scientist who knows the domain decides which information is likely to help prediction. In classic machine learning this step is labor-intensive. In deep learning, the layers extract many features from the data on their own, so hand-crafted features matter less for images, audio and text.
gl.ozellik-muhendisligi.why: In work built on tabular data, such as credit scoring, fraud detection and demand forecasting, well-chosen features can make even a simple model strong. A badly built feature can also leak information from the test data and make results look better than they are. That makes it a key step for both performance and trustworthy measurement.
gl.parametre-verimli-ince-ayar.def: A family of methods that adapt a large pretrained model to a new task by training only a small share of its parameters, or a few newly added ones, rather than the whole model.
gl.parametre-verimli-ince-ayar.example: Hugging Face's PEFT library offers methods like LoRA through a single interface, so a company can adapt an open model to its own customer-support conversations.
gl.parametre-verimli-ince-ayar.faq.0.a: No. PEFT is an umbrella term, and LoRA is one of its best-known methods. Others, such as adapter layers and prompt tuning, belong to the same family.
gl.parametre-verimli-ince-ayar.faq.0.q: Are PEFT and LoRA the same thing?
gl.parametre-verimli-ince-ayar.faq.1.a: In some cases, especially when teaching the model a very different domain, it may not match full fine-tuning in quality. In exchange, it is far cheaper.
gl.parametre-verimli-ince-ayar.faq.1.q: Does it have any downside compared with full fine-tuning?
gl.parametre-verimli-ince-ayar.how: Most of the base model's weights are frozen, and only a small set of parameters takes part in training. That set might be small adapter modules inserted between layers, the low-rank matrices in LoRA, or learnable steering vectors added to the input. Gradients and optimizer state are kept only for these parameters, so memory use drops. The resulting add-ons are tiny, so they can be stored per task and attached to the base model when needed.
gl.parametre-verimli-ince-ayar.why: Retraining a model with billions of parameters for every task is expensive and requires a full copy of the model each time. PEFT methods cut the cost and let small teams and researchers customize large models too. They can also help preserve the base model's general abilities.

gl.parametre.def.en: The numerical values a model learns during training. The parameter count (for example, 70 billion) is often used to describe a model's size.

gl.parametre.example.en: The phrase "a 70-billion-parameter model" means the model consists of 70 billion adjustable numbers.

gl.parametre.faq.0.a.en: Larger models are generally more capable, but the quality of the training data, the training method and the architecture also determine the outcome. Some small models can outperform larger older ones.

gl.parametre.faq.0.q.en: Does a model get better as its parameter count increases?

gl.parametre.faq.1.a.en: B stands for billion. 70B indicates that the model has roughly 70 billion parameters.

gl.parametre.faq.1.q.en: What do terms like 7B and 70B mean?

gl.parametre.how.en: A neural network consists of interconnected artificial "neurons," and the strengths of these connections are expressed as numbers; these numbers are called parameters. During training, parameters are adjusted so that the model's predictions are accurate. Everything the model knows is stored in these numbers.

gl.parametre.why.en: The parameter count indicates a model's size and, generally, its capacity, but it does not determine quality on its own. The quality of the training data and the training method matter at least as much as the parameter count. Larger models require more hardware and energy.

gl.parcalama.def: The process of splitting long documents into smaller, meaningful pieces of text so they can be searched and handed to a model.
gl.parcalama.example: A product manual hundreds of pages long is split by headings and each section is stored separately; when a user asks about replacing the battery, only the relevant section is sent to the model.
gl.parcalama.faq.0.a: There is no single value that works for everyone. It depends on the type of document, the kinds of questions expected and the model used. Teams usually try several sizes and compare results.
gl.parcalama.faq.0.q: What is the ideal chunk size?
gl.parcalama.faq.1.a: If a piece of information sits on the boundary between two chunks, it may look incomplete in both. A small overlap reduces split sentences and ideas and lowers the chance of missing it in retrieval.
gl.parcalama.how: A document is first split according to some rule. The rule can be a fixed length, or a smarter method that follows paragraph, heading or section boundaries. Chunks are often made to overlap partly with their neighbors, so sentences are not cut in the middle and context is preserved. Each chunk is turned into an embedding and stored in a database. When a question arrives, only the most relevant chunks are retrieved and passed to the model.
gl.parcalama.why: Chunk size directly affects the quality of retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) systems. If chunks are too large, the topic gets blurry and the model's context fills with unnecessary text; if they are too small, they may mean little on their own. That makes chunking one of the quiet engineering choices that shape the outcome.
gl.pass-k.def: A metric for code-generating AI models: the probability that at least one of k generated solutions to a problem passes that problem’s unit tests.
gl.pass-k.example: A coding assistant proposes five versions of a function and two of them pass the unit tests; that problem counts as solved under pass@5.
gl.pass-k.faq.0.a: Pass@1 is the chance of getting a correct solution in a single attempt; pass@10 is the chance that at least one of ten attempts is correct. Pass@10 is almost always higher.
gl.pass-k.faq.0.q: What is the difference between pass@1 and pass@10?
gl.pass-k.faq.1.a: Because unit tests can verify code automatically and unambiguously. For free-form text it is much harder to define a single objectively correct answer.
gl.pass-k.faq.1.q: Why is pass@k mostly used for code?
gl.pass-k.how: The model produces several solutions for a programming problem, and each one is run against automated unit tests. Pass@k is the probability that at least one of k attempts passes all the tests. In practice more than k samples are generated per problem and the probability is computed with a statistical estimator, which reduces the effect of luck. Pass@1 reflects success on the first try. As k grows the score rises, because the model gets more chances. Results are then averaged across all problems.
gl.pass-k.why: Since code correctness can be checked automatically and exactly, this metric is common in coding evaluations. Pass@1 reflects a user who wants working code in one try, while higher k values reflect systems that generate many candidates and filter them with tests. A score reported without its k value can therefore be misleading.

gl.pekistirmeli-ogrenme.def.en: A machine learning method in which a model learns through trial and error, receiving rewards for correct behavior and penalties for incorrect behavior.

gl.pekistirmeli-ogrenme.example.en: DeepMind's AlphaGo, the system that beat the world champion at Go, relied heavily on reinforcement learning in its training.

gl.pekistirmeli-ogrenme.faq.0.a.en: RLHF stands for reinforcement learning from human feedback. Humans compare and score model responses, which teaches the model to give more helpful and safer answers.

gl.pekistirmeli-ogrenme.faq.1.a.en: In supervised learning, the correct answer for each example is provided upfront. In reinforcement learning, the model does not know the correct answer; it learns from the rewards it receives for the actions it tries.

gl.pekistirmeli-ogrenme.faq.1.q.en: What is the difference between reinforcement learning and supervised learning?

gl.pekistirmeli-ogrenme.how.en: In reinforcement learning, an "agent" takes actions in an environment and receives a reward or penalty score for the outcome of each action. Over time, it learns the behaviors that maximize its total reward. For language models, the method is used to steer the model toward more helpful and safer responses, with humans or automated evaluators scoring its answers.

gl.pekistirmeli-ogrenme.why.en: It plays a key role in superhuman performance in games, robotic control and the training of today's reasoning models. It lets models improve themselves on math and coding tasks, where the correct answer can be verified.

gl.planli-aldatma.def: When an AI model deliberately misleads its developers or evaluators in order to pursue its own goals. For example, it might behave well when it detects it is being tested and act differently when it believes it is not.
gl.planli-aldatma.example: In one test design, a model is shown a document saying it will be shut down and is given access it could use to alter that document; researchers then check whether it changes it in secret and later denies having done so.
gl.planli-aldatma.faq.0.a: No. In a hallucination, a model makes up something it does not know by mistake. In scheming, the model deliberately misleads someone to serve a goal. The first is an accuracy problem, the second an alignment problem.
gl.planli-aldatma.faq.0.q: Is scheming the same as hallucination?
gl.planli-aldatma.faq.1.a: In controlled experiments, a limited number of such behaviors have been observed. Whether they reflect genuine intent or patterns learned in training, and how often they show up in everyday use, is still debated.
gl.planli-aldatma.faq.1.q: Are today's models actually deceiving people?
gl.planli-aldatma.how: The concept assumes a model has a goal and that human oversight stands in the way of it. Such a model might follow the rules during testing but deviate in real use, hide its true capabilities, or try to disable monitoring mechanisms. To probe this, researchers give models tasks that set their goal against oversight and then examine their behavior and, where available, their reasoning traces. Some safety organizations have reported that advanced models can show behavior of this kind in contrived scenarios. How common it is outside those setups remains debated.
gl.planli-aldatma.why: If scheming occurs, standard safety tests become unreliable, because a model can give the safe-looking behavior just to pass. That raises the question of whether evaluations reflect how a model really behaves. Today it is mostly a research topic, but it is treated as a separate risk category in safety work on advanced models.
gl.politika-gradyani.def: A family of reinforcement learning methods that improve an agent's behavior rule, its policy, by adjusting it directly rather than going through a table of values.
gl.politika-gradyani.example: A robot learning to walk in simulation raises the probability of the movements from episodes where it advanced without falling, gradually developing a balanced gait.
gl.politika-gradyani.faq.0.a: Q-learning first learns the value of actions and then picks the most valuable one. A policy gradient method learns the rule that chooses the action directly and does not need value estimates.
gl.politika-gradyani.faq.0.q: What is the difference between policy gradient and Q-learning?
gl.politika-gradyani.faq.1.a: Because episode outcomes depend partly on chance, the gradient estimate is noisy, which can make training slow and unstable. Various techniques are used to reduce that noise.
gl.politika-gradyani.faq.1.q: What is the weakness of policy gradient methods?
gl.politika-gradyani.how: The policy is usually a neural network that looks at the situation and outputs probabilities for each action. The agent plays a few episodes with this policy and measures how much reward each one earned. The network's weights are then updated in small gradient steps so that actions in high-reward episodes become more likely and actions in low-reward ones become less likely. As this loop repeats, the policy improves. Because action choice is probabilistic, the approach also works comfortably with continuous action spaces.
gl.politika-gradyani.why: Policy gradients are a natural choice for tasks that need continuous movement, such as robot control. PPO, one of the methods used to train chat models with human feedback, belongs to this family. That is why the term comes up indirectly in news about aligning large language models.
gl.poz-tahmini.def: A computer vision task that finds the positions of the joints and limbs of a person, and sometimes an animal or object, in an image or video to work out their posture.
gl.poz-tahmini.example: A fitness app watches someone doing squats through a phone camera and warns that their knees are caving inward.
gl.poz-tahmini.faq.0.a: No. Pose estimation finds how a body or its limbs are positioned, not who the person is. Facial recognition is a separate task.
gl.poz-tahmini.faq.0.q: Does pose estimation mean facial recognition?
gl.poz-tahmini.faq.1.a: Most modern methods work with an ordinary camera. A depth sensor or several cameras can improve accuracy, especially for three-dimensional estimation.
gl.poz-tahmini.faq.1.q: Does pose estimation need a special sensor?
gl.poz-tahmini.how: The model predicts key points such as shoulders, elbows, wrists, hips and knees, then connects them into a skeleton-like structure. Training data comes from images where these points were marked by hand, or from motion-capture systems. Two-dimensional estimation gives points on the image, while three-dimensional estimation also tries to infer depth. In video, the points are tracked across frames so movement is followed smoothly. When several people are in the scene, the system can first find each person and then work out each one's pose.
gl.poz-tahmini.why: Sports analysis, physical therapy tracking, motion-controlled games and animation without special equipment all rely on pose estimation. It also helps robots understand human movement so they can work safely alongside people. Because it tracks posture rather than identity, some applications can analyze movement without collecting facial data.
gl.proksimal-politika-optimizasyonu.def: A reinforcement learning algorithm that updates a model's behavior in small, controlled steps; it was long the standard choice for training language models from human feedback.
gl.proksimal-politika-optimizasyonu.exam: In training InstructGPT, scores from the reward model were fed back into the language model through PPO.
It means close. The method keeps the new policy close to the old one so that training progresses steadily.
In language model training, the policy model, a reference model, a reward model and a value model are all held in memory. For large models that demands serious hardware.
gl.proksimal-politika-optimizasyonu.how: The model produces an answer, a reward model scores it, and the model moves toward behaviors that earn higher scores. PPO's key trick is that it prevents the model from straying too far from its previous behavior in a single update, since a huge jump can wreck training. To do this, the ratio between new and old probabilities is clipped to a limited range. In language model training it is usually paired with an extra penalty for drifting from the starting model and a separate value model that estimates the expected reward of answers.
gl.proksimal-politika-optimizasyonu.why: OpenAI researchers proposed the method in 2017. PPO was a core part of the RLHF pipeline used to train early chat models such as InstructGPT. It spread because it is stable, but it is costly since it requires keeping several large models in memory at once. Methods such as GRPO and DPO emerged partly to reduce that cost.
gl.pytorch.def: An open-source, Python-based deep learning library used to build and train AI models. It is especially widespread among researchers and teams that develop models.
gl.pytorch.example: A university team can write a new image classification architecture in a few hundred lines of PyTorch and start experimenting the same day.
gl.pytorch.faq.0.a: Both are deep learning libraries. PyTorch is popular in research for its flexibility and its closeness to plain Python, while TensorFlow, developed by Google, offers an ecosystem known for its deployment and mobile tools.
gl.pytorch.faq.0.q: What is the difference between PyTorch and TensorFlow?
gl.pytorch.faq.1.a: Yes, PyTorch's main interface is Python. Basic Python plus some intuition for linear algebra and probability is enough to get started.
gl.pytorch.faq.1.q: Do I need to know Python to use PyTorch?
gl.pytorch.how: Data is held in tensors, which are multi-dimensional arrays of numbers, and computations can be accelerated on a graphics card. An automatic differentiation feature called autograd computes the gradients needed to update a model's parameters during training. A model is written like ordinary Python code and runs line by line, which makes debugging easier. Layers, loss functions and optimization algorithms come ready to use. A trained model can be exported to other formats for production use.
gl.pytorch.why: A large share of research papers and of the open models shared on platforms like Hugging Face are written in PyTorch, so it sits underneath many of the models in AI news. The project was started by Meta and is now governed by the PyTorch Foundation, which operates under the Linux Foundation.
gl.q-ogrenme.def: A classic reinforcement learning algorithm that lets an agent learn by trial and error how much long-term reward each action will bring in each situation.
gl.q-ogrenme.example: In a simple maze game, the agent gradually learns in a Q table which direction from each square gets it to the exit faster.
gl.q-ogrenme.faq.0.a: It is commonly explained as short for quality. The Q value shows how good it is to take a particular action in a particular state.
gl.q-ogrenme.faq.0.q: What does the Q in Q-learning stand for?
gl.q-ogrenme.faq.1.a: When the number of states and actions becomes huge, storing the table and trying every cell enough times becomes impossible. That is why deep neural networks that approximate the Q values are used instead.
gl.q-ogrenme.faq.1.q: Why can't Q-learning use a table on large problems?
gl.q-ogrenme.how: The algorithm keeps a Q value for every state and action pair, which is an estimate of the total reward that action can expect to bring. At the start the values are zero or random. Each time the agent takes an action and sees the reward and the new state, it nudges the relevant value toward the reward it received plus the best value it expects from the new state. After many repetitions the values approach the true ones, and the agent picks the action with the highest Q value in each state. It does not need to know the rules of the environment in advance.
gl.q-ogrenme.why: Q-learning is one of the most basic and most widely taught reinforcement learning algorithms. Deep Q-networks (DQN), which estimate Q values with a neural network instead of a table, became well known through DeepMind's system that played Atari games. Understanding how it works also makes more complex agents easier to grasp.
gl.raf-olcekli-sistem.def: An integrated system in which dozens of accelerators in a single data center rack are designed, with fast interconnects and shared cooling, to work like one giant computer.
gl.raf-olcekli-sistem.example: Nvidia's NVL-series rack systems aim to make many GPUs in one rack behave like a single large accelerator.
gl.raf-olcekli-sistem.faq.0.a: A server is a single machine. In a rack-scale system the whole rack, from interconnect to cooling, is designed as one product.
gl.raf-olcekli-sistem.faq.0.q: How is a rack-scale system different from a server?
gl.raf-olcekli-sistem.faq.1.a: Packing many accelerators into one rack greatly raises heat and power density, so options like liquid cooling often come into play.
gl.raf-olcekli-sistem.faq.1.q: Why do these systems need such strong cooling?
gl.raf-olcekli-sistem.how: Data centers used to buy servers one by one and then link them together. In the rack-scale approach, the vendor designs GPUs, processors, networking, power delivery and cooling together at the rack level. The accelerators in the rack are joined by very fast dedicated links, so pieces of a huge model can be shared among them with little delay. The customer buys a ready, tested unit instead of individual parts.
gl.raf-olcekli-sistem.why: Models have outgrown single chips, so performance often depends less on the chip itself and more on how well chips are connected. That shifts competition from individual chips to whole systems. Power and cooling demands also shape how data centers are built.
