gl.rag.def.en: A technique in which a model finds relevant information from a document archive or the web before answering and bases its response on it. It is used to reduce fabricated information.

gl.rag.example.en: An assistant that, when an employee asks about company internal policies, finds the relevant regulation clause and answers based on it is using RAG.

gl.rag.faq.0.a.en: It lets a model answer using current, company-specific information and grounded in documents, without having to retrain the model.

gl.rag.faq.1.a.en: No, but it reduces them noticeably. Errors can still occur if the wrong document is retrieved or the model misinterprets the document.

gl.rag.how.en: In RAG, when a user asks a question, the system first finds relevant passages in a document archive, database or the web. These texts are given to the model along with the question, and the model is asked to base its answer on this information. This way, the model can also use current or private information it did not see in training.

gl.rag.why.en: It is the most common way for companies to build assistants that work with their own documents. There is no need to retrain the model, the information can be updated, and answers can cite sources, which reduces fabricated information.

gl.rastgele-orman.def: A machine learning method that trains many decision trees and combines their predictions by majority vote or averaging to reach a final answer.
gl.rastgele-orman.example: A bank could build a forest of hundreds of trees that look at an applicant's income, debts and payment history, then estimate credit risk from the trees' votes.
gl.rastgele-orman.faq.0.a: A single decision tree can memorize details of the training data and then err on new cases. A random forest takes the joint decision of many different trees, so it is usually more stable, though it is harder to read than one tree.
gl.rastgele-orman.faq.0.q: What is the difference between a random forest and a single decision tree?
gl.rastgele-orman.faq.1.a: Usually not, because they shine in different areas. Deep learning is strong on images, audio and text, while tree-based methods like random forests remain strong choices for tabular data made of rows and columns.
gl.rastgele-orman.faq.1.q: Does a random forest replace deep learning?
gl.rastgele-orman.how: The method first draws many random samples from the training data. A separate decision tree is grown on each sample, and at every split the tree considers only a randomly chosen handful of features rather than all of them. This makes the trees make different mistakes. At prediction time, classification takes a vote across the trees, while numeric prediction averages their answers. It works like the wisdom of crowds: many individually noisy judgments become more stable when pooled.
gl.rastgele-orman.why: A random forest reduces the tendency of a single decision tree to memorize its training data, and it is known for giving good results with little tuning. It remains a common baseline for tabular data such as customer records or loan applications. It can also show which features mattered most, which helps with interpretability.
gl.react.def: A method in which a language model interleaves reasoning with action: the model thinks, uses a tool, sees the result and plans its next step accordingly.
gl.react.example: When asked 'How old is this company's founder?', a model first searches for the founder, then finds the birth year, and finally does the arithmetic to give the answer.
gl.react.faq.0.a: In chain of thought, the model only reasons step by step inside itself. ReAct adds tool use to that reasoning, so the model takes in information from the outside world and changes its plan accordingly.
gl.react.faq.0.q: What is the difference between ReAct and chain of thought?
gl.react.faq.1.a: Yes. Many agent frameworks are built on this loop, where the model thinks, calls a tool, reads the result and continues.
gl.react.faq.1.q: Is ReAct related to AI agents?
gl.react.how: ReAct takes its name from the words reasoning and acting. The model first writes a thought, such as 'I should search to find this information.' Then it takes an action, for example sending a query to a search engine. The returned result is fed back to the model as an observation, and the model continues with a new thought. This loop repeats until an answer is found. That way the model can check facts against outside sources instead of relying only on what it memorized.
gl.react.why: ReAct is considered one of the forerunners of how today's AI agents work. A model that can use a tool and update its plan after seeing the result makes fewer things up than one that answers in a single pass, and it can carry out multi-step tasks. The think, act, observe loop mentioned in agent news mostly builds on this idea.
gl.regresyon.def: A method and task type that aims to predict a continuous numerical value, such as a price, a temperature or demand, from input variables.
gl.regresyon.example: A real estate website can use regression to estimate an apartment’s rent from details such as location, floor area and building age.
gl.regresyon.faq.0.a: Regression predicts a continuous number, while classification picks one of several predefined categories. The answer in the first is something like 23.5 degrees, in the second a label such as “cold” or “warm”.
gl.regresyon.faq.0.q: What is the difference between regression and classification?
gl.regresyon.faq.1.a: The name is a historical convention. Logistic regression computes a probability, and when that probability is turned into a category with a threshold it is used for classification.
gl.regresyon.faq.1.q: Why does logistic regression have regression in its name if it does classification?
gl.regresyon.how: The model learns the relationship between inputs and outcomes from past examples. In its simplest form it draws the line that best fits the data: as a home’s floor area grows, how much does the price rise? The model is adjusted so that the gap between its predictions and the real values gets smaller. More advanced methods and neural networks can handle many inputs and curved relationships. The output is a number rather than a category.
gl.regresyon.why: It sits at the heart of many forecasting jobs: demand forecasting, pricing, risk scores and weather models are some of them. Because it is easy to understand, it is also common in statistics, and simple regression models often have an edge in interpretability over complex ones.
gl.rekabet-hukuku-ve-yapay-zeka.def: The question of how competition rules apply to mergers, partnerships and abuses of dominant positions in the AI industry.
gl.rekabet-hukuku-ve-yapay-zeka.example: A competition authority reviewing whether a large cloud company's investment in an AI startup counts as a merger, and whether it reduces competition in the market, is one example.
gl.rekabet-hukuku-ve-yapay-zeka.faq.0.a: Generally no; existing competition rules also apply to AI markets. Some countries and regions have additional rules for large digital platforms in force or under discussion.
gl.rekabet-hukuku-ve-yapay-zeka.faq.0.q: Is there a separate competition law for AI?
gl.rekabet-hukuku-ve-yapay-zeka.faq.1.a: The Turkish Competition Authority (Rekabet Kurumu) enforces Law No. 4054 on the Protection of Competition. It can review mergers and conduct in digital markets, including AI, under that framework.
gl.rekabet-hukuku-ve-yapay-zeka.faq.1.q: Which authority enforces competition rules in Turkey?
gl.rekabet-hukuku-ve-yapay-zeka.how: Competition authorities usually examine mergers and acquisitions, agreements between companies and the conduct of dominant firms. In AI, several questions stand out. Are computing power, data and talent concentrating in a few companies? Do investments and cloud partnerships between big tech firms and model developers reduce competition? Could pricing algorithms quietly push prices toward each other? Authorities can open investigations, approve deals with conditions or impose fines. Approaches differ from country to country.
gl.rekabet-hukuku-ve-yapay-zeka.why: AI requires heavy capital and infrastructure, which fuels concern that only a few companies can stay ahead. Competition rulings affect which partnerships are allowed and whether new startups can enter the market. At the same time, some argue that excessive intervention could slow investment and innovation.
gl.relu.def: A simple activation function that turns negative inputs into zero and passes positive inputs through unchanged. It is widely used in the hidden layers of deep neural networks.
gl.relu.example: If a neuron's weighted sum comes out as minus 3, ReLU turns it into 0; if it comes out as 2, ReLU leaves it as 2.
gl.relu.faq.1.a: Sigmoid squeezes the output into a range between 0 and 1, while ReLU zeroes out negatives and passes positives through. ReLU is usually easier to train in deep networks.
gl.relu.faq.1.q: What is the difference between ReLU and sigmoid?
gl.relu.how: ReLU applies a very plain rule: if the input is below zero the output is zero, otherwise the output is the input itself. Its graph looks like a line that runs flat until zero and then rises upward. It is very cheap to compute, which speeds up training. Because its slope stays constant for positive values, it suffers less from the problem seen with functions like sigmoid, where the learning signal fades as it moves through the layers. Some neurons can get stuck outputting zero and 'die', which is why variants such as leaky ReLU were developed.
gl.relu.why: ReLU helped make deep networks easier and faster to train, so it became one of the most common components of modern deep learning. Its simplicity keeps computing costs low in large models. Even as newer functions appear, ReLU is often still the default starting point.
gl.risk-sermayesi.def: Funding from investment funds that put money into unproven startups with fast-growth potential in exchange for equity, based on the expectation of high risk and potentially high returns.
gl.risk-sermayesi.example: A fund invests in a startup building AI-assisted legal software and takes shares in return; if the company grows and is sold, the fund turns its stake into cash.
gl.risk-sermayesi.faq.0.a: An angel investor uses personal money, usually at a very early stage. Venture capital firms professionally manage money raised from others and typically invest larger amounts.
gl.risk-sermayesi.faq.0.q: What is the difference between venture capital and an angel investor?
gl.risk-sermayesi.faq.1.a: No. The startup does not have to pay the money back; the investor receives shares in the company. If the company fails, the investor may lose the investment.
gl.risk-sermayesi.how: Venture capital funds raise money from investors such as pension funds, university endowments and wealthy individuals. The fund's managers spread that money across many startups and receive shares in return. Most investments do not pay off; the fund relies on a few big successes to cover the losses. Returns are realized when the company is sold or goes public and the shares are sold. Besides money, funds often offer board support and business connections.
gl.risk-sermayesi.why: Training models and renting computing power is so expensive in AI that many labs and startups depend on venture capital. Which funds back which companies shows where the industry is heading and how competition is taking shape. Investor expectations also influence the product and growth decisions companies make.
gl.robot-ogrenmesi.def: The branch of AI in which robots learn tasks from data, human demonstrations and trial and error instead of being programmed step by step.
gl.robot-ogrenmesi.example: A robot arm can learn to stack cups on a shelf by watching hundreds of recorded demonstrations from a human operator and then doing it on its own.
gl.robot-ogrenmesi.faq.0.a: Machine learning is the broad field. Robot learning applies its methods to systems that act in the physical world, where data is expensive to collect and mistakes can cause physical damage.
gl.robot-ogrenmesi.faq.0.q: How is robot learning different from machine learning?
gl.robot-ogrenmesi.faq.1.a: A simulation cannot fully capture details such as friction, lighting and material behavior. A robot that does well in simulation can therefore be clumsy in the real world.
gl.robot-ogrenmesi.faq.1.q: Why is transferring from simulation to reality hard?
gl.robot-ogrenmesi.how: One common approach is imitation learning: a person remotely operates the robot to show a task, and a model works out what to do from those recordings. Another is reinforcement learning, where the robot tries things out and finds the best behavior guided by a reward signal. Because trying things on a real robot is slow and risky, much of the training usually happens in computer simulation and is then transferred to the physical robot. The gap between simulation and the real world is what makes this transfer hard.
gl.robot-ogrenmesi.why: Hand-written rules fall short against the variety found in homes and warehouses. Learning-based methods offer hope that robots can adapt to new objects and situations. The talk of “robot foundation models” and general-purpose robots in the news builds on this field.
gl.robotaksi.def: A driverless taxi service in which an autonomous vehicle, summoned through an app, takes a passenger from one place to another.
gl.robotaksi.example: Waymo in some US cities and Baidu's Apollo Go in some Chinese cities are examples of companies offering robotaxi services.
gl.robotaksi.faq.0.a: In fully driverless services nobody sits behind the wheel. In some testing phases, a safety operator may be on board.
gl.robotaksi.faq.0.q: Is there a driver inside a robotaxi?
gl.robotaksi.faq.1.a: A robotaxi is a transport service owned and operated by a company. A self-driving personal car is one an individual buys and uses. Because robotaxis work in a limited area, they are considered the more practical model today.
gl.robotaksi.faq.1.q: How is a robotaxi different from a self-driving personal car?
gl.robotaksi.how: The passenger requests a ride in a phone app, and the system dispatches a nearby vehicle. The car uses its sensors and AI software to follow the road on its own, picks up the passenger and drives to the destination. Most services begin in a limited, pre-mapped area of a city. In a tricky situation the car can ask remote operators for help. The company running the fleet handles charging, maintenance and cleaning.
gl.robotaksi.why: Robotaxis are the most visible commercial test of autonomous driving. If they succeed, they could affect urban transport, the taxi industry and habits around owning a car. At the same time, debates continue over safety, the jobs of drivers and the effect on city traffic.
gl.robotik-surec-otomasyonu.def: Software robots that imitate repetitive work people do on a computer screen, such as clicking, copying and filling in forms, and automate it according to fixed rules.
gl.robotik-surec-otomasyonu.example: In a bank, a software robot that pulls reports from several systems every morning, merges them into one table and emails it to the relevant department is a typical RPA use.
gl.robotik-surec-otomasyonu.faq.0.a: No. RPA is an automation method that follows predefined rules and does not learn on its own. AI can be added to RPA for tasks such as reading documents or understanding text.
gl.robotik-surec-otomasyonu.faq.0.q: Are RPA and AI the same thing?
gl.robotik-surec-otomasyonu.faq.1.a: No, it is software running on a computer. The name comes from the way it imitates what a person does on screen.
gl.robotik-surec-otomasyonu.faq.1.q: Is the robot in RPA a physical machine?
gl.robotik-surec-otomasyonu.how: The process to be automated is defined step by step, or the user's actions are recorded. The software robot then works in the interfaces of applications like a person would: it opens files, enters data into fields and moves information between systems. RPA is rule-based, so it can break when an interface changes or something unexpected happens. When AI is added, the robots can also understand and process messy data such as emails or documents.
gl.robotik-surec-otomasyonu.why: The ability to automate work without changing the code of legacy systems has made RPA widespread in organizations. In AI news it is often compared with agents: RPA follows rigid rules, while AI agents can make more flexible decisions. Knowing which one fits where is an important question in automation investments.
gl.robots-txt.def: A plain text file in the root directory of a website that tells search and crawling bots which pages they may visit. It is also used to state preferences toward the bots AI companies use to collect data.
gl.robots-txt.example: A news site could add a Disallow rule covering all pages for GPTBot in its robots.txt file to keep that crawler out.
gl.robots-txt.faq.0.a: Generally it is a technical convention with no binding legal force on its own. In some legal systems, though, it may be treated as a machine-readable form of an opt-out declaration.
gl.robots-txt.faq.1.a: No. The file is a public request, and a bot that ignores it can still reach the content. Real access control needs technical measures such as requiring a login or blocking bots.
gl.robots-txt.how: The file is published publicly at the site's address followed by /robots.txt. It contains a user-agent line naming a bot, along with rules showing which paths that bot is allowed or forbidden to visit. Bots read the file before entering a site and choose whether to follow it. So it works as a courtesy rule rather than a firewall, and a bot that ignores it is not technically stopped. The protocol has been in use since the 1990s and was standardized in 2022.
gl.robots-txt.why: As bots collecting web data for AI training have multiplied, robots.txt has become the best-known tool content owners have for stating their preference. Its legal force is unclear, but whether it counts as an opt-out declaration matters in copyright debates. Its limits are worth knowing, since not every bot obeys it.
gl.roc-egrisi-ve-auc.def: A graph showing how a binary classifier trades off true positive rate against false positive rate as its decision threshold changes, plus a single number summarizing the area under that curve.
gl.roc-egrisi-ve-auc.example: For a model that predicts pneumonia from chest X-rays, lowering the threshold catches more sick patients but also raises false alarms for healthy ones; the ROC curve shows that trade-off in one chart.
gl.roc-egrisi-ve-auc.faq.0.a: There is no single cutoff. 0.5 is chance level and 1 is perfect separation; what is good enough depends on the field and the cost of errors.
gl.roc-egrisi-ve-auc.faq.1.a: Accuracy is the share of correct predictions at one chosen threshold. AUC looks across all possible thresholds and measures how well the model separates the classes.
gl.roc-egrisi-ve-auc.faq.1.q: How does AUC differ from accuracy?
gl.roc-egrisi-ve-auc.how: A model gives each example a probability score, and a threshold decides which scores count as “positive.” The threshold is moved step by step, and at each step the true positive rate (how many real positives are caught) and the false positive rate (how many negatives are wrongly flagged) are calculated. Joining these points produces the ROC curve. The closer the curve hugs the top-left corner, the better the model separates the classes. AUC is the area under the curve: 0.5 matches random guessing and 1 means perfect separation.
gl.roc-egrisi-ve-auc.why: Because AUC lets models be compared without committing to one threshold, it is widely reported in medical diagnosis, fraud detection and credit scoring. A high AUC describes how well a model ranks positives above negatives. When classes are extremely imbalanced the picture can look too rosy, so precision-recall curves are often checked as well.
gl.saas.def: A delivery model in which software is rented over the internet, usually by monthly or annual subscription, instead of being bought and installed once. The program runs on the provider's servers and users access it through a browser or app.
gl.saas.example: A company that uses a customer relationship tool through a browser on a monthly subscription, rather than installing it on its own servers, is using SaaS; ChatGPT's subscription plans are sold on the same logic.
gl.saas.faq.0.a: No. Cloud computing is a broader idea that also covers renting infrastructure such as servers and storage over the internet. SaaS is the layer within it that delivers ready-to-use software directly to end users.
gl.saas.faq.0.q: Is SaaS the same as cloud computing?
gl.saas.faq.1.a: The data generally belongs to the customer but is stored on the provider's servers. The details depend on the contract and privacy terms, so organizations should read them carefully.
gl.saas.faq.1.q: Who owns the data in a SaaS product?
gl.saas.how: The company that builds the software hosts it on its own servers or on a cloud provider's. Customers sign up, log in from a browser or app, and install nothing. Updates, security patches and maintenance are handled by the provider, and the customer pays a recurring fee in return. Pricing usually depends on the number of users or the plan chosen. It resembles renting a home rather than buying one: the landlord handles upkeep, and the tenant can move out when needed.
gl.saas.why: Many AI companies sell their products on a SaaS basis, from chatbots and coding assistants to enterprise AI tools. Generative AI also strains the classic SaaS cost structure, because every use carries a real computing cost. Many debates about AI pricing and profit margins start from this model.
gl.saniye-basina-token.def: A speed measure showing how many tokens an AI model produces each second. A token is the word or word fragment a model uses as its unit of text.
gl.saniye-basina-token.example: A slow model may write at a pace you can read word by word, while a fast serving setup can put hundreds of words on screen in a few seconds.
gl.saniye-basina-token.faq.0.a: There is no single right value. A stream faster than human reading speed is often enough for chat, while agents and long outputs benefit from higher speeds.
gl.saniye-basina-token.faq.0.q: How many tokens per second is enough?
gl.saniye-basina-token.faq.1.a: Not exactly. A token can be a whole word, part of a word or a punctuation mark. In languages with many suffixes, such as Turkish, one word is often split into several tokens.
gl.saniye-basina-token.faq.1.q: Is a token the same as a word?
gl.saniye-basina-token.how: The model writes its answer one token at a time, and the measurement is the number of tokens produced in a given period divided by that time. The value changes with model size, hardware, software optimization and how many users are served at once. It can be measured in two ways: the speed a single user sees, or the server's total output across all users (throughput). The two should not be confused.
gl.saniye-basina-token.why: This number sets how fast text streams onto the screen, and for long outputs such as coding or agent tasks it directly affects total waiting time. For providers it signals how much is being got out of the hardware, and so the cost. It is often highlighted in inference chip launches, but test conditions can differ, so figures should be read carefully.
gl.saskinlik-degeri.def: A metric for how “surprised” a language model is by the next word (token) in a text; the lower the value, the better the model predicts that text.
gl.saskinlik-degeri.example: A researcher measures two small language models on the same Turkish news article; the one with the lower perplexity is better at predicting the next words in it.
gl.saskinlik-degeri.faq.0.a: No. It only shows how well the model predicts that text. Answer quality, accuracy and safety need to be measured separately.
gl.saskinlik-degeri.faq.0.q: Does lower perplexity always mean a better model?
gl.saskinlik-degeri.faq.1.a: Only if the same test text and the same tokenization are used. If the models split text into tokens differently, the numbers are not equivalent.
gl.saskinlik-degeri.faq.1.q: Can perplexity scores of different models be compared directly?
gl.saskinlik-degeri.how: At each step a language model produces a probability distribution over the next token. On a test text, the probabilities the model gave to the tokens that actually appeared are averaged and converted into a number that reflects how many options the model was torn between at each step. A perplexity of ten roughly means the model hesitated between ten equally likely choices. The lower the value, the less surprised the model is. Comparisons are only meaningful when the same text and the same tokenization are used.
gl.saskinlik-degeri.why: Perplexity is a common, cheap way to track progress while training a language model. It does not say whether the model’s answers are correct, useful or safe, so a low value does not prove a model makes a good chat assistant. Modern models are therefore judged with other tests as well.
gl.sdk.def: A package of libraries, sample code, documentation and tools that makes it easier to build software for a particular service or platform.
gl.sdk.example: With the Python packages from OpenAI or Anthropic, a few lines of code are enough to send a question to a model and read the answer.
gl.sdk.faq.0.a: An API is the set of rules and endpoints a service exposes to the outside world. An SDK is a ready-made toolkit that makes using that API easy in a particular programming language.
gl.sdk.faq.0.q: What is the difference between an SDK and an API?
gl.sdk.faq.1.a: No, an API can also be used directly with web requests. An SDK usually saves time and reduces the risk of errors, though.
gl.sdk.faq.1.q: Is it mandatory to use an SDK?
gl.sdk.how: Instead of making developers send raw web requests to an API, AI providers offer ready-made packages in languages such as Python or JavaScript. A developer installs the package, sets an access key and sends a request to the model with a few lines of function calls. The SDK handles details such as authentication, retrying failed requests and turning the response into a tidy data structure. When the provider updates its API, the package is updated too, which makes it easier to keep an application compatible.
gl.sdk.why: It shortens integration time and cuts down on common mistakes. When developers choose a provider, the quality of the SDK, the languages it supports and the clarity of its documentation are important criteria. In news, a new SDK announcement usually means developers can reach a new capability more easily.
gl.semantik-arama.def: A search method that finds content close in meaning to a query instead of looking for exact matches of the query's words.
gl.semantik-arama.example: On a support site, a user searching for my car tyre went flat can reach the tyre replacement guide even if the word flat never appears in it.
gl.semantik-arama.faq.0.a: Keyword search checks whether the words in the query appear in a document. Semantic search looks at similarity of meaning, so it can find content that uses different words for the same topic.
gl.semantik-arama.faq.0.q: What is the difference between semantic search and keyword search?
gl.semantik-arama.faq.1.a: No. For product codes, personal names or exact phrases, keyword search is often more reliable. That is why hybrid search, which combines both, is common.
gl.semantik-arama.how: Texts are converted into vectors, called embeddings, that represent their meaning as numbers. Texts with similar meanings end up with vectors that sit close together. When a user types a query, it is turned into a vector in the same way, and the nearest vectors in the database are retrieved. Vector databases are commonly used for this job. Results are ranked by how similar they are. In practice, many systems combine it with keyword search for cases that need exact matches.
gl.semantik-arama.why: People do not always phrase what they want with the words used in a document. Because semantic search can catch synonyms and different phrasings, it is a core building block in enterprise search, recommendation systems and especially retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), where it finds the information handed to the model.
gl.sembolik-yapay-zeka.def: An approach that tries to build intelligence by manipulating human-readable symbols according to logical rules. Instead of learning from data, it relies on knowledge and rules that people write down explicitly.
gl.sembolik-yapay-zeka.example: A loan program that evaluates applications with hand-written rules like “approve if the applicant is under a certain age and earns more than a certain amount” is a simple example of the symbolic approach.
gl.sembolik-yapay-zeka.faq.0.a: In symbolic AI, people write the knowledge down as rules. In machine learning, the model works out the rules from examples on its own.
gl.sembolik-yapay-zeka.faq.0.q: What is the difference between symbolic AI and machine learning?
gl.sembolik-yapay-zeka.faq.1.a: It is still used. Rule-based decision systems, planning software and verification tools rely on it, and there is ongoing work to combine its ideas with learning-based models.
gl.sembolik-yapay-zeka.faq.1.q: Is symbolic AI no longer used?
gl.sembolik-yapay-zeka.how: Knowledge is written by hand as facts and rules, such as “all birds have wings” and “a sparrow is a bird”. A reasoning engine combines these statements to reach new conclusions, for example “a sparrow has wings”. Because the reasoning can be followed step by step, the system can explain why it gave a particular answer. Its weakness is the messiness of the real world: writing a rule for every situation is laborious, and the system easily gets stuck on cases nobody anticipated.
gl.sembolik-yapay-zeka.why: This approach was the dominant strand of AI research from the 1950s into the 1980s, and today's learning-based systems can partly be read as a reaction to it. Even now, with neural networks in the lead, some researchers want to combine the two, building so-called neuro-symbolic systems, because logic offers explainability and reliability.
gl.sensor-fuzyonu.def: A method of combining data from several sensors, such as cameras, radar and LiDAR, to build a more reliable and complete picture of the surroundings than any single sensor could give.
gl.sensor-fuzyonu.example: On a foggy night, a camera may barely make out the car ahead while radar reports its distance and speed; fusion combines both to confirm the car is there.
gl.sensor-fuzyonu.faq.0.a: No sensor works well in every condition. Combining data from several sensors lets the others cover for one that makes errors or cannot see.
gl.sensor-fuzyonu.faq.1.a: No. Smartphones combine accelerometer and gyroscope data to detect motion, and drones and robots use fusion to work out where they are.
gl.sensor-fuzyonu.faq.1.q: Is sensor fusion used only in vehicles?
gl.sensor-fuzyonu.how: Each sensor has strengths and weaknesses. A camera sees color and texture but struggles to estimate distance, radar measures speed well but offers little detail, and LiDAR captures shape precisely. Fusion software aligns these streams to a common time and position frame, matches each measurement to the object it belongs to, and resolves conflicts based on how trustworthy each source is. Fusion can happen on raw data or on the object lists each sensor produces, and today neural networks can learn it as well.
gl.sensor-fuzyonu.why: Relying on a single sensor means a wrong decision the moment that sensor goes blind. Fusion adds a kind of redundancy that improves safety in self-driving cars, drones and robots. The choice of sensor combination also directly affects cost and system design.
gl.sentetik-medya.def: The general name for content such as images, audio, video and text that is fully produced or substantially altered using AI. It can show something that never happened or a speech that was never given.
gl.sentetik-medya.example: A photo of a person who does not exist, or a news article read aloud in an artificial voice, are examples of synthetic media.
gl.sentetik-medya.faq.0.a: No. Synthetic media is a broad umbrella term that includes harmless content too. A deepfake usually means synthetic content that convincingly imitates a real person, often with deceptive intent.
gl.sentetik-medya.faq.0.q: Is synthetic media the same as a deepfake?
gl.sentetik-medya.faq.1.a: No. It has many legitimate uses, such as dubbing, animation, narration for visually impaired people and film effects. The problem arises when content is presented as real and used to mislead people.
gl.sentetik-medya.how: Generative models learn the patterns of a type of content from a large number of real examples. When a user provides a prompt, a photo or a voice sample, the model produces new output that fits those patterns. Diffusion models are often used for images and video, language models for text and speech synthesis models for audio. The result can be entirely new, or it can be a modified part of an existing recording.
gl.sentetik-medya.why: It lowers costs and expands creative possibilities in advertising, entertainment, education and accessibility. It also magnifies problems of misinformation, impersonation and copyright. That is why labeling content as artificial, watermarking and source verification are debated. Regulations such as the EU AI Act include provisions on disclosing this kind of content.

gl.sentetik-veri.def.en: Data generated by computers or AI rather than collected from the real world, designed to mimic the properties of real data.

gl.sentetik-veri.example.en: An autonomous vehicle company can generate rare real-world crash scenarios in simulation and train its model on these synthetic images.

gl.sentetik-veri.faq.0.a.en: It depends. When well designed, it complements real data and protects privacy; but it may not fully reflect real-world diversity and can amplify errors.

gl.sentetik-veri.faq.0.q.en: Is synthetic data as good as real data?

gl.sentetik-veri.faq.1.a.en: Because it generates records that do not belong to real people, it can reduce privacy risk, but poorly generated synthetic data can carry traces that expose real individuals. Careful evaluation is needed.

gl.sentetik-veri.faq.1.q.en: Does synthetic data protect personal data?

gl.sentetik-veri.how.en: Synthetic data is produced with statistical methods or AI models. For example, records can be generated that mimic the distribution of real customer records but do not belong to real people. Language models can also be trained on questions and answers or math solutions produced by a more powerful model.

gl.sentetik-veri.why.en: It offers a solution when real data is scarce, expensive or unusable for privacy reasons. As high-quality text on the web begins to run out, AI companies are turning to synthetic data more and more. However, training solely on synthetic data can degrade a model's quality.

gl.seri-a-b-c-yatirim-turlari.def: The sequence of investment rounds a startup raises after its seed round, named by letter as it matures; with each letter the company is more established and the round size and expectations usually grow.
gl.seri-a-b-c-yatirim-turlari.example: An AI assistant startup might raise a Series A after landing its first paying customers, and a Series B in later years to multiply its number of enterprise clients.
gl.seri-a-b-c-yatirim-turlari.faq.0.a: The difference is the company's maturity: A is about proving the product works, B about scaling, and C about expanding or preparing for an IPO. The boundaries are not fixed; the labels are a market convention.
gl.seri-a-b-c-yatirim-turlari.faq.0.q: What is the difference between Series A, B and C?
gl.seri-a-b-c-yatirim-turlari.faq.1.a: No. Some companies raise fewer rounds, some become profitable and take no outside money, and others shut down or get acquired along the way.
gl.seri-a-b-c-yatirim-turlari.faq.1.q: Does every startup go through all the rounds?
gl.seri-a-b-c-yatirim-turlari.how: Series A typically comes when early signs show the product works, to support a growing base of revenue and customers. Series B is raised to scale the business, enter new markets and expand the team. Series C and later rounds are used by mature companies to make acquisitions, expand into new countries or prepare for a public listing. In each round new investors buy shares and existing owners' stakes are diluted. The letters are not a strict rule but a naming convention that has settled in the market.
gl.seri-a-b-c-yatirim-turlari.why: In headlines, the round an AI company is in gives a quick sense of how mature it is. As rounds get larger, the company's valuation and investor expectations rise too, pushing it toward fast growth and eventually a sale or an IPO. It also matters to employees, whose equity is valued through these rounds.
gl.ses-kaynagi-ayristirma.def: Splitting a recording in which several sounds are mixed into separate sources, such as speech, vocals, instruments or noise. The goal is to extract each source from the mix as its own recording.
gl.ses-kaynagi-ayristirma.example: When a song's recording is uploaded, a system can return the vocals, drums and bass as separate audio files.
gl.ses-kaynagi-ayristirma.faq.0.a: They are close. Noise reduction is a special case that focuses on separating speech from background sound. Source separation aims to pull out several meaningful sources, such as different instruments, individually.
gl.ses-kaynagi-ayristirma.faq.0.q: Is audio source separation the same as noise reduction?
gl.ses-kaynagi-ayristirma.faq.1.a: Usually not. When sources overlap in the same frequencies, the separated tracks can keep some leakage or an artificial tone. Quality varies with the recording and the model.
gl.ses-kaynagi-ayristirma.how: Sound is usually displayed like an image of time against frequency. A neural network predicts which source each region of that image belongs to and builds a filter for each one. The filter is applied to the mix, and the result is converted back into audio. For training, recordings of the sources made separately are used. They are mixed artificially, and the model learns to recover the original parts from the mix.
gl.ses-kaynagi-ayristirma.why: In music production it makes it possible to isolate vocals and instruments, restore old recordings and make karaoke tracks. It also helps hearing technologies that improve speech clarity in crowds, as well as speech recognition systems. It comes up in debates about artists' rights over their voices too.
gl.ses-klonlama.def: Using AI to learn a person's voice from short recordings and imitate it, so that the person appears to say sentences they never said.
gl.ses-klonlama.example: A scammer can use a short clip from social media to imitate a relative's voice and ask a family for urgent money; a code word the family agreed on in advance can help verify such calls.
gl.ses-klonlama.faq.0.a: There is no sure way. Unusual demands for money or urgent action, odd pauses or flat intonation can be clues, but the safest step is to call the person back on a number you already know.
gl.ses-klonlama.faq.0.q: How can I tell if a voice has been cloned?
gl.ses-klonlama.faq.1.a: It depends on the country, the use and whether consent was given. Imitating someone without permission can raise problems under fraud, personality rights or data protection rules, so legal advice is needed for specifics.
gl.ses-klonlama.how: A voice model learns features such as timbre, emphasis and speaking pace from a recording of the target person. It then reads out written text in that voice, or converts someone else's speech into the target's voice. Some systems can reach a reasonable likeness from very short recordings, and results get more convincing as the recording grows longer and cleaner. Legitimate uses require the person's consent.
gl.ses-klonlama.why: Voice cloning offers real benefits, such as preserving the voice of people who lose the ability to speak, dubbing and accessibility. It can also be abused for fraud and for fake political recordings. Trusting a voice on the phone is no longer enough, which has made extra verification habits more important.
gl.ses-tasarimi-ve-seslendirme.def: The area of audio production that uses AI models to turn text into speech, clone a voice, dub content into other languages, or generate sound effects and music.
gl.ses-tasarimi-ve-seslendirme.example: A game studio can prepare hundreds of lines for minor characters with synthetic speech from text, shortening the recording schedule.
gl.ses-tasarimi-ve-seslendirme.faq.0.a: Technically, even a few minutes of recording can be enough. The legal situation varies by country and by case. In many places a voice may be treated as personal data or fall under personality rights, so a lawyer should be consulted for specifics.
gl.ses-tasarimi-ve-seslendirme.faq.0.q: Can my voice be cloned without permission, and is it legally protected?
gl.ses-tasarimi-ve-seslendirme.faq.1.a: As models improve, it gets harder to tell by ear. Some services add watermarks to generated audio or label the content. For a suspicious recording, verifying the source separately is the safest approach.
gl.ses-tasarimi-ve-seslendirme.faq.1.q: How can I tell an AI voice from a real one?
gl.ses-tasarimi-ve-seslendirme.how: A text-to-speech model turns written text into audio that sounds very close to a human voice, with adjustable tone, speed and emphasis. In voice cloning, a model learns the features of a person's voice from a short recording and reads new sentences in that voice. In AI dubbing, the system transcribes the speech, translates it and reads the translation in a voice close to the original speaker's. Sound effects and music can also be generated from a written description.
gl.ses-tasarimi-ve-seslendirme.why: It speeds up and cheapens the production of podcasts, games, ads and audiobooks. At the same time, voice actors worry about their voices being copied without permission, about copyright problems and about lost work. Synthetic voices can also be misused for fraud. That is why consent and labeling are central questions.
gl.sesli-asistan.def: Software that understands spoken commands and answers by voice, handling tasks such as setting alarms, playing music or answering questions.
gl.sesli-asistan.example: Saying “show me the nearest pharmacy” while driving is a typical case. Alexa, Siri and Google Assistant are well-known voice assistants.
gl.sesli-asistan.faq.0.a: A chatbot talks in text, while a voice assistant works through speech input and output. A voice assistant also often controls device and app functions such as alarms, smart-home devices or music. In newer systems the two are moving closer together.
gl.sesli-asistan.faq.0.q: How is a voice assistant different from a chatbot?
gl.sesli-asistan.faq.1.a: Devices generally wait only for the wake word and try to detect it locally. Details vary by product and settings. Privacy settings let you control whether voice recordings are kept.
gl.sesli-asistan.faq.1.q: Is a voice assistant listening to me all the time?
gl.sesli-asistan.how: In the classic pipeline, a wake word is detected first. A speech recognition model turns the audio into text, and a language understanding step works out what the user wants. The system carries out the request or finds the answer, and speech synthesis reads the reply aloud. With large language models, many assistants have become better at understanding free-form speech. Some newer systems process audio directly and answer in voice without an intermediate text step. Which steps run on the device and which in the cloud matters for privacy.
gl.sesli-asistan.why: Voice assistants help when hands are busy or a screen is out of reach. They also give older people and users with visual impairments better access. On the other hand, how voice recordings are stored and used is debated. As generative AI has advanced, voice assistants have returned to the news.
gl.sesli-mod.def: A feature that lets people talk to an AI assistant instead of typing. The user's speech is turned into text or processed directly, and the reply is spoken back as audio.
gl.sesli-mod.example: Someone with doughy hands in the kitchen can open the assistant's voice mode on their phone, listen to a recipe step by step and ask, 'What can I use instead of butter?'
gl.sesli-mod.faq.0.a: No. A traditional voice command recognizes fixed phrases such as 'set an alarm'. In voice mode, a large language model understands free-form speech and replies conversationally.
gl.sesli-mod.faq.0.q: Is voice mode the same as a traditional voice command?
gl.sesli-mod.faq.1.a: It depends on the product and its settings. Some services may store audio or transcripts, so it is worth checking the privacy settings and policy before use.
gl.sesli-mod.how: In the classic setup, three steps run in sequence: speech recognition turns audio into text, a language model writes the reply, and speech synthesis reads it aloud. Newer approaches use models that can process audio directly, which cuts delay and makes it easier to pick up tone and pauses. Users can usually interrupt mid-answer, and the model stops and moves on to the new question. It works through a phone or computer microphone, so it is handy when typing is difficult.
gl.sesli-mod.why: Speaking is faster than typing and widens access for people who cannot use a keyboard or have their hands full. Voice interfaces are a key part of getting assistants into cars, homes and phones. They also raise questions about audio recording, privacy and the risk of cloned voices (deepfakes).
gl.seyrek-model.def: An AI model in which most parameters are zero, or which activates only a small fraction of its parameters for each input.
gl.seyrek-model.example: Mixture-of-experts architectures such as Mistral's Mixtral models are examples of sparse models: only a portion of the experts is used for each token.
gl.seyrek-model.faq.0.a: In a dense model every parameter is used for every input. In a sparse model only a part of them is used, which makes it possible to build a larger model on the same compute budget.
gl.seyrek-model.faq.0.q: What is the difference between a sparse and a dense model?
gl.seyrek-model.faq.1.a: No. Memory needs often do not shrink, and the speed gain depends on hardware support, so the practical benefit varies from case to case.
gl.seyrek-model.faq.1.q: Is a sparse model always faster?
gl.seyrek-model.how: Sparsity comes in two ways. In the first, methods such as pruning set most of the weights to zero, and only the remaining ones are used in computation. In the second, the model is built from many sub-blocks, or experts, from the start; for each input a router picks just a few experts and the rest stay idle for that step. Mixture-of-experts (MoE) architectures are the typical example of this second kind. The total parameter count can be huge, yet the work done per token stays close to that of a smaller dense model.
gl.seyrek-model.why: Sparsity lets a model's capacity grow without running costs growing at the same rate, which is why it comes up often in large language model news. All the parameters still have to be held in memory, though, and the speed gain depends on how well hardware and software support sparsity.
gl.seyrek-otomatik-kodlayici.def: An auxiliary neural network that learns to reproduce a model's internal activity by breaking it into many simpler components, only a few of which are active at any one time.
gl.seyrek-otomatik-kodlayici.example: Anthropic published a demo in which it amplified a feature linked to the Golden Gate Bridge in a Claude model, making the model bring up the bridge even in unrelated questions.
gl.seyrek-otomatik-kodlayici.faq.0.a: Because only a small number of units are allowed to be active at the same time. That constraint makes it easier for each unit to specialize in a particular concept.
gl.seyrek-otomatik-kodlayici.faq.1.a: No, the original model stays as it is; the autoencoder is a separate tool that reads its internal activity. Experiments that amplify a feature work by intervening in the model's activations.
gl.seyrek-otomatik-kodlayici.faq.1.q: Does a sparse autoencoder change the original model?
gl.seyrek-otomatik-kodlayici.how: First, the activation values of one layer are collected from the language model under study. The sparse autoencoder expands these values into a much wider layer, but during training only a few units are allowed to be active at once, and it then tries to rebuild the original values. This constraint encourages each unit to correspond to a single concept. Researchers assign meaning to a unit by looking at the texts where it activates, and test it by strengthening or weakening it to see how the model's behavior changes.
gl.seyrek-otomatik-kodlayici.why: Individual neurons in a model often carry several concepts mixed together, so they cannot be read directly. Sparse autoencoders are among the most widely used tools in mechanistic interpretability for untangling this mix. Still, not every unit carries a clean meaning, and some information is lost in the reconstruction.
gl.seyreltme.def: A regularization technique that randomly switches off some of a network's neurons during training, which reduces overfitting, where a model memorizes its training data.
gl.seyreltme.example: An image classifier that randomly turns off 20 percent of its neurons at every training step is less dependent on a few neurons, so it may behave more consistently on new photos.
gl.seyreltme.faq.0.a: Usually not. It is applied only during training, and all neurons are active at inference time.
gl.seyreltme.faq.0.q: Is dropout applied when the model is in use?
gl.seyreltme.faq.1.a: It is when a model memorizes details and noise in its training data and then performs poorly on new data. Regularization methods try to reduce it.
gl.seyreltme.how: At each training step, a certain fraction of the network's neurons is chosen at random and set to zero for that step, and the chosen ones change every time. This stops the network from relying too heavily on a single neuron or a small group, so it learns information in a more spread-out and robust way. It can be thought of as training slightly different small networks at each step. When the model is actually used, at inference time, dropout is turned off and all neurons work.
gl.seyreltme.why: Overfitting means a model does well on its training data but poorly on new data, and it is one of the most common problems in practice. Because dropout is simple and cheap, it is one of the widely used regularization methods for neural networks. The right rate is found by experimenting, depending on the model and the amount of data.
gl.sicaklik.def: A setting that controls how random a language model is when choosing the next token. Low values give consistent, predictable replies, while high values give more varied and surprising ones.
gl.sicaklik.example: A customer-support bot typically uses a low temperature, while a tool that suggests slogans or story ideas typically uses a higher one.
gl.sicaklik.faq.0.a: Usually the answers will be very similar, but it is not guaranteed. Hardware and server details can cause small differences.
gl.sicaklik.faq.0.q: If I set temperature to zero, will I always get the same answer?
gl.sicaklik.faq.1.a: It makes output more varied, which is not the same as better creativity. Pushed too high, the text becomes incoherent and may turn nonsensical.
gl.sicaklik.faq.1.q: Does a higher temperature make a model more creative?
gl.sicaklik.how: At each step the model assigns probabilities to possible tokens. Temperature sharpens or flattens that probability distribution. At a low temperature the most likely token dominates and the model almost always takes the same path. At a high temperature the probabilities move closer together, so less likely tokens get chosen more often. Values near zero amount to always picking the single most likely token. Developers usually adjust this setting through an API.
gl.sicaklik.why: Depending on this setting, the same model can act as a precise data-extraction tool or a creative writing partner. It is one of the main controls balancing repeatability against variety. A low temperature does not remove mistakes, though: a model can repeat a wrong claim consistently.

gl.sifir-atisli-ogrenme.def.en: A model's ability to perform a task without seeing any examples (zero-shot) or by working from a few examples given in the prompt (few-shot).

gl.sifir-atisli-ogrenme.example.en: Adding three examples to a prompt to have a company's product codes written in a particular format leads the model to generate the remaining codes in the same format.

gl.sifir-atisli-ogrenme.faq.0.a.en: Few-shot learning means showing the model a few examples within the prompt to explain how to perform a task.

gl.sifir-atisli-ogrenme.faq.1.a.en: In few-shot learning, examples are provided only in the prompt and the model does not change. In fine-tuning, the model is retrained on a large number of examples and its parameters are permanently updated.

gl.sifir-atisli-ogrenme.faq.1.q.en: What is the difference between few-shot learning and fine-tuning?

gl.sifir-atisli-ogrenme.how.en: In zero-shot use, the model is only told the task: "Classify this review as positive or negative." In few-shot use, a few solved examples are added to the prompt, and the model infers the format of the task from them. The model's parameters do not change; learning happens only within that prompt.

gl.sifir-atisli-ogrenme.why.en: It largely removes the need to retrain a model for every new task. A small number of good examples noticeably improves results, especially when a specific output format or style is required.

gl.sifirinci-gun-acigi.def: A security flaw that the software maker does not yet know about or has not yet fixed. The name comes from the fact that developers have had zero days to address it.
gl.sifirinci-gun-acigi.example: A flaw in a web browser that nobody knows about is exploited by attackers, and users remain unprotected until the vendor notices and releases a patch.
gl.sifirinci-gun-acigi.faq.0.a: With a zero-day, the vendor is not yet aware or no patch exists. A known vulnerability has been disclosed and usually patched, and the risk comes from systems that have not installed the fix.
gl.sifirinci-gun-acigi.faq.0.q: What is the difference between a zero-day and a known vulnerability?
gl.sifirinci-gun-acigi.faq.1.a: There are reports of AI tools finding previously unknown flaws. These findings are usually verified by human experts, and the limits of the capability are still being studied.
gl.sifirinci-gun-acigi.how: A researcher or attacker finds a bug in software that the vendor has not noticed. If an attacker builds exploit code for it, defending is very hard because no patch exists. The flaw is either reported to the vendor or quietly used or sold. Once the vendor learns of it and releases a patch, it becomes a known vulnerability, although users still need time to install the update.
gl.sifirinci-gun-acigi.why: Zero-days are among the hardest threats to defend against. In AI news, a model's ability to find previously unknown flaws is treated both as a major capability signal and as a serious risk. That is why the topic comes up often in the safety evaluations run by model developers.
gl.silikon-pul.def: A thin, round, polished disk sliced from a silicon crystal, on whose surface chips are manufactured. A single wafer carries many chips at once.
gl.silikon-pul.example: A 300-millimeter wafer can yield hundreds of small smartphone processors, but far fewer of a very large AI chip.
gl.silikon-pul.faq.0.a: Silicon crystals are grown as cylinders, so the slices come out round. Rectangular chips do not fit a round wafer perfectly, so some space is left unused around the edges.
gl.silikon-pul.faq.1.a: A wafer is the large disk on which many chips are built. When production is done the wafer is cut, and each resulting piece is called a die.
gl.silikon-pul.faq.1.q: What is the difference between a wafer and a die?
gl.silikon-pul.how: Very pure silicon is first melted and grown into a single-crystal cylinder. The cylinder is sliced into thin disks and polished, and these disks are called wafers. Circuits are built up layer by layer on the wafer through steps of light patterning, chemical etching, and doping, with the same pattern repeated many times side by side. In the end the wafer is cut, and each chip piece, called a die, is tested and packaged. Today the common wafer diameter in advanced fabs is 300 millimeters.
gl.silikon-pul.why: Factory capacity is often described in wafers per month, so the word appears often in chip supply news. How many working chips each wafer yields, known as yield, determines cost. Very large AI chips fit fewer to a wafer and are more easily hit by defects, which raises their cost.
gl.simulasyondan-gercege-aktarim.def: The process of taking an AI model or robot controller trained in a virtual environment and getting it to work properly on a physical robot in the real world.
gl.simulasyondan-gercege-aktarim.example: A four-legged robot learns to walk by falling and getting up thousands of times on virtual terrain. The same controller is then loaded onto the real robot.
gl.simulasyondan-gercege-aktarim.faq.0.a: It is the loss of performance caused by a simulation failing to capture the real world fully. A model that works well in simulation can do poorly on a real robot because of differences in physics and perception.
gl.simulasyondan-gercege-aktarim.faq.1.a: No. Success depends on how realistic the simulation is and how varied the training was. Often the model still needs extra tuning or extra data on the real robot.
gl.simulasyondan-gercege-aktarim.faq.1.q: Will any robot trained in simulation work in the real world?
gl.simulasyondan-gercege-aktarim.how: A robot first practices millions of times in a virtual world running on a physics engine, which is fast and safe. The catch is that the virtual world never matches reality exactly: friction, lighting, sensor noise and motor delays all differ. One common way to narrow the gap is domain randomization. During training, values such as friction, weight or color are changed constantly, so the model does not depend on a single virtual world. If needed, the controller is then fine-tuned on the real robot.
gl.simulasyondan-gercege-aktarim.why: Experimenting with a real robot is slow, expensive and wearing, and the robot can fall and break. Simulation cuts that cost sharply. But if the gap between virtual and real is not closed, success in simulation does not carry over to the field. That is why the topic keeps coming up in news about humanoid and four-legged robots.
gl.sinif-dengesizligi.def: A situation where one class in a dataset has far fewer examples than the others, making it hard for a model to learn that rare class.
gl.sinif-dengesizligi.example: If 99.5 percent of items on a production line are fine, a model that labels everything “fine” gets 99.5 percent accuracy yet catches none of the defective items.
gl.sinif-dengesizligi.faq.0.a: Always predicting the majority class already yields high accuracy, even if the rare class is never detected. That is why precision, recall or AUC are checked too.
gl.sinif-dengesizligi.faq.0.q: Why is accuracy misleading on imbalanced data?
gl.sinif-dengesizligi.faq.1.a: It means increasing the number of minority-class examples, by copying them or generating new ones, so the model sees the rare class more often.
gl.sinif-dengesizligi.how: In fraud detection, the vast majority of transactions are legitimate and only a tiny share are fraudulent. During training, most of the error comes from the majority class, so the rare class is easily ignored; even a strategy of “always predict the majority class” can score high accuracy. Remedies include oversampling the minority class, dropping some majority examples, giving classes different weights, or generating synthetic examples. Evaluation also shifts from accuracy to measures such as precision and recall.
gl.sinif-dengesizligi.why: Many important problems, such as rare diseases, fraud and machine failures, are imbalanced by nature. If the issue goes unnoticed, a model can look successful on paper with high accuracy while missing exactly the cases that matter.
gl.siniflandirma.def: The task of predicting which of a set of predefined categories a data example belongs to, such as sorting an email into “spam” or “not spam”.
gl.siniflandirma.example: A model marking an X-ray image as “signs of pneumonia” or “no signs” is a classification task.
gl.siniflandirma.faq.0.a: Classification returns a category, while regression predicts a continuous number. “Is this email spam?” is a classification question, and “what rent will this apartment fetch?” is a regression question.
gl.siniflandirma.faq.0.q: What is the difference between classification and regression?
gl.siniflandirma.faq.1.a: Not always. If 99 percent of the data are healthy cases, a model that calls everyone healthy is 99 percent accurate but finds no sick patients.
gl.siniflandirma.faq.1.q: Does high accuracy mean the model is good?
gl.siniflandirma.how: The model is trained on labeled examples, where the correct category of each one is known. During training it learns which features go with which category. On a new example, the model computes a probability for each category and usually picks the highest. With two categories this is called binary classification, and with more it is multi-class classification. Performance is checked with measures such as accuracy, precision and recall.
gl.siniflandirma.why: It is one of the most common uses of AI: spam filters, diagnostic support, credit application review and content moderation are all examples. The cost of a wrong classification depends on the field; a missed disease in healthcare is far more serious than a spam email that slips through.
gl.sistem-istemi.def: A block of instructions an app developer gives a model before a conversation begins, setting its role, tone and limits. The user typically does not see it.
gl.sistem-istemi.example: In a bank's customer assistant, the system prompt might tell the model to answer only banking questions, be short and polite, and never give investment advice.
gl.sistem-istemi.faq.0.a: The system prompt is written by the developer of the app and shapes the model's overall behavior. A user prompt is the message a person types during the chat and expresses a specific request.
gl.sistem-istemi.faq.0.q: What is the difference between a system prompt and a user prompt?
gl.sistem-istemi.faq.1.a: Normally not, but the model can sometimes be persuaded to reveal it. That is why sensitive information such as passwords or secret keys should never go into a system prompt.
gl.sistem-istemi.faq.1.q: Can users see the system prompt?
gl.sistem-istemi.how: Before each reply, the model reads the system prompt, the conversation history and the user's latest message together. The system prompt is usually placed in a slot the model has been trained to treat as higher priority than user messages. It can include the model's role, speaking style, off-limits topics, answer format and the tools it may use. There is no guarantee the model always obeys, though; cleverly written user messages can sometimes override the rules or get the model to reveal the text itself.
gl.sistem-istemi.why: The same model can become very different products with different system prompts, so understanding a chatbot's behavior means looking at its system prompt. News stories sometimes report leaked system prompts, a reminder that secrets should never be placed inside one.
gl.sistemik-risk-tasiyan-model.def: In the EU AI Act, the most powerful general-purpose AI models, considered capable of causing wide-scale harm across society because of their capabilities and reach.
gl.sistemik-risk-tasiyan-model.example: A company developing a frontier language model trained with very large computing power would face extra testing and incident-reporting duties if the model is deemed to carry systemic risk.
gl.sistemik-risk-tasiyan-model.faq.0.a: No. The category applies only to the most advanced models that meet the set high-impact criteria. Most small and mid-sized models fall outside it.
gl.sistemik-risk-tasiyan-model.faq.0.q: Is every large model a systemic-risk model?
gl.sistemik-risk-tasiyan-model.faq.1.a: No. It can be placed on the market, but its provider must meet heavier obligations. Bans apply to the unacceptable practices covered under a separate heading of the Act.
gl.sistemik-risk-tasiyan-model.faq.1.q: Is a model in this category banned?
gl.sistemik-risk-tasiyan-model.how: The Act determines whether a model carries systemic risk by looking at its high-impact capabilities. Criteria such as the computing power used in training play an important role, and the European Commission can also designate a model as falling into this category. Providers of these models must meet the general-purpose model obligations plus additional ones: model evaluation, adversarial testing, reporting of serious incidents and cybersecurity safeguards. Systemic risks include dangers that could affect society broadly, such as helping enable cyberattacks or models escaping human control.
gl.sistemik-risk-tasiyan-model.why: Harm from the most powerful models does not stay within one product; it can reach millions of users and many sectors. The Act therefore places extra responsibility on the large labs. How accurate the thresholds and criteria are remains a matter of debate between safety advocates and industry representatives.
gl.sivi-sogutma.def: A cooling method that removes the heat produced by chips and servers with a liquid instead of air. It is increasingly common in heavily loaded AI servers.
gl.sivi-sogutma.example: Gaming PCs with a water block on the processor use the same principle on a small scale; in large AI data centers the same idea is spread across hundreds of racks.
gl.sivi-sogutma.faq.0.a: Usually not. In the common approach, liquid runs through sealed pipes to a cold plate on the chip and never enters the server itself. Only in immersion cooling are servers submerged, and then in a special liquid that does not conduct electricity.
gl.sivi-sogutma.faq.0.q: Does liquid cooling mean dunking servers in water?
gl.sivi-sogutma.faq.1.a: As chips get more powerful, more heat comes out of a small area. Air carries heat poorly compared with liquid, so it takes very strong fans and wide spacing, which becomes inefficient and costly in floor space.
gl.sivi-sogutma.faq.1.q: Why is air cooling not enough for AI servers?
gl.sivi-sogutma.how: Liquid carries heat far more effectively than air. In the most common setup, cold plates sit on top of processors and accelerators, and water or a special coolant flowing through them carries the heat to a heat exchanger. In immersion cooling, servers are submerged in a liquid that does not conduct electricity. The warmed liquid is cooled elsewhere and the loop starts again. With air cooling, fans push heat into the room air, which can fall short at high power density.
gl.sivi-sogutma.why: AI accelerators draw a lot of power, and the heat per rack is pushing the limits of air cooling. Liquid cooling allows racks to be packed more densely, can cut fan energy, and can improve a facility's overall efficiency. That is why it comes up so often in the design of new AI data centers.

gl.sizma-testi.def.en: The authorized practice of probing a system for security vulnerabilities using the same methods a real attacker would use.

gl.sizma-testi.example.en: Testing, with authorization, whether the login form of a company's web application can be abused is a penetration test.

gl.sizma-testi.faq.0.a.en: It is legal when performed with the system owner's written permission and within the agreed scope. Tests carried out without permission can constitute a crime.

gl.sizma-testi.faq.1.a.en: AI tools help security teams with code review, vulnerability scanning and test scenario generation. Because attackers can use the same capabilities, the topic is controversial.

gl.sizma-testi.faq.1.q.en: How is AI used in penetration testing?

gl.sizma-testi.how.en: In a penetration test, security experts attack a website, application or network the way a real attacker would, with the permission of the system's owner. The goal is to find and report vulnerabilities before malicious actors do. Tests are conducted within a defined scope and set of rules.

gl.sizma-testi.why.en: AI agents can now automate parts of penetration testing, which makes security testing faster and cheaper. Because the same capabilities can also be used maliciously, the area is being watched closely.

gl.softmax.def: A function that converts the raw scores produced by a neural network into probabilities that add up to one. It is used in multiclass classification and when language models choose the next token.
gl.softmax.example: If an image classifier produces scores of 2.0, 1.0 and 0.1 for cat, dog and rabbit, softmax turns them into roughly 66 percent, 24 percent and 10 percent.
gl.softmax.faq.0.a: Sigmoid turns a single score into a value between 0 and 1 and is usually used for two-class problems or independent labels. Softmax handles several classes at once and produces probabilities that sum to one.
gl.softmax.faq.0.q: What is the difference between softmax and sigmoid?
gl.softmax.faq.1.a: Not always. The output is in the form of probabilities, but neural networks can assign high probability to wrong answers too.
gl.softmax.faq.1.q: Does softmax show how confident the model really is?
gl.softmax.how: The network's final layer gives a raw score for each option, and these scores can be negative or very large. Softmax first applies an exponential to each score so that all of them become positive, then divides each by the total to get proportions. As a result, every option gets a share between 0 and 1, and the shares add up to one. The highest score receives the largest probability, and gaps between scores become more pronounced in the process.
gl.softmax.why: Softmax turns a model's answer into probabilities that are easy to interpret, so it is almost the standard last step of classification models. Large language models also use it to produce a probability distribution over possible next tokens at each step. Generation settings such as 'temperature' change how sharp that distribution is.

gl.sohbet-botu.def.en: Software that can converse with a user in natural language, in writing or by voice. Current chatbots are based on large language models.

gl.sohbet-botu.example.en: ChatGPT, Claude and Gemini are general-purpose chatbots; the digital assistant in a bank's app is a chatbot customized for a specific job.

gl.sohbet-botu.faq.0.a.en: Chatbot is a combination of the English words chat and bot; in Turkish it is used as sohbet botu. It is software that communicates with a user by typing or speaking.

gl.sohbet-botu.faq.1.a.en: It depends on the job. Different bots can stand out in tasks such as writing, coding, research and images; the most reliable approach is to try a few of them on your own work.

gl.sohbet-botu.how.en: Older chatbots worked with pre-written question-and-answer templates and got stuck on questions outside those templates. Today's chatbots are based on large language models: they read the user's message and the conversation history and generate a new response. Companies can connect these bots to their own documents (RAG) so that they can answer questions specific to their products.

gl.sohbet-botu.why.en: It is the most widespread AI application for 24/7 customer service support, quick access to information and assistance with everyday tasks. Because of the risk of giving incorrect information, human oversight is still needed on critical matters.

gl.somutlasmis-yapay-zeka.def: AI that has a body, sensors and actuators, as in a robot, and that learns and makes decisions by interacting directly with the physical world.
gl.somutlasmis-yapay-zeka.example: A robot arm moving boxes in a warehouse, or an autonomous vehicle that senses obstacles and finds its way, are examples of embodied AI.
gl.somutlasmis-yapay-zeka.faq.0.a: No. An industrial robot that repeats fixed, pre-programmed movements and does not learn from what it senses hardly counts. The core idea is a learning loop between perception and action.
gl.somutlasmis-yapay-zeka.faq.0.q: Is every robot an example of embodied AI?
gl.somutlasmis-yapay-zeka.faq.1.a: Usually not, since they have no body and no direct interaction with the physical world. But the same language models can become part of an embodied system when connected to a robot.
gl.somutlasmis-yapay-zeka.faq.1.q: Do chatbots count as embodied AI?
gl.somutlasmis-yapay-zeka.how: The system perceives its surroundings through sensors such as cameras, touch and balance. An AI model chooses an action based on that data, and motors carry it out. The result of the action is perceived again, and the loop continues. Training can happen on a real robot, or first in simulation because it is safer and faster. Language and vision models are increasingly added to this loop so robots can understand instructions.
gl.somutlasmis-yapay-zeka.why: Models trained only on text do not directly experience the physical world. Embodied AI is seen as the key to making robots useful in warehouses, factories and homes. The physical world is unpredictable and mistakes can be costly, which makes the field hard.
gl.sonraki-token-tahmini.def: The task of estimating, from the text so far, which small unit of text (token) is likely to come next. It is the core training objective of large language models.
gl.sonraki-token-tahmini.example: After the phrase “The weather today is very”, a model gives high probability to words like “nice” or “hot” and very low probability to a word like “book”.
gl.sonraki-token-tahmini.faq.0.a: For pretraining, yes, that is the basic task. To do it well, though, the model has to absorb grammar, facts and reasoning patterns. Many models are also fine-tuned afterwards with human feedback.
gl.sonraki-token-tahmini.faq.0.q: Does the model really only predict the next piece of text?
gl.sonraki-token-tahmini.faq.1.a: No. A token can be a whole word, part of a word, a punctuation mark or a space. The tokenizer decides how text is split.
gl.sonraki-token-tahmini.faq.1.q: Is a token the same as a word?
gl.sonraki-token-tahmini.how: The model reads text as a sequence of tokens and assigns a probability to every token in its vocabulary. During training the real next token is known, so each wrong guess nudges the model's internal weights in a better direction. This is repeated across enormous collections of text. At use time, one token is chosen, appended to the sequence, and the same step runs again. A reply therefore emerges one token at a time.
gl.sonraki-token-tahmini.why: Chatbots, coding assistants and summarization tools are mostly built on this simple objective. It also explains why models can sound fluent yet be wrong: the goal is to produce a plausible continuation, not to verify facts. It is a useful starting point for understanding the “hallucination” debate in AI news.
gl.sorumlu-olcekleme-politikasi.def: A written commitment framework in which an AI company sets out in advance which safety measures it will take as its models become more capable, and under what conditions it will pause development or deployment.
gl.sorumlu-olcekleme-politikasi.example: A company's policy might state that if a model passes a certain level of skill at automating cyberattacks, it will not be released widely until extra safeguards are in place.
gl.sorumlu-olcekleme-politikasi.faq.0.a: Generally no. These are voluntary commitments by companies, and a company can update its policy. Legal obligations come from national or regional rules, such as the EU AI Act.
gl.sorumlu-olcekleme-politikasi.faq.0.q: Is a responsible scaling policy legally binding?
gl.sorumlu-olcekleme-politikasi.faq.1.a: The core idea is similar: set capability thresholds and match safeguards to them. Names and details differ by company, and responsible scaling policy is the term Anthropic uses.
gl.sorumlu-olcekleme-politikasi.faq.1.q: Is it the same as frameworks like a frontier safety framework?
gl.sorumlu-olcekleme-politikasi.how: The framework is usually tiered. The company defines capability thresholds, such as a model giving meaningful help toward making a biological weapon. Each new model is tested against these thresholds during training and before release. If a threshold is crossed, stricter safeguards kick in, such as better protection of model weights and added defenses against misuse. If the safeguards are not adequate, training or deployment is delayed. The name became widely used after Anthropic published its policy in 2023, and other companies have released similar frameworks under different names.
gl.sorumlu-olcekleme-politikasi.why: These policies aim to make safety decisions in advance rather than under commercial pressure in the moment. They also give governments and the public a yardstick for judging companies. Critics point out that the commitments are voluntary, written by the companies themselves and can be revised later, so they are no substitute for legal regulation.
gl.sorumlu-yapay-zeka.def: An organizational approach and set of processes aimed at developing, using and managing AI in line with ethical principles, safety expectations and legal requirements.
gl.sorumlu-yapay-zeka.example: An insurance company might put a new claims assessment model through a bias test, a privacy review and an internal approval board before releasing it.
gl.sorumlu-yapay-zeka.faq.0.a: AI ethics is the field that debates principles and values. Responsible AI is the effort to turn those principles into an organization's processes, checklists and assigned duties.
gl.sorumlu-yapay-zeka.faq.0.q: How is responsible AI different from AI ethics?
gl.sorumlu-yapay-zeka.faq.1.a: No. The scale may differ, but any organization using AI, however small, should identify its risks and put basic safeguards in place.
gl.sorumlu-yapay-zeka.faq.1.q: Is responsible AI only for large companies?
gl.sorumlu-yapay-zeka.how: It carries ethical principles into day-to-day work. While a product is built, teams run risk assessments, document data and models, and carry out bias and safety tests. Sensitive uses get human oversight, and responsibilities are assigned to named people. Many organizations run this through internal policies, review boards and approval stages. After launch, monitoring continues, and if something goes wrong the incident is reported and the system is fixed.
gl.sorumlu-yapay-zeka.why: Once AI products reach users, mistakes can repeat at large scale. As regulation tightens and customers ask for assurances, responsible practice is moving from an option to a condition of doing business. Preserving trust also helps products gain long-term adoption.
gl.sozcuk-gommesi.def: A way of turning words into lists of numbers (vectors) so that words with similar meanings end up close together. Word2Vec, introduced by Google researchers in 2013, popularized the idea.
gl.sozcuk-gommesi.example: In a trained embedding space, “doctor” and “physician” sit close together, while “doctor” and “bicycle” are far apart.
