gl.sozcuk-gommesi.faq.0.a: Word2Vec assigns one vector per word, so the different meanings of a word like “bank” are blended into one vector. Current language models produce a different vector for a word depending on the sentence it appears in.
gl.sozcuk-gommesi.faq.0.q: How do Word2Vec and today's embeddings differ?
gl.sozcuk-gommesi.faq.1.a: No. Tokenization splits text into pieces and numbers them. An embedding then attaches a meaning-carrying vector to each of those pieces.
gl.sozcuk-gommesi.faq.1.q: Is an embedding the same as tokenization?
gl.sozcuk-gommesi.how: The method learns meaning from a word's surroundings. Across a huge body of text, the model tries to predict a word's neighbors from the word, or the word from its neighbors, and each word's list of numbers is adjusted along the way. Words that appear in similar contexts end up with similar vectors, so they sit near each other in the vector space. In a famous example, “king” minus “man” plus “woman” lands near “queen”. Word2Vec gives each word a single vector regardless of context.
gl.sozcuk-gommesi.why: Embeddings let computers measure relationships between words numerically and became a foundation for search, recommendation and translation systems. Token embeddings in modern language models continue the same idea, but they are sensitive to context. Understanding them is a first step toward understanding semantic search and retrieval-augmented systems.
gl.spekulatif-kod-cozme.def: A technique in which a small, fast model guesses several upcoming tokens and the large model verifies them in a single pass, speeding up text generation without changing the quality of the output.
gl.spekulatif-kod-cozme.example: In code completion, a draft model can easily guess boilerplate such as a function header, and the large model approves it in one step.
gl.spekulatif-kod-cozme.faq.0.a: Not when implemented correctly, because the large model always has the final say. Wrong guesses from the draft model are rejected.
gl.spekulatif-kod-cozme.faq.0.q: Does speculative decoding reduce answer quality?
gl.spekulatif-kod-cozme.faq.1.a: If the draft model's guesses are rejected often, the gain shrinks. The extra computation can even cancel out the benefit.
gl.spekulatif-kod-cozme.faq.1.q: Why doesn't it speed things up every time?
gl.spekulatif-kod-cozme.how: Normally a large model produces tokens one after another. Here, a small “draft” model first proposes several tokens in a row. The large model checks all of them at once, accepts the part that matches what it would have chosen, and at the first mismatch stops and writes the correct token. Because checking can be done in parallel, several tokens can cost about as much as one step when the guesses are good. With a proper acceptance rule, the result follows the same distribution the large model would produce alone.
gl.spekulatif-kod-cozme.why: Response latency is one of the main problems for large models, affecting both user experience and server costs. This technique aims to add speed without shrinking the model or sacrificing quality. How much it helps depends on how often the draft model's guesses are accepted.
gl.stil-aktarimi.def: An AI technique that keeps the content of one image while applying the artistic style of another, such as its colors, brushwork and texture.
gl.stil-aktarimi.example: A photo of a city skyline can be transformed to look as if it had been repainted with the swirling brushstrokes of Van Gogh’s “The Starry Night.”
gl.stil-aktarimi.faq.0.a: Simple filters apply the same color or effect settings to every image. Style transfer learns the style of another image and adapts it to the content, so the results are more varied and painterly.
gl.stil-aktarimi.faq.0.q: Is style transfer just an ordinary photo filter?
gl.stil-aktarimi.faq.1.a: Yes, phrases such as “in a watercolor style” can give a similar result. Unlike classic style transfer, which matches two images directly, this relies on the model reproducing styles it learned during training.
gl.stil-aktarimi.faq.1.q: Can text-to-image models do style transfer too?
gl.stil-aktarimi.how: Neural networks process an image in layers: deeper layers capture what is depicted, while layers closer to the surface capture style features like color and texture. In style transfer, content information is taken from one image and style information from another. The system then refines a new image step by step so that its content resembles the first and its style resembles the second. The people and objects in the photo stay in place, but the picture looks as if a different painter had made it.
gl.stil-aktarimi.why: It allows quick creative experiments, which is why it shows up in photo apps and filters. Imitating the style of living artists without permission, however, raises copyright and ethical debates. Whether a style alone can be protected by copyright is treated differently from country to country.
gl.super-bilgisayar.def: A system built by linking thousands of processors together to solve extremely large computations, delivering performance far beyond that of ordinary computers.
gl.super-bilgisayar.example: A national weather agency can produce its forecasts by running atmospheric simulations on a supercomputer.
gl.super-bilgisayar.faq.0.a: Not exactly, but they overlap. A supercomputer is a general term for machines built for scientific computing; a GPU cluster is a structure made mostly of GPUs and is also used for AI training. Many modern supercomputers contain GPUs.
gl.super-bilgisayar.faq.0.q: Is a supercomputer the same as a GPU cluster?
gl.super-bilgisayar.faq.1.a: Yes, GPU-based supercomputers are also used for model training. Still, clusters built specifically for AI are often optimized for that job.
gl.super-bilgisayar.faq.1.q: Can an AI model be trained on a supercomputer?
gl.super-bilgisayar.how: A supercomputer is made by joining many servers, called nodes, with a fast network. Each node holds processors and, often, GPUs. A problem is split into small pieces, the pieces are distributed across nodes, and the results are combined. Weather forecasting, climate modeling, drug research and physics simulations are classic uses. Performance is usually measured in floating-point operations per second and ranked in lists such as the TOP500.
gl.super-bilgisayar.why: As AI companies build clusters that resemble supercomputers for large models, the line between the two concepts has blurred. In news coverage, the word supercomputer is sometimes used for marketing as well. These machines are also considered strategic for national investment and scientific research capacity.
gl.surec-odul-modeli.def: A type of reward model that evaluates and scores each intermediate step of a chain of reasoning, not just the final result, helping to find where an error was made.
gl.surec-odul-modeli.example: If a five-step geometry solution uses a wrong formula in the third step, a process reward model gives high scores to the first two steps and a low one to the third.
gl.surec-odul-modeli.faq.0.a: An outcome reward model scores only the final answer. A process reward model evaluates each intermediate step of the solution separately.
gl.surec-odul-modeli.faq.0.q: What is the difference between a process reward model and an outcome reward model?
gl.surec-odul-modeli.faq.1.a: Collecting step-level labels is expensive, and the correctness of intermediate steps is not clear in every task. Some teams therefore prefer simpler methods that check the outcome automatically.
gl.surec-odul-modeli.faq.1.q: Why aren't process reward models used everywhere?
gl.surec-odul-modeli.how: The model solves a problem step by step, and the process reward model scores whether each step is correct and sensible. For training data, people mark the steps of a solution one by one, or step labels are produced with automated methods. An outcome reward model, by contrast, looks only at the final answer. Process scores can be used to pick the most solid solution among several candidates, or to let a model stop at a flawed step and change course.
gl.surec-odul-modeli.why: Looking only at the outcome also rewards solutions that reach the right answer by accident through faulty reasoning. Step-by-step feedback helps a model reason more reliably and makes it clearer where a mistake occurred. The cost is that step labeling is expensive and the correctness of an intermediate step is not clearly defined in every domain.
gl.surekli-ogrenme.def: An approach in which a model learns new data and tasks one after another over time without losing what it learned earlier, aiming for something like human lifelong learning.
gl.surekli-ogrenme.example: A spam filter has to learn new phishing tricks as they appear without losing its ability to spot the older ones.
gl.surekli-ogrenme.faq.0.a: They are close but not identical. Online learning describes data arriving as a stream with the model updated continuously. Continual learning focuses specifically on keeping old knowledge intact while new tasks arrive.
gl.surekli-ogrenme.faq.0.q: Is continual learning the same as online learning?
gl.surekli-ogrenme.faq.1.a: It is when a neural network updates its weights for a new task and in doing so disrupts the settings that worked for an earlier task, so its performance on that earlier task drops.
gl.surekli-ogrenme.how: A classic model is trained once and then frozen. If training simply continues on new data, the model can quickly forget the old material, a problem known as catastrophic forgetting. Continual learning methods try to prevent this. Examples include storing small samples from earlier tasks and replaying them, limiting changes to the weights that matter most, or reserving a separate part of the network for each task. The goal is to add new knowledge while keeping the old.
gl.surekli-ogrenme.why: The real world does not stand still: user habits, language and fraud tactics keep changing, and retraining a model from scratch each time is costly. Continual learning could reduce that cost, but forgetting remains an open research problem, and large models are still mostly updated through retraining or fine-tuning.
gl.surus-otomasyonu-seviyeleri.def: A classification from zero to five that describes how much of the driving task a vehicle handles itself, most commonly based on the SAE International standard.
gl.surus-otomasyonu-seviyeleri.example: A driver-assist package that steers and controls speed but requires the driver to watch the road is level 2, while a driverless robotaxi service is classified as level 4.
gl.surus-otomasyonu-seviyeleri.faq.0.a: The driver-assistance systems common in privately owned cars are mostly level 2. Higher levels tend to appear in limited areas and specific services.
gl.surus-otomasyonu-seviyeleri.faq.0.q: Which level is most common in cars people buy?
gl.surus-otomasyonu-seviyeleri.faq.1.a: At level 3 the system may ask the driver to take over, so the driver must be ready. At level 4 the system can bring the car to a safe stop on its own within its defined area, so no human intervention is needed.
gl.surus-otomasyonu-seviyeleri.faq.1.q: What is the difference between level 3 and level 4?
gl.surus-otomasyonu-seviyeleri.how: At level 0 there is no automation and the driver does everything. At level 1 the system assists with either steering or speed. At level 2 it assists with both, but the driver must monitor constantly. At level 3 the car takes over driving under certain conditions, though the driver must take back control when the system asks. At level 4 the car drives without a human inside a defined area and set of conditions. Level 5 means full automation everywhere and in all conditions.
gl.surus-otomasyonu-seviyeleri.why: Marketing terms like “autopilot” or “full self-driving” can cause confusion. The levels give people a shared language for what a vehicle expects from its driver and where responsibility lies. They are also essential for making sense of terms like “level 2” or “level 4” in the news.
gl.swe-bench.def: A benchmark that measures how well AI models can resolve bugs and feature requests in real software projects. Its tasks come from the GitHub records of popular open-source Python projects.
gl.swe-bench.example: A bug report on an open-source library saying 'the program crashes on this input' could serve as a SWE-bench task in which the model is asked to write the fix.
gl.swe-bench.faq.0.a: It is a subset of tasks that humans reviewed to confirm they are solvable and clearly specified. It aims to reduce the effect of ambiguous or flawed tasks on scores.
gl.swe-bench.faq.1.a: HumanEval contains short, single-function problems. SWE-bench requires understanding and changing multiple files in a large codebase.
gl.swe-bench.faq.1.q: How does SWE-bench differ from HumanEval?
gl.swe-bench.how: In each task, the model receives a project's code repository and an issue report filed on GitHub. It produces a code change, called a patch, that is meant to resolve the issue. The patch is applied and the project's own tests are run, and if they pass, the task counts as solved. The score is the share of tasks solved. The benchmark was introduced in 2023 by a team that included researchers from Princeton University, and a human-reviewed subset called 'Verified' is widely used.
gl.swe-bench.why: Coding assistants and 'software engineer agents' appear often in the news, and SWE-bench is one of the best-known ways to test such claims on real projects. Because the work is more realistic than writing a single function, it is valuable for showing agent capabilities. Results can vary with the setup and tools used, so scores should be compared with care.
gl.tahmine-dayali-analitik.def: An approach that uses statistics and machine learning to learn patterns from historical data and estimate the likelihood of future outcomes, such as customer churn or equipment failure.
gl.tahmine-dayali-analitik.example: A telecom operator can identify customers likely to leave and offer them a tailored deal.
gl.tahmine-dayali-analitik.faq.0.a: No. Predictive analytics is a purpose. It often uses AI methods such as machine learning, but classical statistical methods are used too.
gl.tahmine-dayali-analitik.faq.0.q: Is predictive analytics the same as artificial intelligence?
gl.tahmine-dayali-analitik.faq.1.a: They are not certain; they usually give probabilities. Success depends on data quality and on how closely future conditions resemble the past.
gl.tahmine-dayali-analitik.how: First, past records with known outcomes are collected, such as which customers canceled a subscription. The model learns the relationship between the features in those records and the outcome. When a new customer arrives, the model is asked about them, and the output is usually a probability or risk score rather than a firm verdict. That score is then used to make decisions, such as offering a deal to customers at high risk. As conditions change the model goes stale, so it should be monitored and retrained regularly.
gl.tahmine-dayali-analitik.why: Companies use it in inventory, risk, maintenance and marketing to prepare in advance instead of reacting after the fact. But predictions rest on patterns from the past, so they can mislead if conditions shift or the data is biased.
gl.taklit-ogrenmesi.def: A way of training an AI system to perform a task by copying behavior demonstrated by human experts, rather than by trial and error guided by rewards.
gl.taklit-ogrenmesi.example: An operator shows a robot arm how to fold a shirt dozens of times. From these recordings the robot learns which movement goes with which camera view.
gl.taklit-ogrenmesi.faq.0.a: In imitation learning the model learns from examples shown by an expert. In reinforcement learning it learns by trying things and adjusting to the rewards it receives. The two are often used together.
gl.taklit-ogrenmesi.faq.0.q: How is imitation learning different from reinforcement learning?
gl.taklit-ogrenmesi.faq.1.a: The model is generally limited to the range of behaviors it was shown. When it meets a situation far from its training data it can make mistakes, and those mistakes can grow in later steps. That is why collecting varied, plentiful examples matters.
gl.taklit-ogrenmesi.faq.1.q: What is the main limit of imitation learning?
gl.taklit-ogrenmesi.how: While an expert performs a task, the situation they are in (a camera image, sensor readings) and the action they take are recorded together. The model learns to predict what the expert would do in a given situation. In its simplest form this is supervised learning, often called behavior cloning. Once trained, the model produces actions similar to the expert's in new situations. Its weakness is that when it ends up in a situation the expert never demonstrated, errors can pile up. So more data is collected, or the method is combined with other techniques.
gl.taklit-ogrenmesi.why: Programming every movement by hand, or designing a good reward function, is very hard for a robot. Teaching by showing is more natural and faster. That is why imitation learning sits at the base of much robot AI research. It is also used in self-driving research.
gl.talimat-ayari.def: Fine-tuning of a language model on pairs of instructions and desired responses, so that it can understand and follow commands written in natural language, such as “summarize this” or “translate that”.
gl.talimat-ayari.example: Given the instruction “Summarize the email below in three sentences”, a model that writes an actual three-sentence summary instead of simply continuing the email has most likely gone through instruction tuning.
gl.talimat-ayari.faq.0.a: In practice, instruction tuning is a kind of supervised fine-tuning. The difference is that the data takes the form of instructions and responses, and the aim is to build instruction-following ability.
gl.talimat-ayari.faq.0.q: Is instruction tuning the same as supervised fine-tuning?
gl.talimat-ayari.faq.1.a: Instruction tuning learns from ready-made example responses. RLHF learns from human preferences between different responses and is usually applied after instruction tuning.
gl.talimat-ayari.faq.1.q: How is instruction tuning different from RLHF?
gl.talimat-ayari.how: A pre-trained model knows how to continue text but not that it is supposed to carry out a command. In instruction tuning, the model is shown many instructions covering a wide range of tasks, each paired with a suitable example response. From these pairs it learns the pattern of doing the requested job when a request arrives. The data can be written by people or generated with other models. The more varied the tasks, the better the model handles instructions it has never seen.
gl.talimat-ayari.why: Instruction tuning is one of the key steps that turns a raw language model into a tool ordinary users can talk to comfortably. It is part of why models can be directed in everyday language without carefully engineered prompts.
gl.talimat-modeli.def: A version of a base model that has been trained further so it can understand human requests, follow them and give helpful answers.
gl.talimat-modeli.example: Telling a base model “Write me a short email” may be treated like the start of a document to continue, while an instruct model simply writes the email.
gl.talimat-modeli.faq.0.a: Often they are very close. A chat model can be thought of as an instruct model tuned especially for multi-turn conversation, though naming varies from company to company.
gl.talimat-modeli.faq.0.q: Is a chat model the same as an instruct model?
gl.talimat-modeli.faq.1.a: For everyday use, yes, because it follows requests. But developers who want to fine-tune for a specialized domain may prefer the base model because it is more flexible.
gl.talimat-modeli.faq.1.q: Is an instruct model always better than a base model?
gl.talimat-modeli.how: An instruct model is built starting from a base model. First comes supervised fine-tuning on many pairs of instructions and example answers written or selected by people. Then methods that draw on preferences, such as which answer humans or other models judge better, are applied. Through this the model learns to answer questions, follow steps, adopt a suitable tone and decline harmful requests. Most chat assistants are built on this kind of model.
gl.talimat-modeli.why: Almost every product that people interact with directly uses an instruct model. How helpful, safe and consistent a model feels is largely decided at this stage. When news stories mention chat or assistant versions of a model, they usually mean models that have gone through this process.
gl.talimat-takibi.def: An AI model's ability to carry out the directions it is given, such as format, length, tone or restrictions, accurately and completely.
gl.talimat-takibi.example: If a user asks the model to summarize a text in under a hundred words, in a formal tone and without bullet points, and the model respects all three rules, it has followed the instruction well.
gl.talimat-takibi.faq.0.a: No. Instruction following is a capability of the model, while prompt engineering is about how the user writes a request to get good results. The two complement each other.
gl.talimat-takibi.faq.0.q: Is instruction following the same as prompt engineering?
gl.talimat-takibi.faq.1.a: Instructions can be contradictory, vague or very long, and the model's ability is limited. Safety rules can also take priority over certain requests.
gl.talimat-takibi.faq.1.q: Why does a model sometimes ignore an instruction?
gl.talimat-takibi.how: Language models learn patterns in text during initial training, and instruction following is usually sharpened in later stages. The model is fine-tuned on pairs of instructions and desired responses, then trained with methods based on human ratings, such as reinforcement learning from human feedback, to learn which answers fit a request better. Results also depend on how clear the instruction is: a precise request like 'three bullets, one sentence each' works more reliably than a vague one. When many rules are given at once, models may miss some of them.
gl.talimat-takibi.why: No matter how knowledgeable a model is, it is not useful if it will not answer in the requested format and within limits. Companies that plug AI into customer service or automation depend on consistent, predictable behavior. That is why instruction following is one of the abilities most often measured when models are compared.
gl.talimat-veri-seti.def: A dataset of examples that pair an instruction or question with the response that is wanted. It is used to teach a language model to follow what users ask of it.
gl.talimat-veri-seti.example: A company could collect real customer-service questions and approved answers into an instruction dataset to adapt a model to its own domain.
gl.talimat-veri-seti.faq.0.a: An instruction dataset gives one example response per prompt, and the model learns to imitate it. Preference data marks which of several responses to the same prompt is better.
gl.talimat-veri-seti.faq.0.q: What is the difference between an instruction dataset and preference data?
gl.talimat-veri-seti.faq.1.a: Yes, a strong model can produce example instructions and responses to train another model. The accuracy and variety of the generated data still need to be checked.
gl.talimat-veri-seti.faq.1.q: Can a model generate an instruction dataset?
gl.talimat-veri-seti.how: Each example usually has an instruction, an input text if needed, and an ideal response, such as the instruction “Summarize this text in three sentences” paired with a good summary. People can write the examples, or another model can generate them and people review them. A model that has finished pretraining is then trained further on these examples, a step called supervised fine-tuning. As a result, instead of merely continuing a piece of text, the model learns to understand a request and answer it appropriately.
gl.talimat-veri-seti.why: This is one of the key steps that make chat assistants useful. The quality and variety of the dataset directly shape the model's behavior, and flawed, biased or narrow examples are passed on to the model. Preparing instruction data is therefore a significant effort and cost in its own right.
gl.tarayici-ajani.def: An AI agent that works inside a web browser on a user's behalf, browsing pages, searching, filling in forms and clicking. Rather than just answering a question, it tries to carry out the task from start to finish.
gl.tarayici-ajani.example: A user can ask an agent to compare hotel prices on three sites and add a suitable room to the cart; the agent visits each site, summarizes the results and leaves the payment for the user to approve.
gl.tarayici-ajani.faq.0.a: A chatbot mostly provides information and generates text. A browser agent moves through web pages and performs actions itself, such as clicking, typing and submitting forms.
gl.tarayici-ajani.faq.0.q: How is a browser agent different from a chatbot?
gl.tarayici-ajani.faq.1.a: Because it can reach accounts where you are signed in, mistakes or manipulation by a malicious page can cause harm. Asking for approval on important actions and limiting its access reduce that risk.
gl.tarayici-ajani.faq.1.q: Is it risky to trust a browser agent?
gl.tarayici-ajani.how: The agent reads a page either through its underlying structure (HTML) or as a screenshot. The language model looks at the user's goal and picks the next step, such as clicking a link, typing into a search box or filling in a form. After the action is carried out, the updated page is fed back to the model and the loop repeats. Because the agent often runs in a browser where the user is already signed in, it can reach accounts, so asking for confirmation at critical steps like payment is a common design choice.
gl.tarayici-ajani.why: Much of daily work happens on the web, so browser agents promise to take over tedious jobs such as searching, comparing and filling in forms. They are also exposed to prompt injection, where instructions hidden in a page try to steer the agent. That is why security is a frequent topic in coverage of the technology.
gl.tehlikeli-yetenek-degerlendirmesi.def: Systematic testing to measure how far an AI model has capabilities that could cause serious harm, such as aiding biological or chemical threats, carrying out cyberattacks, manipulating people or evading oversight.
gl.tehlikeli-yetenek-degerlendirmesi.exa: A model is tested with questions written by biology experts to measure whether it could give meaningful help to a novice trying to produce a harmful agent.
gl.tehlikeli-yetenek-degerlendirmesi.faq: They are close but not identical. Red teaming pushes a model to find harmful behavior and weaknesses. A dangerous capability evaluation aims to measure the level of specific risky abilities. In practice the two complement each other.
Is a dangerous capability evaluation the same as red teaming?
It depends on the company's policy and applicable rules. Extra safeguards may be added, access may be restricted, or the release may be delayed.
What happens if a model scores as dangerous?
gl.tehlikeli-yetenek-degerlendirmesi.how: Evaluation teams give the model question and task sets prepared by experts in risky domains. In a cybersecurity task, for example, they check whether the model can find a vulnerability in a system. The key is to bring out the model's best performance: suitable prompting, tool access and, where needed, fine-tuning are used, since a bad actor could do the same. Results are compared against thresholds set in advance. The tests can be run by companies' internal teams, independent organizations and government-linked safety institutes.
gl.tehlikeli-yetenek-degerlendirmesi.why: These tests underpin decisions about whether a model is released and with what safeguards. They also form the measurement side of responsible scaling policies. But tests can fall short: a model may show less than its real ability, or a way of using it may go untested. Results are therefore best read as a risk estimate, not a guarantee.
gl.tekrarlayan-sinir-agi.def: A type of neural network that reads input one step at a time and carries an internal state, called the hidden state, forward from earlier steps. It is used for sequential data such as text, audio and time series.
gl.tekrarlayan-sinir-agi.example: An RNN reading the words 'Last night we went to the' uses the hidden state it has built up so far to predict a likely next word such as 'cinema'.
gl.tekrarlayan-sinir-agi.faq.0.a: An RNN processes text step by step and carries the past in a single hidden state. A Transformer looks at all the tokens at once, which makes training easier to parallelize and long context easier to handle.
gl.tekrarlayan-sinir-agi.faq.0.q: What is the main difference between an RNN and a Transformer?
gl.tekrarlayan-sinir-agi.faq.1.a: In large language models they have mostly been replaced by Transformers. They are still used in small, resource-limited applications and some time-series tasks, and newer recurrent designs are being researched.
gl.tekrarlayan-sinir-agi.how: The network takes each element of the sequence in order. At every step it combines the new input with the hidden state left over from the previous step to produce a new hidden state and, if needed, an output. The same weights are reused at every step, which is where the word recurrent comes from. In training, the error is propagated backward through the time steps. As sequences grow longer, this signal can fade or blow up, which makes it hard to learn long-range dependencies.
gl.tekrarlayan-sinir-agi.why: Before Transformers, RNNs were the basic building block for language, speech and translation. Because they process data in sequence, training is hard to parallelize and they struggle to carry long contexts, which helped speed the rise of Transformers. Still, the idea continues to inspire today's state space models.
gl.teleoperasyon.def: The real-time control of a robot or machine by a human operator at a distance. In AI it is also a method for collecting demonstration data to teach robots.
gl.teleoperasyon.example: An operator guides a robot arm with a VR headset and hand controllers to open a drawer. The recording is later used so the robot can learn to do the same task by itself.
gl.teleoperasyon.faq.0.a: No. In teleoperation a human makes the decisions and the movements. In an autonomous system the decision comes from the robot's own software. Many systems sit somewhere in between, with humans and software sharing the work.
gl.teleoperasyon.faq.0.q: Is teleoperation the same as autonomy?
gl.teleoperasyon.faq.1.a: Because what a person does turns directly into examples a robot can learn from. It is one of the more practical ways to collect robot skill data, though it takes labor and time.
gl.teleoperasyon.faq.1.q: Why is teleoperation used to train robots?
gl.teleoperasyon.how: The operator uses a controller, a glove, a virtual reality headset or a leader arm that mirrors the robot arm's movements. Their movements are sent to the robot, which carries them out. The operator works by watching the images from the robot's cameras. In an AI setting, the camera images and movement commands are recorded during this process. The recordings are then used to train a model through imitation learning. In some systems the robot mostly works on its own and a human steps in during hard moments.
gl.teleoperasyon.why: One of the biggest bottlenecks in robot AI is the shortage of good training data, and teleoperation is one of the main ways to produce it. It also keeps people out of harm's way in dangerous settings. And it raises a fair question about robot demos billed as “autonomous”: how much human intervention is actually involved?
gl.telif-hakki-ve-yapay-zeka.def: The legal area dealing with whether training AI models on copyrighted works is allowed, and whether what models produce can itself be protected by copyright. Authors, artists, news organizations and tech companies are on opposing sides of the debate.
gl.telif-hakki-ve-yapay-zeka.example: In 2023, The New York Times sued OpenAI and Microsoft, claiming its articles were used to train models without permission. The companies argue that the use is lawful.
gl.telif-hakki-ve-yapay-zeka.faq.0.a: The general trend is that protection depends on human creativity. For example, the US Copyright Office does not register works generated entirely by AI. If a person made a meaningful creative contribution, the assessment may differ.
gl.telif-hakki-ve-yapay-zeka.faq.0.q: Can an AI-generated image be protected by copyright?
gl.telif-hakki-ve-yapay-zeka.faq.1.a: There is no single answer. Some countries have exceptions that allow it, while elsewhere the question is still before the courts. The result depends on the country, the data used and the way it is used.
gl.telif-hakki-ve-yapay-zeka.faq.1.q: Is training AI on copyrighted works illegal?
gl.telif-hakki-ve-yapay-zeka.how: The debate centers on two points. The first is input: models are trained on large collections of books, news articles, images and code, and rights holders ask whether that requires permission. The second is output: it is unclear whether a text or image generated by a model is protected when the human contribution is limited. Countries answer these questions differently, mostly through court rulings and statutory exceptions, and many issues remain unsettled.
gl.telif-hakki-ve-yapay-zeka.why: The outcome will determine how AI companies get training data and whether they must pay the people who created it. It affects the income and rights of many groups, from news publishers to authors, which is why it appears so often in AI news.
gl.temel-bilesen-analizi.def: A statistical method that summarizes data with many features by projecting it onto new axes that capture the most variation. The data becomes simpler while the loss of information stays limited.
gl.temel-bilesen-analizi.example: Hundreds of measurements of a customer's shopping habits can be reduced to a few principal components and plotted on a two-dimensional chart, where groups of similar customers become visible.
gl.temel-bilesen-analizi.faq.0.a: No. Feature selection keeps some of the existing columns, while PCA combines all of them to build new axes.
gl.temel-bilesen-analizi.faq.0.q: Is PCA the same as feature selection?
gl.temel-bilesen-analizi.faq.1.a: It assumes that variation carries information and it captures only linear structure. It can perform poorly on curved structures, or on features with very different scales if they are not standardized first.
gl.temel-bilesen-analizi.faq.1.q: Does PCA work on every dataset?
gl.temel-bilesen-analizi.how: The method first finds the direction in which the data spreads out the most; this is the first principal component. It then picks a direction perpendicular to it that carries the largest share of the remaining variation, and so on. Each component is a weighted mix of the original features. Keeping the first few components and dropping the rest represents the data with far fewer numbers. It resembles photographing an object from several angles and choosing the most informative one. The method is linear, meaning it relies only on straight axes.
gl.temel-bilesen-analizi.why: It is one of the most common preprocessing steps for visualization, noise reduction and shortening training time. It is a classic way to cope with the curse of dimensionality. Because components are hard to interpret in terms of the original features, though, there is a tradeoff between simplification and explainability.
gl.temel-model.def: A general-purpose AI model trained at large scale on broad and varied data, which can then be adapted to many different jobs such as chat, translation, coding or image understanding.
gl.temel-model.example: A company can use the same language model under three separate products: a customer service chatbot, a contract summarizer and a coding assistant.
gl.temel-model.faq.0.a: Every large language model can be considered a foundation model, but not every foundation model is a language model; there are also ones that work with images, audio or several data types at once.
gl.temel-model.faq.0.q: Is a foundation model the same as a large language model?
gl.temel-model.faq.1.a: A foundation model is defined by being general-purpose and adaptable. A frontier model is one at the leading edge of capability at a given time; frontier models are usually foundation models as well.
gl.temel-model.faq.1.q: What is the difference between a foundation model and a frontier model?
gl.temel-model.how: A foundation model is first pretrained on internet-scale data such as text, images, audio or code, usually through self-supervised learning. This stage takes enormous computing power and gives the model broad knowledge of language and the world. The resulting model is not built for one particular job; through fine-tuning, prompting or further training it becomes the base for many different applications. It is called a foundation because many products rest on a model trained once.
gl.temel-model.why: Most of the large language models in the news are foundation models. Having one model underpin many products lowers costs, but it also means that errors and biases can carry over to all of those products. In regulatory debates, these models are often treated as a category of their own.
gl.temel-surum-model.def: A raw language model that has learned to predict the next piece of text from a huge body of data, but has not yet been tuned to follow instructions or hold a conversation.
gl.temel-surum-model.example: If you type “What is the capital of France?” into a base model, it may continue with more similar questions, such as “What is the capital of Italy?”, instead of answering.
gl.temel-surum-model.faq.0.a: A base model only predicts the continuation of text. An instruct model is built on top of it with extra training so that it understands requests and gives helpful answers.
gl.temel-surum-model.faq.0.q: What is the difference between a base model and an instruct model?
gl.temel-surum-model.faq.1.a: Developers use them as a starting point for fine-tuning on their own data. Because they have not been shaped into a chat style, they are also useful for studying a model's raw capabilities.
gl.temel-surum-model.faq.1.q: Why are base models still released?
gl.temel-surum-model.how: A base model is trained in a stage called pretraining, on a very large collection of text gathered from the web, books and code repositories. Its only job is to predict which piece of text comes next. That is why, when given a command, it tends to continue the text rather than carry out the request. With later fine-tuning and human feedback, it becomes an instruct model. The base model is the first and most compute-hungry link in that chain.
gl.temel-surum-model.why: Most of a model's knowledge and abilities form at this stage, and later tuning mostly makes that knowledge usable. Open model releases often include the base version separately. Researchers and companies can fine-tune it for their own domains to build specialized tools.
gl.temellendirme.def: Tying an AI model's answers to reliable sources, documents or data. The goal is for the model to rely on verifiable information rather than inventing details from its own memory.
gl.temellendirme.example: A bank's customer assistant answers an interest-rate question using a section of the bank's current product document and shows that document; if the document does not contain the information, it says it does not know.
gl.temellendirme.faq.0.a: No. Grounding is the goal: connecting answers to sources. RAG is one of the methods used to reach that goal.
gl.temellendirme.faq.0.q: Is grounding the same as RAG?
gl.temellendirme.faq.1.a: No. It reduces the chance of made-up answers, but the model can still misread or under-report a source, and the source itself may be wrong.
gl.temellendirme.how: When the model generates an answer, relevant texts, database records or search results are added to its input, and it is instructed to write based on that material. Many systems show source links or citations alongside the answer so readers can check it. The most common route is retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), and instructions telling the model to answer only from the supplied documents are also used. It works like an open-book exam: the answer should rest on what the book says.
gl.temellendirme.why: Language models can produce fluent but wrong statements, known as hallucinations. Grounding lowers that risk without removing it, because a model can still misread a source. In fields like health, law and finance, being able to point to a source is a big part of whether a tool is usable at all.
gl.tensor-cekirdegi.def: A specialized compute unit inside a GPU, built to run AI math such as matrix multiplication very fast. Nvidia uses the name for the units in its graphics processors.
gl.tensor-cekirdegi.example: When a chatbot generates a reply, the billions of multiply-and-add operations involved are mostly carried out in the tensor cores on Nvidia GPUs.
gl.tensor-cekirdegi.faq.0.a: CUDA cores are the GPU's general-purpose parallel compute units. Tensor cores are specialized only for matrix operations and are much faster at them.
gl.tensor-cekirdegi.faq.0.q: What is the difference between a tensor core and a CUDA core?
gl.tensor-cekirdegi.faq.1.a: The term belongs to Nvidia. Chips from other makers also have similar matrix compute units, but they go by different names.
gl.tensor-cekirdegi.faq.1.q: Are tensor cores found only in Nvidia chips?
gl.tensor-cekirdegi.how: The basic operation in neural networks is multiplying and adding tables of numbers (matrices), and a tensor is the general name for such tables in many dimensions. Ordinary GPU cores do this with individual numbers, while a tensor core processes a small block of a matrix in a single step. Part of the speedup comes from lower-precision number formats: working with 16-bit or smaller numbers often gives enough accuracy for AI and also saves memory. Software libraries route the model's operations to these cores.
gl.tensor-cekirdegi.why: How long a large model takes to train and what it costs to run depends on how efficient these specialized units are. They are one of the main reasons modern AI GPUs have moved away from traditional graphics processors. Chip comparisons in the news often come down to how fast these units are.
gl.tensor.def: A data structure that arranges numbers as a single value, a vector, a matrix, or an array with even more axes. In AI, nearly everything, from text and images to model weights, is stored as tensors.
gl.tensor.example: A 256 × 256 pixel color photo is fed to a model as a three-axis tensor of shape 256 × 256 × 3.
gl.tensor.faq.0.a: A matrix is the special case of a tensor with two axes. The tensor concept places no limit on the number of axes; it can have three, four or more.
gl.tensor.faq.0.q: Is a tensor the same as a matrix?
gl.tensor.faq.1.a: In mathematics and physics, tensors are defined by how they transform under changes of coordinates. In AI software the word usually just means a multi-dimensional array of numbers, and that meaning is enough for practical purposes.
gl.tensor.faq.1.q: Is a tensor in AI the same as a tensor in physics?
gl.tensor.how: A tensor's number of axes is called its rank or number of dimensions. A single number has zero axes, a row of numbers (a vector) has one, and a table of rows and columns (a matrix) has two. A color photo is a three-axis tensor of height, width and color channel, and a batch of photos adds a fourth axis. Libraries such as PyTorch and TensorFlow are built to process tensors in bulk on GPUs.
gl.tensor.why: Neural networks do all their computation on tensors, so training and inference speed depends on how efficiently hardware handles them. Nvidia's GPUs and Google's TPU chips are designed around this kind of work. Terms in the news such as 'tensor cores' come from the same idea.
gl.tensorflow.def: A deep learning library developed by Google and released as open source in 2015. It offers a broad toolkit for training models and deploying them on many kinds of devices.
gl.tensorflow.example: A phone app can run a model shrunk with TensorFlow Lite directly on the device and recognize objects in photos without an internet connection.
gl.tensorflow.faq.0.a: Keras is a high-level interface that makes building models easier. TensorFlow is the computation engine underneath; Keras now ships with TensorFlow and is its most common entry point.
gl.tensorflow.faq.0.q: What is the difference between TensorFlow and Keras?
gl.tensorflow.faq.1.a: Yes, especially in production systems and in mobile or edge device applications. New research projects more often choose PyTorch.
gl.tensorflow.how: Computations are laid out as a graph of operations over tensors, and that graph can run on a processor, a graphics card or Google's TPU chips. With a high-level interface called Keras, a model can be defined and trained in a few lines. In TensorFlow 2, code runs step by step by default and is converted to graph form when speed is needed. The ecosystem includes TensorFlow Lite for mobile devices, TensorFlow.js for the browser and TensorFlow Serving for publishing models on servers.
gl.tensorflow.why: Ready-made tools for moving a trained model onto a phone, into a browser or into a large server system have kept TensorFlow in place in production environments. Many companies' existing systems are built on it. In the research community, PyTorch has become more common in recent years.
gl.tercih-verisi.def: Comparison records showing which of several responses to the same prompt is better. They are usually marked by people, and sometimes by another model.
gl.tercih-verisi.example: If a chat assistant shows two responses side by side and asks the user to pick the better one, that choice can be recorded as preference data.
gl.tercih-verisi.faq.0.a: No. Preference data is the raw material that methods like RLHF use. RLHF is the process of training a reward model on that data and then improving the main model against that reward.
gl.tercih-verisi.faq.0.q: Is preference data the same as RLHF?
gl.tercih-verisi.faq.1.a: No. Another AI model can also judge responses and generate preferences. In that case the judge model's own errors and biases can leak into the data.
gl.tercih-verisi.faq.1.q: Is preference data produced only by people?
gl.tercih-verisi.how: A model is given a prompt and produces several different responses. An evaluator ranks them or picks one over another based on criteria such as helpfulness, accuracy or safety. The accumulated comparisons can be used to train a reward model that scores responses, and some methods tune the model directly on these pairs. The approach known as reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF) relies on this kind of data.
gl.tercih-verisi.why: Writing out a perfect answer is hard, but saying which of two answers is better is usually easier. That makes preference data an important tool for shaping a model's tone and safety behavior. The personal and cultural leanings of the evaluators can also carry over into the model.
gl.terminal-bench.def: A benchmark that measures how well AI agents complete real software and system tasks in a command-line terminal.
gl.terminal-bench.example: An agent is asked to take a downloaded project and get it compiled and running; the task passes only if the build actually succeeds.
gl.terminal-bench.faq.0.a: SWE-bench focuses mainly on writing patches that fix bugs in open-source repositories. Terminal-Bench covers a broader range of terminal tasks, including installation, configuration, and system work.
gl.terminal-bench.faq.0.q: How is Terminal-Bench different from SWE-bench?
gl.terminal-bench.faq.1.a: A terminal is text-based, so typing commands and reading output comes naturally to a model. The correctness of the result can also be checked clearly with automated tests.
gl.terminal-bench.faq.1.q: Why are agents tested in a terminal?
gl.terminal-bench.how: Each task is given to the agent in an isolated terminal environment, such as building a piece of software, configuring a server, or repairing a broken setup. The agent types commands, reads the output, and changes its approach when needed. When it finishes, pre-written tests check whether the environment reached the desired state, and a task counts as solved only if the result is correct. The success rate is calculated over the number of tasks.
gl.terminal-bench.why: As more software work is handed to agents, it matters not just that a model can write code but that it can use tools in a real environment and carry a job through to the end. Terminal-Bench measures that end-to-end ability. Its results are often cited when comparing agent-based coding products.
gl.test-seti.def: A portion of data that the model never sees during training or tuning, used after development is finished to measure its final performance in an unbiased way.
gl.test-seti.example: For a medical imaging model, X-rays from different hospitals that were never used in training are set aside as the test set, and the model's final accuracy is reported on them.
gl.test-seti.faq.0.a: Usually yes. If the model is changed after each look at the results, the test set indirectly becomes part of tuning and the score turns optimistic. That is why it is used as sparingly as possible.
gl.test-seti.faq.0.q: Is it a problem to use the test set more than once?
gl.test-seti.faq.1.a: There is no fixed rule; with smaller datasets, 10 to 20 percent is common. What matters is that it has enough examples for a reliable result and represents real-world use.
gl.test-seti.faq.1.q: How big should a test set be?
gl.test-seti.how: The data is split at the start and the test set is put aside. The model is trained and tuned using the validation set, and the test set is used only at the very end, ideally once. The result approximates how the model will behave on new data in the real world. If the model is changed after looking at test results, the set loses its neutrality, because the developer unknowingly adapts the model to it. The test data should also reflect real use and contain no copies of the training data.
gl.test-seti.why: A claim about a model's performance only means something if it is measured on data the model has not seen. Headlines saying a model scored a certain number on a certain test rest on this logic. If the test set leaks into training or is reused over and over, results look better than they really are.
gl.tohum-yatirim-turu.def: The first formal investment round a startup raises to turn an idea into a product, usually from angel investors or small funds that take an ownership stake in exchange for early, modest funding.
gl.tohum-yatirim-turu.example: A three-person team builds a prototype of an AI text-summarizing tool and raises its first funding from an angel investor and a small fund; that is a seed round.
gl.tohum-yatirim-turu.faq.0.a: Not exactly. An angel investor is an individual investing personal money, while a seed round describes the stage of funding. Both angels and small funds can take part in a seed round.
gl.tohum-yatirim-turu.faq.0.q: Is a seed round the same as angel investment?
gl.tohum-yatirim-turu.faq.1.a: The amount varies widely by country, period and sector. Because training AI models is expensive, some rounds can be large, but there is no single standard figure.
gl.tohum-yatirim-turu.faq.1.q: How much money goes into a seed round?
gl.tohum-yatirim-turu.how: Founders approach investors with an idea, a small team and often an early prototype. The investor buys a slice of the company's shares, or uses an instrument such as a convertible note that later turns into shares. The money goes toward the first engineers' salaries, building the prototype and finding early customers. Revenue at this stage is usually tiny or zero, so investors focus on the founders' track record, the size of the market and how fast the team moves.
gl.tohum-yatirim-turu.why: Many AI startups begin with a seed round, so who gets that first check shows early where the industry is heading. When headlines mention a 'record seed round,' it reflects how much investors value a team even at the founding stage. Still, a significant share of companies at this stage never make it further.
gl.token-basina-fiyatlandirma.def: A pricing scheme for language model services in which the charge depends on the number of text pieces, called tokens, that the model reads and writes. A unit price is set for a given quantity of tokens.
gl.token-basina-fiyatlandirma.example: When a developer asks a model to summarize a ten-page contract, both the contract text and the generated summary are counted as tokens, and the bill is based on that total.
gl.token-basina-fiyatlandirma.faq.0.a: There is no fixed ratio; it depends on the language and on how the model splits text. In languages with heavy suffixing, such as Turkish, words are often cut into more pieces, so the same text can use more tokens.
gl.token-basina-fiyatlandirma.faq.0.q: How many words is one token?
gl.token-basina-fiyatlandirma.faq.1.a: Many providers price them separately because reading a prompt and generating a reply put different loads on the hardware. The details vary by provider.
gl.token-basina-fiyatlandirma.faq.1.q: Why are input and output tokens priced separately?
gl.token-basina-fiyatlandirma.how: The model splits text into small pieces called tokens; a token can be a whole word, part of a word or a punctuation mark. The text a user sends (input) and the reply the model produces (output) are counted separately. Providers typically publish a unit price for a set number of tokens, and input and output prices may differ. The total bill is the token counts multiplied by the unit prices. Sending a long document or asking for a long answer uses more tokens and therefore costs more.
gl.token-basina-fiyatlandirma.why: For teams building AI applications, token consumption is a core line in cost planning. Writing a shorter prompt, avoiding unnecessary context and choosing a smaller model for the same job all affect the bill directly. Model prices are often in the news, but they change over time, so current figures are best checked on the provider's own page.

gl.token.def.en: The small units language models use to process text; a token can be a word or part of a word. API prices are usually set per million tokens.

gl.token.example.en: An API price of "$1.50 per million input tokens" is the fee paid for every million tokens of text sent to the model.

gl.token.faq.0.a.en: It varies by language. In English, a word averages around one token; in agglutinative languages such as Turkish, a word is often split into more than one token.

gl.token.faq.0.q.en: How many tokens is a word?

gl.token.faq.1.a.en: API fees, the context window limit and response time all depend on the number of tokens.

gl.token.faq.1.q.en: Why does the token count matter?

gl.token.how.en: Language models process text not directly as letters or words but in pieces called tokens. Common words may be a single token, while rare words are split into several pieces. In agglutinative languages such as Turkish, a single word often takes up more than one token.

gl.token.why.en: API pricing, the context window and model speed are all measured in tokens. Because the same content can take more tokens in Turkish than in English, using Turkish can be somewhat more expensive.

gl.tokenlestirme.def: The process of splitting text into small units called tokens and representing each one as a number. Language models read text as this sequence of numbers.
gl.tokenlestirme.example: A word like the Turkish “Okullarımızdan” (“from our schools”) might be split into pieces such as “Okul”, “larımız” and “dan”.
gl.tokenlestirme.faq.0.a: There is no fixed ratio. It depends on the language and the tokenizer. In languages with many suffixes, one word often takes more than one token.
gl.tokenlestirme.faq.0.q: How many tokens is one word?
gl.tokenlestirme.faq.1.a: Splitting by letter makes sequences very long and expensive to process. Splitting by whole word makes the vocabulary huge and cannot handle unseen words. Subword pieces are a middle ground.
gl.tokenlestirme.faq.1.q: Why isn't text split letter by letter or word by word?
gl.tokenlestirme.how: A tokenizer has a pre-built vocabulary of text pieces. It splits incoming text into those pieces: common words often become a single token, while rarer words are broken into several parts. Each piece has an ID number, and the model sees only these numbers, not words or letters. When the model produces output, the numbers are converted back into text. The tokenizer is prepared separately from the model and usually stays fixed during training.
gl.tokenlestirme.why: Usage fees and context-window limits are measured in tokens, so cost and capacity depend directly on this step. Efficiency varies by language and by tokenizer. In languages such as Turkish, which add many suffixes, a single word often takes several tokens, so the same text can be slower and costlier to process.
gl.top-p-ornekleme.def: A way of choosing the next token in which the model samples only from the smallest group of likely candidates whose probabilities add up to a threshold (p). It is also called nucleus sampling.
gl.top-p-ornekleme.example: With p set to 0.9, if the three most likely tokens have probabilities of 50, 30 and 15 percent, they add up to 95 percent, so the pool stops at those three and the choice is made only among them.
gl.top-p-ornekleme.faq.0.a: Top-k always keeps a fixed number of the most likely tokens. Top-p changes the size of the pool depending on how the probabilities add up.
gl.top-p-ornekleme.faq.0.q: What is the difference between top-p and top-k?
gl.top-p-ornekleme.faq.1.a: Yes. Temperature reshapes the distribution, while top-p cuts off its unlikely tail. Often adjusting just one is enough, and changing both makes results harder to predict.
gl.top-p-ornekleme.faq.1.q: Can top-p and temperature be used together?
gl.top-p-ornekleme.how: The model ranks tokens by probability from highest to lowest. Starting at the top, it adds up the probabilities and stops once the total reaches p, for example 0.9. The tokens in that group form the candidate pool and the rest are discarded. A token is then picked at random from the pool according to its probability. When the model is confident the pool is small, and when it is unsure the pool is wide, so the pool size adjusts itself. In top-k sampling, by contrast, the pool size is fixed.
gl.top-p-ornekleme.why: It keeps text fluent by excluding very unlikely, nonsensical tokens while still leaving room for variety. It is a common setting alongside temperature in text-generation interfaces. Because of its effect on output quality and diversity, it is a basic control for people building products on language models.
gl.toplu-isleme-api-si.def: A type of programming interface where many AI requests are submitted together and the answers are prepared in the background and returned within a set time window rather than instantly.
gl.toplu-isleme-api-si.example: An online retailer sends several hundred thousand product reviews from last year to a batch job for sentiment analysis overnight and finds the results ready in the morning.
gl.toplu-isleme-api-si.faq.0.a: A regular API answers within seconds, while a batch API prepares the answers in the background over a longer period. Those willing to wait are usually offered a lower price.
gl.toplu-isleme-api-si.faq.0.q: What is the difference between a batch API and a regular API?
gl.toplu-isleme-api-si.faq.1.a: It does not suit tasks where a user expects an instant reply, such as chatbots, live assistants or interactive search. It makes sense for bulk jobs where delay does not matter.
gl.toplu-isleme-api-si.faq.1.q: Which tasks is it not suited for?
gl.toplu-isleme-api-si.how: A developer collects hundreds or thousands of requests into a single file and uploads it to the provider. The provider queues the jobs and runs them on spare server capacity without disrupting live chat traffic. When the job finishes, the results are downloaded as a file, and each result carries an ID that ties it to its original request. Providers usually allow a waiting window of several hours. In return, many of them charge less than for normal calls.
gl.toplu-isleme-api-si.why: For work that is not urgent, such as labeling a document archive, classifying customer reviews or generating test data, it can cut costs noticeably. It also makes large volumes easier to handle without running into the rate limits of real-time calls. That is why companies using AI at scale often rely on it.
gl.tops.def: A measure of how many trillion operations a chip can perform each second, used especially to describe the power of the AI processors (NPUs) in phones and laptops.
gl.tops.example: Two laptops may list different TOPS values on their spec pages, but if one was measured with 8-bit numbers and the other with 4-bit numbers, the figures do not reflect the same kind of work.
gl.tops.faq.0.a: TOPS counts operations of any kind, mostly integer operations, while FLOPS counts only floating-point operations. FLOPS is more common for large accelerators, TOPS for on-device NPUs.
gl.tops.faq.0.q: What is the difference between TOPS and FLOPS?
gl.tops.faq.1.a: No. TOPS is a theoretical ceiling. Memory bandwidth, software support and the structure of the model determine real-world speed.
gl.tops.faq.1.q: Does higher TOPS always mean faster AI?
gl.tops.how: TOPS expresses the maximum number of operations a chip can perform per second, in trillions. The figure is a theoretical ceiling derived from the number of processing units on the chip and the speed they run at. The operations are usually done with low-precision numbers such as 8-bit integers, because that is often enough for running AI models. TOPS figures given without saying which number type was used are therefore hard to compare directly.
gl.tops.why: When new devices are launched, AI performance is mostly advertised in TOPS. Real speed also depends on memory, software and the model itself, so this number alone does not say how well a device will handle AI tasks.

gl.tpu-npu.def.en: Processors designed specifically for AI computations. The TPU is the chip Google uses in its data centers; an NPU is the unit that runs AI tasks in phones and computers.

gl.tpu-npu.example.en: Tasks such as removing an object from a photo or transcribing a voice note on a phone can be done on the NPU without going online.

gl.tpu-npu.faq.0.a.en: A GPU is a general-purpose processor that can be used for graphics and many different computations. A TPU is a chip Google designed specifically for AI computations and can be more efficient for those workloads.

gl.tpu-npu.faq.0.q.en: What is the difference between a TPU and a GPU?

gl.tpu-npu.faq.1.a.en: Some AI features (such as image editing, live captions and noise cancellation) can run faster and with less battery use, without sending data to cloud servers.

gl.tpu-npu.faq.1.q.en: What is the benefit of having an NPU in my computer?

gl.tpu-npu.how.en: GPUs are general-purpose parallel processors suited to many different computations. TPUs and NPUs are designed specifically to perform large matrix multiplications, the core operation of AI, with less energy. Google uses TPUs in its own data centers to train and run its models and also rents them to cloud customers. NPUs are built into phone and laptop processors.

gl.tpu-npu.why.en: Because demand for AI chips has increased dependence on Nvidia's GPUs, big tech companies are developing their own chips. NPUs allow AI to run on the device itself, without an internet connection and more privately.

gl.transfer-ogrenme.def: Reusing the knowledge a model gained on one task for a related task, so that work on the new problem starts from an existing foundation rather than from scratch.
gl.transfer-ogrenme.example: A hospital can take a model trained on general image datasets and adapt it with only a few thousand X-rays to build a system that flags abnormalities in chest scans.
gl.transfer-ogrenme.faq.0.a: Fine-tuning is a common way of doing transfer learning: the weights of a pretrained model are updated with new data. Transfer learning is the broader idea and covers any way of carrying knowledge over to another task.
gl.transfer-ogrenme.faq.0.q: What is the difference between transfer learning and fine-tuning?
gl.transfer-ogrenme.faq.1.a: No. If the source and target tasks are very different, the transferred knowledge may not help and can even make results worse.
gl.transfer-ogrenme.how: A model is first trained on a broad dataset, for example learning to recognize objects from millions of images. Its weights are then used as the starting point for a new task. Either only the last layers are trained on the new data, or the whole model is fine-tuned with small updates. Because the lower layers already know general features such as edges, textures or language patterns, the new task needs far less data. Someone who plays piano picking up the organ faster is a fair analogy.
gl.transfer-ogrenme.why: Many organizations lack the data or computing power to train a large model from nothing. Transfer learning lets them adapt ready-made models to specialized jobs with little data and at low cost. The common practice of fine-tuning pretrained models today is a direct result of this approach.

gl.transformer.def.en: A neural network architecture introduced in 2017 that uses an "attention" mechanism to evaluate the relationships among all the words in a text at once. Nearly all large language models are based on this architecture.

gl.transformer.example.en: Models such as ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini and Llama all use different variants of the transformer architecture; the architecture has also become widespread in image and audio models.

gl.transformer.faq.0.a.en: GPT is the abbreviation of generative pre-trained transformer; the T stands for the transformer architecture.

gl.transformer.faq.0.q.en: What does the T in GPT stand for?

gl.transformer.faq.1.a.en: It is the method that calculates how much importance a model should give to which other words in the text while processing a given word. It forms the basis of understanding context.

gl.transformer.how.en: The transformer uses the "attention" mechanism to calculate how related each word in a sentence is to every other word. This lets it determine the meaning of a word like "bank" in a sentence such as "He sat on the bank" by looking at the surrounding words. Unlike older methods, it processes text in parallel rather than word by word in sequence, which allows very large models to be trained efficiently on GPUs.

gl.transformer.why.en: Introduced in the 2017 paper "Attention Is All You Need" by Google researchers, this architecture forms the foundation of today's large language models. The "T" in GPT also comes from transformer.

gl.turing-testi.def.en: A thought experiment proposed by Alan Turing in 1950 that measures whether a machine can behave so much like a human in written conversation that it cannot be told apart from one.

gl.turing-testi.example.en: A user being unable to tell whether the party they are chatting with in customer service is a human or a bot is an everyday reflection of the Turing test.

gl.turing-testi.faq.0.a.en: Some studies have reported that current language models can convince a significant share of participants that they are human in short conversations. However, results depend on how the test is set up, and the test's value for measuring intelligence is disputed.

gl.turing-testi.faq.0.q.en: Has ChatGPT passed the Turing test?

gl.turing-testi.faq.1.a.en: He was a British mathematician and one of the founders of computer science. He proposed the Turing test in his 1950 paper "Computing Machinery and Intelligence."

gl.turing-testi.how.en: In the test, an evaluator converses in writing only with two parties, one human and one machine, and tries to work out which is the machine. If the evaluator cannot reliably tell the machine apart, the machine is considered to have passed. Turing proposed this as a measurable question to replace "Can machines think?"

gl.turing-testi.why.en: It is one of the best-known benchmarks in artificial intelligence. As today's language models can write in a human-like way, the meaning of the test is being debated again: many researchers argue that being able to imitate a human does not show real intelligence or understanding.

gl.turkce-benchmark-ve-veri-setleri.def: Test sets and text collections built to measure and train language models in Turkish. Turkish has an agglutinative structure and relatively fewer online resources than English, so it is a distinct area of interest.
gl.turkce-benchmark-ve-veri-setleri.exam: When choosing a chatbot for customer service, a Turkish bank might compare candidates by their results on Turkish question-answering and inference tests rather than by their English scores.
A translated test may read unnaturally and cover topics that do not fit a Turkish context. Tests written natively in Turkish better reflect everyday language and local knowledge.
What is the difference between a translated test and a native Turkish test?
No. A score only shows the skills the test measures, and the model may have seen the test data during training. It is still worth trying a model on the real use case.
Is a model with a high benchmark score good at everything?
gl.turkce-benchmark-ve-veri-setleri.how: A benchmark is a fixed test that gives a model questions or tasks and compares its answers with the correct ones. For Turkish, some tests are written from scratch in Turkish, while others come from translating English tests or from the Turkish portions of multilingual tests such as XNLI. On the training side, Turkish corpora are drawn from sources such as web crawls, Wikipedia, and news text. Translated tests can introduce linguistic and cultural distortions, so quality control matters.
gl.turkce-benchmark-ve-veri-setleri.why: Strong performance in English does not carry over to Turkish automatically. Turkish is agglutinative, and there is far less Turkish content online than English content. Without local tests, it is hard to know how useful a model really is in Turkish. Public institutions, companies, and startups need these measurements when choosing a model.
gl.uc-bilisim.def: An approach in which data is processed on devices or local servers close to where it is produced, rather than being sent to a distant data center.
gl.uc-bilisim.example: A voice recognition feature on a phone can run on the device's own processor without sending the recording to a server.
gl.uc-bilisim.faq.0.a: No, the two complement each other. Training large models and heavy storage stay in the cloud, while instant decisions are made at the edge.
gl.uc-bilisim.faq.0.q: Does edge computing replace cloud computing?
gl.uc-bilisim.faq.1.a: Shrunken models can run on devices such as phones and laptops. The largest models need heavy hardware, so they usually run in the cloud.
gl.uc-bilisim.faq.1.q: Can large language models run on edge devices?
gl.uc-bilisim.how: In edge computing, processing happens at points near the data, such as a phone, a camera, a vehicle or a small server on a factory floor. Because data does not have to travel to the cloud, latency drops and network traffic eases. In AI, a small model trained earlier in the cloud is placed on the device, and the device runs inference locally. The cloud and the edge often work together: heavy training happens in the cloud, and fast decisions happen at the edge.
gl.uc-bilisim.why: In areas where delay is critical, such as self-driving cars, industrial cameras or medical devices, edge computing can be necessary. Keeping data on the device can also offer a privacy advantage. Small AI models that run on-device come up often in the news for this reason.
gl.ulusal-yapay-zeka-stratejisi.def: An official roadmap, usually published by a government, describing how a country intends to develop and govern AI across research, the economy, education and public services.
gl.ulusal-yapay-zeka-stratejisi.example: A country's strategy might aim to raise the number of graduate scholarships in AI, launch pilot projects in healthcare and set ethical principles for public agencies.
gl.ulusal-yapay-zeka-stratejisi.faq.0.a: No. It is a policy document that sets out a government's goals and priorities. It carries no direct penalties; regulation is done separately through legislation.
gl.ulusal-yapay-zeka-stratejisi.faq.0.q: Is a national AI strategy a law?
gl.ulusal-yapay-zeka-stratejisi.faq.1.a: Yes, Turkey has an official national AI strategy document. For its current goals and implementation status, the relevant institutions' official announcements are the best source.
gl.ulusal-yapay-zeka-stratejisi.faq.1.q: Does Turkey have an AI strategy too?
gl.ulusal-yapay-zeka-stratejisi.how: Governments typically prepare a strategy by consulting experts, universities and industry representatives. The document usually covers talent development, research funding, data and computing infrastructure, use in the public sector, ethics and regulation. Goals and responsible agencies are named, and some countries back the plan with an action plan and a budget. A strategy is not a binding law but a statement of policy direction. How much it achieves depends on the resources assigned and on follow-up mechanisms.
gl.ulusal-yapay-zeka-stratejisi.why: A strategy shows which areas a country wants to benefit from AI and where it plans to direct resources. Because it influences investment, education and regulatory decisions, it is a useful signal for companies and researchers. It also helps explain how competition between countries over AI gets framed in the news.
gl.unicorn.def: A privately held startup valued at more than one billion dollars; the name comes from the mythical creature because companies reaching that size were once very rare.
gl.unicorn.example: An AI lab that started with little revenue or no product yet raises a new round at a valuation above one billion dollars and is declared a unicorn.
gl.unicorn.faq.0.a: A unicorn is a private startup valued at over one billion dollars. A decacorn is a less common label for one valued at over ten billion dollars.
gl.unicorn.faq.0.q: What is the difference between a unicorn and a decacorn?
gl.unicorn.faq.1.a: No. A valuation reflects investor expectations, and many unicorns still operate at a loss.
gl.unicorn.faq.1.q: Does being a unicorn mean the company is profitable?
gl.unicorn.how: The valuation comes from the price investors put on the company's shares in its latest funding round, not from the cash in its bank account. When a startup crosses the one-billion-dollar line, it is called a unicorn. Companies valued above ten billion dollars are sometimes called decacorns. The term was popularized by investor Aileen Lee in 2013. Publicly listed companies do not count; to be a unicorn a company has to be private.
gl.unicorn.why: AI startups becoming unicorns in a short time shows how much money is flowing into the sector. But a valuation is an estimate, and being a unicorn does not mean a company is profitable or sustainable. When reading the news, it helps to remember the figure reflects market expectations.
gl.uretim-sureci.def: The name for the generation of manufacturing technology used to make a chip. Traditionally given in nanometers, a smaller number generally means a more advanced process and a denser packing of transistors.
gl.uretim-sureci.example: When a chipmaker announces that its new model is built on a more advanced process than the previous generation, it is signaling that it fits more transistors into the same area and aims for higher performance at lower energy.
gl.uretim-sureci.faq.0.a: A nanometer is one billionth of a meter; a human hair is tens of thousands of times thicker. Even so, the nanometer names used in chipmaking today no longer point directly to the size of any one transistor.
gl.uretim-sureci.faq.1.a: It usually means higher density and efficiency, but cost rises too. Since naming differs between manufacturers, the numbers from different companies cannot be compared directly.
gl.uretim-sureci.faq.1.q: Does a smaller nanometer number always mean a better chip?
gl.uretim-sureci.how: Each new process generation allows transistors to be packed more closely, so more of them fit in the same area, which can improve speed and energy efficiency. The nanometer figure once corresponded to an actual transistor dimension; today it is largely a generation label, and processes from different makers carrying the same number may not be equivalent. A real comparison looks at measures such as transistor density. Advanced generations require new transistor structures and extreme ultraviolet (EUV) lithography machines.
gl.uretim-sureci.why: A chip's speed, power consumption, and cost depend heavily on the process it is made with. For AI chips, access to more advanced processes is a competitive advantage. Export restrictions and the investment race also center on these leading-edge processes.
gl.uretken-motor-optimizasyonu.def: The set of practices aimed at making content more likely to be cited, featured and described accurately in answers produced by AI-powered search and chat systems.
gl.uretken-motor-optimizasyonu.example: A courier company publishes a help page with short, clear, sourced answers to common questions, hoping to raise the chance of being cited in AI search results.
gl.uretken-motor-optimizasyonu.faq.0.a: No, though they are related. SEO targets a page's position in search results; GEO targets being cited in AI-generated answers. Good, trustworthy content helps in both.
gl.uretken-motor-optimizasyonu.faq.0.q: Is GEO the same as SEO?
gl.uretken-motor-optimizasyonu.faq.1.a: No. How models choose sources is not fully known and changes over time. GEO tries to raise the odds; it cannot promise an outcome.
gl.uretken-motor-optimizasyonu.faq.1.q: Can GEO guarantee a place in AI answers?
gl.uretken-motor-optimizasyonu.how: Classic search engine optimization (SEO) tries to lift a page in a list of results; GEO tries to get a page used as a source in a model's answer. In practice, people test things like clear and verifiable facts, descriptive headings, citations to reliable sources, structured data, and consistent mentions of a brand across many sites. Because these systems are not transparent and change often, the effect cannot be measured precisely, and much of the advice rests on experiments and observation.
gl.uretken-motor-optimizasyonu.why: As users get answers directly from AI, visibility for brands and publishers moves to a new arena, which is why GEO draws so much attention in marketing and media. But no method is guaranteed, and there are ethical and trust debates about attempts to manipulate models.

gl.uretken-yapay-zeka.def.en: AI that can produce new text, images, audio, video or code based on the examples it has learned from. ChatGPT and image-generating models fall into this category.

gl.uretken-yapay-zeka.example.en: A chat assistant that writes an email, a tool that creates a poster image from a single sentence and models that produce video from a short text are examples of generative AI.
