gl.uretken-yapay-zeka.faq.0.a.en: Classical systems generally classify or predict (is this email spam?). Generative AI, on the other hand, creates new content (write a reply to this email).

gl.uretken-yapay-zeka.faq.0.q.en: What is the difference between generative AI and classical AI?

gl.uretken-yapay-zeka.faq.1.a.en: No. Models can produce fluent but incorrect information (hallucination). Important information should always be verified against a reliable source.

gl.uretken-yapay-zeka.faq.1.q.en: Is content produced by generative AI always accurate?

gl.uretken-yapay-zeka.how.en: Generative models learn patterns in their training data and produce new content that fits those patterns. Language models generate text by predicting the most likely next word in a passage; image models typically start from noise and build a meaningful picture step by step. The user describes what they want with a prompt.

gl.uretken-yapay-zeka.why.en: It cuts creative work that only humans could do before, such as writing, design, coding, music and video, down to minutes. While this boosts productivity, it also raises new debates over copyright, fake content and the effects on professions.

gl.uzman-sistem.def: A computer program that stores a human expert's knowledge as rules and uses it to answer questions or recommend decisions in a specific field. Expert systems became widespread in the 1970s and 1980s.
gl.uzman-sistem.example: MYCIN, developed at Stanford University in the 1970s, was a well-known research prototype that used a set of rules to suggest which antibiotic to give for blood infections.
gl.uzman-sistem.faq.0.a: In an expert system, people write the rules; in machine learning, the model learns from examples. That makes expert systems easy to trace but laborious to keep up to date.
gl.uzman-sistem.faq.0.q: What is the difference between an expert system and machine learning?
gl.uzman-sistem.faq.1.a: They are less often called by that name, but rule-based decision support and automation software is still used at many organizations.
gl.uzman-sistem.how: An expert system has three main parts: a knowledge base that holds the rules, an inference engine that chains those rules together to reach a conclusion, and an interface for talking to the user. Knowledge engineers interview the expert and write rules like “if this symptom is present, this diagnosis becomes more likely”. As the user answers questions, the engine fires the relevant rules in sequence and produces a recommendation. It can often also show which rules led to that result.
gl.uzman-sistem.why: Expert systems were among the first serious commercial uses of AI and drew heavy corporate investment in the 1980s. But the difficulty of keeping the rules up to date and their brittleness in unforeseen situations contributed to disappointed expectations and, eventually, an AI winter. They can be seen as ancestors of today's rule-based decision software.

gl.uzmanlar-karisimi.def.en: An architecture in which a model consists of many sub-networks (experts) and only a few of them run for each input. It makes it possible to run large models at lower compute cost.

gl.uzmanlar-karisimi.example.en: A model with 600 billion total parameters, of which about 30 billion run for each token, is an example of a mixture-of-experts architecture.

gl.uzmanlar-karisimi.faq.0.a.en: It is the number of parameters actually used when processing a token in mixture-of-experts models. Speed and compute cost depend largely on active parameters.

gl.uzmanlar-karisimi.faq.1.a.en: No. Generally, all experts need to be kept ready in memory. The savings come not from memory but from the amount of computation performed at each step.

gl.uzmanlar-karisimi.faq.1.q.en: Do MoE models use less memory?

gl.uzmanlar-karisimi.how.en: In a mixture-of-experts model, some of the layers consist of many parallel sub-networks (experts). A router selects only a few of these experts for each token. So even if the model's total parameter count is very large, only a small fraction of them runs at each step.

gl.uzmanlar-karisimi.why.en: It makes it possible to build models that carry more knowledge at lower compute cost. Many current open-weight models use this architecture, which is why model cards distinguish between "total parameters" and "active parameters."

gl.uzun-baglam-testi.def: A test that checks whether a model can find a single piece of information placed inside a long text. It aims to show how reliably a model recalls information across its large context window.
gl.uzun-baglam-testi.example: An unrelated sentence like 'The meeting will be held on Tuesday' is hidden in a report hundreds of pages long, and the model is asked when the meeting will take place.
gl.uzun-baglam-testi.faq.0.a: No, it only shows that the model can locate a fact. Tasks like combining several facts or summarizing are harder and are measured with separate tests.
gl.uzun-baglam-testi.faq.0.q: Does this test prove a model understands a long document?
gl.uzun-baglam-testi.faq.1.a: It refers to the idiom about the difficulty of finding something small in a large pile. The haystack is the long text and the needle is the hidden fact.
gl.uzun-baglam-testi.faq.1.q: Why is it called 'needle in a haystack'?
gl.uzun-baglam-testi.how: The setup starts with a very long text, usually unrelated to the question, which is the haystack. A small piece of information, such as a single sentence, is inserted at a chosen spot; this is the needle. The model is then asked a question about that information. The test is repeated while changing the needle's position and the text's length, and the results are often shown as a heat map. This reveals at which lengths and positions the model tends to miss the information.
gl.uzun-baglam-testi.why: A large context window does not mean the model uses everything inside it well. The test offers a basic reliability signal for applications that work with long documents, such as contracts or code repositories. Still, finding one fact is a relatively easy task and does not measure complex reasoning.
gl.uzun-baglam.def: The ability of an AI model to take in a very large amount of text at once, meaning a large context window. Long documents, code repositories or hours-long conversations can be given to the model together.
gl.uzun-baglam.example: A lawyer can upload a several-hundred-page contract in one go and ask the model to find conflicting clauses, without splitting it into parts, because the model has a long context.
gl.uzun-baglam.faq.0.a: No. The context window is the text the model can see in the current conversation, and the model usually does not keep it on its own once the session ends. Persistent memory is a separate feature.
gl.uzun-baglam.faq.0.q: Is a context window the same as memory?
gl.uzun-baglam.faq.1.a: Not always. Cost and latency go up, and accuracy can drop on very long inputs. Sometimes selecting only the relevant section gives better results.
gl.uzun-baglam.faq.1.q: Is a bigger context window always better?
gl.uzun-baglam.how: Language models split text into small pieces called tokens and produce each answer by looking at the tokens in front of them. The context window sets the upper limit on how many of these pieces the model can see. As the window grows, a model can read a whole book, a long contract or a large software project from start to finish. However, longer inputs cost more to process and take longer, and the model may sometimes overlook details buried in the middle of a very long text.
gl.uzun-baglam.why: Long context widens the range of work AI can do, such as scanning legal documents, understanding large codebases or summarizing lengthy reports. Window size often features in model announcements, but a big window does not mean the model uses every piece of information correctly. For users, the real question is how reliably a model handles long input.
gl.uzun-kisa-sureli-bellek.def: A type of recurrent neural network equipped with gate mechanisms that let it hold on to information for a long time. It was proposed in 1997 by Sepp Hochreiter and Jürgen Schmidhuber.
gl.uzun-kisa-sureli-bellek.example: In a long sentence, remembering whether the subject at the start was singular or plural until the verb at the end is the kind of problem the LSTM's gates were designed to handle.
gl.uzun-kisa-sureli-bellek.faq.0.a: An LSTM is a type of RNN; the difference is its gates and cell state. These let it carry information over long distances better than a plain RNN.
gl.uzun-kisa-sureli-bellek.faq.0.q: What is the difference between an LSTM and an RNN?
gl.uzun-kisa-sureli-bellek.faq.1.a: The name refers to the fact that the short-term memory, meaning the hidden state, can be preserved for a long time. Although it is short-term memory, the gates let it persist across many steps.
gl.uzun-kisa-sureli-bellek.how: An LSTM cell carries a cell state in addition to the hidden state of a standard RNN; this works like a conveyor line along which information can flow through many steps almost unchanged. Gates control what enters the cell, what leaves it and what old information is forgotten. Based on the current input, the gates decide what to keep, what to erase and what to pass on. This design reduces how much the error signal vanishes as it travels back through time, making long-range dependencies easier to learn.
gl.uzun-kisa-sureli-bellek.why: LSTM was one of the core building blocks of the period when deep learning made its mark in speech recognition and machine translation. It stopped being the leading choice once Transformers took over, but its ideas about memory and gating continue to influence later architectures.
gl.uzun-ufuklu-gorevler.def: Tasks that cannot be finished in a single response and need many steps, tool uses and a long stretch of time. They require an AI agent to keep a plan going until the goal is reached and to change course based on intermediate results.
gl.uzun-ufuklu-gorevler.example: When a software agent is told to find a bug in a project, fix it, run the relevant tests and report back, it goes through dozens of steps of reading, editing and trying files.
gl.uzun-ufuklu-gorevler.faq.0.a: Errors accumulate step by step, context information can overflow, and the goal can get lost along the way. A small mistake in a short question is easy to spot, but in a long chain it can surface later and spoil the whole job.
gl.uzun-ufuklu-gorevler.faq.0.q: Why are long-horizon tasks hard for AI?
gl.uzun-ufuklu-gorevler.faq.1.a: Not by itself. A larger window helps the model hold more information, but it also needs to keep to a plan, recover from errors and choose the right tools.
gl.uzun-ufuklu-gorevler.faq.1.q: Does a longer context window solve this?
gl.uzun-ufuklu-gorevler.how: Such a task is usually broken into sub-steps. At each step the model decides what to do, calls a tool, reads the result and updates its plan. Because every step carries a small chance of error, mistakes pile up as the number of steps grows. The context window can also fill up, and the model may lose sight of the original goal. To cope, systems use note-taking, memory writes, checkpoints and splitting the job among sub-agents.
gl.uzun-ufuklu-gorevler.why: Models can be impressive at short question-and-answer exchanges, yet most real work takes many steps over hours. Whether agents are actually useful depends largely on their reliability here. That is why the ability to stay consistent on long tasks comes up so often when model capability is discussed in the news.
gl.varlik-adi-tanima.def: A natural language processing task that finds proper names and specific items in text, such as people, organizations, places, dates and amounts of money, and labels each one by type.
gl.varlik-adi-tanima.example: In the sentence 'Ayşe Yılmaz visited Ege University in İzmir in March,' the system marks Ayşe Yılmaz as a person, March as a date, İzmir as a place and Ege University as an organization.
gl.varlik-adi-tanima.faq.0.a: No. Keyword extraction picks out the important words in a text, while named entity recognition also assigns a type, such as person, place or organization, to each expression it finds.
gl.varlik-adi-tanima.faq.0.q: Is named entity recognition the same as keyword extraction?
gl.varlik-adi-tanima.faq.1.a: It is common in scanning news and archives, reviewing contracts and case files, and hiding personal details in patient records or customer messages.
gl.varlik-adi-tanima.faq.1.q: Where is named entity recognition used?
gl.varlik-adi-tanima.how: The model splits the text into small pieces and predicts a label for each: person, organization, location or none. Context is decisive here, since a sentence shows whether 'Apple' means the fruit or the company. Training uses text that people have labeled by hand. Today, pretrained language models are usually fine-tuned for the job, and large language models can also do it when given the right prompt. The output lists each expression with its position in the text and its type. Turkish word endings, as in 'Ankara'dan' (from Ankara), make the task harder.
gl.varlik-adi-tanima.why: It is one of the basic steps for pulling structured information out of news archives, legal documents and medical records. It is used in search engines, knowledge graphs and automatic masking of personal data. It helps AI systems turn plain text into usable data.
gl.varolussal-risk.def: The risk of a catastrophe that could cause human extinction or permanently and drastically limit humanity's future. In AI, it refers to scenarios where very advanced systems escape human control or are misused on a massive scale.
gl.varolussal-risk.example: In 2023, many prominent figures, including leading AI researchers, signed a short statement saying that reducing the risk of extinction from AI should be a global priority alongside other societal-scale risks such as pandemics and nuclear war.
gl.varolussal-risk.faq.0.a: No. Discrimination, misinformation and privacy violations are harms happening now. Existential risk concerns more advanced systems and scenarios that are uncertain in likelihood but potentially catastrophic. The two topics are not mutually exclusive.
gl.varolussal-risk.faq.0.q: Is existential risk the same as the harms AI causes today?
gl.varolussal-risk.faq.1.a: No. It rests on reasoning from current trends and scenario analysis, not on direct measurement. Experts disagree substantially about both how likely it is and how urgent it is.
gl.varolussal-risk.faq.1.q: Has existential risk from AI been scientifically proven?
gl.varolussal-risk.how: The concept deals with outcomes that cannot be undone, not ordinary product failures. One scenario discussed is a system more capable than humans whose goals do not match human values and which resists being shut down. Another is the misuse of powerful models for harmful purposes, such as helping develop biological weapons. Researchers disagree sharply on how likely these scenarios are. Some consider the risk real and urgent, while others call it speculative and argue it distracts from concrete harms happening today.
gl.varolussal-risk.why: The term appears often in AI companies' safety commitments, in government debates over regulation and in open letters from experts. It raises the question of how much effort a risk deserves when its probability may be low but its consequences would be extreme. It is also part of the debate over how to balance this against present-day problems such as discrimination, misinformation and job loss.
gl.varyasyonel-otomatik-kodlayici.def: A kind of autoencoder that compresses data into a probability distribution in latent space rather than a single point, so that sampling from that space produces new data.
gl.varyasyonel-otomatik-kodlayici.exampl: In a VAE trained on handwritten digits, moving through latent space from the point for “3” toward the point for “8” produces images in which the digit gradually changes shape.
A plain autoencoder squeezes each input into one point and is not well suited to generating new samples. A VAE learns a distribution, so picking a random point in its latent space gives meaningful new samples.
How does a VAE differ from a plain autoencoder?
Training minimizes the average reconstruction error, so the model drifts toward an averaged image instead of sharp details. This is most visible in images, which come out soft.
Why are VAE outputs often blurry?
gl.varyasyonel-otomatik-kodlayici.how: The encoder maps an input not to a single point but to a region of latent space described by a mean and a spread. A random point is drawn from that region, and the decoder tries to rebuild the input from it. Training asks for two things at once: the reconstruction should resemble the original, and the latent space should stay smooth and well organized. Because of that smoothness, moving between two points yields meaningful in-between samples.
gl.varyasyonel-otomatik-kodlayici.why: VAEs are an established and stable family of generative models. They are easier to train than GANs, though their outputs tend to be blurrier. Many modern image generation systems use a VAE-like component to compress images into a compact latent representation.

gl.vektor-veritabani.def.en: A database that stores embedding vectors and makes it possible to quickly find the content most similar in meaning. It is used in document search and RAG systems.

gl.vektor-veritabani.example.en: A law firm can load thousands of contracts into a vector database and quickly find relevant documents with queries such as "lease agreements with a termination clause."

gl.vektor-veritabani.faq.0.a.en: Regular databases search by exact match or specific values. Vector databases calculate the proximity between vectors to find content that is similar in meaning.

gl.vektor-veritabani.faq.0.q.en: What is the difference between a vector database and a regular database?

gl.vektor-veritabani.faq.1.a.en: No. If there are only a few documents, all of them can be given directly to the model. For large, constantly updated document archives, a vector database is more efficient.

gl.vektor-veritabani.faq.1.q.en: Is a vector database necessary for every AI project?

gl.vektor-veritabani.how.en: Documents are first split into chunks, and each chunk is converted into a vector by an embedding model. The vector database stores these vectors. When a user asks a question, the question is also converted into a vector, and the database finds the document chunks closest in meaning within milliseconds. The retrieved chunks are then given to the language model as context.

gl.vektor-veritabani.why.en: It is a core building block for companies to build AI assistants that give current, accurate answers based on their own documents. It makes it possible to add new information without retraining the model.

gl.veri-artirma.def: A way of expanding a training set by transforming existing data or generating new examples from it. The goal is to let a model see more varied examples without collecting new data.
gl.veri-artirma.example: For a model that reads handwritten digits, each digit image is slightly tilted and shifted to make several variants, so the model gets used to different handwriting styles.
gl.veri-artirma.faq.0.a: No, though the line is blurry. Augmentation modifies existing examples, while synthetic data is usually generated from scratch by a model or a simulation.
gl.veri-artirma.faq.0.q: Is data augmentation the same as synthetic data?
gl.veri-artirma.faq.1.a: No. Transformations that corrupt the label cause harm; flipping a 6 can make it look like a 9, for example. The transformations need to fit the task.
gl.veri-artirma.how: With images, small changes such as rotating, flipping, cropping and adjusting brightness are applied. With text, some words are swapped for synonyms, or a sentence is translated into another language and back. With audio, noise is added or the speed is changed. The key rule is that the change must not break the label: a rotated photo of a cat is still a cat. Sometimes generative models create entirely new examples as well. The model sees the same content in different forms, so it does not get stuck on one appearance.
gl.veri-artirma.why: Collecting and labeling data is expensive, and augmentation eases that burden. In fields with few examples, such as medical imaging, it helps keep a model from overfitting, meaning memorizing its training data. Poorly chosen transformations can still hurt by showing the model unrealistic examples.
gl.veri-bilimi.def: A discipline that combines statistics, programming and domain knowledge to draw meaning and value from data. Its aim is to turn data into information that helps people make decisions.
gl.veri-bilimi.example: A telecom operator builds a model that predicts which subscribers are likely to cancel their line, then offers those customers special deals.
gl.veri-bilimi.faq.0.a: A data scientist usually does analysis, experiments and modeling. A machine learning engineer focuses on moving models into products and running them at scale. Roles vary from company to company.
gl.veri-bilimi.faq.0.q: What is the difference between a data scientist and a machine learning engineer?
gl.veri-bilimi.faq.1.a: The two fields overlap, but neither is a subset of the other. Data science focuses on extracting knowledge from data, while AI focuses on building systems that show intelligent behavior. Machine learning is a tool they share.
gl.veri-bilimi.faq.1.q: Is data science a part of artificial intelligence?
gl.veri-bilimi.how: Work begins by defining a problem. The relevant data is then collected, cleaned and examined through exploratory analysis. Next, statistical or machine learning models are built and evaluated, and the results are presented to decision makers through charts and reports. If a model proves useful, it is built into a product or process. Python and SQL are common tools. In organizations, data scientists, data engineers and analysts usually work on this together.
gl.veri-bilimi.why: It lets organizations base decisions on evidence instead of intuition and gives AI projects a solid footing. Machine learning is an important tool of data science, but data science also covers defining the problem, data quality and interpreting results. That is why it has become one of the most sought-after skill areas in business.
gl.veri-duvari.def: The idea that the supply of high-quality training data, especially human-written text, is limited, so the growth of AI models could stall at some point.
gl.veri-duvari.example: If a company has already trained on books, news archives and scientific papers, it may struggle to find enough new text of comparable quality to scale its next model.
gl.veri-duvari.faq.0.a: Opinions differ. Some argue that high-quality human-written data is approaching exhaustion, while others believe synthetic data and new data types can get around the limit.
gl.veri-duvari.faq.0.q: Does the data wall really exist?
gl.veri-duvari.faq.1.a: It may help in part, but there is no guarantee. If generated data is low in quality or variety, a model can reinforce its own mistakes and drift away from the real world.
gl.veri-duvari.faq.1.q: Can synthetic data solve the data wall?
gl.veri-duvari.how: Large language models generally tend to improve as they are trained on more data. But the amount of original, high-quality text on the internet is finite, and once duplicates, spam and low-quality content are filtered out, the usable share shrinks further. As the data appetite of models grows, the stock is said to be getting close to exhausted. Proposed ways around it include synthetic data generated by models, other data types such as images and audio, private data deals and training methods that use data more efficiently.
gl.veri-duvari.why: The data wall sits at the center of the debate over whether AI progress can continue through bigger models and more computing power alone. It also helps explain why companies seek content deals with publishers and data owners. Some researchers see the problem as serious, while others think it can be overcome.
gl.veri-etiketleme.def: The work of adding correct answers or descriptions to raw data such as images, text or audio so that a model can learn from it. Labels show the model what to look at and what it should learn.
gl.veri-etiketleme.example: A team building a self-driving system has people mark pedestrians, traffic lights and lane lines in camera footage one by one to prepare examples the model can learn from.
gl.veri-etiketleme.faq.0.a: Yes, some methods learn from unlabeled data, as in the first training stage of language models. Even so, labeled data remains important for improving a model on specific tasks.
gl.veri-etiketleme.faq.0.q: Can a model be trained without labeling?
gl.veri-etiketleme.faq.1.a: Partly. Models can suggest first-pass labels, but human review is usually still needed for quality control and for difficult examples.
gl.veri-etiketleme.faq.1.q: Can AI do the labeling itself?
gl.veri-etiketleme.how: Labelers, mostly people and sometimes people working alongside helper models, mark examples one by one. A box is drawn around an object in a photo, a review is classified as positive or negative, an audio recording is transcribed. For consistency, detailed guidelines are written and the same example is often labeled by several people so differences can be checked. For language models, people also contribute by ranking the model's responses according to quality.
gl.veri-etiketleme.why: The quality of labels directly affects how well a model performs. Wrong or careless labels lead to wrong learning. The pay and working conditions of the people who do this work are also part of the debate around the AI industry, while companies try to automate labeling in part.
gl.veri-kaymasi.def: A gradual change in the statistical properties of the data a model sees in use, so that it differs from the data the model was trained on.
gl.veri-kaymasi.example: A model that reads chest scans in a hospital may face images with different characteristics when the hospital switches to a new brand of scanner, so it ends up working on a distribution it has not seen before.
gl.veri-kaymasi.faq.0.a: No. In data drift, the distribution of the inputs changes. In concept drift, the relationship between the inputs and the correct answer changes, for example when what counts as spam shifts over time.
gl.veri-kaymasi.faq.0.q: Is data drift the same as concept drift?
gl.veri-kaymasi.faq.1.a: The distribution of live inputs is compared with the training data at regular intervals. If the difference passes a preset threshold, an alert is sent to the team.
gl.veri-kaymasi.how: Training data is like a snapshot of the world the model learned from. Once the model is live, incoming inputs can stop resembling that snapshot: a new camera model, a different customer base or newly emerging words are all examples. Teams measure the gap with statistical tests and monitoring dashboards that compare the distribution of live inputs with that of the training data. If the gap grows, the data is refreshed and the model is retrained. Drift does not necessarily mean accuracy has dropped, but it is a warning sign.
gl.veri-kaymasi.why: Because true labels often arrive late, noticing a change in inputs gives an early warning before a drop in performance can be measured. This makes data drift one of the core monitoring concerns for keeping AI systems reliable after deployment.
gl.veri-kurasyonu.def: The process of collecting, cleaning, filtering, labeling, and balancing the data used to train a model. The goal is to turn a raw pile of data into a high-quality, consistent training set that fits its purpose.
gl.veri-kurasyonu.example: A company takes billions of web pages, removes duplicates, spam, and pages containing personal information, then blends the remaining text by topic balance to train a language model.
gl.veri-kurasyonu.faq.0.a: No. Cleaning covers fixing errors and removing duplicates, while curation also includes broader decisions such as source selection, filtering, labeling, and mixing proportions.
gl.veri-kurasyonu.faq.0.q: Is data cleaning the same as data curation?
gl.veri-kurasyonu.faq.1.a: No. Adding more low-quality data may not improve performance and can even hurt it. Smaller, carefully selected sets can often give better results.
gl.veri-kurasyonu.faq.1.q: Does more data always mean a better model?
gl.veri-kurasyonu.how: The process usually starts with choosing sources. Duplicate content is then removed, broken, low-quality, or harmful text is filtered out, and personal information is scrubbed. If needed, people or automated systems label and rate the examples. Finally, the mix of topics, languages, and genres is adjusted. It works a bit like a librarian who cares less about how many books there are than about having the right books on the shelves. The resulting set largely determines what the model will learn.
gl.veri-kurasyonu.why: The performance of models with the same architecture often depends on data quality, which is why companies invest heavily in curation. Debates over bias, copyright, and privacy also largely come down to decisions made at this stage. The principle of 'garbage in, garbage out' applies fully here.
gl.veri-lisans-anlasmasi.def: A contract, usually paid, in which a content or data owner permits an AI company to use its data for model training or in products under agreed terms.
gl.veri-lisans-anlasmasi.example: The Associated Press was reported in 2023 to have agreed with OpenAI to license part of its news archive. Other publishers and platforms have made similar deals.
gl.veri-lisans-anlasmasi.faq.0.a: Largely, for the uses the license covers. Risk remains for any data not included in the agreement.
gl.veri-lisans-anlasmasi.faq.0.q: Does a licensing deal remove a company's copyright lawsuit risk?
gl.veri-lisans-anlasmasi.faq.1.a: No. Some involve fees, while others may offer technology access, visibility or joint products in return. The terms are often not disclosed.
gl.veri-lisans-anlasmasi.faq.1.q: Do these deals always involve money?
gl.veri-lisans-anlasmasi.how: The parties set out in the contract which content may be used, for what purpose and for how long. The scope varies: it may cover training only, or also displaying content and giving credit inside a product. Payment can be a fixed fee, a usage-based fee or some other form of return. The AI company avoids legal uncertainty, and the content owner earns income from its data. Most terms are not made public.
gl.veri-lisans-anlasmasi.why: These deals show that a data market is forming in the AI industry while copyright lawsuits are still unresolved. They are a new revenue source for media and platform companies and a more dependable, up-to-date supply of data for AI companies. Whether smaller publishers can get a seat at the table is debated.
gl.veri-madenciligi.def: The process of discovering hidden patterns, relationships and unusual records in large data sets using statistics and machine learning methods.
gl.veri-madenciligi.example: A supermarket chain studies its basket records to find which products are often bought together and arranges its shelves accordingly.
gl.veri-madenciligi.faq.0.a: Data mining focuses more on discovering unknown patterns in existing data. Machine learning aims to build models that learn from data and make predictions for new situations. The two share many methods.
gl.veri-madenciligi.faq.0.q: What is the difference between data mining and machine learning?
gl.veri-madenciligi.faq.1.a: No. Data mining is one of the techniques data science uses. Data science is a broader field that stretches from collecting data to presenting results.
gl.veri-madenciligi.faq.1.q: Are data mining and data science the same?
gl.veri-madenciligi.how: Data is first collected, cleaned and made ready for analysis. Then methods such as clustering, classification, association rules and outlier detection are used to search through it. Clustering groups similar records, association rules find which things tend to show up together, and outlier detection catches records that stand apart from what is expected. Experts then interpret the patterns that come out, because not every relationship found is meaningful. The mining metaphor points to digging valuable pieces out of a huge pile.
gl.veri-madenciligi.why: Many business decisions, such as fraud detection, customer segmentation and inventory planning, rest on data mining results. Its methods overlap heavily with machine learning. Two points deserve care: a relationship found in data does not necessarily mean causation, and privacy must be respected when working with personal data.
gl.veri-merkezi-su-tuketimi.def: The water consumed directly to cool servers in data centers, plus the water used indirectly at the power plants that supply them with electricity.
gl.veri-merkezi-su-tuketimi.example: A large data center planned in an arid region can spark debate with residents and local authorities over the water it would use for cooling.
gl.veri-merkezi-su-tuketimi.faq.0.a: There is no single figure; it depends on the cooling method, the climate and what the calculation includes. That is why estimates from different sources should be compared with care.
gl.veri-merkezi-su-tuketimi.faq.0.q: How much water does an AI query use?
gl.veri-merkezi-su-tuketimi.faq.1.a: Yes. Options include closed-loop systems, using wastewater or recycled water, and building in cooler climates. Some of these methods can require more electricity.
gl.veri-merkezi-su-tuketimi.faq.1.q: Can data centers reduce their water use?
gl.veri-merkezi-su-tuketimi.how: Running servers get very hot, so data centers must get rid of that heat. In one common method, warm water is evaporated in cooling towers; the evaporated water is lost from the system and replaced with fresh supply. Air cooling or closed-loop liquid cooling can use less water but usually needs more electricity. Water used by the power plants that generate the electricity counts as indirect consumption. Companies calculate figures in different ways, so comparisons can be difficult.
gl.veri-merkezi-su-tuketimi.why: Water is one of the main reasons for local pushback against data center projects, especially in dry regions. As AI services grow, so does cooling demand, and companies announce water efficiency and replenishment goals. Because there is a trade-off between water and electricity, the best solution varies by location.

gl.veri-merkezi.def.en: A facility where thousands of servers and storage and networking equipment operate together. AI models are trained and run on GPUs in these facilities.

gl.veri-merkezi.example.en: A company announcing that it is building a "200 MW AI data center" is a typical infrastructure news item.

gl.veri-merkezi.faq.0.a.en: Thousands of GPUs run at high power at the same time and require intensive cooling. That is why the electricity consumption of large AI data centers is compared to that of small cities.

gl.veri-merkezi.faq.0.q.en: Why do AI data centers consume so much energy?

gl.veri-merkezi.faq.1.a.en: Turkey has a number of data centers, and investment plans for AI infrastructure are being announced; you can follow the latest developments in our Turkey section.

gl.veri-merkezi.faq.1.q.en: Are there AI data centers in Turkey?

gl.veri-merkezi.how.en: Data centers are facilities that house thousands of servers, storage systems and the networking equipment that connects them. AI data centers need very high electrical power and advanced cooling systems to run large numbers of GPUs together. Their capacity is usually expressed in megawatts (MW).

gl.veri-merkezi.why.en: Because AI models are trained and used in data centers, investment in these facilities has reached record levels. Their energy consumption, water use and which countries they are built in are also the subject of major policy debates.

gl.veri-paralelligi.def: A parallelization method in which every accelerator holds a full copy of the model and processes a different slice of the training data at the same time, speeding up training.
gl.veri-paralelligi.example: An image classification model trained on eight GPUs has the same model on every GPU, each looking at a different group of photos; the gradients are averaged and sent back to all of them.
gl.veri-paralelligi.faq.0.a: No. It speeds up training but does not increase model size. Since each chip holds a copy of the model, the model must fit on one chip; otherwise model parallelism or memory-sharding techniques are needed.
gl.veri-paralelligi.faq.0.q: Can data parallelism make a model bigger?
gl.veri-paralelligi.faq.1.a: In data parallelism the model is copied and the data is split. In model parallelism the model itself is divided into parts and placed on different chips.
gl.veri-paralelligi.faq.1.q: What is the difference between data parallelism and model parallelism?
gl.veri-paralelligi.how: Each chip carries an identical copy of the model and works on its own batch of data (a mini-batch). The chips then share the corrections they computed, called gradients, average them and all apply the same update, so the copies stay in sync. Because this happens over a network, communication overhead grows as more chips are added. Techniques such as FSDP and ZeRO reduce the memory burden by sharding training state across chips.
gl.veri-paralelligi.why: It is the simplest and most common form of parallelism, so it is the starting point for most training setups. Adding chips this way is the most direct route to shorter training times. It is not enough on its own when a model does not fit in a single chip's memory, which is where model parallelism comes in.
gl.veri-seti.def: A collection of examples gathered and organized to train, test or evaluate an AI model. It can take the form of text, images, audio or tables.
gl.veri-seti.example: MNIST, made up of images of handwritten digits, is a small, well-known dataset that has long been used to try out image recognition models.
gl.veri-seti.faq.0.a: No. A database is a system for storing and querying data. A dataset is a collection of examples put together for a specific modeling task, often fixed in form.
gl.veri-seti.faq.0.q: Is a dataset the same as a database?
gl.veri-seti.faq.1.a: A model can memorize the examples it saw during training. Measuring it on unseen examples gives a more honest picture of how well it will work in real use.
gl.veri-seti.faq.1.q: Why is test data kept separate from training data?
gl.veri-seti.how: Examples are collected from various sources, cleaned and, where needed, labeled. They are then usually split into three parts: the model learns from the training portion, its settings are tuned on the validation portion, and its performance on examples it has never seen is measured on the test portion. A dataset's value depends not only on its size but on its quality, its diversity and how well it reflects real-world conditions.
gl.veri-seti.why: A model's behavior comes largely from the data it was trained on. Gaps and biases in the dataset carry over into the model. Copyright, personal data and consent are also frequently debated dataset issues in AI news. In short, it is hard to build a good model from bad data.
gl.veri-temizleme.def: The preparation step in which errors, duplicate records, missing values and noise in raw data are found and then fixed or removed. It happens before model training and makes the data trustworthy.
gl.veri-temizleme.example: In a bank's customer table, the same person listed twice with different spellings, or an age column that says 250, would be caught and fixed during cleaning.
gl.veri-temizleme.faq.0.a: Not exactly. Preprocessing is the broader term. Besides cleaning, it includes normalization, scaling and converting data into a form the model can use.
gl.veri-temizleme.faq.0.q: Is data cleaning the same as data preprocessing?
gl.veri-temizleme.faq.1.a: Yes. Deleting real but unusual examples, or records that represent certain groups, can leave the model with an incomplete view of the world and increase bias.
gl.veri-temizleme.faq.1.q: Can cleaning too much cause problems?
gl.veri-temizleme.how: The process usually starts by scanning the data for copied records, badly formatted rows, empty fields and inconsistent values. These are then deleted, corrected or filled in with a reasonable value. With text data, leftover HTML, repeated sentences, unwanted languages and passages containing personal information are also filtered out. Rules, statistical checks and sometimes small classifier models do the work. It resembles washing and trimming vegetables before cooking: the prep decides how the dish turns out.
gl.veri-temizleme.why: A model learns from what it sees, so if the data is wrong, the model learns the errors too. For large language models, training data quality is often seen as just as decisive as model size. Data scientists spend a large share of their time on this work. Removing duplicates and personal data also matters for privacy and for reducing memorization.
gl.veri-yerellestirme.def: A legal or regulatory requirement that certain types of data, especially personal or sensitive data, be stored and processed on servers inside a country's borders.
gl.veri-yerellestirme.example: A bank may have to buy an AI provider's service from a data center inside the country in order to use an AI tool that works on customer data.
gl.veri-yerellestirme.faq.0.a: Transfer rules allow data to leave the country under certain conditions. Localization is built on keeping data inside the country and largely limits it from leaving.
gl.veri-yerellestirme.faq.0.q: How does data localization differ from rules on cross-border transfers?
gl.veri-yerellestirme.faq.1.a: For personal data, Turkey has a transfer regime rather than a general localization rule. Some sectors, such as banking and payment services, have separate rules that call for systems to be kept in the country.
gl.veri-yerellestirme.faq.1.q: Does Turkey have a data localization requirement?
gl.veri-yerellestirme.how: The rule requires data to be kept in a data center within the country. In some places data may only be stored domestically, while in others a copy can go abroad as long as the primary record stays at home. Scope varies by country and sector, and banking, health and government data are the most common targets. Companies then either build local data centers or use the in-country regions offered by cloud providers.
gl.veri-yerellestirme.why: Localization is defended on grounds of national security, easier oversight and digital sovereignty. Critics say it raises costs, makes it harder for small firms to reach global services, and does not always improve data security. Because training and running AI models depends on large cloud infrastructure, the topic comes up often in AI news.
gl.veri-yonetisimi.def: The set of policies, roles and processes that determine who collects, stores, uses and shares an organization’s data, under which rules and for what purposes.
gl.veri-yonetisimi.example: Before using customer data in a credit model, a bank sets up a committee that decides which fields may be used, who gets access and how long the data is kept.
gl.veri-yonetisimi.faq.0.a: No. Data management covers the day-to-day technical work of storing and processing data. Governance is the higher-level framework that sets the rules and responsibilities for that work.
gl.veri-yonetisimi.faq.0.q: Is data governance the same as data management?
gl.veri-yonetisimi.faq.1.a: Yes, scaled to their size. Even a simple data inventory, access rules and retention periods reduce risk.
gl.veri-yonetisimi.faq.1.q: Do small organizations need data governance?
gl.veri-yonetisimi.how: Data governance starts with defining ownership and responsibility: who is accountable for which data and who may access it. Standards for data quality, retention periods, access rights, security and privacy are then put in writing. The origin of data and the transformations it goes through are recorded. Regular audits and logs help monitor compliance. In AI projects this framework helps ensure that training data is authorized, accurate and documented.
gl.veri-yonetisimi.why: AI models are only as trustworthy as the data they learn from, and copyright, personal-data and discrimination risks often begin at the data stage. Compliance with rules such as Turkey’s personal data protection law (KVKK) and EU regulations also pushes organizations to build clear governance. Without it, legal and reputational risks grow.
gl.veri-zehirlenmesi.def: An attack that deliberately slips corrupted, misleading or harmful examples into a model's training or fine-tuning data to push the model's behavior in the attacker's chosen direction.
gl.veri-zehirlenmesi.example: A spam filter that learns from user feedback can be dulled over time if an attacker marks hundreds of malicious messages as “not spam.”
gl.veri-zehirlenmesi.faq.0.a: No. Data poisoning is a method, aimed at degrading or steering a model. A model backdoor is one possible result of it: hidden behavior that appears only when a specific trigger is present.
gl.veri-zehirlenmesi.faq.0.q: Is data poisoning the same as a model backdoor?
gl.veri-zehirlenmesi.faq.1.a: Not always. The bad examples may be a small part of the data and may not show up in ordinary tests. Keeping records of data origin, scanning the data and testing the model in varied situations lower the risk.
gl.veri-zehirlenmesi.how: Models learn from their data, so bad examples that get in are learned too. An attacker might flip labels, publish web pages full of particular claims, or add crafted examples to open datasets. The effect can be a general drop in accuracy, or a wrong answer on one specific topic. Systems that keep updating from user feedback can be poisoned the same way. Defenses include auditing data sources, filtering, and detecting unusual examples.
gl.veri-zehirlenmesi.why: Large models are trained on data gathered from the web at huge scale, so the trustworthiness of the data pipeline is part of model security. If poisoning goes unnoticed, flawed or biased outputs can reach the final product. That is why being able to trace and verify where data came from matters to organizations.
gl.vibe-coding.def: A way of building software where, instead of writing code line by line, a person describes what they want in plain language and mostly accepts the AI-generated code without studying its details, steering by feel.
gl.vibe-coding.example: A founder can produce a working booking-page prototype for a designer friend just by describing it, never looking at how the code is written and only typing new requests based on what they see on screen.
gl.vibe-coding.faq.0.a: Not exactly. In AI-assisted programming, the developer usually reads the generated code and takes responsibility for it. In vibe coding, the code is largely accepted unread, judged by whether the result seems to work.
gl.vibe-coding.faq.0.q: Is vibe coding the same as AI-assisted programming?
gl.vibe-coding.faq.1.a: It can suit prototypes and personal tools. Products that need security, data privacy and long-term maintenance require the code to be understood and tested.
gl.vibe-coding.faq.1.q: Can vibe coding be used for serious projects?
gl.vibe-coding.how: A person types into a chat box or coding tool that they want, say, a to-do list app. The AI generates the code, the person runs it to see the result, and describes in words anything they dislike. This round repeats many times, and the person looks at what appears on screen rather than reading the code itself. The term was popularized by Andrej Karpathy. The core idea is to leave the details of coding to the model and guide it by feel.
gl.vibe-coding.why: Vibe coding draws attention because it lets people who do not know programming build simple apps and prototypes. At the same time, code accepted without being understood can hide bugs, security holes and maintenance problems. It can work for small experiments, but care is needed for critical systems, which is why opinions on it are divided.
gl.video-anlama.def: The ability of an AI system to grasp the objects, people, actions and events in a video along with how they relate over time. It goes beyond recognizing a single frame to working out what happened, when and why.
gl.video-anlama.example: Given a recording of a football match and asked when the goal was scored, a system can locate the relevant moment and answer.
gl.video-anlama.faq.0.a: Image recognition looks at what is in a single frame. Video understanding must also interpret motion, sequence and cause and effect across frames.
gl.video-anlama.faq.0.q: What is the difference between video understanding and image recognition?
gl.video-anlama.faq.1.a: A video holds far more data than a single image, and events can stretch over a long time. The model has to follow both detail and overall flow while keeping computing costs reasonable.
gl.video-anlama.faq.1.q: Why is video understanding considered difficult?
gl.video-anlama.how: The video is sampled into frames at set intervals, and each frame is passed through a visual encoder that turns it into a numerical representation. Audio and any captions are processed in the same way. The model tracks order and change across these pieces to interpret motion and the flow of events. In many current systems, these representations are fed to a language model, which can then answer questions about the video or write a summary.
gl.video-anlama.why: It reduces the need to watch hours of footage by hand in areas such as security cameras, sports analysis, educational video and content search. Long videos demand a lot of computing power, so it remains a hard research area. It often comes up in news about multimodal models.
gl.vllm.def: An open-source inference library built to run large language models on servers with less memory and higher throughput. It lets the same hardware serve more users at once.
gl.vllm.example: A company running an open-weight language model on its own servers can expose its chat assistant through vLLM and serve more employees at the same time on the same GPUs.
gl.vllm.faq.0.a: No. vLLM is serving software that runs existing models, not a model itself. It can be used with many open models.
gl.vllm.faq.1.a: It is a technique for managing the language model's cache of earlier tokens in small blocks. This wastes less GPU memory and allows more requests to be processed at once.
gl.vllm.how: While a model generates a reply, it keeps intermediate results for earlier tokens, known as the KV cache, in GPU memory. Traditional approaches reserve large contiguous blocks for this cache up front, so a lot of memory goes unused. vLLM's PagedAttention splits the cache into small blocks, much like paging in an operating system, and allocates them only as needed. Continuous batching also lets a new request take the place of a finished one right away, so the GPU rarely sits idle.
gl.vllm.why: Serving a model to millions of users can cost as much as training it. Inference efficiency means answering more requests on the same GPUs and lowering the cost per request. Because vLLM is open source, it is a common choice for companies hosting their own models.
gl.vram.def: Fast memory located on a graphics card that the graphics processor (GPU) accesses directly. In AI it holds a model's weights and the intermediate data produced during computation.
gl.vram.example: A model with about seven billion parameters stored as 16-bit numbers needs roughly 14 GB for its weights alone, so it will not run as is on a card with 8 GB of VRAM.
gl.vram.faq.0.a: RAM is the processor's main memory. VRAM belongs to the graphics card and feeds the GPU with data at a much higher speed.
gl.vram.faq.0.q: What is the difference between VRAM and RAM?
gl.vram.faq.1.a: The model either fails with an error or runs with part of it moved to main memory. In the second case, speed usually drops noticeably.
gl.vram.faq.1.q: What happens if there is not enough VRAM?
gl.vram.how: While a GPU computes, the data needs to sit in fast memory close to the processor, so separate memory chips are placed on the card itself. When a model is run, its weights are first loaded into VRAM. The space needed depends on the number of parameters and how many bits each number uses, and the cache reserved for the conversation history takes room too. If the model does not fit in VRAM, it either will not run or slows down sharply because part of it spills into slower main memory. Techniques such as quantization reduce the space required.
gl.vram.why: For people who want to run AI models locally, VRAM is often the first number checked when choosing a graphics card. In data centers, the memory per accelerator likewise determines how large a model can run on a single card.
gl.wafer-olcekli-cip.def: A chip design that, instead of cutting a silicon wafer into many small pieces, uses almost the entire wafer as one giant processor.
gl.wafer-olcekli-cip.example: The Wafer Scale Engine chips from the US company Cerebras are the best-known example of this approach.
gl.wafer-olcekli-cip.faq.0.a: A giant single piece is hard and expensive to manufacture, power and cool. The software ecosystem has also matured mostly around GPUs.
gl.wafer-olcekli-cip.faq.0.q: Why aren't wafer-scale chips more common?
gl.wafer-olcekli-cip.faq.1.a: It is a thin disk of silicon on which chips are built. In conventional manufacturing, many chips come from one wafer.
gl.wafer-olcekli-cip.how: Normally a silicon wafer carries hundreds of small chips, which are cut apart and packaged separately. In a wafer-scale design, the cores and memory are built together on a single piece covering most of the wafer. Because communication between cores stays inside the chip, it can be much faster than links between separate chips connected by cables. Manufacturing defects, which are unavoidable, are handled with spare cores and routing that skips faulty regions.
gl.wafer-olcekli-cip.why: With large models, moving data can cost as much as the computation itself. The wafer-scale approach tries to keep that movement on the chip to gain speed and efficiency. It offers an alternative to common GPU clusters, though manufacturing, cooling and software compatibility remain challenges.
gl.web-kazima.def: The automated process of using a program to pull information from web pages and turn it into an organized form such as a table or database. It is the automated version of copying and pasting by hand.
gl.web-kazima.example: A price comparison site pulls product prices from retailers' pages at regular intervals and shows them in a single list.
gl.web-kazima.faq.0.a: There is no single answer. It depends on the country, the type of content, whether personal data is involved and the site's terms of use. A specific case calls for legal advice.
gl.web-kazima.faq.1.a: A crawler follows links to discover and collect pages. Scraping focuses on extracting specific information from a page as structured data. The two are often used together.
gl.web-kazima.faq.1.q: What is the difference between web scraping and a web crawler?
gl.web-kazima.how: A program downloads a page, parses its HTML and picks out the wanted fields, such as titles, prices or reviews, and saves them. It usually targets specific sites and specific information. Sites may respond with rate limits, login requirements or robots.txt rules. Scraping often works together with crawlers: the crawler finds pages, and the scraper extracts the needed content from them. The resulting data is then cleaned and used for analysis or model training.
gl.web-kazima.why: Training data for AI models, price comparison and research all lean on web scraping. But debates continue over copyright, personal data and sites' terms of use. Content owners argue their work is used without permission, while developers stress the value of access to publicly available information.
gl.web-tarayici-bot.def: Software that automatically browses web pages by following links and collects their content. It is the core tool of search engines and large-scale data collection projects.
gl.web-tarayici-bot.example: Googlebot, which browses web pages for Google's search results, is a typical example of a crawler.
gl.web-tarayici-bot.faq.0.a: It is a text file at the root of a site that tells bots which sections they should stay out of. Technically it is a statement of rules rather than a barrier; whether to follow it is up to whoever runs the bot.
gl.web-tarayici-bot.faq.1.a: No. Archive projects, researchers and AI companies also run their own crawlers. Who operates a bot can often be seen from the user-agent name in its request.
gl.web-tarayici-bot.faq.1.q: Does every crawler belong to a search engine?
gl.web-tarayici-bot.how: A crawler starts with a list of seed addresses, downloads a page, finds the links inside it and adds them to a queue of pages to visit. Details that matter include not revisiting the same page, not overloading sites and deciding how often pages should be refreshed. Well-behaved crawlers follow the limits a site sets in its robots.txt file, though compliance is voluntary. The collected pages are then indexed for search or archived.
gl.web-tarayici-bot.why: Search engines could not work without crawlers. In the AI era, bots that gather training data for language models have become a point of dispute with publishers, and many sites choose to restrict their access. The traffic load these bots create and concerns about unauthorized use are part of that debate.
gl.yalnizca-kod-cozucu-model.def: A type of language model that uses a single Transformer stack and predicts the next piece of text by looking only at the pieces before it. Most of the large language models behind today's chatbots follow this design.
gl.yalnizca-kod-cozucu-model.example: Models in the GPT and Llama families are of this type: when a user types 'The weather today', the model produces the most likely continuation one token at a time.
gl.yalnizca-kod-cozucu-model.faq.0.a: BERT is an encoder that looks at both sides of a word to work out its meaning. Decoder-only models see only the preceding tokens and are built to generate text.
gl.yalnizca-kod-cozucu-model.faq.0.q: What is the difference between a decoder-only model and BERT?
gl.yalnizca-kod-cozucu-model.faq.1.a: No. They build context while reading the earlier part of a sequence, and at large scale they have done well at both understanding and generation tasks. Still, researchers continue to debate which architecture suits which job best.
gl.yalnizca-kod-cozucu-model.faq.1.q: Are these models bad at understanding input?
gl.yalnizca-kod-cozucu-model.how: The model reads text from left to right, and at each position it can see only what came before; later pieces are hidden by a mask. The training task is simple: predict the next token in the sequence. When generating, the model picks a token from a probability distribution, appends it to the sequence and repeats the process to extend the text. The prompt and the answer are not separate sections but consecutive parts of one sequence.
gl.yalnizca-kod-cozucu-model.why: Because the design is simple and scales well with very large amounts of data, it became the dominant choice for large language models. The same model can translate, summarize or write code just by changing the prompt. Many of the names that appear in the news, such as GPT and Llama, belong to this family.
gl.yanlilik-varyans-dengesi.def: The tension between a model capturing the detail in its training data and staying consistent on new data. Simpler models make more systematic errors, while more complex ones become overly sensitive to the data they saw.
gl.yanlilik-varyans-dengesi.example: When predicting house prices, a model that looks only at floor area will consistently underestimate pricey neighborhoods (high bias), while one that memorizes every street and floor number will stumble on new listings (high variance).
gl.yanlilik-varyans-dengesi.faq.0.a: Rarely in practice; as one falls, the other usually rises. More data and good regularization can improve the balance, but they do not remove the tradeoff entirely.
gl.yanlilik-varyans-dengesi.faq.0.q: Can bias and variance both be driven to zero?
gl.yanlilik-varyans-dengesi.faq.1.a: Overfitting is the typical sign of high variance, and underfitting is the typical sign of high bias. The tradeoff describes both problems within a single framework.
gl.yanlilik-varyans-dengesi.faq.1.q: How does this relate to overfitting?
gl.yanlilik-varyans-dengesi.how: Bias is the systematic error a model makes when it assumes the underlying pattern is simpler than it really is, like describing a curve with a straight line. Variance measures how much the model's predictions shift when the training data changes slightly. A very flexible model memorizes even the noise in its training set, so its variance rises. In practice, as model complexity grows, bias falls and variance climbs. Error on validation data is usually lowest somewhere in the middle, where the two curves cross.
gl.yanlilik-varyans-dengesi.why: This is the core idea behind the discussion of overfitting and underfitting. Choices about model type, regularization and how much data to collect are made with this balance in mind. It also sits quietly behind explanations of why large models need so much data.
gl.yapay-noron.def: A computing unit loosely inspired by the biological nerve cell: it multiplies its inputs by weights, adds them up, and passes the result through an activation function to produce a single output.
gl.yapay-noron.example: In a network that predicts house prices, one neuron combines inputs such as floor area and number of rooms, each with its own weight, into a single number.
gl.yapay-noron.faq.0.a: Only loosely. An artificial neuron is a simple mathematical operation, while a biological cell works in a much more complicated way.
gl.yapay-noron.faq.0.q: How similar is an artificial neuron to a real neuron?
gl.yapay-noron.faq.1.a: It is an adjustable constant added to the neuron's weighted sum and set during training. It shifts how easily the neuron activates.
gl.yapay-noron.how: A neuron takes in several numbers as inputs. Each input has a weight that determines how much influence it has. The neuron adds up the weighted inputs, adds a tunable constant called a bias, and feeds the result into an activation function. The number that comes out becomes an input to neurons in the next layer. What a network learns during training is these weights and biases, and they make up most of its parameters.
gl.yapay-noron.why: Everything in an artificial neural network is built by repeating this small unit thousands or millions of times. When people talk about a model's 'parameter count', they largely mean the weights between neurons. The resemblance to a biological neuron is only loose inspiration, since a real brain is far more complex.

gl.yapay-sinir-agi.def.en: A mathematical model, inspired by the neurons in the brain, that consists of many simple computing units in interconnected layers and learns from data.

gl.yapay-sinir-agi.example.en: A small neural network that recognizes handwritten digits is often used as the first example in AI courses.

gl.yapay-sinir-agi.faq.0.a.en: It is only loosely inspired by it. Artificial neural networks consist of mathematical calculations and are a highly simplified model of the biological processes in the brain.

gl.yapay-sinir-agi.faq.0.q.en: Does an artificial neural network work like the human brain?

gl.yapay-sinir-agi.faq.1.a.en: The weights of the connections in a neural network are the model's parameters. For example, a model with 70 billion parameters has that many adjustable values.

gl.yapay-sinir-agi.faq.1.q.en: What is the relationship between parameters and a neural network?

gl.yapay-sinir-agi.how.en: A neural network consists of an input layer, one or more hidden layers and an output layer. Each unit multiplies the numbers it receives by certain weights, sums them and passes the result to the next layer. During training, the network's prediction is compared with the correct answer, and the weights are updated backward to reduce the error (backpropagation).

gl.yapay-sinir-agi.why.en: Neural networks are the building blocks of deep learning and, by extension, of today's language, image and audio models. What we call a model's "parameter count" is the number of weights in this network.

gl.yapay-super-zeka.def: A theoretical level of AI that would far surpass human intelligence in nearly every field, including scientific creativity and general reasoning. No such system exists today.
gl.yapay-super-zeka.example: A single system that designs new drugs, solves physics problems and runs a company far better than the best human experts would count as ASI, but for now that remains science fiction.
gl.yapay-super-zeka.faq.0.a: AGI describes a system that can do a broad range of tasks at a human level. Superintelligence would go beyond that level and be far more capable than any human.
gl.yapay-super-zeka.faq.0.q: What is the difference between superintelligence and artificial general intelligence (AGI)?
gl.yapay-super-zeka.faq.1.a: Nobody knows. Experts' estimates range from several decades to never, so anyone offering a firm timeline deserves some skepticism.
gl.yapay-super-zeka.how: Since superintelligence is still hypothetical, how it would work is not settled; the discussion usually treats it as a stage after artificial general intelligence. One scenario goes like this: a system that reaches human level improves its own design, the improved system does so even faster, and progress quickly leaves humans behind. Other researchers consider such a rapid leap unlikely and expect progress to be slow, gradual, or held back by limits in hardware, data and energy.
gl.yapay-super-zeka.why: Superintelligence sits at the center of debates about AI safety and alignment. Some people regard it as a serious long-term risk that warrants precautions today; others think the focus distracts from present-day problems such as bias and effects on jobs. Knowing this divide helps when reading news claims about it.

gl.yapay-zeka-ajani.def.en: An AI system that carries out a given goal by planning the steps itself and using tools, such as searching the web, filling in forms or running code.

gl.yapay-zeka-ajani.example.en: Systems that search for restaurants and make reservations on a user's behalf, or complete an online purchase after getting approval, are AI agents.

gl.yapay-zeka-ajani.faq.0.a.en: A chatbot answers questions. An agent uses tools to do work on the user's behalf, such as searching, filling in forms, editing files or shopping.

gl.yapay-zeka-ajani.faq.0.q.en: What is the difference between an AI agent and a chatbot?

gl.yapay-zeka-ajani.faq.1.a.en: It depends on the authority they are given. Requiring approval for important actions, limiting the agent's access and tracking what it does reduce the risks.

gl.yapay-zeka-ajani.how.en: An AI agent combines a language model with tools: it can search the web, read files, fill in forms, run code or use other applications. It breaks the goal it is given into steps, decides on the next one by looking at the result of each step, and continues until the job is done.

gl.yapay-zeka-ajani.why.en: Agents turn AI from an assistant that only answers questions into a colleague that does work on the user's behalf. They are spreading quickly in areas such as shopping, appointment booking, software development and customer service, and questions about security and accountability come with them.

gl.yapay-zeka-arama-motoru.def: A search service that, instead of returning a list of links, gathers information from the web or other sources, summarizes it with a language model, and gives a direct answer with cited sources.
gl.yapay-zeka-arama-motoru.example: A user asks how to extend a laptop's battery life; the service shows a short list of tips drawn from several sites, each with a link to its source.
gl.yapay-zeka-arama-motoru.faq.0.a: A traditional search engine ranks links and leaves the finding to the user. An AI search engine reads and summarizes pages to produce a direct answer.
gl.yapay-zeka-arama-motoru.faq.0.q: How is an AI search engine different from a traditional one?
gl.yapay-zeka-arama-motoru.faq.1.a: No. The model can summarize a source wrongly or rely on a weak one. Checking the cited links is a good habit, especially on important topics.
gl.yapay-zeka-arama-motoru.faq.1.q: Are AI search engine answers always correct?
gl.yapay-zeka-arama-motoru.how: The user types a question; the system interprets it, rewrites it if needed, and pulls relevant pages from a search index. The retrieved passages are passed to a language model, which combines them into a short answer and usually shows its sources as numbered citations. The user can ask follow-up questions and keep the conversation going. Underneath, it follows the logic of retrieval-augmented generation (RAG).
gl.yapay-zeka-arama-motoru.why: The way people reach information is shifting: instead of opening pages one by one, they can read a ready-made answer. That is convenient for users but can affect publishers' traffic and advertising revenue. Risks of faulty summaries and copyright disputes are also recurring themes in news about this area.
gl.yapay-zeka-arkadasi.def: An AI application designed to chat with a user over time, offering emotional support, friendship or role play. It usually has a persistent personality, name and appearance, and is built to remember earlier conversations.
gl.yapay-zeka-arkadasi.example: Replika and Character.AI are among the best-known apps in this space; users can hold long-running conversations with a character they choose.
gl.yapay-zeka-arkadasi.faq.0.a: A chatbot usually performs a task, such as answering customer questions. A companion app focuses on building a relationship, with continuity and a sense of personality.
gl.yapay-zeka-arkadasi.faq.0.q: What is the difference between an AI companion and a chatbot?
gl.yapay-zeka-arkadasi.faq.1.a: It depends on the person and how the app is used. It helps to check how personal data is stored and to remember that the app does not replace real human relationships. In serious distress, professional support is needed.
gl.yapay-zeka-arkadasi.faq.1.q: Is it safe to use an AI companion?
gl.yapay-zeka-arkadasi.how: Behind the app there is usually a large language model. Developers give the model a persona, a speaking style and rules, while the app stores what the user shares in a kind of memory and adds it to later conversations. Some products also include voice chat, avatars or images. Users can pick or create their own character. Although replies feel personal, the model does not experience real feelings or a relationship; it generates fitting words based on context.
gl.yapay-zeka-arkadasi.why: Many people use these apps. Possible benefits include easing loneliness and practicing social skills, but there are also debates about emotional dependence, the privacy of personal data and the protection of young users. Regulators and researchers are watching the area closely.
gl.yapay-zeka-asistani.def: Software built on artificial intelligence that responds to requests given in natural language, answering questions, writing text and helping with many kinds of tasks. It is usually used through a chat interface.
gl.yapay-zeka-asistani.example: Apps such as ChatGPT, Gemini and Claude are AI assistants; a user can ask one to draft an email or summarize a long report.
gl.yapay-zeka-asistani.faq.0.a: They are similar but not identical. Voice assistants mostly responded to predefined commands, while today's AI assistants use large language models to understand free-form speech and help with a wider range of tasks. Many voice assistants are being rebuilt on such models.
gl.yapay-zeka-asistani.faq.0.q: Is an AI assistant the same as a voice assistant?
gl.yapay-zeka-asistani.faq.1.a: It is often useful, but it can give wrong or made-up information. For topics like health, law and finance, check the answer against reliable sources.
gl.yapay-zeka-asistani.faq.1.q: Can I trust the information an AI assistant gives?
gl.yapay-zeka-asistani.how: Behind an assistant sits a large language model. The user types or speaks a request, and the model weighs it together with the earlier conversation to produce a reply. Some assistants connect to tools such as web search, file reading or a calendar, so they can do more than just talk. Companies can add their own instructions and information to tailor an assistant to a particular job. The quality of the answers depends on the model, the information it is given and how clear the request is.
gl.yapay-zeka-asistani.why: AI assistants are the form of AI most ordinary users meet. By speeding up writing, summarizing, translation and research, they are changing how individuals and companies work. Because they can still produce wrong information, answers on important matters need to be checked.
gl.yapay-zeka-avatari.def: A talking digital character, often human-like, that is generated or driven by AI. On screen it presents a script or chats with a user using its face, voice and expressions.
gl.yapay-zeka-avatari.example: A company turns one script into an employee training video in dozens of languages, presented by an avatar host.
gl.yapay-zeka-avatari.faq.0.a: Similar methods can be involved, but purpose and consent differ. An avatar is usually a character shown openly as synthetic and made with permission. A deepfake usually means imitating a real person without consent or in a misleading way.
gl.yapay-zeka-avatari.faq.0.q: Is an AI avatar the same as a deepfake?
gl.yapay-zeka-avatari.faq.1.a: Many services let you create a personalized avatar from a short video recording and your consent. Since face and voice can count as personal data, it is worth checking how the data is stored and used.
gl.yapay-zeka-avatari.faq.1.q: Can I make an avatar of myself?
gl.yapay-zeka-avatari.how: The system has two parts: content and appearance. The script is written by hand or generated by a language model. A speech synthesis model turns it into spoken audio, and an image-generation model animates the face, lip movements and head or hand gestures to match the voice. An avatar can be built from a short video recording of a real person (with their consent) or be entirely fictional. Some systems respond in real time, while others render a video in advance.
gl.yapay-zeka-avatari.why: In training videos, customer service and multilingual presentations, avatars cut the cost of cameras and studios. On the other hand, there is debate over using someone's likeness without permission, over deepfakes and over deception. Telling viewers that the content is synthetic is part of that debate.
gl.yapay-zeka-balonu.def: The claim or concern that expectations around AI companies and infrastructure investment have run far ahead of real revenue and profit potential, pushing prices up to unsustainable levels.
gl.yapay-zeka-balonu.example: The dot-com bubble of the late 1990s is a common comparison: the internet really did change the world, but many companies lost most of their value and plenty shut down.
gl.yapay-zeka-balonu.faq.0.a: Not necessarily. The internet kept developing after the dot-com crash; what fell was mostly prices and weak business models. The lasting value of a technology and the sustainability of company valuations are separate questions.
gl.yapay-zeka-balonu.faq.0.q: If an AI bubble bursts, does the technology disappear?
gl.yapay-zeka-balonu.faq.1.a: There is no definitive answer. It is a matter of forecasting, opinions are divided, and a bubble is usually only acknowledged once prices have fallen.
gl.yapay-zeka-balonu.faq.1.q: Is there actually an AI bubble?
gl.yapay-zeka-balonu.how: In a bubble, investors buy assets at prices far above current real earnings, trusting a story of future growth. As prices rise, more people join in and expectations feed on themselves. If the expected revenue does not arrive, confidence cracks, selling speeds up and prices can fall. In AI, the debate centers on whether the enormous spending on chips and data centers will be matched by enough revenue to justify it.
gl.yapay-zeka-balonu.why: The topic touches a wide range of areas, from stock market values and startup funding to energy and chip demand and employment. Experts disagree: some analysts see parallels with past technology bubbles, while others argue the technology brings real productivity gains. Whether it is a bubble usually becomes clear only in hindsight.
gl.yapay-zeka-bilgisayari.def: A personal computer with a dedicated AI processor, usually called an NPU, so it can run AI tasks on the device itself instead of relying on a cloud connection.
gl.yapay-zeka-bilgisayari.example: Blurring the background in a video call or transcribing a meeting on the device are tasks an NPU-equipped laptop can handle while keeping battery use low.
gl.yapay-zeka-bilgisayari.faq.0.a: No. Cloud services like ChatGPT work in a browser on almost any computer. An NPU mainly helps when AI tasks should run efficiently on the device itself.
gl.yapay-zeka-bilgisayari.faq.0.q: Do you need an NPU to use AI on a PC?
gl.yapay-zeka-bilgisayari.faq.1.a: A GPU is a more general-purpose, high-power parallel processor. An NPU is a low-energy unit specialized for AI calculations.
gl.yapay-zeka-bilgisayari.faq.1.q: What is the difference between an NPU and a GPU?
gl.yapay-zeka-bilgisayari.how: In a traditional computer, AI workloads fall mostly on the CPU or the graphics card (GPU). An AI PC adds a neural processing unit (NPU), a chip designed around the math of neural networks. The NPU aims to do the same work with far less energy, so tasks such as background blur, live captions, local speech recognition or small language models can run without draining the battery. The software then spreads each job across the NPU, GPU or CPU depending on the situation.
gl.yapay-zeka-bilgisayari.why: Running AI locally can keep data on the device, let features work offline and reduce cloud costs. That is why chipmakers and PC brands position new laptops around it. Real benefits still depend on how much apps actually make use of the NPU.
gl.yapay-zeka-cipi.def: A processor designed or adapted to run the heavy matrix calculations needed to train and operate AI models quickly and efficiently.
gl.yapay-zeka-cipi.example: Nvidia's data center GPUs and Google's own TPUs are well-known examples of the chips on which large language models are trained and run.
gl.yapay-zeka-cipi.faq.0.a: A GPU is the most widely used type of AI chip, but not every AI chip is a GPU. Purpose-built accelerators such as TPUs are used for the same work.
gl.yapay-zeka-cipi.faq.0.q: Is a GPU the same as an AI chip?
gl.yapay-zeka-cipi.faq.1.a: For small models, yes, and many people run models on their own machines. For training large models, memory capacity and chip-to-chip connection speed fall short, which is why data center chips are used.
gl.yapay-zeka-cipi.faq.1.q: Can a home computer's graphics card do AI work?
gl.yapay-zeka-cipi.how: Neural network computation rests largely on multiplying and adding huge numbers of values. A general-purpose processor handles tasks one after another and flexibly, while AI chips carry out those multiply-and-add operations simultaneously across many compute units. Moving data to those units is also a bottleneck, so the chips are paired with very fast memory.
