Graphics processing units (GPUs) are the most common example, though purpose-built chips such as Google's TPU exist too. Designs can also differ for training and for inference.
gl.yapay-zeka-cipi.why: The time and cost of training large models depend heavily on how many of these chips are available and how powerful they are. When supply is tight, companies' product plans are affected. That is why export controls, companies designing their own chips, and chip procurement are staple topics in AI news.
gl.yapay-zeka-copu.def: Low-quality text, images and video produced with generative AI at minimal effort and care, then dumped onto the internet, often only to attract clicks and revenue.
gl.yapay-zeka-copu.example: Mass-produced images with warped details, posted only to farm engagement, are a typical case, as are 'guide' pages that repeat the same sentences.
gl.yapay-zeka-copu.faq.0.a: No. Accurate, useful content that is carefully reviewed is not slop even if AI helped produce it. The term describes careless, mass-produced output.
gl.yapay-zeka-copu.faq.1.a: They are close but not identical. Spam is unsolicited, usually bulk messaging, while AI slop describes low-quality content produced in volume with AI, and it can be used for spam purposes.
gl.yapay-zeka-copu.faq.1.q: Is AI slop the same as spam?
gl.yapay-zeka-copu.how: Generative tools make producing content almost free, so some people and sites use them to chase clicks, ad revenue or better placement in search results. The outcome is repetitive, generic writing that sometimes contains errors, images with odd details, and meaningless videos that fill social media feeds and search results. The term is used much like 'spam'. Using AI does not by itself make content slop; carelessness and intent are what matter.
gl.yapay-zeka-copu.why: This flood of material makes good sources harder to find and pushes search engines and platforms to filter more aggressively. The spread of AI output online also raises questions about the quality of data future models will be trained on. For readers, it calls for a bit more skepticism toward what they see.
gl.yapay-zeka-denetimi.def: An independent examination of whether an AI system complies with laws, standards and an organization's own principles, and whether it works fairly, safely and in a documented way. Internal teams or outside bodies can carry it out.
gl.yapay-zeka-denetimi.example: A hiring platform has its resume-screening algorithm audited by an independent firm, which checks whether equally qualified candidates receive different scores depending on gender.
gl.yapay-zeka-denetimi.faq.0.a: Testing focuses on the model's technical performance. An audit is broader: besides tests, it covers data, processes, documentation and the structure of responsibility.
gl.yapay-zeka-denetimi.faq.0.q: Is an AI audit the same as testing a model?
gl.yapay-zeka-denetimi.faq.1.a: Internal audit teams, independent audit firms, academics or authorized bodies can do it. The more independent the auditor, the more trust the results usually earn.
gl.yapay-zeka-denetimi.faq.1.q: Who carries out an AI audit?
gl.yapay-zeka-denetimi.how: An auditor first looks at the system's purpose, the data it uses and its decision processes. Then they test whether the model gives similar results across different user groups, how often its outputs are wrong, whether it has security weaknesses and whether records are adequate. Specially crafted inputs may be fed to the model. The results go into a report, fixes are recommended and progress is followed up later. Audits can also be done without access to the model's internals, but they reveal less.
gl.yapay-zeka-denetimi.why: AI systems often look like black boxes from the outside. Independent audits are one way to verify companies' claims and catch problems such as discrimination early. Some regulations make such assessments mandatory for certain systems, while auditing standards are still settling.
gl.yapay-zeka-destekli-kimlik-avi.def: The use of generative AI by scammers to trick people through fake messages, emails, calls or videos into handing over data such as passwords and payment details.
gl.yapay-zeka-destekli-kimlik-avi.exampl: An employee receives an email imitating the manager's writing style that asks for an urgent payment, and can verify the request by calling the manager through a different channel.
Language is no longer a reliable clue. When a message creates urgency or asks for information or money, confirm the sender through an official channel before clicking any link.
How can I spot AI-powered phishing?
The basic method is the same; the difference is scale and quality. AI makes messages more convincing and personal while lowering the cost of producing them.
How is it different from traditional phishing?
gl.yapay-zeka-destekli-kimlik-avi.how: In classic phishing, language errors and generic wording often gave the attack away. Generative AI can quickly write near-flawless, personalized messages that include a person's name, job and interests. Voice cloning and fake video carry the attack onto phone calls and video meetings. An attacker can automate all this for large numbers of targets at almost no cost. The core trick stays the same: rush the recipient into clicking a link or sending money.
gl.yapay-zeka-destekli-kimlik-avi.why: Old warning signs such as spelling mistakes are losing their value. That makes awareness training and technical safeguards equally important for individuals and companies. Habits like multi-factor authentication and confirming requests through a second channel protect people however convincing a message looks.
gl.yapay-zeka-destekli-siber-saldiri.def: A cyberattack in which attackers use AI tools to speed up or scale stages such as reconnaissance, phishing and malware development. AI acts as an assistant or accelerator for the attack.
gl.yapay-zeka-destekli-siber-saldiri.exa: Instead of a clumsy foreign-language scam email, an employee might receive a flawless phishing message that uses the company's internal jargon and their correct name.
gl.yapay-zeka-destekli-siber-saldiri.faq: It can automate some stages to a large degree, but in most cases a human chooses the target and steers the process. How far automation will go is still closely watched.
Can AI carry out an attack from start to finish on its own?
They use it to detect suspicious behavior, scan logs and prioritize alerts. It is expected to ease the heavy workload of security teams.
gl.yapay-zeka-destekli-siber-saldiri.how: Language models can write fluent, error-free phishing emails tailored to a target. Code generation tools can make it easier to prepare simple malware. Open-source information about a target can be gathered quickly, and weak points in systems can be scanned automatically. In most cases a human operator still directs the process, but as automation improves, models are becoming able to carry out longer chains of tasks on their own. Defenders use the same technology for threat detection.
gl.yapay-zeka-destekli-siber-saldiri.why: AI can lower both the cost of attacking and the expertise required. The old habit of spotting a fake email by its language mistakes works less well than it used to. Model developers try to monitor and limit misuse. The true scale of the effect is still debated among experts.
gl.yapay-zeka-duzenlemesi.def: The whole body of efforts to frame how AI is developed and used through laws, rules and standards. The aim is to protect safety, fundamental rights and accountability without blocking innovation.
gl.yapay-zeka-duzenlemesi.example: An AI system that scores job candidates in a company's hiring process is treated as high-risk under the EU AI Act and faces additional obligations.
gl.yapay-zeka-duzenlemesi.faq.0.a: It is the EU law adopted in 2024 that classifies AI systems by risk level and sets obligations accordingly. Its provisions are coming into effect in stages.
gl.yapay-zeka-duzenlemesi.faq.0.q: What is the EU AI Act?
gl.yapay-zeka-duzenlemesi.faq.1.a: Views differ. One side says a heavy compliance burden strains smaller companies in particular, while the other argues that clear rules build trust and support adoption.
gl.yapay-zeka-duzenlemesi.faq.1.q: Does regulation slow down innovation in AI?
gl.yapay-zeka-duzenlemesi.how: Countries take different routes. The EU's AI Act, adopted in 2024, uses a risk-based approach: some applications are banned, high-risk ones face strict obligations, and low-risk ones face light rules. Other countries rely on sector-specific rules, guidance or voluntary commitments instead of one comprehensive law. China and some others have issued their own specific rules for generative AI. Existing laws on data protection and copyright also apply to AI.
gl.yapay-zeka-duzenlemesi.why: Regulation determines which products companies can offer and how, what checks they must pass, and who is responsible for possible harm. A debate continues between those who say overly strict rules slow innovation and those who argue that loose rules can cause social harm. It is among the most common topics in AI news.
gl.yapay-zeka-etigi.def: An interdisciplinary field that asks what is right, fair and acceptable in building and using AI systems, and produces principles and practices to guide those choices.
gl.yapay-zeka-etigi.example: A company that asks its ethics board for an opinion before deciding which customers may buy its face recognition technology is applying AI ethics in everyday practice.
gl.yapay-zeka-etigi.faq.0.a: No. Law sets binding rules and enforces them, while ethics is a broader discussion about what is right and often looks at areas the law does not yet cover.
gl.yapay-zeka-etigi.faq.0.q: Is AI ethics the same as law?
gl.yapay-zeka-etigi.faq.1.a: Some critics argue principles often never reach practice, while others point to cases where ethics work changed real product decisions. The value of the principles depends on whether they become measurable processes.
gl.yapay-zeka-etigi.faq.1.q: Is AI ethics just a public relations exercise for companies?
gl.yapay-zeka-etigi.how: Discussions usually revolve around principles such as fairness, transparency, privacy, accountability, safety and respect for human rights. These principles turn into company guidelines, product design decisions, ethics boards and impact assessments. Researchers, lawyers, philosophers, engineers and civil society groups all take part. Principles sometimes collide, for instance when more accurate results and more privacy are both wanted, and then a balance has to be struck for the specific context.
gl.yapay-zeka-etigi.why: AI is entering decision processes in hiring, healthcare, education, security and more. Not everything that can be built technically should be built, and drawing that line requires a shared vocabulary. Ethical debate also lays the groundwork for laws and organizational policies.
gl.yapay-zeka-fabrikasi.def: A large data center designed from the ground up to train and run AI models, organized like a production line. Data and electricity go in; trained models and AI-generated answers come out.
gl.yapay-zeka-fabrikasi.example: A single facility where a company links many GPUs with a dedicated network, trains a language model there and also serves answers to users is a typical AI factory.
gl.yapay-zeka-fabrikasi.faq.0.a: A traditional data center hosts many kinds of applications. In an AI factory the hardware, networking and cooling are designed around AI workloads, and the key measure is the amount of models and answers produced.
gl.yapay-zeka-fabrikasi.faq.0.q: How is an AI factory different from a traditional data center?
gl.yapay-zeka-fabrikasi.faq.1.a: No. It is an industry phrase popularized especially by Nvidia's messaging, and it has no formal standard or single agreed definition.
gl.yapay-zeka-fabrikasi.faq.1.q: Is AI factory an official technical standard?
gl.yapay-zeka-fabrikasi.how: Many graphics processors (GPUs) work side by side, linked by a very fast internal network. Storage, power distribution, cooling and management software are designed together around this single purpose. A traditional data center hosts a wide mix of workloads such as email, websites and databases, while an AI factory focuses on training models and producing their responses. Efficiency is often measured by how many tokens of output it produces per unit of energy.
gl.yapay-zeka-fabrikasi.why: As demand for AI grows, companies and governments are investing heavily in these facilities, and electricity, cooling and chip supply are frequent news topics. The concept shows that AI is increasingly seen less as software and more as industrial infrastructure. The term is partly a marketing phrase, though; technically it describes a large data center built for AI.
gl.yapay-zeka-filigrani.def: Adding a marker, often invisible to people, to AI-generated images, audio, video or text so that the content can later be identified as machine-made.
gl.yapay-zeka-filigrani.example: Google DeepMind's SynthID tool adds a mark that people cannot see to images made by its own models, and a dedicated detector can look for that mark later.
gl.yapay-zeka-filigrani.faq.0.a: No. A watermark is embedded in the content itself, while content credentials are a signed record attached to the file. The two can complement each other.
gl.yapay-zeka-filigrani.faq.0.q: Is a watermark the same as content credentials?
gl.yapay-zeka-filigrani.faq.1.a: Yes. Heavy editing, regeneration or rewriting can weaken or strip it. That is why a watermark is treated as a helpful clue rather than conclusive proof.
gl.yapay-zeka-filigrani.faq.1.q: Can an invisible watermark be removed?
gl.yapay-zeka-filigrani.how: With invisible watermarking, a pattern is hidden in the content while it is being generated. In an image it may be tiny, regular shifts in pixel values; in text it is a statistical bias built into the model's word choices. A detection tool later looks for that pattern and, if it finds it, reports which system produced the content. The pattern is designed to survive routine changes such as resizing or compression. Heavy editing, rewriting or regenerating the content with another tool can still erase it.
gl.yapay-zeka-filigrani.why: Realistic fakes are making it harder to tell whether an image or voice is synthetic. Watermarks give platforms and researchers a way to check content at scale. They are not a complete solution, though, because only systems that choose to watermark can mark their own output.
gl.yapay-zeka-geri-bildirimiyle-pekistir: A training method that improves a language model using preferences and scores given by another AI model instead of human raters.
When a chatbot gives two answers to a harmful request, another model picks the one that better follows the safety principles, and those choices become training data.
The difference is who gives the feedback. In RLHF humans set the preferences, while in RLAIF an AI model does.
What is the difference between RLAIF and RLHF?
No. Humans still write the evaluation principles and criteria and check the results. What shrinks is the burden of labeling individual answers by hand.
Does RLAIF remove humans from the process entirely?

The process resembles reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF), but a model takes over the labeler's role. The model being trained produces two answers to the same prompt. A second model acting as a judge says which one is better according to set principles or criteria. These comparisons are used either to train a reward model or directly as a reward signal. The main model is then updated to favor the answers the judge preferred.

Human labeling is expensive, slow and hard to scale. AI feedback eases that bottleneck and lets the evaluation criteria be spelled out in written principles. On the other hand, the judge model's own mistakes and biases can leak into training, so it remains debated whether the method can fully replace human oversight.
gl.yapay-zeka-guvenligi.def: The field of research and practice that aims to make sure AI systems behave in line with human intentions and values, without causing unintended harm.
gl.yapay-zeka-guvenligi.example: A chatbot refusing to give dangerous instructions, such as how to build a weapon, is the result of safety training and testing done before release.
gl.yapay-zeka-guvenligi.faq.0.a: No. Safety is about a model behaving as intended without causing harm, while security is about protecting the system from attackers. The two overlap but have different focuses.
gl.yapay-zeka-guvenligi.faq.0.q: Is AI safety the same as AI security?
gl.yapay-zeka-guvenligi.faq.1.a: No. The field also covers present-day problems such as misinformation, bias and misuse. How much priority long-term risks deserve is debated among experts.
gl.yapay-zeka-guvenligi.faq.1.q: Is AI safety only about risks in the distant future?
gl.yapay-zeka-guvenligi.how: Several methods stand out. Alignment work steers a model toward behavior that matches human expectations, and training with human feedback is a common example. In red teaming, experts deliberately push a model to find cases where it gives harmful answers. Interpretability research tries to understand how a model reaches its decisions internally. Pre-release evaluations and usage policies also aim to limit misuse.
gl.yapay-zeka-guvenligi.why: As models become more capable and more autonomous, the cost of mistakes or misuse rises. What the field should focus on is debated: some stress present-day harms such as misinformation and bias, while others give priority to risks from far more powerful systems in the future. Many companies and governments now put resources into this area.
gl.yapay-zeka-guvenlik-enstitusu.def: The general name for public bodies that governments set up to evaluate the risks of advanced AI models and conduct safety research. The United Kingdom, the United States and other countries have created similar units.
gl.yapay-zeka-guvenlik-enstitusu.example: An institute might run a standard test suite measuring how much a new chat model could help write malicious software, then share the results with the company.
gl.yapay-zeka-guvenlik-enstitusu.faq.0.a: Usually not. Most institutes do testing and research, and their power to make binding decisions or ban products is limited. Their role varies from country to country.
gl.yapay-zeka-guvenlik-enstitusu.faq.0.q: Is an AI Safety Institute a regulator?
gl.yapay-zeka-guvenlik-enstitusu.faq.1.a: The United Kingdom and the United States are the best-known examples, and other countries have set up or discussed similar bodies. Their names and structures can change over time.
gl.yapay-zeka-guvenlik-enstitusu.faq.1.q: Which countries have AI safety institutes?
gl.yapay-zeka-guvenlik-enstitusu.how: These institutes agree with companies building frontier models to get access before or after release, and run tests in areas such as cyberattacks, biological risk and loss of control. They develop testing methods, publish findings and share information across countries. The aim is to make models' capabilities understandable to regulators and the public. Their enforcement powers are generally limited, and the work relies largely on companies' voluntary cooperation.
gl.yapay-zeka-guvenlik-enstitusu.why: As frontier models grow more capable, independent public evaluation capacity matters more. The institutes aim to avoid leaving risk assessment solely to a developer's own claims. Names and mandates of these bodies can change, so news readers should check which country's unit is meant.
gl.yapay-zeka-hizlandiricisi.def: Hardware designed to run the heavy math behind training and running AI models faster and more efficiently than general-purpose processors.
gl.yapay-zeka-hizlandiricisi.example: A company training a new language model runs thousands of GPUs together in one cluster inside a data center.
gl.yapay-zeka-hizlandiricisi.faq.0.a: Not exactly. A GPU is the best-known type of accelerator, but tensor processors such as TPUs and other custom chips also count.
gl.yapay-zeka-hizlandiricisi.faq.0.q: Is a GPU the same as an AI accelerator?
gl.yapay-zeka-hizlandiricisi.faq.1.a: A CPU is good at handling varied tasks one after another with a few powerful cores. AI workloads need huge numbers of simple operations done at once, which is what accelerators are built for.
gl.yapay-zeka-hizlandiricisi.faq.1.q: Why is a regular processor (CPU) not enough?
gl.yapay-zeka-hizlandiricisi.how: Neural network computation is made up largely of matrix multiplications, which can be split into many small operations and done at the same time. Accelerators are built with a large number of compute units and high memory bandwidth to carry out this parallel work. Graphics processing units (GPUs), tensor processors such as Google's TPU, and various custom chips all fall into this class. Large models are typically trained on clusters where hundreds or even thousands of accelerators are linked by fast connections.
gl.yapay-zeka-hizlandiricisi.why: How quickly large AI models can be developed, and at what cost they can be offered, depends heavily on this hardware. That is why chip manufacturing, export restrictions and data center investment keep appearing in AI news, and why chip companies like Nvidia are so often in the headlines.
gl.yapay-zeka-icerik-etiketleme-zorunlul: Rules or platform policies that require text, images, audio and video made or altered with AI to be disclosed to users as such.
A social media platform adding a 'created with AI' label beneath a realistic AI-generated video is a typical case.
No. Labels help, especially alongside watermarking, but bad actors can strip them or use tools that do not apply them. Labeling alone is not considered a complete solution.
Does labeling completely stop fake content from spreading?
Generally not. Rules tend to focus on realistic content that could mislead; minor edits or clearly fictional works may fall outside the scope. Details vary by country.
Does every piece of AI-assisted content have to be labeled?

Labeling works in two main ways. Visible labels place a notice such as 'made with AI' on or next to the content. Invisible methods embed information in a file's metadata or add a watermark that can be detected later. A requirement can come from law, or platforms can set it in their own rules. Responsibility may fall on the creator, the publisher or the platform. There are technical limits too: watermarks can be removed, and some tools produce unlabeled content.

Deepfakes and misleading images create risks in elections, fraud and reputational attacks. Labeling helps people judge how far to trust what they see. The EU AI Act, adopted in 2024, includes transparency obligations for this kind of content. At the same time, there are criticisms about free expression, artistic use and how enforceable the rules are.
gl.yapay-zeka-icerik-tespiti.def: The general name for software and methods that try to estimate whether a text, image, audio clip or video was produced by AI. The result is given as a probability, not a verdict.
gl.yapay-zeka-icerik-tespiti.example: A teacher may see a high 'AI probability' after uploading an essay to a detector, but that score does not prove the text came from AI; talking with the student is a sounder step.
gl.yapay-zeka-icerik-tespiti.faq.0.a: None are flawless. They can raise false alarms and miss content that was partly edited or rewritten. Their results should not be used alone to make decisions.
gl.yapay-zeka-icerik-tespiti.faq.0.q: How reliable are AI detection tools?
gl.yapay-zeka-icerik-tespiti.faq.1.a: No. Detection infers from the content's characteristics, while watermark checking looks for a mark added at creation. A watermark usually gives a clearer answer but only works for systems that add one.
gl.yapay-zeka-icerik-tespiti.faq.1.q: Is detection the same as watermarking?
gl.yapay-zeka-icerik-tespiti.how: Most detection tools are classifiers trained on examples of human-made and AI-made content. In images they look for lighting inconsistencies or texture patterns, in audio for unnatural transitions, and in text for word choices that are too regular and predictable. The tool combines these clues into a score such as the likelihood of being synthetic. As generation models improve, older clues stop working, so detectors need constant updating. For content that carries a watermark, the tool can look for the mark directly.
gl.yapay-zeka-icerik-tespiti.why: Schools, media organizations and platforms want to know where content comes from, yet detectors can produce false positives and false negatives. A student's own homework being labeled as AI-written can cause real unfairness. Results should therefore be treated as a clue, not as proof on their own.
gl.yapay-zeka-ile-goruntu-duzenleme.def: Using AI models to handle tasks such as removing objects, swapping backgrounds, retouching and color correction in photos and other images, often with a brush stroke or a written command.
gl.yapay-zeka-ile-goruntu-duzenleme.exam: An online seller can replace the cluttered background of a product photo with a plain studio backdrop using a single command.
In traditional tools, the user changes pixels by hand or with preset filters. In AI-assisted tools, the model predicts the requested result and generates missing or new detail itself.
How is AI image editing different from traditional editing software?
Not always easily. Some platforms and tools add labels or metadata showing that AI was used, but these can be stripped, so checking the source remains important.
Can you tell whether an edited image is real?
gl.yapay-zeka-ile-goruntu-duzenleme.how: These tools rely on models that have learned how images look from millions of examples. The user selects a region or types a command such as “turn the sky into a sunset,” and the model reads the image and the instruction together and regenerates the relevant pixels. Some operations use classic algorithms, while others use generative models. With generative methods, the system does more than adjust existing pixels; it invents detail that was not there. The result usually appears within a few seconds.
gl.yapay-zeka-ile-goruntu-duzenleme.why: Retouching that once took expertise and hours can now be done with tools almost anyone can use. This speeds up e-commerce, advertising and social media production. The same ease also makes it simpler to create fake or misleading images, which keeps image authenticity at the center of the debate.
gl.yapay-zeka-ile-guvenlik-acigi-bulma.d: The use of AI models to examine software code or systems and identify security flaws. It is a dual-use capability that both defenders and attackers can exploit.
gl.yapay-zeka-ile-guvenlik-acigi-bulma.e: A developer has a model review an open-source project's code and receives a list of possible memory errors; the team checks each item by hand and fixes the real ones.
gl.yapay-zeka-ile-guvenlik-acigi-bulma.f: For now it is seen as a complementary tool. A model can produce many possible findings, but deciding which ones are real and serious still takes an expert.
The usual approach is responsible disclosure: the flaw is first reported to the software maker, a reasonable time is given for a patch, and details are made public afterwards.
gl.yapay-zeka-ile-guvenlik-acigi-bulma.h: A model reads source code, looks for risky coding patterns and explains how a flaw might be exploited. It can also help generate malformed or unexpected inputs to stress a program, a technique known as fuzzing. Traditional scanners work from fixed rules, while language models can grasp the context of code, but they can also produce findings that are not real. That is why an expert needs to verify the results.
gl.yapay-zeka-ile-guvenlik-acigi-bulma.w: Finding flaws before attackers do is one of the core goals of software security. AI can speed this up and lighten the load on small teams. The same ability also helps malicious actors, which is why sharing findings responsibly, by notifying the software owner first, matters.
gl.yapay-zeka-ile-muzik-uretimi.def: The use of AI models to create new music, instrument sounds or vocals from inputs such as a written description, a melody or an audio sample.
gl.yapay-zeka-ile-muzik-uretimi.example: A video creator can type “a calm background track with acoustic guitar” and listen to several alternative tracks within minutes.
gl.yapay-zeka-ile-muzik-uretimi.faq.0.a: It varies by country and by the terms of the service used, and the legal debate is still ongoing. It is worth reading the service’s terms before using a track commercially.
gl.yapay-zeka-ile-muzik-uretimi.faq.0.q: Who owns the copyright to AI-generated music?
gl.yapay-zeka-ile-muzik-uretimi.faq.1.a: Opinions differ. Some see the tools as an aid to the creative process, while others worry about lost work in areas such as background music and about the use of artists’ work as training data.
gl.yapay-zeka-ile-muzik-uretimi.how: These models are trained on large collections of music and learn how notes, rhythms and timbres follow one another over time. When a user types something like “a slow piano piece for a film scene,” the model produces an audio waveform or a note sequence that fits the description. Some systems output audio directly, while others first generate note data such as MIDI and then render it as sound. The result depends on how detailed the prompt is and on the data the model was trained on.
gl.yapay-zeka-ile-muzik-uretimi.why: Because it cuts the cost and time of producing music, video makers, game studios and advertisers are paying attention. At the same time, there are open debates about which recordings the models were trained on and how artists’ rights should be protected. The two issues often appear together in the news, since the technology raises legal and ethical questions along with its creative possibilities.
gl.yapay-zeka-ile-verimlilik-artisi.def: The ability to do the same work faster, with less effort, or to produce more with the same effort by using AI tools. Productivity describes output relative to the effort put in.
gl.yapay-zeka-ile-verimlilik-artisi.exam: If an accounting office employee has AI draft routine email replies to clients and only reviews them, they can handle more clients in the same day.
No. The time saved can also lead a company to produce more, improve service quality or move staff to other tasks. Which of these happens depends on the company's choices.
Do productivity gains automatically mean fewer employees?
It is not guaranteed. In work where outputs must be checked closely or mistakes are costly, the gains may be limited. The effect varies with the task and with how the tool is used.
Does AI increase productivity in every job?
gl.yapay-zeka-ile-verimlilik-artisi.how: AI creates productivity gains by speeding up tedious, repetitive tasks. Drafting text, summarizing meeting notes, suggesting code or scanning documents are typical examples. The worker has the tool prepare a first draft and spends their own time reviewing and making decisions. The gain is not the same for every task. When a tool produces flawed output, the time spent fixing it can eat into the savings. The effect therefore depends on the type of work and on how well the person uses the tool.
gl.yapay-zeka-ile-verimlilik-artisi.why: Productivity gains are the most commonly cited reason companies invest in AI. Economists also debate whether the technology will raise overall productivity over time. Because results reported in the news vary by study, sector and measurement method, relying on a single figure can be misleading.
gl.yapay-zeka-kaynakli-zararlardan-sorum: The question of who, among developers, distributors, operators and users, can be held legally responsible when an AI system causes financial, physical or reputational harm.

When a vehicle with an AI-assisted driving system is involved in a crash, how responsibility is shared among the manufacturer, the software provider and the driver is debated, and the outcome varies by country and circumstances.
Under current legal systems, AI is not a legal person. Liability falls on the individuals or organizations that develop, operate or use it.
Can an AI system itself be held legally liable?
It depends on the circumstances, the terms of use and the law of the country concerned. There is no single answer, and for a specific case it is best to consult a lawyer.
Who is responsible if a chatbot gives wrong information and causes harm?

Existing legal systems generally apply rules that are not specific to AI, such as fault-based liability, product liability and contract law. Harm may stem from a model error, misuse, poor data or inadequate oversight, and with many parties along the chain, assigning responsibility is hard. Because it can be difficult to explain why a model made a decision, proving what went wrong can also be a problem. Some jurisdictions are discussing or adopting AI-specific liability rules to reduce this uncertainty.

In areas such as self-driving cars, medical advice systems and hiring algorithms, errors can cause real harm. Uncertainty about liability affects both victims' ability to seek compensation and companies' decisions about releasing products. Rules that are too strict or too loose can upset the balance between protection and innovation.
gl.yapay-zeka-kisi.def: A period in which unmet, overblown expectations cause interest, investment and research funding for AI to drop sharply. The term describes the boom-and-bust pattern in the field's history.
gl.yapay-zeka-kisi.example: In the 1980s, companies selling expert systems and firms building specialized AI computers such as Lisp machines lost customers and saw their market shrink as cheaper general-purpose computers rose.
gl.yapay-zeka-kisi.faq.0.a: People usually speak of two major ones, in the 1970s and in the late 1980s. Historians do not agree on their exact boundaries, and smaller downturns are also mentioned.
gl.yapay-zeka-kisi.faq.0.q: How many AI winters have there been?
gl.yapay-zeka-kisi.faq.1.a: Nobody can say for sure. Some commentators think inflated expectations could cause another letdown; others argue that real, widespread use of today's technology makes this period unlike the earlier ones.
gl.yapay-zeka-kisi.faq.1.q: Will there be another AI winter?
gl.yapay-zeka-kisi.how: The cycle tends to run the same way: a new method brings big promises, money flows in, results fall short of expectations, disappointment sets in and funding is cut. History usually points to two major winters: roughly the 1970s, and the stretch from the late 1980s into the early 1990s. In the second, the collapse of the expert system market and of the market for specialized hardware played a part. Research never stopped completely during these winters; many ideas kept developing in a quieter climate.
gl.yapay-zeka-kisi.why: The term often comes up when today's wave of AI investment is discussed. One view holds that inflated expectations could lead to another downturn; another says things are different now because today's systems are actually used by large numbers of people. History cannot predict the future, but it is a useful reminder about managing expectations.
gl.yapay-zeka-okuryazarligi.def: The ability to understand what everyday AI systems do, how they work and where they can go wrong, and to use, question and evaluate them thoughtfully.
gl.yapay-zeka-okuryazarligi.example: A student checks the source a chatbot cited, finds that it does not exist, and does not use the answer as is in the assignment.
gl.yapay-zeka-okuryazarligi.faq.0.a: No. The core is understanding what these systems can and cannot do and how far to trust their output; writing code is not required.
gl.yapay-zeka-okuryazarligi.faq.0.q: Do you need to know how to code to be AI literate?
gl.yapay-zeka-okuryazarligi.faq.1.a: Try the tools on your own tasks and watch for their mistakes, compare outputs with reliable sources, and follow trustworthy educational material.
gl.yapay-zeka-okuryazarligi.how: It does not require technical expertise; it is built from a few basic habits. One is knowing that models learn from data, so they can make mistakes and reflect biases in that data. Another is knowing that generative AI can sound convincing while being wrong, and checking sources accordingly. It also includes knowing which personal or confidential information should not be shared with these tools. Schools, companies and public institutions try to build these skills through training programs.
gl.yapay-zeka-okuryazarligi.why: As AI shows up more at work, in school and in the news, there is a growing need for people who can use the tools without trusting them blindly. The skill is also seen as part of protecting oneself against misinformation, privacy risks and bad decisions.
gl.yapay-zeka-olay-veritabani.def: A public archive that collects harms, failures and misfires caused by AI systems. Its purpose is to build a shared memory so the same mistakes are not repeated.
gl.yapay-zeka-olay-veritabani.example: A chatbot giving a user harmful advice, or a facial recognition system matching the wrong person, are the kinds of cases that can appear in such an archive as incident records.
gl.yapay-zeka-olay-veritabani.faq.0.a: Researchers, journalists, policymakers and product teams use it. It is a source people turn to for real-world examples when assessing risk.
gl.yapay-zeka-olay-veritabani.faq.0.q: Who uses an AI incident database?
gl.yapay-zeka-olay-veritabani.faq.1.a: No. Usually the entries are cases that caused real harm or came close to it. The exact criteria vary from one archive to another.
gl.yapay-zeka-olay-veritabani.faq.1.q: Is every AI error recorded as an incident?
gl.yapay-zeka-olay-veritabani.how: Incidents are compiled from news reports, research papers and user submissions. Each entry records what happened, which system was involved, who was affected and what kind of harm resulted. Entries are categorized, so researchers and journalists can search by sector or type of failure. Much like accident reporting in aviation, patterns can be drawn out of many individual cases. One of the best-known examples is the AI Incident Database project.
gl.yapay-zeka-olay-veritabani.why: AI failures often remain scattered news stories and are soon forgotten. A shared archive shows which risks have actually materialized, so regulators, companies and researchers can rely on recorded cases rather than guesses. It also gives product teams a practical way to learn from past mistakes.

gl.yapay-zeka-onyargisi.def.en: When an AI system systematically produces erroneous or unfair results against certain people or groups. It mostly stems from imbalances in the training data.

gl.yapay-zeka-onyargisi.example.en: A résumé-screening system trained on data in which mostly male candidates were hired in the past may systematically score female candidates lower.

gl.yapay-zeka-onyargisi.faq.0.a.en: The main methods are diversifying the training data, testing results separately for different groups, auditing decisions regularly and keeping human oversight in critical decisions.

gl.yapay-zeka-onyargisi.faq.0.q.en: How can AI bias be reduced?

gl.yapay-zeka-onyargisi.faq.1.a.en: Building a completely unbiased system is very difficult, because data and definitions come from people. The goal is to measure bias, be transparent and minimize its harmful effects.

gl.yapay-zeka-onyargisi.how.en: When certain groups are underrepresented in the training data or the data contains past discriminatory decisions, a model learns and repeats these imbalances. Bias can arise from data collection, labeling, the model's design or the way it is used.

gl.yapay-zeka-onyargisi.why.en: In areas that affect people's lives, such as hiring, credit assessment, healthcare and security, biased decisions can lead to serious injustices. That is why regulations such as the EU AI Act impose data quality and oversight requirements on high-risk systems.

gl.yapay-zeka-sarmalayicisi.def: A product that uses another company's AI model through an API and adds its own interface and features, instead of building a model of its own. It is often seen as a thin layer on top of someone else's technology.
gl.yapay-zeka-sarmalayicisi.example: An app that lets users chat with uploaded PDF files is a typical wrapper if it calls a provider's language model behind the scenes.
gl.yapay-zeka-sarmalayicisi.faq.0.a: Not in itself. Many successful software products are built on someone else's technology. What matters is how much original value the product adds beyond the model.
gl.yapay-zeka-sarmalayicisi.faq.0.q: Is being a wrapper a bad thing?
gl.yapay-zeka-sarmalayicisi.faq.1.a: A wrapper usually calls an off-the-shelf model as it is and builds a product around it. Fine-tuning adapts a model with additional data for a specific job. The two are not mutually exclusive, and a product can use both.
gl.yapay-zeka-sarmalayicisi.faq.1.q: How is a wrapper different from a fine-tuned model?
gl.yapay-zeka-sarmalayicisi.how: The app takes the user's input, combines it with instructions it has prepared, and sends it to a provider's model through an API. It then formats the reply, perhaps blends it with its own data sources, and presents it through a tidy interface. Because the model is rented, the product is relatively quick and cheap to build. The trade-off is that the company depends on the model's pricing, usage rules and version changes.
gl.yapay-zeka-sarmalayicisi.why: The term is used both as a neutral description and as a criticism. Critics say such products are easy to copy and that the model provider could add the same feature to its own product. Defenders argue that a good interface, proprietary data and a workflow tailored to a specific field create real value. The debate comes down to how durable AI startups can be.
gl.yapay-zeka-sermaye-harcamasi.def: Money companies spend on long-lived assets for AI, such as data centers, chips, servers and networking, which is reported separately from everyday operating costs in financial statements.
gl.yapay-zeka-sermaye-harcamasi.example: When a cloud company reports quarterly results and says it will raise capital spending on new data centers and GPU purchases, that is an AI capex headline.
gl.yapay-zeka-sermaye-harcamasi.faq.0.a: Capex is investment in assets used over a long period, while opex covers everyday costs like salaries, rent and cloud services. If a company buys GPUs it is usually capex; if it rents them, it usually shows up as opex.
gl.yapay-zeka-sermaye-harcamasi.faq.0.q: What is the difference between capex and operating expenses (opex)?
gl.yapay-zeka-sermaye-harcamasi.faq.1.a: Because the spending is enormous and the payoff is still uncertain. One view is that demand will justify it; another is that there is a risk of overinvestment.
gl.yapay-zeka-sermaye-harcamasi.how: Capex, or capital expenditure, is money a company spends on assets it will use for many years. In AI this mostly means accelerator chips such as GPUs, servers, cooling and power infrastructure, and the construction of new data centers. Large cloud companies usually record this spending as an asset and spread its cost over time through depreciation, instead of expensing it all at once. Each quarter, companies report their capex and outlook to investors.
gl.yapay-zeka-sermaye-harcamasi.why: Much of the AI race is being run through this spending, so capex announcements from companies such as Microsoft, Alphabet, Amazon and Meta show the pace of the industry. Investors debate whether the spending will bring enough revenue. It also feeds wider debates about electricity, chip and water demand.
gl.yapay-zeka-siber-guvenligi.def: The effort to protect AI systems from attack and manipulation; in a broader sense it also covers the use of AI in cyberattacks and defense.
gl.yapay-zeka-siber-guvenligi.example: An AI assistant that summarizes a company's emails could be steered by a command hidden inside an incoming message, which is a typical prompt injection.
gl.yapay-zeka-siber-guvenligi.faq.0.a: It is an attack in which a model mistakes hidden instructions, from a user or from content it reads, for legitimate commands and drifts from its real task. It is especially risky for assistants that browse the web or read documents.
gl.yapay-zeka-siber-guvenligi.faq.1.a: Security focuses on protecting the system from attackers. Safety is about the model behaving as intended and avoiding harm even when no attack is happening.
gl.yapay-zeka-siber-guvenligi.faq.1.q: How is AI security different from AI safety?
gl.yapay-zeka-siber-guvenligi.how: Attackers can target the model itself or the systems around it. Prompt injection diverts a model from its real task using instructions hidden in a web page or document. Data poisoning adds harmful examples to training data, and model theft and leaking of training data are also known risks. On the defense side, teams use input and output filters, access controls, limits on what the model is permitted to do, and regular penetration testing. In the other direction, AI is also used to write phishing emails or to detect threats.
gl.yapay-zeka-siber-guvenligi.why: As companies connect AI assistants to email, documents and internal systems, a hijacked model can become a door to real damage. Traditional security measures do not cover all of these new attack types. For that reason, organizations have begun to treat AI systems as a separate risk area.
gl.yapay-zeka-yatirim-getirisi.def: A measure of what an organization gains from an AI project compared with the money and effort put into it. The gain can be cost savings, higher revenue or time saved.
gl.yapay-zeka-yatirim-getirisi.example: An insurance company using an AI tool to summarize claim files can estimate ROI by comparing how much the time spent per file has fallen against the tool's total cost.
gl.yapay-zeka-yatirim-getirisi.faq.0.a: Because some of the benefits are indirect and do not show up right away. Results like staff spending time on higher-value work or improved customer satisfaction need assumptions to be converted into money.
gl.yapay-zeka-yatirim-getirisi.faq.0.q: Why is AI ROI hard to measure?
gl.yapay-zeka-yatirim-getirisi.faq.1.a: Yes. Even at a small scale, comparing a tool's cost with the time it saves is a good enough starting point for deciding whether to keep using it.
gl.yapay-zeka-yatirim-getirisi.faq.1.q: Is this calculation meaningful for a small business too?
gl.yapay-zeka-yatirim-getirisi.how: The calculation compares two sides. The cost side includes software or model usage fees, infrastructure, data preparation, integration and staff training. The benefit side counts outcomes such as faster task completion, fewer errors or increased sales. Some of these gains are easy to put a price on, while others, like customer satisfaction, are indirect. For that reason, companies often start with a small pilot, measure the results first and scale up afterward.
gl.yapay-zeka-yatirim-getirisi.why: Spending on AI tools has grown quickly, so executives want to see what they are getting for it. The ROI debate that appears often in the news reflects the distance between the technology's promise and results that organizations can actually measure. Projects without a clear yardstick can stall at the experiment stage.
gl.yapay-zeka-yerlisi-sirket.def: A company that builds its product, workflows and organization around AI from the start. AI is not a feature added later but the foundation of how the business operates.
gl.yapay-zeka-yerlisi-sirket.example: A legal technology startup that takes requests in plain language and runs contract review through an AI model fits the description; an older software package that later gained a chat box usually does not.
gl.yapay-zeka-yerlisi-sirket.faq.0.a: AI-enabled companies add AI functions to products that already exist. In AI-native companies the product is built so that it could not exist without AI. There is still no agreed standard for where the line falls.
gl.yapay-zeka-yerlisi-sirket.faq.0.q: What is the difference between AI-native and AI-enabled?
gl.yapay-zeka-yerlisi-sirket.faq.1.a: No. Many use models built by others through an API and create value through product design, data and workflow.
gl.yapay-zeka-yerlisi-sirket.faq.1.q: Do all AI-native companies build their own models?
gl.yapay-zeka-yerlisi-sirket.how: These companies design their products by taking what AI models can do as the starting point. The product is shaped around the model's responses and its ability to carry out parts of a task on its own. Internally, AI tools are used routinely for work such as software development, customer support or analysis. Established companies, by contrast, usually add AI features to products that already exist. A rough test of the difference is whether the product still makes sense once the AI is taken away.
gl.yapay-zeka-yerlisi-sirket.why: The phrase turns up often in startup and investment coverage as a way to tell whether a company has truly put AI at its core. There is no precise definition, though, and it is sometimes just marketing language. It is more useful to look at how dependent the product really is on AI than at the label.
gl.yapay-zeka-yonetisimi.def: The set of rules, processes and lines of responsibility that determine how AI systems are built, used and overseen by organizations and governments. It ranges from internal company policies to international agreements.
gl.yapay-zeka-yonetisimi.example: Before deploying a credit scoring model, a bank gets approval from a risk committee, keeps records of the decisions and assigns a team to review appeals.
gl.yapay-zeka-yonetisimi.faq.0.a: No. Ethics debates what is right; governance turns those principles into practice through responsibilities, processes and oversight mechanisms.
gl.yapay-zeka-yonetisimi.faq.0.q: Is AI governance the same as AI ethics?
gl.yapay-zeka-yonetisimi.faq.1.a: No. Any organization that uses AI has to decide who uses which tool, with what data and for what purpose, even if it does so informally. Only the level of formality differs.
gl.yapay-zeka-yonetisimi.faq.1.q: Does governance only concern large companies?
gl.yapay-zeka-yonetisimi.how: Inside a company, governance is made up of parts such as committees that decide which AI applications may be used, risk assessments, documentation for data and models, and incident reporting procedures. Each system gets an owner, and responsibility for problems is written down in advance. At the national and international level, laws, standards and voluntary principles serve the same goal. The layers complement each other: law sets the minimum bar, and internal policy ties daily practice to that bar.
gl.yapay-zeka-yonetisimi.why: AI systems now affect people directly, from hiring to credit decisions. Without governance, mistakes, discrimination and data breaches can grow unnoticed. For companies it also means legal compliance, customer trust and reputational risk, and regulatory debates in the news usually fall under this heading.

gl.yapay-zeka.def.en: The general name for technologies that enable computers to perform tasks that normally require human intelligence, such as learning, reasoning, understanding language, seeing and making decisions.

gl.yapay-zeka.example.en: Your phone's face unlock, the spam filter in your email, a navigation app's traffic predictions and chat assistants such as ChatGPT are examples of AI in daily life.

gl.yapay-zeka.faq.0.a.en: No. Artificial intelligence is the name of the overall field; machine learning is today's most common way of achieving AI. Deep learning is a subfield of machine learning.

gl.yapay-zeka.faq.0.q.en: Are artificial intelligence and machine learning the same thing?

gl.yapay-zeka.faq.1.a.en: Today's AI systems do not think consciously like humans; they make predictions and generate output based on the patterns they have learned. Although they surpass human level on some tasks, they can make simple mistakes on others.

gl.yapay-zeka.how.en: Artificial intelligence is not a single technology but an umbrella term for many methods. Older systems ran on rules written one by one by people; most of today's systems use machine learning to learn patterns in large datasets on their own. A language model learns the structure of language from billions of sentences, and an image model learns what objects look like from millions of photos, then applies that knowledge to new inputs.

gl.yapay-zeka.why.en: It is changing the way business is done in nearly every sector, from search engines to banking, healthcare to advertising. Alongside opportunities such as productivity gains, new products and a transformation of the labor market, it brings risks such as misinformation, privacy and security; for this reason, governments are drafting laws to regulate AI.

gl.yapay-zekanin-enerji-tuketimi.def: The total electricity used to train AI models and serve them to users, mostly by the servers and cooling systems in data centers.
gl.yapay-zekanin-enerji-tuketimi.example: A single question to a chatbot uses little electricity, but when the same service answers millions of people every day, the data center's power bill and grid load rise noticeably.
gl.yapay-zekanin-enerji-tuketimi.faq.0.a: No. The same amount of electricity produces very different emissions depending on whether it comes from coal or renewables. The data center's location and the regional energy mix therefore matter.
gl.yapay-zekanin-enerji-tuketimi.faq.0.q: Does AI's carbon footprint depend only on how much electricity it uses?
gl.yapay-zekanin-enerji-tuketimi.faq.1.a: For a given model, training is intense but happens once. If the model is used very widely, though, inference can add up to more than training over time. The balance depends on the model and its usage.
gl.yapay-zekanin-enerji-tuketimi.faq.1.q: Does training or inference use more energy?
gl.yapay-zekanin-enerji-tuketimi.how: Energy is spent in two phases. In training, thousands of accelerator chips run intensively for weeks. In inference, the model runs every time it answers a user's question; a single query is small, but with millions of users the total becomes large. Cooling, needed to remove the heat servers produce, uses electricity too. Overall consumption depends on model size, hardware efficiency and how heavily the service is used.
gl.yapay-zekanin-enerji-tuketimi.why: Data centers' power demand can strain local grids, which brings new power plant investments and energy deals onto the agenda. Estimates vary widely depending on method. More efficient chips and smaller models reduce energy per task, but rising total usage can offset those gains. The topic sits at the center of both climate and economic debates.
gl.yapay-zekanin-istihdama-etkisi.def: The effect AI has on which occupations change, which jobs shrink and which new jobs emerge. It is a shared concern for workers, companies and governments.
gl.yapay-zekanin-istihdama-etkisi.exampl: If AI answers frequently asked questions at a call center, agents' work may shift from routine queries toward complex complaints, while the company makes its own decision about team size.
No one can say for certain. The current debate is mostly about some tasks being automated and jobs changing, rather than whole occupations disappearing. Experts do not agree on the scale of the effect.
Commonly suggested steps are learning to use AI tools in one's own field and investing in distinctly human skills such as judgment, communication and domain knowledge. These are general approaches, not guarantees.
How can workers prepare for the change?
gl.yapay-zekanin-istihdama-etkisi.how: To understand the effect, it helps to think of a job as a bundle of tasks rather than a single block. AI can take over some tasks and leave others to people. If most of an occupation's tasks can be automated, the number of jobs in that area may fall. If only some tasks are handed off, the job usually transforms instead. Technology can also create new kinds of work. Outcomes vary by sector, company choices, education levels and regulation, and they cannot be predicted with certainty.
gl.yapay-zekanin-istihdama-etkisi.why: Worry about job loss is one of the most closely followed parts of the AI debate. Researchers and institutions put forward different scenarios: some expect major disruption, while others argue the effect will be slow and gradual. Because of this uncertainty, skills training and worker protection policies remain on the agenda.
gl.yapilandirilmis-cikti.def: A language model responding in a predefined format, such as JSON with specific fields, instead of free text. The output can be read and processed directly by software.
gl.yapilandirilmis-cikti.example: An app that reads an invoice image asks the model for a JSON object with date, amount and vendor name fields instead of a free paragraph, and passes it straight to the accounting system.
gl.yapilandirilmis-cikti.faq.0.a: No. The format can be made to follow the schema, but the accuracy of the information inside must be checked separately. A model can return a wrong value in a perfectly valid format.
gl.yapilandirilmis-cikti.faq.0.q: Does structured output guarantee the content is correct?
gl.yapilandirilmis-cikti.faq.1.a: They are close but not identical. Structured output means the response itself takes a set format. In function calling, the model states in a structured form which function should be run and with what parameters.
gl.yapilandirilmis-cikti.faq.1.q: Is structured output the same as function calling?
gl.yapilandirilmis-cikti.how: The developer defines the expected fields and their types in a schema. With some providers, a constraint is applied during generation so the model can only pick next pieces that fit the schema. In other cases the format is requested in the prompt and the output is validated afterward, with a retry if it does not match. A valid format does not mean the content is correct: every field can be filled in and the values can still be wrong.
gl.yapilandirilmis-cikti.why: Language models write fluent text meant for people, but software systems need orderly data. Structured output is the bridge between the two, making it possible to pass a model's result safely into a database, a form or another program. It is one of the basic requirements for automation in business applications.
gl.yardimci-pilot.def: An AI tool that works alongside a user and offers suggestions while leaving the final decision and control with the human. The name comes from the second pilot who assists the captain of an aircraft.
gl.yardimci-pilot.example: GitHub Copilot offers suggestions while a developer writes code, and the developer decides whether to accept them.
gl.yardimci-pilot.faq.0.a: A copilot works with the user step by step, and the person stays in control. An agent, given a goal, carries out a multi-step job more independently, using tools and making intermediate decisions itself.
gl.yardimci-pilot.faq.0.q: What is the difference between a copilot and an AI agent?
gl.yardimci-pilot.faq.1.a: Both. Companies such as Microsoft and GitHub use Copilot as a product name, but lowercase copilot is also a general term for any AI tool that works alongside a person.
gl.yardimci-pilot.faq.1.q: Is Copilot a brand name or a general term?
gl.yardimci-pilot.how: A copilot is built into the application the user is working in and sees the current context, such as the code being written, the open document or an email. Based on that context, it produces a draft, a correction or a suggested next step. The user can accept, edit or reject the suggestion. The workflow stays in the user's hands while the AI adds speed and ideas. Unlike an autonomous agent, it keeps working with the person instead of chaining steps together and finishing on its own.
gl.yardimci-pilot.why: The copilot approach is common in business because it keeps human oversight in place against AI errors while still saving time. Companies add such features to their products to offer AI without pulling users out of their usual environment. However, Copilot is also a product brand for some companies, so the general meaning and the brand name can get mixed up.
gl.yari-denetimli-ogrenme.def: A machine learning approach that trains a model using a small amount of labeled data together with a large amount of unlabeled data. It sits between supervised and unsupervised learning.
gl.yari-denetimli-ogrenme.example: A hospital might have radiologists label only a few hundred X-rays, then add thousands of unlabeled X-rays to training in the hope of getting a better model.
gl.yari-denetimli-ogrenme.faq.0.a: Semi-supervised learning has at least a few labeled examples, and the model learns its target from them. Unsupervised learning has no labels at all.
gl.yari-denetimli-ogrenme.faq.0.q: What is the difference between semi-supervised and unsupervised learning?
gl.yari-denetimli-ogrenme.faq.1.a: No. If its assumptions fail, for example if the unlabeled data differs from the labeled data, results can get worse, so the method is not helpful for every problem.
gl.yari-denetimli-ogrenme.faq.1.q: Does semi-supervised learning always give better results?
gl.yari-denetimli-ogrenme.how: The process starts with an initial model trained on a small labeled set. The structure of the unlabeled data then comes into play, drawing on assumptions such as the tendency of similar examples to share the same label. In one common method, the model makes predictions on unlabeled examples, treats the ones it is confident about as provisional labels, and retrains itself on the enlarged dataset. This lets most of the costly labeling work be skipped.
gl.yari-denetimli-ogrenme.why: Producing labels often takes expert effort; for instance, only doctors can label medical images correctly. Semi-supervised learning promises to cut that cost. Still, if a model treats its own wrong predictions as labels, errors can reinforce themselves, so careful validation is needed.
gl.yari-iletken.def: A class of material whose electrical conductivity sits between that of a conductor and an insulator and can be controlled. It is the basic substance of transistors and therefore of all modern chips.
gl.yari-iletken.example: The processor, memory, and camera sensor in a smartphone are all made from semiconductors, and AI accelerators rely on the same basic class of material.
gl.yari-iletken.faq.0.a: Not exactly. A semiconductor is a class of material, while a chip is a circuit made from it. In everyday language and in news stories the two are often used interchangeably.
gl.yari-iletken.faq.0.q: Is a semiconductor the same thing as a chip?
gl.yari-iletken.faq.1.a: No. Silicon is by far the most common, but materials such as gallium nitride, silicon carbide, and gallium arsenide are also used in power electronics, lighting, and high-frequency applications.
gl.yari-iletken.faq.1.q: Are semiconductors made only of silicon?
gl.yari-iletken.how: The conductivity of a semiconductor such as silicon can be tuned by adding tiny amounts of other atoms (doping) and by applying an electric field. This lets the material act like a switch that turns current on and off. A transistor is a very small version of that switch; a chip arranges billions of them side by side to carry out computation and memory functions. Chips are made on silicon wafers through many steps involving light patterning and chemical processing.
gl.yari-iletken.why: AI chips, memory, and networking gear all rest on semiconductors. Advanced manufacturing capacity is concentrated in a few companies and countries, so supply chains, export controls, and investment incentives come up often in AI news. In everyday usage, the word also refers to the industry itself.
gl.yas-dogrulama.def: A general name for methods that check whether a person using an online service meets the required age limit. It is used to keep children away from inappropriate content and risky AI applications.
gl.yas-dogrulama.example: Instead of relying on a simple checkbox, a chatbot app might turn to a verification service that asks users for an ID document or a face scan.
gl.yas-dogrulama.faq.0.a: No. With self-declaration the user simply states their age and nobody checks it. Verification confirms it through an ID document, a trusted record or facial analysis.
gl.yas-dogrulama.faq.0.q: Is self-declared age the same as age verification?
gl.yas-dogrulama.faq.1.a: It can. Collecting ID or face data carries risk, so approaches that do not store the data, or that share only a yes-or-no age confirmation, are often preferred.
gl.yas-dogrulama.faq.1.q: Does age verification create privacy problems?
gl.yas-dogrulama.how: The simplest method is letting users type in their own birth date, but that is easy to get around. Stricter approaches involve uploading an ID document, confirming age through a trusted source such as a bank or mobile carrier, or estimating age from a selfie. Some systems only issue a confirmation that the person is above a certain age, without passing identity details to the service. Which method is chosen depends on the balance between safety needs and privacy.
gl.yas-dogrulama.why: Chatbots and generative AI apps have spread quickly among children and teenagers, raising the question of whether age limits can really be enforced. Age verification aims to protect minors, but collecting ID or face data raises privacy concerns of its own, which is why the topic is contested.
gl.yasakli-yapay-zeka-uygulamalari.def: AI applications that the EU AI Act bans outright because they pose unacceptable risk and conflict with fundamental rights and human dignity.
gl.yasakli-yapay-zeka-uygulamalari.examp: A company using an AI system at work to infer employees' emotional states from their facial expressions would be engaging in a practice the Act lists as prohibited.
gl.yasakli-yapay-zeka-uygulamalari.faq.0: For most of them, no. For some, such as real-time biometric identification in public spaces, law enforcement gets narrow exceptions tied to strict conditions. The details are in the text of the Act.
Are there any exceptions to the prohibited practices?
gl.yasakli-yapay-zeka-uygulamalari.faq.1: The Act provides for the highest level of administrative fines for these violations. The exact amounts and procedures depend on the text of the Act and the relevant authorities.
What happens to those who break the ban?
gl.yasakli-yapay-zeka-uygulamalari.how: The Act lists these practices one by one. They include social scoring that rates people by their social behavior, systems that manipulate people through subliminal techniques, applications that exploit the vulnerabilities of certain groups, building facial-image databases by scraping the internet or camera footage, emotion recognition in workplaces and schools, and real-time remote biometric identification in public spaces. For the last one, law enforcement is given narrow exceptions. The bans are among the first provisions of the Act to take effect.
gl.yasakli-yapay-zeka-uygulamalari.why: The bans draw the clearest line against using AI for surveillance and manipulation. Which applications fall within them is debated because it touches the balance between security and freedoms; the biometric identification exceptions in particular have drawn criticism.
gl.yeniden-beceri-kazandirma.def: Workers learning a new set of skills so they can move into a different role when their current jobs change or disappear. It is about preparing for another kind of work, not about getting deeper in the same field.
gl.yeniden-beceri-kazandirma.example: A bank that trains its branch-operations staff in customer data analysis and moves them to a different department as digital channels spread is carrying out reskilling.
gl.yeniden-beceri-kazandirma.faq.0.a: Reskilling means learning different skills in order to move into a new role. Upskilling means improving skills within the current role. In practice the two often overlap.
gl.yeniden-beceri-kazandirma.faq.0.q: What is the difference between reskilling and upskilling?
gl.yeniden-beceri-kazandirma.faq.1.a: That is debated. Some argue it falls to employers, others to governments and others to individuals. In practice it usually takes shared effort.
gl.yeniden-beceri-kazandirma.how: The process begins when a company or institution identifies which skills are declining and which will be needed. Workers are then offered routes such as courses, workshops, on-the-job training or certificate programs. For example, someone who does data entry might be moved toward data analysis, and a customer service agent toward overseeing AI systems. Programs are run by employers, public agencies or educational institutions. Success is judged by whether what was learned turns into a real job.
gl.yeniden-beceri-kazandirma.why: Because AI is rapidly changing what jobs consist of, reskilling is seen as one of the main ways to reduce the cost of the transition that automation creates. For companies it can be an alternative to hiring from outside, and for workers it can mean job security. Who should pay for it is a separate debate.
gl.yeniden-siralama-modeli.def: A model that takes candidate documents found by a search and examines them more closely against the query, reordering them from most to least relevant.
gl.yeniden-siralama-modeli.example: In an internal document assistant, embedding search returns 50 paragraphs, the reranker picks the five most relevant ones, and only those are sent to the language model.
gl.yeniden-siralama-modeli.faq.0.a: An embedding model encodes the query and documents separately, which is fast but coarser. A reranker reads the query and document together, which is more accurate but slower. They are usually used together.
gl.yeniden-siralama-modeli.faq.0.q: What is the difference between an embedding model and a reranker?
gl.yeniden-siralama-modeli.faq.1.a: No. For a small, well-organized collection, embedding search may be enough. If results are often off-topic or the collection is large, adding a reranker usually makes a difference.
gl.yeniden-siralama-modeli.faq.1.q: Does every RAG system need a reranker?
gl.yeniden-siralama-modeli.how: Search is often done in two stages. In the first, a fast method such as an embedding model pulls dozens or hundreds of candidates from a large collection. In the second, the reranker reads the query together with each candidate and assigns a relevance score. Because the query and document are examined jointly, the judgment is more accurate, but also slower. For that reason it is applied only to the short candidate list, and the highest-scoring results are kept.
gl.yeniden-siralama-modeli.why: A language model can only take in a limited amount of text, and irrelevant passages lower the quality of its answer. In retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) systems, reranking is a cheap and effective way to pass along just the few passages that truly help.
gl.yerel-dil-modeli.def: A large language model that runs on the user's own computer, phone or company server instead of connecting to a cloud service.
gl.yerel-dil-modeli.example: A law firm runs an open-weight model on its own server to summarize contracts, so client documents never leave the building.
gl.yerel-dil-modeli.faq.0.a: ChatGPT is a service that runs on OpenAI's servers and is used over the internet. A local model is downloaded and runs on your own device, so data stays with you, but its power is limited by your hardware.
gl.yerel-dil-modeli.faq.0.q: What is the difference between a local LLM and ChatGPT?
gl.yerel-dil-modeli.faq.1.a: No. Small quantized models run on an ordinary laptop. Larger and more capable models need a graphics card with plenty of memory.
gl.yerel-dil-modeli.faq.1.q: Do I need a very powerful computer to run a local model?
gl.yerel-dil-modeli.how: A model whose weights are publicly shared is downloaded and run with tools such as Ollama, llama.cpp or LM Studio. To fit the model into memory, quantization is applied: numbers are stored with fewer bits, so the file shrinks and quality may drop a little. Speed and the largest model you can run depend on graphics card memory and system RAM. Small models can run on an ordinary laptop, while larger ones need powerful hardware. Because everything happens on the device, prompts and documents are not sent elsewhere.
gl.yerel-dil-modeli.why: Privacy is the strongest argument for local models, since sensitive data stays with the person or company. Working offline and paying no per-use fees are further advantages, though there are hardware costs and setup effort. Local models are generally less capable than the largest cloud models.
gl.yerel-minimum.def: A point in a loss function that is lower than everything around it but is not necessarily the lowest point of the whole function. During training, an optimization algorithm can get stuck there.
gl.yerel-minimum.example: Training the same neural network twice with different random starting values can send it into different pits of the loss surface and produce slightly different results.
gl.yerel-minimum.faq.0.a: A local minimum is lower only than the points in its immediate neighborhood. The global minimum is the lowest value of the function over its whole domain. Every global minimum is also a local minimum, but not the other way around.
gl.yerel-minimum.faq.0.q: What is the difference between a local minimum and a global minimum?
gl.yerel-minimum.faq.1.a: Techniques such as momentum, learning rate schedules and the noise from mini-batch stochastic gradient descent can reduce the chance of getting stuck in pits. Training several times from different starting values is also used. None of them guarantees finding the global minimum.
gl.yerel-minimum.faq.1.q: How can training avoid getting stuck in a local minimum?
gl.yerel-minimum.how: A loss function can be pictured as a mountainous landscape: each parameter setting of the model is a location and the loss is the height. Gradient descent moves in the steepest downhill direction at each step. When it reaches a pit, every direction leads uphill and the slope approaches zero, so the algorithm stops. If that pit is not the deepest point in the landscape, the algorithm has landed in a local minimum. The lowest point of the entire landscape is the global minimum. Convex functions have only one minimum, while the loss surfaces of deep networks are far more complicated.
gl.yerel-minimum.why: This is a basic idea for understanding why optimization can fail. Still, in high-dimensional deep networks, research suggests that what makes training hard is often saddle points and flat regions rather than bad local minima. The topic is still being studied.
gl.yetenek-satin-alimi.def: A deal in which a company buys a startup, or hires its founders and employees, mainly to gain the team and its expertise rather than the startup's product.
gl.yetenek-satin-alimi.example: Microsoft's 2024 hiring of Inflection AI's founders and a large part of its team is often cited as an example of this kind of deal.
gl.yetenek-satin-alimi.faq.0.a: In a regular acquisition the goal is usually the product, customers or market share. In an acqui-hire the main target is the team, and the product often takes a back seat.
gl.yetenek-satin-alimi.faq.0.q: How is an acqui-hire different from a regular acquisition?
gl.yetenek-satin-alimi.faq.1.a: Usually the team moves to the buyer, but details depend on the deal. Equity, pay and the fate of those left behind differ from case to case.
gl.yetenek-satin-alimi.faq.1.q: What happens to employees in an acqui-hire?
gl.yetenek-satin-alimi.how: A large company wants to add a small startup's engineers and researchers to its own staff. It can do so through a full acquisition, or by hiring the founders and team and paying a licensing fee for the startup's technology. The startup's product is often shut down or left in the background. What investors receive depends on how the deal is structured. Because qualified AI researchers are scarce, this route is seen as a fast shortcut in the race to hire talent.
gl.yetenek-satin-alimi.why: Acqui-hires show how valuable skilled researchers are in AI. Some deals built on licensing and hiring have drawn the attention of competition authorities, because they can follow a different path from traditional merger review. Outcomes for employees and investors can also vary with the deal.
gl.yigin-boyutu.def: The number of training examples a model processes at once before it updates its parameters a single time. It affects training speed, memory use and how noisy the updates are.
gl.yigin-boyutu.example: A team whose training crashes with batches of 64 because the graphics card memory is full can drop the batch size to 16 and keep training.
gl.yigin-boyutu.faq.0.a: No. A large batch uses hardware more efficiently and gives a steadier gradient, but it needs more memory and can sometimes generalize worse. The best value depends on the task and the hardware.
gl.yigin-boyutu.faq.0.q: Is a larger batch size always better?
gl.yigin-boyutu.faq.1.a: The batch size can be reduced, or a technique called gradient accumulation can be used. It sums the gradients of several small batches and makes a single update, with an effect similar to one large batch.
gl.yigin-boyutu.faq.1.q: What can be done if memory is not enough?
gl.yigin-boyutu.how: Training data is fed to the model not one example at a time or all at once, but in groups of, say, 32 or 256 examples. The model computes the error for every example in the group, averages the gradients and makes one update. A large batch makes better use of the parallel power of graphics cards and gives a less noisy gradient estimate, but needs more memory. A small batch uses less memory and adds noise to the updates, which can sometimes help generalization.
gl.yigin-boyutu.why: Batch size determines how efficiently hardware is used, how fast training runs and whether a model fits in memory. For large models, graphics card memory is limited, so this value is a practical constraint. It is also linked to the learning rate; when the batch size changes, the rate may need retuning.
gl.yillik-tekrarlayan-gelir.def: The yearly value of a company's regular, expected-to-repeat income from subscriptions or contracts, commonly used as a size measure for software and AI service companies.
gl.yillik-tekrarlayan-gelir.example: An AI software company with 100,000 dollars in monthly recurring subscription revenue has an ARR of 1.2 million dollars.
gl.yillik-tekrarlayan-gelir.faq.0.a: No. ARR covers only revenue expected to repeat; one-off sales can appear in total revenue but not in ARR. ARR is also a forward-looking figure, not accounting revenue.
gl.yillik-tekrarlayan-gelir.faq.0.q: Is ARR the same as total revenue?
gl.yillik-tekrarlayan-gelir.faq.1.a: MRR is monthly recurring revenue and ARR is annual. ARR is roughly twelve times MRR.
gl.yillik-tekrarlayan-gelir.faq.1.q: What is the difference between ARR and MRR?
gl.yillik-tekrarlayan-gelir.how: In the simplest calculation, monthly recurring revenue is multiplied by twelve. One-off sales, setup fees and consulting that will not repeat are left out. New customers raise ARR, while cancellations and lost customers lower it. For AI services billed by usage, revenue can swing from month to month, so some companies annualize recent revenue into a run-rate figure; as a result, ARR numbers are not always calculated the same way from one company to another.
gl.yillik-tekrarlayan-gelir.why: ARR is one of the main measures investors and news coverage use to track the commercial progress of AI startups.
